digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-24
digests.theme: The best papers today all insist on identifying the real object before optimizing, compressing, or auditing it. World models of environment, agent and joint agent-environment systems says a world model is not defined only by what variables it predicts, but by which channel it models. The Exceedance Design Effect says threshold guarantees care about same-side exceedance correlation at the operating level, not ordinary score correlation. STCO says future-state prediction for control should condition on target-time interventions, not pretend observed history already fixes the future. Bern2Edge says the useful representation is the one you can both synthesize and inspect, not the one you patch for hardware later. StateSight says format-valid multimodal answers can still fail to reconstruct the latent spatial state that the task actually requires.
digests.overview: This Monday, August 24, 2026 run inspected full text for all five ranked papers below: PDF full text for World models of environment, agent and joint agent-environment systems, and arXiv HTML full text for the other four. Four papers earn preserved notes. StateSight is the strongest adjacent runner-up because the benchmark is clean and the failure signal is real, but it is still more diagnostic infrastructure than reusable mechanism. Most relevant today: World models of environment, agent and joint agent-environment systems.
digests.takeaway: The August 24 lesson is that a lot of ML slop comes from optimizing a nearby object and then pretending it was the real one all along. A world model is not just "something that predicts future stuff"; it is a model of a particular channel. A threshold guarantee is not about raw score correlation; it is about threshold-side agreement at the operating level. A control surrogate is not just a forecaster; it must answer intervention-conditioned queries. A deployable model is not just an accurate one; it must live in a representation that hardware and symbolic tooling can actually use. A multimodal benchmark is not just an answer sheet; it should isolate the latent state the model needs to recover. Same rule everywhere: identify the object first, then do the math.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-23
digests.theme: The strongest papers today all refuse to let a local heuristic impersonate the real object being optimized. Phantom Gains says transition-level self-improvement claims need measured nulls, not noisy gain-loss folklore. Optimal Skill Selection says skill routing is a budgeted set optimization problem, not top-k relevance. Harness Continual Learning says agent adaptation lives in a mutable harness that can forget even when the model is frozen. Forgetting, plasticity, and co-observation says retention and plasticity still do not recover joint-training generalization when the data is never seen together. Levy Attention says uncertainty should come out of the attention operator itself rather than being bolted on with extra heads or extra passes.

digests.takeaway: The August 23 lesson is that you should optimize the real state transition, not the prettiest local proxy. A transition statistic without a measured null manufactures self-improvement. Skill routing without set-level budgeting wastes context and degrades execution. Harness adaptation without retention gates quietly breaks earlier behavior. Continual learning without co-observation never recovers the structure joint training got from seeing things together. Attention without surfaced evidence and disagreement cannot say how much a query should be trusted. Same rule all day: if the mechanism does not preserve or optimize the real object, the headline result is partly fake.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-19
digests.theme:
Today's useful pattern is state has to survive the moment it is not convenient. The best papers do not ask whether a model can emit plausible surface behavior. They ask whether the hidden state, task state, or evaluation state remains explicit enough to be checked when the easy observation disappears.

I kept robotics/VLA work as a lane rather than the center. The scan deliberately covered video world-model evaluation, tool-using agents, generative-model evaluation, diffusion-LM transparency, surgical/medical deployment, neurosymbolic counterfactuals, long-video temporal reasoning, spatial tool-use agents, skill mining, and physical-AI serving. No robotics/VLA paper landed in the top three today.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable for individual paper pages, but the fetched content was mostly title/navigation stubs rather than useful related-paper text. I used the arXiv API, arXiv new listings, individual AlphaXiv title checks, and direct arXiv PDFs for full-text inspection. Discovery may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

Full-text PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core, LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents, The FID Lottery, How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?, TimeProVe, GEN-Guard, DeepSWIP, MemoryWAM, S-Agent, SoftSkill, Automating SKILL.md Generation, and Execution-State Capsules. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core is the most relevant paper today. It turns "world model" into an intervention test: move the camera away, return, and ask whether the object state kept evolving while unobserved. Across 9,600 videos from 23 models, the answer is mostly no; visible quality and re-observation access do not imply re-observed state correctness.

LedgerAgent is the cleanest agent-systems mechanism. It stores successful read-tool returns in a typed ledger, renders that observed state back into the prompt, and checks environment-changing calls against executable policy predicates before they touch the external system. It is not glamorous, but it is exactly the kind of explicit state boundary tool agents usually fake.

The FID Lottery is the strongest evaluation paper today. It treats FID as a random variable over both training seeds and sampling seeds, then shows that retraining the same recipe moves FID much more than redrawing samples from one fixed model. The useful lesson is not just "report error bars"; it is that many single-seed generative-model gains sit below the evaluation noise floor.

Several other papers were worth reading but stayed below the preservation line. How Transparent is DiffusionGemma? is a strong foundation-model behavior audit: the token bottleneck between denoising steps appears much more interpretable than the worst-case latent-reasoning story, but algorithmic transparency remains hard because the model can revise the whole canvas non-chronologically. GEN-Guard is a useful surgical-AI deployment paper because it names "performance leakage" in federated model selection and tests a client-blocked detection/correction stack; I kept it below the top three because the mechanism is more specialized. TimeProVe is a good long-video evidence search system, reducing VLM calls and cost through propose-then-verify temporal grounding, but it is less conceptually sharp than LedgerAgent today. MemoryWAM was the best robotics/VLA candidate, with hybrid recent-frame, anchor-frame, and gist-token memory for long-horizon manipulation, but it did not beat the non-robotics top three on transfer value.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all punish fake state. Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core asks whether a video model keeps an event endpoint alive when the camera is not watching. LedgerAgent asks whether a tool agent has a real observed-state object before it changes the world. The FID Lottery asks whether a generative-model claim survives the hidden state of training randomness. Different domains, same standard: if the state matters, isolate it, perturb observability, and make it carry the claim.

digests.theme:

I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work as one lane rather than the center. The scan covered interpretability, structured inference, medical uncertainty and clinical decision support, 3D scene understanding, active multimodal perception, scientific ML for climate emulation, deepfake-detector evaluation, VLA knowledge retention, and user simulation.

Explaining Attention with Program Synthesis is the most relevant paper today. It asks whether an attention-head explanation can be a runnable Python program, not a loose natural-language label. The important part is the causal check: high-fit programs can replace a meaningful fraction of real attention heads while preserving perplexity and downstream QA behavior.

Structured Inference with Large Language Gibbs is the cleanest mechanism paper. It treats an LLM's local conditionals as transition operators over a structured state, then uses Gibbs-style resampling to reduce fixed-order autoregressive bias. The paper's useful lesson is simple: a ranking metric can look excellent while the actual confidence signal is unsafe for a treatment-critical class.

OneCanvas is a strong adjacent 3D representation paper: lift multi-view patch features into a shared equirectangular canvas with metric 3D position embeddings, then let a VLM read the result as one image. digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-17
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is aggregate success is not evidence of the right mechanism. The strongest papers ask whether a memory system used reachable evidence, whether a medical VLM used the image, and whether deception leaves a different internal state than ordinary wrongness. I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work as one lane rather than the center. The scan covered agent memory, clinical AI, interpretability, source/provenance verification, prompt-injection sanitization, agent-search scaling, VLM reliability, clinical speech, environment-model RL, code-reasoning diagnostics, 3D/CAD data, and a list-level robotics/VLA pass.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv's lightweight search route returned a 404 page again. Individual AlphaXiv paper pages were reachable for some candidates, but the fetchable text exposed only title/navigation stubs, so it was not useful for discovery or related-paper branching. I used arXiv new listings, the arXiv API, and direct arXiv PDFs for the serious candidates.

Full-text PDFs were available for the papers I considered preserving. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitation sections, for MemTrace: Probing What Final Accuracy Misses in Long-Term Memory, Vision-language models for chest radiography do not always need the image, Rift: A Conflict Signature for Deception in Language Models, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents, PARSE, Beyond Parallel Sampling, Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories, Visuals Lie, Consistency Speaks, SpeechDx, EnvRL, and From Brewing to Resolution. The robotics/VLA scan found several plausible candidates, including technical reports and VLA memory/control papers, but none beat the best non-robotics papers today on mechanism, evidence quality, and future usefulness.

MemTrace is the most relevant paper today. It changes the unit of long-term memory evaluation from independent QA rows to knowledge points: a single user fact probed across age, question type, and evidence condition. The important result is not merely that memory systems forget. It is that most hard failures are evidence-use failures after relevant evidence is already reachable.

Vision-language models for chest radiography do not always need the image is the strongest healthcare/evaluation paper in the scan. The paper builds an interventional audit using label-matched image swaps, radiologist-box target masks, and irrelevant masks to test whether a correct answer causally depends on the radiograph. The uncomfortable result is that a text-only model lands close to the best multimodal system, and several medical VLMs either ignore the image or use it only selectively.

Rift is the most provocative interpretability paper today, but I am keeping it below the two preserved notes because it needs replication and has a narrow experimental regime. The mechanism is interesting: residual rank rises during deceptive forward passes relative to both honest answers and naive wrong answers. The paper controls for wrongness and tests roleplay, strategic bluffing, concealment prompts, length, and cross-domain probes. That is worth attention. It is not yet a deployment-ready lie detector.

Several other papers were useful but stayed below the preservation line. ProvenanceGuard is highly aligned with MCP-style agents because it verifies not just whether a claim is supported somewhere, but whether it is attributed to the right tool/source. PARSE is a practical warning that prompt-injection defenses proven on synthetic tasks may collapse on real enterprise documents. DivInit is a clean agent-search trick: diversify first-turn queries before parallel rollouts instead of letting threads collapse onto the same retrieval path. Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories is valuable as an agent-harness paper, but the paper is partly a systems report around one harness. SpeechDx is a strong benchmark contribution for clinical speech AI, but today's two preserved notes have sharper mechanism transfer.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are all refusing a lazy metric. MemTrace says memory is not row-level accuracy; it is fact-level behavior across time, question type, and evidence condition. Chest radiography VLMs do not always need the image says medical VQA accuracy is not evidence of image use; grounding needs causal intervention. Rift says wrongness is not the same as deception; compare a model lying while knowing against a model that is merely wrong. The shared lesson is simple and useful: before trusting a success number, identify the mechanism that was supposed to produce it and test that mechanism directly.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-16
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is diagnostic interfaces beat aggregate success. The strongest papers do not merely report higher task scores. They expose where a model thinks it is on track, whether an answer is grounded in the supplied context, and where a scientific evidence pipeline loses eligible studies. I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work as one lane rather than the center. The scan looked first at interpretability, agent grounding, healthcare/evidence synthesis, search-agent security, KV-cache context management, generative world models, representation learning, and medical imaging, then used the robotics papers as comparison cases.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight /search route returned a 404 page, so it was not useful for discovery today. I used the arXiv API plus direct arXiv PDFs. Full-text PDFs were available for the leading candidates. I inspected the method, result, and limitation sections for The Value Axis: Language Models Encode Whether They're on the Right Track, Context-Aware RL for Agentic and Multimodal LLMs, Benchmarking LLM Agents on Meta-Analysis Articles from Nature Portfolio, How Much Can We Trust LLM Search Agents?, and KVEraser. I did lighter full-text skims for DreamX-World 1.0, Selection Without Signal, Recovery Through Expression, T-Rex, and adjacent technical candidates including posterior-score inverse problems, urban inverse rendering, phase in neural representations, and non-contrast abdominal CT diagnosis.

The Value Axis is the most relevant paper today. It constructs a linear activation direction in Qwen3-8B from synthetic in-context RL conversations, then shows that the direction tracks and causally modulates confidence-like behavior across math, code, DPO word preferences, SFT domains, and evaluation-awareness settings. This should not be treated as a general truth detector: it is one model, one axis-construction recipe, and a set of selected validation domains. But it is exactly the right kind of interpretability object for cabbageland: an internal state variable that can be measured, steered, and audited against external behavior.

Context-Aware RL is the strongest training-method paper in the scan. The method adds a context-selection loss to GRPO: given a query, an answer, and two similar contexts, the policy is rewarded for identifying which context actually supports the answer. The important part is not the contrastive data by itself. The paper shows that supervised augmentation can collapse an agentic policy and outcome-only RL mostly fails to use the signal; the bounded auxiliary loss is what preserves the policy while improving grounding.

MetaSyn is the strongest healthcare/scientific-evidence evaluation paper today. It builds a benchmark from 442 Nature Portfolio meta-analyses, a PubMed-anchored corpus of 140,585 articles, 8,674 corpus-matched positives, hard negatives, and PI/ECO-structured inclusion criteria. The headline is sharp: retrieval can reach 90.9% Recall@200, but no end-to-end pipeline recovers more than 52.7% of included studies. The bottleneck is not "can it retrieve relevant papers?" but "can it screen topically similar distractors against protocol criteria?"

SearchGEO is a strong security/evaluation warning. It tests whether manipulated web evidence becomes user-facing endorsement in LLM search agents. The useful result is the source-diversity effect: distinct corroborating attacker pages move endorsement far more than repetition of one source. I did not preserve a detailed note because today's top two papers are more reusable as model-training and model-debugging mechanisms, but SearchGEO is worth revisiting for agent-search hardening.

KVEraser is a very relevant systems paper, but just below the preservation line today. It learns local KV-cache steering states to erase a harmful, stale, or retracted span without recomputing the entire suffix. The mechanism is attractive for long-running agents because "forget this tool observation" should be an actual cache edit, not a polite instruction appended after contamination. I did not write a note today because the two preserved papers were more central and the pipeline is already audio-heavy, but this one should stay in the follow-up queue.

The robotics lane had one genuinely strong candidate: T-Rex: Tactile-Reactive Dexterous Manipulation. It combines human egocentric pretraining, a 100-hour tactile-rich teleoperation dataset, a variable-rate Mixture-of-Transformers, and a temporal tactile VQ-VAE for high-frequency residual tactile refinement. On a robotics-only day it would likely deserve a note. Today it stays out of the top three because the non-robotics candidates are stronger for general mechanism transfer.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are about making hidden interfaces visible. The Value Axis finds a candidate internal gauge for whether a model thinks its current trajectory will succeed. Context-Aware RL trains models to bind answers to the context that actually supports them. MetaSyn shows that scientific-agent pipelines fail at protocol screening even when retrieval is strong. The shared lesson is that end scores are too blunt: the useful object is the stage, span, head, cache state, or activation direction where the failure can actually be localized.

Patches Talk Through Registers, Local Coverage Governs Memorization in Diffusion Models, Memento: Reconstruct to Remember for Consistent Long Video Generation, A Low-Rank Subspace Analysis of LLM Interventions, and Compressed Computation is (probably) not Computation in Superposition. I preserved detailed notes for When Errors Become Narratives and Gaze Heads.

When Errors Become Narratives is the most relevant paper today. It is a single-system case study, so the frequencies should not be generalized casually, but the mechanism taxonomy is exactly the right object: environment quirks, design-assumption mismatches, swallowed/diluted errors, fail-plausible fabrication, and operational/forensic blind spots. The strongest idea is the trigger/amplifier/concealer decomposition. Fixing the trigger is usually cosmetic; the durable work is removing the amplifier and making the concealer impossible. The paper is unusually close to cabbageland's own agent-runtime concerns, but that is not why it wins. It wins because the observed failures are concrete, longitudinal, and architecturally reusable.

Gaze Heads is the cleanest mechanistic model paper in the scan. In Qwen3-VL-8B, fewer than 9% of attention heads track the image region currently being described, and forcing those heads to attend to a chosen region steers the VLM's answer toward that region at 83.1% accuracy on six-panel comics. The intervention also works dynamically mid-generation and transfers imperfectly to natural COCO images and several VLM families. The caveat is that the testbed is heavily shaped by comics and the mechanism is not universal: some frozen-encoder architectures show no comparable head set. Still, this is real causal interpretability, not merely heatmap poetry.

ClinHallu is the strongest medical/evaluation paper today. It builds 7,031 validated medical VQA instances with structured traces split into Visual Recognition, Knowledge Recall, and Reasoning Integration, then uses stage-replacement interventions to diagnose where hallucinations enter. That decomposition is more useful than a final-answer hallucination score because it says whether the model is seeing wrong, remembering wrong, or combining evidence badly. The limitation is that the benchmark leans on generated traces, LLM-as-judge filtering/evaluation, and VQA-style tasks, so it is a diagnostic testbed rather than clinical deployment evidence.

When Good Verifiers Go Bad is the best deployment warning. It shows verifier-driven self-DPO can silently regress VLM students on MMMU even while DPO loss decreases, and argues that task-rubric verifier accuracy should be measured before running the loop. The single-family Qwen ladder and small verifier scale limit the claim, but the warning is practical: a verifier is not a moral authority. If it is confidently wrong on the target task, preference optimization can amplify the wrong direction.

Neither Parallel Nor Sequential is a useful foundation-model behavior audit. By hooking DiffusionGemma's own commit mechanism, it finds partial, granularity-dependent left-to-right token commitment rather than clean parallel or block-autoregressive decoding. The paper's most portable contribution is methodological: commit-order studies need to handle EOS padding artifacts, same-call ties, non-monotonic commits, pooling traps, and block-size sensitivity.

AgentSpec is aligned but broader and less decisive. It treats embodied LLM agents as typed compositions of perception, memory, reasoning, reflection, action, and learning modules, then compares scaffold combinations across interactive benchmarks. The useful lesson is that scaffold compatibility matters: memory helps only when matched to the reasoner and task, and policy optimization should train against the scaffold expected at deployment. I did not preserve it today because it is more framework-plus-sweep than sharp mechanism.

RATS and Local Coverage Governs Memorization are strong adjacent representation papers. RATS turns register tokens into a bottleneck that surfaces unsupervised part-level visual structure under a DINO objective. Local Coverage reframes diffusion memorization as a local data-coverage phenomenon rather than a global model property. Both are useful, but today's preserved notes are more directly actionable for agent reliability and multimodal control.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is When Errors Become Narratives because it treats production agent failures as mechanism classes, not embarrassing one-offs. Gaze Heads is the mechanistic ML note to keep because it finds a small causal control surface for VLM grounding. ClinHallu is the healthcare/evaluation reminder that hallucination diagnosis needs stage-local interventions, not just final-answer scoring. The common thread is diagnostic resolution: systems get better when they expose where the failure entered, how it propagated, and which interface can actually be repaired.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-14
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is small interfaces beat decorative generality when they are tested honestly. There is no fresh Sunday arXiv batch in the scoped categories, so today's scan revisited the current June 10-11 arXiv robotics/CV/AI/CL batch and avoided papers already preserved in the June 12-13 digests. muVLA is the strongest paper because it isolates recurrence itself inside a pretrained VLA and shows exactly where minimal latent memory helps and where it fails. Sparse2Act is the strongest representation note because it uses task-space robot actions as supervision for sparse 3D features, rather than hoping reconstruction or downstream behavior cloning will discover control relevance. DIRECT is the best adjacent systems note: test-time compute should be routed by task demand, not paid uniformly as a tax.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight fetched /search URL returned 404 again, so it was not useful for discovery. The arXiv API submittedDate:[202606120000 TO 202606142359] query over relevant categories returned zero entries even though the arXiv recent category pages listed the Friday June 12 batch, so today's discovery used arXiv recent category pages plus direct arXiv pages and PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for muVLA: On Recurrent Memory for Partially Observable Manipulation in VLA Models, Improving Robotic Generalist Policies via Flow Reversal Steering, Sparse2Act: Learning Action-Aligned Sparse 3D Representations for Cross-Domain Robot Manipulation, Mana: Dexterous Manipulation of Articulated Tools, DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?, SERF: Spatiotemporal Environment and Robot Feature Map for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation, and MCR-Bionic Hand: Anatomical Structural Priors for Dexterous Manipulation. muVLA and Sparse2Act are preserved today.

muVLA is the strongest direct hit. It adds a small bank of recurrent memory tokens to OpenVLA-OFT and deliberately avoids retrieval modules, compression heads, hierarchical memory, and auxiliary objectives. The payoff is a cleaner measurement: minimal recurrence lifts partially observable MIKASA-Robo training tasks sharply, transfers modestly to held-out tasks with matching memory semantics, and mostly fails when the memory semantics change. That limit is the value. The paper gives future VLA memory work a baseline and a warning: if a fancier memory system cannot beat tiny recurrent tokens under the same cadence and latency budget, it is probably ornament.

Sparse2Act is the best representation paper today. It pretrains sparse point-cloud encoders by masking 3D tokens and predicting one-step task-space end-effector actions, then transfers only the encoder initialization into downstream policies. The ablations are the useful part: action-only and reconstruction-only help, but masked action alignment helps far more, and the gain persists with simplified downstream decoders. The design lesson is portable: use robot action to organize geometry around control, then let the downstream policy choose its own action parameterization.

DIRECT is adjacent but practically important. It treats the high-level embodied planner as a routed variable across reasoning depth, model size, and memory history. The paper's best claim is not "bigger reasoning helps"; it is the opposite: compute axes help on different task types and can hurt or waste latency elsewhere. A lightweight multimodal router recovers much of the expensive planner's success at lower cost in simulation and Franka DROID experiments. This is more systems and deployment than core representation, so I did not preserve a separate note today, but the framing is worth stealing.

Flow Reversal Steering is good policy-improvement material. It reverses a flow-matching VLA from coarse reference actions into latent noise, then denoises back into in-distribution actions that follow the rough semantic direction. It is especially useful for turning human or VLM guidance into noise-space BC or RL warm starts. I am not preserving it today because it is a steering wrapper over a behavioral prior rather than a stronger state, memory, or representation interface.

SERF is a strong explicit-memory mobile-manipulation paper, but with simulation caveats. It builds a spatiotemporal feature map of environment and robot neural points, updates environment points by object-level SE(3) tracking and robot points by forward kinematics, then conditions a VLA on map tokens. The idea is aligned with cabbageland: persistent spatial memory should be an input, not hidden in image history. The limitation is also clear: prior map features, privileged simulator instance labels, rigid-object updates, and no real-world mobile-manipulation validation yet.

Mana and MCR-Bionic Hand are useful physical-structure papers. Mana turns articulated tool manipulation into an animation-like data pipeline: human marks functional affordances, the system samples grasp keyframes, plans geometric phases, and uses RL only for short contact-rich transitions before training a point-cloud diffusion policy for zero-shot sim-to-real. MCR-Bionic is more hardware/anatomy than learning: it argues that wrist-finger tenodesis, extensor hoods, and intrinsic pathways are physical computation, not mere biomimetic decoration. Both are adjacent inspiration for "structure does work," but neither displaces today's two preserved representation/memory papers.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is muVLA because it gives VLA memory a controlled lower bound: tiny recurrent tokens can be powerful, but they do not magically generalize to new memory semantics. Sparse2Act is the representation note to keep because it uses robot action to shape sparse 3D geometry around control before downstream policy training. DIRECT is the adjacent systems lesson: expensive reasoning, bigger planners, and longer memory should be routed by task demand. The common thread is that useful long-horizon systems need small explicit interfaces with honest budgets, not bigger hidden mush.

Sparse2Act: Learning Action-Aligned Sparse 3D Representations for Cross-Domain Robot Manipulation

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-13
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is trust and memory need explicit budgets. There does not appear to be a fresh Saturday arXiv batch in the scoped robotics/CV/AI categories, so today's scan widened across the current week and avoided papers already preserved in the June 10-12 digests. Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon is the strongest paper because it turns world-model trust into a predictable-horizon certificate rather than an average rollout score. Action-Effect Memory Pretraining is the best practical robotics note because it learns a compact action-conditioned history state before policy training. Learning What to Remember is adjacent but useful: it makes the forgetting decision blind to future queries and learns a multi-factor value for retention rather than leaning on recency or query similarity.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level. The arXiv API query for submittedDate:[202606120000 TO 202606132359] over the relevant AI/CV/robotics categories returned no entries, so discovery quality today is a current-week fallback rather than a true new-Saturday batch. I used arXiv API search plus direct arXiv PDFs, and inspected extracted full PDFs for Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon: Certified Predictability for Equivariant World Models, Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory, Bounding Boxes as Goals: Language-Conditioned Grasping via Neuro-Symbolic Planning, Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation, ProPlay: Procedural World Models for Self-Evolving LLM Agents, TetherCache: Stabilizing Autoregressive Long-Form Video Generation with Gated Recall and Trusted Alignment, and MoVerse: Real-Time Video World Modeling with Panoramic Gaussian Scaffold. Scale Buys and AEM are preserved today.

Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon is the strongest direct hit. The paper argues that an equivariant latent world model can certify how far a rollout remains trustworthy: exact equivariance makes rollout error constant over symmetry orbits, while approximate equivariance yields a finite per-channel horizon controlled by the latent predictor's Lyapunov spectrum. The best idea is the distinction between a universal audit and an a-priori guarantee. Any smooth latent loop can be spectrally audited, but exact structure is what makes the number trustworthy without a held-out divergence check. I did not independently verify the proofs, so the note preserves the framing and caveats rather than treating the theorem stack as settled law.

Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation is the best robot-memory note. AEM interleaves visual and action tokens, masks aligned action-effect timesteps, and trains a Mamba encoder to compress history into the encoded final vision token. That one vector is then concatenated with current perception inside Diffusion Policy or ManiFlow. The results are useful because the paper compares against no-history policies, direct DINOv2 feature stacking, randomized scenes, and memory-dependent tasks. The caveat is that the real-world result prose has inconsistent averages, so I trust the direction more than every exact margin.

Learning What to Remember is adjacent inspiration for long-running agents. Its useful point is methodological: if a retention policy scores memory relevance against the held-out future question, it is measuring retrieval with an oracle, not forgetting. In the blind consolidation regime, a learned multi-factor value over reliability, emotion, self/user relevance, and goal/session relevance beats recency and single-factor policies on LongMemEval gold-evidence retention. I am not preserving a separate note today because the evaluation is still retention-only, three of the seven factors are inert in the API-free setup, and final QA/task return is left for follow-up. Still, the oracle-vs-blind distinction is worth remembering.

MoVerse is the strongest 3D adjacent paper. It turns a single narrow-FOV image into a gravity-aligned panorama, lifts it into a persistent panoramic 3D Gaussian scaffold, and uses a distilled causal video renderer for interactive roaming. The representation lesson is excellent: keep long-range spatial memory in explicit geometry and let the video model repair local rendering quality. I am not preserving it today only because the paper is mostly a large staged system with qualitative-heavy evidence, while today's two kept papers are sharper for trust and robot-memory interfaces.

TetherCache is useful citation material for long-form video/world-model memory. Its sink/memory/recent cache split, attention-diversity recall, and trusted statistic alignment are sensible for drift-resistant autoregressive video. It is less central to cabbageland today because the mechanism is cache management for generation rather than embodied state or planning.

ProPlay is useful agent-memory/planning material. It builds a procedure graph with reliability records, preplays likely procedural trajectories, and updates the graph after environment feedback. The idea is aligned with procedural world models for LLM agents, but the abstraction remains natural-language procedural guidance over public text/game benchmarks, not a stronger direct hit than today's preserved papers.

Bounding Boxes as Goals is mostly citation material. It compiles language into bounding-box goal states and uses GroundingDINO plus closed-loop proportional control. The explicit goal-state interface is nice, but the evaluated robot task is still mostly grasp-and-lift; full end-to-end sorting and goal-similarity verification are left to future work.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon because it gives world-model trust a shape: a per-situation horizon that structure can certify and generic latents must cross-check. Action-Effect Memory Pretraining is the robot-memory note to keep because it compresses vision-action history into a small pretrained state that downstream policies can actually use. Learning What to Remember is the agent-memory warning label: do not evaluate forgetting with future-query information. The common lesson is that long-horizon systems need explicit budget interfaces, whether the budget is rollout trust, history length, or memory survival.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-12
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is world models are being judged by the interfaces they expose to control, not by rollout aesthetics alone. WEAVER is the strongest paper because it treats a robotic world model as a learned simulator that must support policy evaluation, synthetic policy improvement, and test-time planning under latency constraints. MaskWAM is the cleanest object-centric WAM paper: masks are both a future prediction target and an optional first-frame spatial prompt, so the model predicts what matters, not only what happens. EA-WM is the predicate-level companion: it adds event prediction and verification on top of feature-space rollouts so a planner can score imagined futures by task progress rather than feature distance alone.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight fetched /search URL returned 404, so it was not useful for discovery today. Discovery and inspection for this run used the arXiv API over the June 11, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for WEAVER, Better, Faster, Longer: An Effective World Model for Robotic Manipulation, RepWAM: World Action Modeling with Representation Visual-Action Tokenizers, MaskWAM: Unifying Mask Prompting and Prediction for World-Action Models, EA-WM: Event-Aware World Models with Task-Specification Grounding for Long-Horizon Manipulation, NavWAM: A Navigation World Action Model for Goal-Conditioned Visual Navigation, World Tracing: Generative Pixel-Aligned Geometry Beyond the Visible, SpatialClaw: Rethinking Action Interface for Agentic Spatial Reasoning, SPARC: Reliable Spatial Annotations from Robot Demonstrations at Scale, VISA: VLM-Guided Instance Semantic Auditing for 3D Occupancy World Models, Real-Time Execution with Autoregressive Policies, See Selectively, Act Adaptively, and LabVLA / RoboGenesis. WEAVER, MaskWAM, and EA-WM are preserved today.

WEAVER is the best direct hit. Its central claim is practical and useful: a manipulation world model should jointly satisfy fidelity, temporal consistency, and inference speed because the downstream uses are policy evaluation, policy improvement, and online planning. The architecture combines multi-view visual latents, proprioception prediction, sparse long-term memory, short-term history, flow-matched latent dynamics, diffusion-forcing style noise, accelerated denoising, and latent reward/critic heads. The paper is strongest where it connects the world model to decisions: predicted rollouts correlate with real success after finetuning, synthetic segments improve a pi0.5 policy without extra real interaction, and latent best-of-4 steering improves test-time task success.

MaskWAM is the strongest object-centric WAM interface paper. It treats masks as first-class latent streams, jointly predicting future RGB, future masks, and action chunks. That makes target regions explicit during training and enables a deployment-time mask prompt for language-ambiguous manipulation. The best result is not the tiny LIBERO gain over other strong baselines; it is the ablation showing that a mask prompt without future-mask prediction collapses in ambiguous tasks, while joint mask prediction plus prompting stays robust across distractors, novel instances, and lighting shifts.

EA-WM is worth preserving with caveats. The mechanism is exactly aligned with explicit-state taste: roll out candidate actions in frozen visual-feature space, decode task-grounded event predicates, and score futures with task, semantic, physical, and uncertainty terms before CEM or hybrid selection. The red flag is that event supervision is simulator-derived, LIBERO online evaluation is short-window rather than full autonomous episodes, and Goal10 gains are modest. Still, the design pattern is useful: visual-feature closeness is not the same as event progress.

RepWAM is directly relevant but not preserved as a separate note today. It trains a representation visual-action tokenizer aligned to a visual foundation model, then learns latent actions as transitions inside that semantic visual space. The ablations are useful, especially the two-stage latent-action training result, but the paper overlaps with the last few days of WAM interface/alignment papers and is less sharply explicit than MaskWAM or EA-WM.

NavWAM is strong adjacent direct work for navigation. It represents current state, goal image, future observations, action chunk, future state, and goal-progress value as a shared latent canvas inside a Cosmos Predict2-style video model. It beats CEM-style navigation world-model baselines and reports 19/24 real-world image-goal navigation successes. I am not preserving it today because the strongest cabbageland thread is manipulation/world-action interfaces, but NavWAM is good citation material for "future prediction is useful when trained with action and value targets."

World Tracing is the best 3D/geometry paper in the batch. It predicts layered pixel-aligned 3D point stacks, where layer 0 is the visible surface and deeper layers complete occluded intersections along each input ray. This is a serious representation paper, especially for input-faithful hidden geometry, but it is adjacent to today's robotics-control thread rather than the main preserved story.

SpatialClaw, SPARC, and VISA are useful citation material. SpatialClaw argues that code in a persistent kernel is a better spatial-reasoning action interface than single-pass code or fixed tool calls. SPARC scores robot-demo annotations by phase-aware object motion, 3D gripper proximity, and robot-overlap filtering. VISA converts offline VLM object audits into voxel-grounded semantic supervision for 3D occupancy world models. All three are useful, but none displace today's WAM/control-interface papers.

Real-Time Execution with Autoregressive Policies, See Selectively, Act Adaptively, and LabVLA / RoboGenesis are mostly baseline/framing material for deployment, bimanual routing, and synthetic lab robotics data. The ideas are useful, but they are less central than today's top three.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is WEAVER because it asks whether a world model can do real policy work: evaluate trajectories, generate useful synthetic improvement data, and steer actions online quickly enough to matter. MaskWAM is the clean object-centric complement, showing that predicting and prompting masks gives the action head a target-specific interface instead of a generic RGB future. EA-WM is the event-level complement, using predicted predicates and verifier scores to judge whether imagined futures make task progress. The common lesson is blunt: world models become useful when their hidden state is exposed as the right control object, whether that object is a value-scored latent rollout, a future target mask, or a task-event scorecard.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-11
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is the world-action interface is becoming the actual research object. Making Foresight Actionable is the strongest paper because it does not accept "the world model made a plausible video" as evidence that the action head can use the representation. It probes where action attention and causal sensitivity land, then regularizes WAM hidden states toward spatially coherent DINOv2 features so the action decoder reads task-relevant interaction regions. World Pilot is the complementary integration recipe: route a WAM's scene-evolution latent into VLA hidden states and its anticipated trajectory into the action generator as a soft prior. DAM-VLA is the sensor-time version of the same idea: stop forcing vision, language, force, proprioception, and action onto one synchronous clock, and let each modality keep its own buffer and update rhythm.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the site level. Discovery and inspection for this run used arXiv API search over the June 8-10, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for Making Foresight Actionable: Repurposing Representation Alignment in World Action Models, World Pilot: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models with World-Action Priors, DAM-VLA: Decoupled Asynchronous Multimodal Vision Language Action model, PLUME: Probabilistic Latent Unified World Modeling and Parameter Estimation for Multi-Finger Manipulation, DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?, Slots, Transitions, Loops: Learning Composable World Models for ARC, World Model Self-Distillation: Training World Models to Solve General Tasks, VICX: Generalizable Robot Manipulation via Video Generation and In-Context Operator Network, VLGA: Vision-Language-Geometry-Action Models for Autonomous Driving, ATM: Action-Consistency Transfer Matrix for Diagnosing and Improving Latent World Models, Plan-and-Verify Video Reward Reasoning with Spatio-Temporal Scene Graph Grounding, ISAP-3D: Identity-Slot Aligned Part-Aware 3D Generation, and CP4D: Compositional Physics-aware 4D Scene Generation. AGRA, World Pilot, and DAM-VLA are preserved today.

Making Foresight Actionable is the strongest direct hit. The paper diagnoses a concrete failure mode in world-action models: a WAM can generate a plausible future while the action decoder attends to background, static hands, or other task-irrelevant regions. AGRA adds an auxiliary alignment loss between selected video-diffusion hidden states and DINOv2 patch features, which makes the feature field more spatially coherent and action-readable. The paper's best contribution is not the headline success number; it is the attention plus causal-intervention audit that turns "world model features" into something testable.

World Pilot is the best companion integration paper. It keeps the WAM frozen and injects two priors into a VLA: Latent Steering routes the scene-evolution latent through residual cross-attention into VLM hidden states, while Action Steering compresses the WAM's anticipated trajectory into a single prefix token for the flow-matching action generator. The ablations are useful: latent injection beats decoded future images, a single trajectory token beats per-step or raw trajectory conditioning, and even a scene-prediction-only Cosmos model helps before action post-training.

DAM-VLA is the strongest asynchronous multimodal VLA paper. Its argument is clean: a synchronous VLA oversamples slow vision and language, undersamples fast contact signals, and gates action generation on a complete observation bundle. DAM-VLA keeps per-modality latent buffers, refreshes them at their sensor rates, and lets the action head read them continuously through gated cross-attention. The real-robot evidence is small but sharp: seven contact-rich tasks, 15 trials each, and a large gap between the full model and synchronous or concatenation baselines.

PLUME is strong adjacent inspiration and may deserve a later dedicated note. It learns a latent belief over physical parameters and rewards, updates that belief online with a flow-matching world model, and plans with likelihood-penalized rollouts. The hardware screwdriver result is especially relevant for explicit physical state. I am not preserving it today because the top three form a tighter VLA/WAM interface story, not because PLUME is weak.

DIRECT is strong systems framing for embodied planner deployment. The key point is that test-time compute has different capability profiles depending on whether it is reasoning depth, model size, or memory history. The router is useful, but it is more about compute allocation for high-level planners than about state/action representation.

Loop-OWM is useful compositional-reasoning inspiration. It frames ARC as object-centric transition learning over structured visual-symbolic states. I am not promoting it above today's robotics papers because the internal recurrent steps are not yet semantically stable, and the result is more a controlled reasoning lens than an embodied mechanism.

World Model Self-Distillation, VICX, VLGA, ATM, SG-PVR, ISAP-3D, and CP4D are all citation material for narrower purposes: data-free video-world-model task transfer, video-plan-to-trajectory grounding, dense driving geometry supervision, latent-world-model diagnostics, structured video reward reasoning, identity-slot 3D parts, and physics-aware 4D composition. None displaced the three preserved notes today.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is Making Foresight Actionable because it makes the world-action interface inspectable: a useful future representation should focus the action head on interaction regions and be causally robust to irrelevant background changes. World Pilot is the matching integration recipe, routing WAM latents and trajectory priors into different parts of a VLA. DAM-VLA generalizes the same taste to multimodal timing, with per-modality buffers and gated updates instead of synchronous token mush. The common lesson is blunt: a "world model" only matters when its hidden state reaches the control computation in the right form, at the right layer, and at the right time.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-10
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is predictive structure is being pushed closer to the hidden state that actually matters for action. Next Forcing is the strongest paper because it changes the training target for autoregressive video world models: instead of denoising only the current chunk, it asks lightweight auxiliary heads to predict multiple future chunks and backpropagate longer-range temporal pressure into the main model. TacForeSight is the strongest contact-world-model paper because it uses force/torque as a leading signal to forecast tactile latent dynamics before local contact changes fully appear. LIBERO-Occ is the best VLA robustness paper because it turns occlusion into a controlled partial-observability benchmark, then tests whether generated complementary views can recover task-relevant evidence.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the site level, but discovery and inspection for this run used arXiv API search over the June 9, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for Next Forcing: Causal World Modeling with Multi-Chunk Prediction, TacForeSight: Force-Guided Tactile World Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation, LIBERO-Occ: Evaluating and Improving Vision-Language-Action Models under Scene-Induced Occlusion via Viewpoint Imagination, MV-Actor: Aligning Multi-View Semantics and Spatial Awareness for Bimanual Manipulation, IMPACT: Learning Internal-Model Predictive Control for Forceful Robotic Manipulation, WorldOlympiad: Can Your World Model Survive a Triathlon?, P3D-Bench: Benchmarking MLLMs for Parametric 3D Generation and Structural Reasoning, and Bridging Semantics and Physical Execution: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Multi-Pair Robotic Assembly. Next Forcing, TacForeSight, and LIBERO-Occ are preserved today.

Next Forcing is the strongest direct hit. Its claim is simple and useful: teacher-forced next-chunk denoising lets high-frame-rate video world models lean on appearance copying, so the model needs a denser target that makes dynamics unavoidable. The method adds multi-chunk prediction modules for next1, next2, and next3 chunks, chains them causally, fuses intermediate main-model layers, and optionally keeps the depth-1 module at inference to generate the next video chunk in parallel. The results are strong on RoboTwin, PhyWorld, and a general video pretraining setting, though the training scale and proprietary data mean I trust the mechanism more than any single headline number.

TacForeSight is the best contact-rich manipulation note. It treats wrist force/torque as a high-frequency global cue that can precede local tactile deformation, then predicts future tactile latents and feeds them into a flow-based policy through current-future tactile cross-attention and adaptive visuo-tactile gating. The real-robot results are much stronger than the baselines across five contact tasks and three perturbation settings. The caveat is that the system assumes force and tactile hardware, and the evaluation is specialized, but the mechanism is exactly the kind of explicit physical foresight worth remembering.

LIBERO-Occ is the strongest VLA evaluation/framing note. The benchmark physically instantiates occluders in LIBERO scenes, verifies visibility/validity/executability, and separates manipulated-object, receptacle, and dual occlusion. The main empirical point is blunt: models that look strong on standard LIBERO collapse under scene-induced occlusion. VIM then imagines a complementary viewpoint from the occluded primary view and conditions action prediction on both observed and generated evidence. It improves substantially, but the paper is honest that this is a simulation benchmark and generated views remain bounded by learned priors.

IMPACT is strong adjacent inspiration and may deserve a later control note. It decouples high-level diffusion-policy planning from low-level force compensation by learning an online internal model from joint torque residuals, then applying feedforward wrench compensation. It is not a VLA/world-model paper in the narrow sense, but it is a very clean example of putting hidden physical state into a control interface instead of expecting imitation learning to absorb payload dynamics implicitly.

MV-Actor is useful citation material for multi-view bimanual perception. It aligns semantic tokens across physically corresponding camera regions, injects feed-forward reconstruction features for spatial awareness, and repairs noisy depth. I am not preserving it as a top note because it is mostly a perception-front-end improvement, while today's stronger thread is predictive hidden-state completion for action.

WorldOlympiad and P3D-Bench are good benchmark papers, not today's core preserved mechanisms. WorldOlympiad is useful for evaluating whether video world models preserve physics, 3D consistency, and interaction state. P3D-Bench is useful for checking whether code-generating MLLMs recover parametric 3D structure rather than merely producing plausible shapes. Both may be worth citing when framing evaluation, but they do not change the architecture/control story as directly as today's top three.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is Next Forcing because it changes what a causal video world model is forced to learn: multi-horizon dynamics rather than local chunk copying. TacForeSight is the tactile/contact note to remember because it predicts future tactile latents from force/torque, giving the policy physical foresight instead of reactive fusion. LIBERO-Occ is the VLA robustness note because it turns occlusion into a real partial-observability test and uses imagined complementary views as inspectable missing evidence. The common lesson is that hidden state should not be left as a hope inside a giant latent. Make the missing future, contact, or view into an explicit interface.

TacForeSight: Force-Guided Tactile World Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-09
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is world models are becoming structured memory and action interfaces, not just future-frame generators. MemoryVLA++ is the most relevant paper because it gives a VLA an explicit past-present-future temporal interface: perceptual/cognitive memory for past context, current working tokens, and latent future imagination for action prediction. iMaC is the sharpest action-conditioning paper because it turns robot actions into rendered motion images and two contact-distance image streams instead of asking a video model to infer contact from a compact vector. Latent Spatial Memory / Mirage is the best video-world-model memory paper because it stores a 3D cache directly in diffusion latent space, avoiding the expensive RGB point-cloud render-and-reencode loop.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv pages for the main candidates returned HTTP 403 in this environment. Discovery therefore used arXiv API search over the June 8, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full PDFs for MemoryVLA++: Temporal Modeling via Memory and Imagination in Vision-Language-Action Models, Latent Spatial Memory for Video World Models, iMaC: Translating Actions into Motion and Contact Images for Embodied World Models, Echo-Memory: A Controlled Study of Memory in Action World Models, AHA-WAM: Asynchronous Horizon-Adaptive World-Action Modeling with Observation-Guided Context Routing, omega-EVA: Envision, Verify, and Act with Latent Interactive World Models, Prisma-World: Camera-Controllable Multi-Agent Video World Model, MotionWAM: Towards Foundation World Action Models for Real-Time Humanoid Loco-Manipulation, FF-JEPA: Long-Horizon Planning in World Models with Latent Planners, and Your Model Already Knows: Attention-Guided Safety Filter for Vision-Language-Action Models. MemoryVLA++, iMaC, and Latent Spatial Memory are preserved today.

MemoryVLA++ is the strongest direct hit. It builds a full temporal VLA interface: current RGB and language become perceptual and cognitive working-memory tokens; a Perceptual-Cognitive Memory Bank stores low-level details and high-level semantics from past interaction; a manipulation-adapted video world model provides compact latent future imagination; and a diffusion action expert consumes the fused temporal tokens. The evidence is broad: Libero, SimplerEnv, Mikasa-Robo, Calvin, Libero-Plus, and several real-robot task categories. The paper is not perfectly controlled across all comparisons, but the ablations support the useful mechanism: both memory retrieval/consolidation and memory-guided imagination matter.

iMaC is the most concrete action-world-model interface paper. It asks a better question than whether generated robot videos look plausible: can a learned world model rank policy checkpoints in the same direction as real hardware? The method renders future robot motion from URDF and forward kinematics, predicts/uses depth, and builds two contact-image streams from scene-to-gripper and robot-to-scene distances. Across eight real-robot tasks, world-model scores are strongly positively correlated with real-world performance on most tasks, while the two weaker tasks expose missing-observation failure modes rather than generic metric noise.

Latent Spatial Memory / Mirage is the strongest memory-system paper for camera-controllable video world models. Instead of accumulating an RGB point cloud and repeatedly rendering it back to pixels before VAE encoding, Mirage stores VAE latent tokens at 3D world coordinates. Readout is a latent-resolution projection into the target camera view, then a ControlNet-style branch injects the memory into the diffusion backbone. The result is both a representation claim and a systems claim: better or competitive consistency on WorldScore and RealEstate10K, with much lower cache read cost and memory.

Echo-Memory is strong citation material and may deserve a later synthesis note. Its most useful result is that replay fidelity is not a proxy for revisit memory: spatial memory can win replay PSNR while failing open-domain return, and block-wise state-space recurrence can win semantic return while losing replay metrics. I am not preserving it as a full note today because it is mainly an evaluation/design-space study, while today's three notes provide more directly reusable architecture surfaces.

AHA-WAM is useful but not preserved. The two-timescale split between a slow video-DiT planner and fast action-DiT executor is a good deployment idea, and the latency story is concrete. I am treating it as adjacent because it is close to yesterday's action/world-model interface thread, and part of the result is systems optimization rather than a cleaner representation mechanism.

omega-EVA is also useful but not preserved. The proposal-conditioned Envision-Verify-Act loop is conceptually aligned with CAPE from June 8: make the policy inspect a latent consequence of its own proposed action before execution. The evidence is mostly simulation and the Stage 3 deltas are real but modest, so it is citation material rather than one of today's top three.

Prisma-World is adjacent for multi-agent video simulation. Its joint denoising, multi-agent RoPE, relative camera geometry, and minimap conditioning address cross-view consistency, but it is less directly tied to robot memory/planning than the preserved papers.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is MemoryVLA++ because it makes temporal modeling in VLAs explicit enough to reason about: past memory, present tokens, and future imagination each have a job. iMaC is the action-conditioning note to remember because it converts actions into robot motion and contact geometry before asking a video model to simulate manipulation. Latent Spatial Memory is the video-world-model note to keep because it treats persistent 3D memory as latent features rather than RGB cache clutter. The common lesson is blunt: world models get more useful when their memory and action interfaces expose the structure that decisions actually depend on.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-08
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is the action interface is becoming the real planning interface. CAPE is the strongest paper because it trains a latent world model around action-conditioned future differences instead of dense visual reconstruction. Coarse-to-Control is the best VLA planning paper because it puts the intermediate plan into the action-token vocabulary rather than text or image space. Spline Policy is the cleanest output-representation paper because it turns a raw action chunk into a continuous motion object that can be resampled, corrected, constrained, and connected to controllers.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider, but it returned missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv paper pages for the preserved candidates returned HTTP 200 but exposed only minimal page metadata through the fetcher. Discovery therefore used arXiv API/category search plus direct arXiv pages and PDFs. At 08:00 Pacific on Monday, June 8, 2026, the Monday arXiv announcement had not landed yet, so the live recent window was still dominated by the June 5 batch. I filtered that leftover cluster rather than pretending there was a fresh Monday release.

I inspected arXiv PDFs for CAPE: Contrastive Action-conditioned Parallel Encoding for Embodied Planning, Coarse-to-Control: Action-Token Planning for Vision-Language-Action Models, Spline Policy: A Structured Representation for Robot Policies, Skill-3D: Evolving Scene-Aware Skills for Agentic 3D Spatial Reasoning, LARA: Latent Action Representation Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models, MemDreamer: Decoupling Perception and Reasoning for Long Video Understanding via Hierarchical Graph Memory and Agentic Retrieval Mechanism, Native3D: End-to-End 3D Scene Generation via Unified Mesh-Texture Modeling and Semantic Alignment, AnchorWorld: Embodied Egocentric World Simulation with View-based Evolution Customization, Streaming Video Generation with Streaming Force Control, Dash2Sim: Closed-Loop Driving Simulation from in-the-wild Dashcam Videos, M3Exam: Benchmarking Multimodal Memory for Realistic User-Agent Interactions, The Sim-to-Real Gap of Foundation Model Agents: A Unified MDP Perspective, and Planning-aligned Token Compression for Long-Context Autonomous Driving. CAPE, Coarse-to-Control, and Spline Policy are preserved today. Skill-3D and LARA are useful adjacent notes, but I am not preserving full notes for them in this run because today's stronger common thread is action/world-model interface design.

CAPE is the strongest direct hit. It argues that embodied planning needs predictive representations that distinguish action-induced future outcomes, not models that reconstruct every visually salient future detail. It predicts an entire future latent trajectory in parallel from the current visual context and candidate action sequence, then trains with a goal-convergent contrastive objective. The reported DROID retrieval gains are large, and the planning-time result is the practical point: CAPE stays near-flat from 335 ms at horizon 1 to 356 ms at horizon 5 in the reported CEM setup.

Coarse-to-Control is the cleanest VLA planning interface today. It first predicts coarse long-horizon action tokens, then predicts executable short-horizon action tokens conditioned on that plan. Both live in a shared discrete action vocabulary. The key result is not just the 97.9 LIBERO average or 83.3 SimplerEnv-WidowX average; it is the tokenizer-sharing ablation showing that a shared action vocabulary helps the plan act as control-native guidance rather than an abstract hint.

Spline Policy is worth keeping because it asks a basic but under-discussed question: what should a robot policy emit? Its answer is spline parameters rather than fixed-resolution action chunks. That output can be decoded into a continuous trajectory, queried at different temporal resolutions, edited or constrained in parameter space, and in the quadratic case converted into a local corrective flow field. The benchmark story is modest, which I like: comparable performance with lower output dimensionality and more execution structure, not universal magic.

Skill-3D is good adjacent agent-memory/tool-use work. It constructs a Scene Memory of tool-use trajectories and co-evolves scene-aware skills with failure lessons, improving effective tool usage in 3D spatial reasoning. I am not preserving a full note today because it overlaps yesterday's agent-memory/tool-state thread, and its main value is tool-routing workflow memory rather than action/world-model interface design.

LARA is useful VLA data-alignment context. Jointly aligning a latent action model and a diffusion VLA is a real reciprocal-supervision idea, especially for using unlabeled videos and limited robot data. I am leaving it as citation material today because CAPE and Coarse-to-Control give sharper planning-interface lessons.

MemDreamer and AnchorWorld are also relevant but not preserved. MemDreamer has a hierarchical graph memory and agentic retrieval loop for hours-long video, but it sits close to the LongSpace note from June 7. AnchorWorld's pose-associated anchor views for egocentric world customization are interesting, but the paper is mainly video-simulator controllability rather than a reusable planning or memory mechanism.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is CAPE because it makes latent world modeling answer the action-selection question directly. Coarse-to-Control is the strongest VLA planning note because it makes the plan a coarse action-token object rather than a semantic flourish. Spline Policy is the output-interface note to remember because it turns learned actions into a continuous motion object that downstream control can actually work with. The common lesson is blunt: planning and control improve when the intermediate object is built for the job it must do.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-07
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is memory and world models are becoming selection-and-state interfaces, not just bigger context. PatchWorld is the most directly relevant paper because it turns logged text-agent trajectories into executable belief-state programs that can be replayed, patched, and used for planning. Worth Remembering is the best embodied-memory paper because it gives memory formation a causal, unsupervised write gate based on surprise in a predictive video-feature space. LongSpace is the strongest benchmark/method note because it asks whether video MLLMs can preserve spatial evidence across long room-tour sequences rather than merely accept more frames.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider, but it returned missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv paper pages for screened candidates returned HTTP 200, and direct arXiv pages/PDFs were used for primary-source inspection. The arXiv weekend cadence means there was no genuinely new Sunday batch; I therefore searched the recent June arXiv cluster plus one slightly older but still relevant paper that had not been preserved.

I inspected arXiv PDFs for PatchWorld: Gradient-Free Optimization of Executable World Models, Worth Remembering: Surprise-Gated Robot Episodic Memory, LongSpace: Exploring Long-Horizon Spatial Memory from Perception to Recall in Video, HyperVis: Continuous Latent Visual Relational Graphs on the Lorentz Hyperboloid for Compositional Reasoning, LatentSkill: From In-Context Textual Skills to In-Weight Latent Skills for LLM Agents, and Where Should Knowledge Enter? A Layered Framework for Knowledge Infusion in Multimodal Iterative Generative Models. PatchWorld, Worth Remembering, and LongSpace are preserved today. HyperVis and LatentSkill are useful citation material, but I am not preserving full notes for them in this run. The knowledge-infusion paper is a decent taxonomy, but not close enough to the repo's embodied/world-model center to spend a note slot today.

PatchWorld is the strongest direct hit. It induces Python world models with explicit symbolic belief state, transition rules, correction logic, and readout logic from offline text-agent trajectories. Prediction failures become typed counterexamples for code repair. The most important result is not just better text prediction; it is the observed frontier between observation fidelity and planning utility. The residual-memory variant predicts surface text better, while the simpler symbolic variant gives better live one-step planning utility.

Worth Remembering is the cleanest embodied-memory mechanism. It computes surprise in V-JEPA-2 latent space with a causal sliding-window Gaussian surrogate, stores only thresholded local maxima as visual episodes, and augments a 4D scene-graph memory. On OC-NaVQA, the surprise-gated memory improves question accuracy over DAAAM from 0.711 to 0.796 while storing about 1.7% of frames. The caveat is that the causal predictive model is still a simple Gaussian over embeddings, not a rich action-conditioned video world model.

LongSpace is worth keeping as benchmark and architecture pressure. LongSpace-Bench contains 445 room-tour videos, about 159 hours, and 4,073 QA pairs covering scene perception, spatial relations, and spatial memory. LongSpace combines 3D spatial-token injection with layer-aware hierarchical KV memory. The key result is that long-memory inference reaches 49.2 on LongSpace-Bench versus 36.1 for uniform 32-frame sampling and 37.7 for recent-window inference, with gains growing on longer videos.

HyperVis is a good citation for continuous relational structure. Its strongest point is that textual scene-graph triplets can hurt VLM accuracy, while continuous hyperbolic relation tokens improve compositional scoring. I am not preserving it today because it is static-image VQA/compositional scoring rather than embodied memory, planning, or world modeling.

LatentSkill is useful adjacent agent-systems material. Converting textual skills into LoRA adapters is a real interface move, but the current evidence is mainly ALFWorld and Search-QA efficiency/composition. It belongs in a future agent-skill synthesis more than today's paper daily note set.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is PatchWorld because it makes a world model into an executable belief-state object that can be inspected, tested, repaired, and used for planning. Worth Remembering is the best embodied-memory mechanism because it gives memory writes a causal surprise gate and beats same-budget uniform/random episodic storage. LongSpace is the benchmark/method to remember because it separates long-context video processing from real spatial memory. The common lesson is clean: useful memory is not accumulation, and useful world modeling is not reconstruction theater. The object being stored, updated, retrieved, or repaired has to be explicit enough to do work.

VASO is the strongest direct hit. It represents each LLM-generated robot skill as a semantic contract with a temporal-logic local rule, proposition-aligned labeling function, and planner-facing template. The useful move is that model-checker counterexamples become textual gradients for updating the reusable skill contract. The caveat is important: the verification guarantee depends on the correctness of the proposition-aligned mapping from low-level robot behavior to symbolic propositions.

Astra is strong adjacent-to-direct world-model reasoning work. It couples an RL-trained VLM policy with a Bagel-based world simulator that generates novel views from camera-motion queries. The key point is not merely "generate another view"; off-the-shelf generation is not enough, and forced simulator use can hurt. Astra improves by training the simulator for view consistency and training the policy to decide when, where, and how to imagine.

PACT is the simplest stealable agent architecture idea today. It treats inter-agent communication as a public state-update problem. Agents may reason privately, but only an action, grounded state/evidence, and result enter shared history. The evidence is practical: across controlled multi-agent settings PACT improves the performance-cost frontier, and in OpenHands/SWE-agent ports it reduces cost per solved SWE-bench Verified instance.

MAGE is worth remembering as memory citation material. Its hierarchical execution-state tree, with Grow, Compress, Maintain, and Revise operations, is conceptually good. I am not preserving it as a full note today because PACT carries a cleaner minimal interface lesson, and VASO/Astra are stronger against the repo's embodied/world-model taste.

DexFuture is good adjacent robotics context. It amortizes future target generation for bimanual dexterous tool use instead of running slow online CEM over action-conditioned world-model rollouts. The target-interface idea is useful, but the paper is narrower than today's top three.

Discrete-WAM is relevant world-action modeling for autonomous driving, with a shared discrete token space for visual states, decisions, and actions. It is not weak, but the result stack is more benchmark- and system-heavy than the cleaner mechanism papers preserved today.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is VASO because it turns formal verification from a post-hoc safety check into a reusable skill-optimization signal. Astra is the most interesting world-model reasoning paper because it makes imagined observations answer an evidence question and shows that simulator access alone is not enough. PACT is the most directly reusable agent-systems design because it keeps private reasoning private and turns public communication into compact action-state records. The common lesson is blunt: state interfaces matter. The good papers today do not just add more generation or more agent chatter; they define what must be exposed, verified, imagined, or passed forward.

digests.theme: Today's strongest pattern is world models are being pulled into the evaluation and control loop, not just the video-generation stack.
