# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-01

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **judge the supervision channel before trusting the model it trains**. QVal asks whether dense intermediate scores actually order actions by downstream value before spending a full RL run on them. HealthAgentBench asks whether healthcare agents can execute full clinical workflows in raw environments instead of answering static vignette questions. AdaJEPA asks whether a frozen latent world model should be allowed to keep planning after its own prediction errors reveal that the environment has shifted.

I kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan deliberately covered agent evaluation, healthcare agents, adaptive world models, interpretability, continual self-supervised memory, medical multimodal reasoning, 3D/generative world-model benchmarks, and a small robotics lane. Fresh robotics/manipulation titles were present, but the strongest non-robotics papers had cleaner mechanisms and broader reuse value today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv pages for candidate IDs were reachable and useful for quick metadata / summary checks. arXiv PDFs were accessible and used for primary-source inspection.

No preserved note today is abstract-only. I acquired and inspected the arXiv PDFs for **QVal**, **AdaJEPA**, **HealthAgentBench**, **Self-Study Reconsidered**, **CLIMB**, **WorldRoamBench**, **SemRF**, and **Resolving superposition in AI for interpretability and cross-modal alignment in patient-neuronal images**. I read the main method, evaluation, results, and limitations / conclusion where present; I did not audit every appendix table for the longer benchmark papers.

**QVal** is the most directly useful paper today. It gives a cheap, training-free testbed for asking whether dense supervision signals for long-horizon LLM agents are aligned with reference Q-values.

**HealthAgentBench** is the strongest healthcare / deployment-evaluation paper. It replaces static medical QA with terminal-based healthcare tasks over X-rays, CT volumes, pathology slides, trial protocols, and EHR data, then scores agents by binary task success.

**AdaJEPA** is the strongest adaptive world-model mechanism. It inserts self-supervised test-time adaptation inside the model predictive control loop: plan, act, use the observed transition to update the latent world model, then replan.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **QVal: Cheaply Evaluating Dense Supervision Signals for Long-Horizon LLM Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the cleanest methodological contribution today.

Why it matters: dense supervision for agents is usually judged only after an expensive training pipeline, which mixes up signal quality with optimizer and implementation effects. QVal isolates the signal: given state-action pairs, does the score rank actions the same way a strong reference continuation policy's Q-values do? The uncomfortable result is useful: simple direct prompting beats many recent dense-supervision methods.

### 2. **HealthAgentBench: A Unified Benchmark Suite of Realistic Agentic Healthcare Environments for Challenging Frontier AI Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for agent evaluation and healthcare deployment realism.

Why it matters: it treats healthcare-agent capability as environment interaction, not bedside-manner multiple choice. The benchmark has 54 tasks across 7 categories with raw clinical artifacts and terminal environments. Even the best evaluated agent, Codex GPT-5.5 in their setup, reaches only about 42 percent task success, with imaging and large-search compositional tasks still ugly.

### 3. **AdaJEPA: An Adaptive Latent World Model**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for world models, but more adjacent than QVal for immediate agent tooling.

Why it matters: it makes world-model calibration an online loop rather than a pretraining artifact. The mechanism is simple and transferable: after each MPC action, use the observed transition as the same latent prediction target used in training, update a small subset of parameters, and replan. The caveat is that it is still a controlled benchmark story, not a proof that deployment-time updates are safe in messy environments.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** QVal.

The steal is the evaluation contract: before turning a heuristic score into a training signal, ask whether it is aligned with the value notion you actually need. For cabbageland agents, that means not treating confidence, critique quality, embedding similarity, verifier prose, or self-distilled ratings as "dense feedback" until they pass a direct alignment check against downstream success.

HealthAgentBench gives the environment-design analogue: evaluate agents in raw, tool-using workflows where success requires search, decomposition, data inspection, and exact output constraints. AdaJEPA gives the world-model analogue: when the model's own action produces evidence that its prediction was wrong, the system should have a principled way to adapt rather than keep rolling out a stale imagination.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**QVal** is strong because it names the hidden confounder in dense-supervision work. Downstream training performance does not tell us whether the intermediate signal was good; it tells us the whole recipe worked or did not. QVal fixes datasets, contexts, reference labels, and model backbones, then compares 21 scoring methods across FrozenLake, ALFWorld, OpenApps, and TerminalBench. The main caveat is that Q-alignment is only as good as the reference policy and sampled state-action distribution. TerminalBench labels depend on strong-model rollouts rather than true optimal policies, so this is a practical proxy, not a theorem about all agent training.

**HealthAgentBench** is strong because it builds tasks that look like real work: inspect files, query databases, view images, write outputs, and pass a verifier. The design choices are mostly right: low chance success, anti-cheat mounting, minimal instructions, raw clinical artifacts, and binary task success. The caveat is evaluation ecology. The reported Codex / Claude / Copilot rankings are tied to 2026 harnesses, costs, and disabled web access; the durable contribution is the benchmark framing, not the leaderboard gossip.

**AdaJEPA** is strong because the intervention sits exactly where the failure occurs. Frozen world models produce prediction errors under visual, geometry, dynamics, or layout shifts; AdaJEPA uses those newly observed transitions to reduce prediction error before the next plan. The method reports consistent gains across PushT / PushObj and PointMaze variants with one gradient step per MPC replan and only small latency. The caveat is representation coverage: if the pretrained latent space lacks the features needed for the new environment, light adaptation can improve behavior but cannot invent a missing ontology.

**Self-Study Reconsidered** was the best synthetic-data runner-up. It shows that document-generated QA is an implicit evidence-selection policy, not neutral preprocessing. Coverage saturates, artifacts attract questions, and instruction-like spans in the source can hijack the answer stage. Useful, but I kept it as a runner-up because QVal was a cleaner general evaluation mechanism.

**CLIMB** was the strongest continual-learning runner-up. Its bounded hierarchical centroid memory plus replay distillation is a real memory mechanism for online continual self-supervised learning. I did not preserve it today because the evaluation is mostly Split CIFAR/ImageNet representation learning, so it is adjacent inspiration rather than immediate agent/world-model design.

**WorldRoamBench** is useful for evaluating interactive world models over long-horizon action following, visual stability, physics, and memory. I did not preserve it because it is a large benchmark paper and the core idea is easier to cite than steal today.

**SemRF** is conceptually aligned with interpretability, but it reads more like a formal framing paper than a tested mechanism. **Resolving superposition in patient-neuronal images** is intriguing in its attempt to connect sparse autoencoders, biological image representations, and transcriptomic alignment, but the claims are broad enough that it needs slower biological-method scrutiny before becoming a preserved note.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all make evaluation more local and less theatrical. QVal asks whether the feedback signal orders intermediate actions by value. HealthAgentBench asks whether agents can actually operate inside clinical workflows rather than charm a static benchmark. AdaJEPA asks whether a world model can use its own prediction miss as a test-time correction signal. The common lesson is blunt: do not trust a polished downstream outcome until you have inspected the mechanism that produced the signal, the environment, or the rollout.

- [HealthAgentBench note](../paper_notes/healthagentbench_agentic_healthcare_environments.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-21

## Theme

Today’s strongest signal is **explicit interfaces that actually constrain behavior**. The best paper is **ECHO: Continuous Hierarchical Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models** because it tries to make long-horizon memory retrieval more typed and hierarchy-aware instead of treating memory as a flat nearest-neighbor sludge heap. **Jointly Learning Predicates and Actions Enables Zero-Shot Skill Composition** is the more intellectually honest neurosymbolic paper today, because it does not pretend end-to-end action generation alone will magically support composition. **GaussianDream** is useful adjacent material, but it overclaims the phrase “world model” for what is mostly a geometry-heavy training-time supervision scaffold.

## Short overview

Brave Search and AlphaXiv were not available in this run, and browser automation was unavailable because the OpenClaw browser gateway timed out, so discovery used direct inspection of current arXiv recent-category listings plus full-text arXiv HTML/PDF reads where accessible. I fully inspected arXiv full text for **ECHO**, **Jointly Learning Predicates and Actions Enables Zero-Shot Skill Composition**, and **GaussianDream**. Confidence is solid on their mechanisms, training setup, and headline results, and weaker on fine implementation details I did not separately re-derive from appendices.

**ECHO** is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is to store successful robotic experiences in a continuous hyperbolic hierarchy, retrieve them with entailment-aware tree search, and fuse the retrieved memory back into a frozen π0-style policy through residual injection and gating. The part that matters is not “hyperbolic” by itself. The useful claim is that long-horizon reuse gets better when memory is organized by abstraction level instead of thrown into a flat retrieval pool.

**Jointly Learning Predicates and Actions Enables Zero-Shot Skill Composition** is the cleanest structure paper in the set. It learns a single generative skill model over both action trajectories and predicate-belief trajectories, then uses the predicted predicate rollout as an online symbolic interface for planning, monitoring, and recomposition. That is much better than stapling a separate classifier onto a policy after the fact. The limitation is obvious but important: the predicate vocabulary and symbolic planning domain are still manually specified.

**GaussianDream** is competent, but I do not buy the strongest framing. It adds a feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction and short-horizon future Gaussian prediction module during training, then discards the heavy decoding heads at inference while keeping a learned spatiotemporal prefix for action generation. That is a useful way to inject geometric supervision into a VLA. But calling it a “world model” risks overstating how much explicit predictive state is actually used during control.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **ECHO: Continuous Hierarchical Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it treats memory organization as an interface-design problem for long-horizon control, not as a generic retrieval garnish.

### 2. **Jointly Learning Predicates and Actions Enables Zero-Shot Skill Composition**

**Verdict:** useful direct material.

Why it matters: it makes symbolic outcome traces part of the skill model itself instead of outsourcing composition to a brittle post hoc layer.

### 3. **GaussianDream: A Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian World Model for Robotic Manipulation**

**Verdict:** skimmable adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it is a good example of geometry-heavy training supervision helping manipulation, even though the “world model” label is doing more work than the deployed control loop.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** ECHO: Continuous Hierarchical Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models.

What makes ECHO worth attention is not the hyperbolic branding, it is the narrower systems claim underneath it. The paper argues that manipulation memory should be organized so that coarse task semantics, subgoals, and local action experience are retrievable at different abstraction levels, with hierarchy-aware filtering before action priors are injected back into the policy. On LIBERO-Long, that setup improves the reproduced π0 baseline from 80.7 percent to 93.5 percent, and the ablation path is actually informative: short-term buffering helps a lot, flat memory helps only a little, hyperbolic organization helps more, and entailment-aware tree retrieval plus consolidation helps most.

This matters for cabbageland because it is a real attempt to replace flat latent mush with **typed reusable memory structure that changes retrieval behavior**. The paper is still scaffold-heavy and depends on VLM-mediated subgoal extraction and verification, so it is not cleanly learned end to end. But the structural burden is at least legible and testable.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update is that **memory papers should be judged by retrieval contract, not by sentimental talk about long-term context**. ECHO earns partial credit because its ablation isolates what the hierarchy is buying over short-term context and flat memory. That is much stronger than papers that call something “hierarchical memory” when they merely add another cache.

PACTS sharpens a second point. If you want compositional skill reuse, a symbolic interface should appear inside the rollout object itself, not as a separately trained monitor glued on afterward. Jointly generating actions and predicate-belief traces is a more defensible design than training a policy and then hoping a detached symbolic layer can explain it.

GaussianDream provides the negative calibration. Strong geometry-aware supervision can improve manipulation, but that is not the same thing as giving the deployed agent a planning-grade explicit state model. The paper looks useful as a training recipe and less convincing as a world-model paper in the stricter sense.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **ECHO** because it makes a real argument that long-horizon manipulation benefits from hierarchy-aware memory retrieval rather than flat similarity search, and it backs that claim with a meaningful ablation path. **PACTS** is the more principled compositionality paper, because it builds symbolic outcome traces directly into the skill model and uses them for planning and monitoring, though it still depends on hand-designed predicates and operators. **GaussianDream** is a solid geometry-supervision paper masquerading a little too hard as a world model. The shared lesson is simple: explicit structure matters when it narrows the interface between experience, control, and reuse in a way that can actually be inspected.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-28

## Theme

Today’s useful pattern is **making long-horizon control legible by changing the interface**, not by stapling more scale onto the policy. The strongest paper is **PrimitiveVLA** because it tries to move VLA fine-tuning away from monolithic instruction-to-trajectory imitation and toward reusable motion units with explicit assembly logic. **ProgVLA** is the best compact-policy paper of the batch because it adds a real progress signal and aggressive token compression instead of just shrinking the model and hoping for the best. **MentalMap** is not a robotics paper, but it is a sharp diagnostic reminder that text-only “world model” claims still collapse badly once viewpoint transformation and active spatial construction enter the loop.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in spirit, but no Brave Search tool is configured in this run, so I could not actually use it here. AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable as a live tool surface in this environment. Discovery therefore fell back to recent arXiv API results, direct arXiv HTML full-text pages when available, and direct arXiv abstract pages otherwise.

I inspected substantial arXiv HTML full text for **PrimitiveVLA: Learning Reusable Motion Primitives for Efficient and Generalizable Robotic Manipulation**, **ProgVLA: Progress-Aware Robot Manipulation Skill Learning**, and **Do LLMs Build World Models From Text? A Multilingual Diagnostic of Spatial Reasoning**. Confidence is reasonably good on the main mechanism and evaluation setup for all three. Confidence is lower on appendix-only hyperparameters and on the exact robustness of some reported gains.

**PrimitiveVLA** is the most relevant paper today. Its core claim is that standard VLA fine-tuning wastes data by binding high-level instructions directly to task-specific low-level trajectories, which makes reusable motion patterns hard to share across tasks. The paper’s answer is to disassemble demonstrations into an explicit library of 11 primitives, train the VLA on primitive-conditioned masked observations, and then reassemble tasks at inference time with a VLM planner plus switching logic. I like the pressure it puts on the decomposition interface: if compositionality is real, the reusable unit should exist both during training and during execution.

The caveat is that PrimitiveVLA gets a lot of its structure from external scaffolding. Primitive sequences come from VLM reasoning over demonstrations, and boundary logic is generated as code from primitive definitions plus state traces. That is not fake, but it does mean the paper is less “the VLA discovered primitives” and more “the system was carefully forced into a primitive regime.” Honestly that is fine. Forced structure is still structure, and it is much better than vague claims that modularity just emerges.

**ProgVLA** is less ambitious conceptually, but more disciplined than most compact-VLA work. It uses two-stage Perceiver resampling to aggressively compress multimodal context, then adds progress heads that predict normalized remaining horizon and near-completion success, using those signals to reweight a flow-matching imitation objective. This is not a world model and not a deep memory paper. But it does make long-horizon progress estimation an internal training signal instead of an external evaluator, which is a respectable way to attack the “small policies lose the thread” problem.

**MentalMap** is the best framing paper of the day. It shows a strong, multilingual L3 cliff in pure-text spatial reasoning: models can recover local facts but break when asked to perform viewpoint transformation or active spatial construction. That matters because people keep talking as if text-only LLMs already have robust internal world models. This benchmark does not prove they do not have any such structure, but it does show that the structure is much weaker and less stable than the branding suggests.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **PrimitiveVLA: Learning Reusable Motion Primitives for Efficient and Generalizable Robotic Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it pushes compositionality into the actual training and execution interface instead of merely naming experts, subgoals, or stages after the fact.

### 2. **ProgVLA: Progress-Aware Robot Manipulation Skill Learning**

**Verdict:** useful, with a real mechanism.

Why it matters: it gives compact VLAs an explicit internal notion of progress and does so in a way that directly changes training weights on long-horizon behavior.

### 3. **Do LLMs Build World Models From Text? A Multilingual Diagnostic of Spatial Reasoning**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration and framing-important.

Why it matters: it is a good antidote to lazy “text world model” rhetoric, especially around viewpoint reasoning and spatial construction.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** PrimitiveVLA.

The interesting part is not the primitive vocabulary by itself. Plenty of papers can write down a list of verbs. The meaningful move is that PrimitiveVLA tries to align three things at once: the supervision unit during fine-tuning, the execution unit during inference, and the canonicalized representation that is supposed to make reuse possible across tasks. That is the kind of decomposition that actually changes computation.

I also like that the paper is honest about the problem it is solving. It is not claiming fully open-ended invention. It is claiming that if you teach a VLA reusable motion patterns like grasp, pull, press, and rotate, and you preserve object-relevant context with masks plus canonical instructions, then the model can recombine those patterns better than a monolithic trajectory imitator can. That is a narrower claim, but a cleaner one.

My confidence is decent because I inspected the accessible full arXiv HTML through the method section, including the primitive library, disassembly pipeline, state-based boundary segmentation, canonical representation, and the main reported results. My main skepticism is not about whether the system works better than baseline in the paper’s setting. It is about how much of the gain comes from good decomposition versus from fairly strong external supervision and hand-held switching rules.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**PrimitiveVLA** matters because it raises the bar for compositional-robotics claims. If a paper says a VLA is compositional, it should be fair to ask what the reusable unit is, how it is supervised, where it appears in the computation, and how it is reassembled at execution time. PrimitiveVLA gives a concrete, inspectable answer.

**ProgVLA** is useful baseline pressure on compact VLAs. It suggests that a small model does not have to be stupid if the sequence bottleneck is managed carefully and if the policy has an internal training signal for temporal progress. That is not the same thing as solving memory or planning, but it is a real architectural improvement over plain model shrinkage.

**MentalMap** is a framing correction. It suggests that a lot of “LLMs have world models from text” discourse is still overconfident. The benchmark’s most useful contribution is not the headline itself, but the sharper division between static fact recall and active spatial construction.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **PrimitiveVLA** because it makes compositionality concrete at the actual interface where reuse must happen: demonstrations are disassembled into reusable motion primitives during training and reassembled during execution. **ProgVLA** is the cleanest compact-policy paper because it couples aggressive multimodal compression with an internal progress signal that directly reweights long-horizon imitation. **MentalMap** is the best adjacent paper because it punctures mushy text-world-model claims by showing a persistent viewpoint-reasoning cliff across languages. The common lesson is that explicit structure matters when it changes the policy’s real control loop or the benchmark’s real failure diagnosis, not when it is just better branding for a latent blob.

- [ProgVLA note](../paper_notes/progvla_progress_aware_robot_manipulation_skill_learning.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-12

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **do not keep or update the whole state when only the decision-relevant delta matters**. When Does Continual Learning Require Learning separates world change into domain shift, temporal drift, and agent-generated experience, then shows that different update mechanisms win in different regimes. Certified Interventional Fidelity says interpretability claims should be written as explicit causal estimands and certified under repeated monitoring, not reported as one convenient point estimate. DeltaV replaces full intermediate image generation with compact visual state updates, so the model spends tokens on what changed instead of repainting the entire scene. Robust Bayesian Decision Making under Adversarial Uncertainty shifts active learning away from nominally optimal but brittle decisions toward decisions that stay stable under plausible hidden perturbations. Harrison.Rad 1.5 treats radiology reporting as a multimodal report-drafting problem with priors, context, and certification-style evaluation rather than generic medical VQA.

I kept robotics / VLA out of the ranked five again today. The scout deliberately inspected non-robotics lanes: continual learning, mechanistic interpretability, uncertainty and decision-making, healthcare / radiology foundation models, multimodal reasoning, object-centric representation learning, and grokking / measurement-validity work. The strongest robotics-adjacent candidates were **Native Video-Action Pretraining for Generalizable Robot Control**, **LEEVLA**, **WCog-VLA**, **Dual Latent Memory in Vision-Language-Action Models**, and **GIRAF**. Some were plausible, but none clearly beat the non-robotics papers below on mechanism, evidence, and future usefulness.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. I used live arXiv category pages, direct arXiv title lookups, and full arXiv HTML papers for discovery and inspection. Discovery quality is narrower than a healthy Brave-first run, but no preserved note today is abstract-only.

For the preserved notes, I inspected the full arXiv HTML papers for **When Does Continual Learning Require Learning**, **Certified Interventional Fidelity**, **DeltaV**, and **Robust Bayesian Decision Making under Adversarial Uncertainty**. I read the framing, method, benchmark or experiment design, main results, and at least one meaningful caveat section for each. I also inspected the full arXiv HTML papers for **Harrison.Rad 1.5**, **When Structured Sparse Autoencoders Learn Consistent Concepts Across Modalities**, and **At-Grok Is Not Converged** as ranked or runner-up candidates. I did not audit released code, reproduce results, or verify every appendix table independently.

**When Does Continual Learning Require Learning** is the most relevant paper today. Its useful move is to stop treating continual learning as one scalar capability and instead ask what kind of world change is happening, then compare prompt updates, weight updates, RL updates, and context-compression methods under one protocol.

**Certified Interventional Fidelity** is the strongest evaluation paper. It turns activation patching and similar interpretability claims into bounded causal estimands with confidence intervals and anytime-valid confidence sequences, including adaptive intervention sampling.

**DeltaV** is the strongest architecture paper. The interesting claim is not "generate more intermediate images," but "only model the visual change that matters for the next reasoning step."

## Ranked papers

### 1. **When Does Continual Learning Require Learning**

**Verdict:** must read for continual learning and agent adaptation.

Why it matters: The paper reframes continual learning as increasing competence as the world changes along two axes: space, where new domains arrive, and time, where the same task drifts. It then recasts standard LLM evaluations as sequential problems and compares prompt optimization, supervised fine-tuning, online RL, and context-compression methods on a shared Qwen3-8B backbone. The core result is the useful part: prompt-based methods fit fast but damage future performance, distillation-like methods accumulate knowledge but resist updates, context compression improves efficiency without teaching new tasks, and online RL adapts best to factual change but is reward-sensitive.

### 2. **Certified Interventional Fidelity: Anytime-Valid, Adaptive Evaluation of Causal Claims in Mechanistic Interpretability**

**Verdict:** strong interpretability-evaluation paper.

Why it matters: CIF wraps interventional interpretability metrics in explicit causal statistics. Instead of reporting one patching number, it defines the target as an expectation over a stated input and intervention distribution, then attaches confidence intervals and anytime-valid confidence sequences that remain valid under repeated monitoring. The variance-adaptive betting sequences are the real engineering win: the paper reports 10-30x lower certification cost than the conservative Hoeffding-style alternative on MNIST abstractions and GPT-2 Small IOI circuits.

### 3. **DeltaV: Thinking with Visual State Updates in Unified Large Multimodal Models**

**Verdict:** strong direct-relevance multimodal reasoning paper.

Why it matters: DeltaV argues that interleaved multimodal reasoning wastes capacity when it regenerates whole images at every step. The model instead predicts compact visual update tokens conditioned on past visual states, and the TSIM Router dynamically stops allocating tokens when reconstruction gains flatten out. The paper reports 55.6% fewer newly generated visual tokens on average, a 3.3 point reasoning gain over full-image intermediate generation, and a 5.9 point gain over Qwen3-VL-2B on external multimodal understanding and reasoning benchmarks. The most important negative result is also useful: naive full-image intermediate generation can be worse than text-only reasoning.

### 4. **Robust Bayesian Decision Making under Adversarial Uncertainty**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent paper for uncertainty-aware decision support.

Why it matters: This paper is about active learning and experiment design for stable decisions, not just good posterior fit. It formalizes adversarially robust decision utility and derives a Bayesian acquisition criterion that targets decision stability under plausible hidden perturbations. The paper's best message is that conventional decision-aware design can reach high confidence around a fragile optimum, while the robustness-aware criterion spends samples around brittle regions instead. The caveat is honest too: at very large perturbation budgets, the robust method can become overly conservative and lose out to simpler baselines.

### 5. **Harrison.Rad 1.5 Technical Report: A radiology foundation model that can draft reports from images, priors and clinical context**

**Verdict:** useful healthcare / foundation-model report; lighter recommendation.

Why it matters: Harrison.Rad 1.5 is more interesting as a clinically aligned evaluation and workflow report than as a generic "medical LLM beats baseline" paper. The system is trained on roughly 6 million image-report instances, integrates priors and clinical context, and evaluates report quality with a Findings-Diagnosis score plus certification-style FRCR simulations. The strongest headline is that HR1.5 and its agentic variant are the only systems in the report to clear the simulated FRCR 2B Short Case passing threshold. The reason it stays fifth is that the load-bearing evidence is still partly internal and proprietary, the FRCR exams are simulated rather than official sittings, and the model is explicitly not cleared for clinical use.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** When Does Continual Learning Require Learning.

The steal is the framing boundary. Continual learning is not "can the agent remember more?" It is "what changed in the world, and which update surface is the right one?" Some changes want prompt or context updates. Some want weight updates. Some need policy learning. Some only look like memory problems until you measure whether competence actually increased. That maps directly onto OpenClaw-style agents, long-running tooling tasks, mutable user constraints, and dynamic external systems.

CIF provides the evaluation complement: if we claim an interpretability or intervention effect, we should specify the intervention distribution and report uncertainty that survives repeated monitoring. DeltaV provides the representation complement: do not regenerate the whole visual state when the useful supervision is in the delta. Robust Bayesian decision-making provides the uncertainty complement: do not collect data only where the nominal optimum looks strongest; collect data where the decision might flip.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**When Does Continual Learning Require Learning** is strong because it refuses the usual forgetting-only framing. The important move is the two-axis decomposition of change, plus one mechanism-agnostic evaluation protocol that compares prompt, weight, RL, and context methods on equal ground. The result that context compression barely helps with new-task acquisition is especially relevant for agent builders who keep hoping better memory packing is the same thing as learning. Caveats: the comparison is still tied to a single backbone family and a specific selection of update methods, and the sequentialized tasks remain laboratory versions of deployment drift.

**Certified Interventional Fidelity** is strong because it changes the reporting contract around mechanistic-interpretability claims. The paper does not invent a new explanation metric; it makes existing intervention scores statistically explicit and monitor-safe. That is more useful than another patching heatmap. The caveat is that CIF certifies the chosen estimand, not the truth of the underlying explanation itself. A bad intervention target can still be certified precisely.

**DeltaV** is strong because it isolates the actual waste in interleaved multimodal reasoning: unchanged visual content. Modeling only the visual update is a cleaner interface than asking the model to repaint the whole scene. The TSIM Router gives the idea a concrete budget controller instead of a hand-wavy compression story. The caveat is that the paper still lives inside the authors' StructCoT setup and image-generation loop, and routed updates do not beat text-only reasoning on every subtask.

**Robust Bayesian Decision Making under Adversarial Uncertainty** is useful because it shifts the optimization target from nominal utility to decision stability. That matters for high-stakes decision support, scientific design, and any system where the best nominal action may be locally brittle. The paper is also refreshingly honest about the price of robustness: larger adversarial budgets can make the method too conservative. The limitations are exactly where you would expect them - adversarial-variable modeling choices, modest experimental scope, and synthetic structure around the most controlled results.

**Harrison.Rad 1.5** earns the fifth slot because it is more field-shaped than the usual medical benchmark paper. Its best contribution is the combination of workflow framing, report-generation task definition, and certification-style evaluation. I am keeping it as a lighter recommendation because the strongest evidence depends on a proprietary stack, internally constructed FRCR simulations, and internal datasets, while the paper itself says the system is not approved for clinical use.

**When Structured Sparse Autoencoders Learn Consistent Concepts Across Modalities** was a strong runner-up. I like the move of adding exclusive sparsity for inter-region disentanglement and group sparsity for intra-region consistency, then checking whether the visual-side regularization improves cross-modal monosemanticity too. I left it below the ranked five because the evaluation remains surrogate-heavy and the practical downstream payoff is less immediate than CIF or DeltaV.

**At-Grok Is Not Converged** was another strong runner-up. Its main point is sharp: reading effective rank at the grokking transition is a measurement-validity error because compression keeps moving long after accuracy flips. I did not preserve it today mainly because CIF already occupied the evaluation-audit slot and had broader mechanism transfer.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all punish lazy state accounting. Continual learning should be measured against the kind of world change that actually happened. Interpretability claims should survive repeated monitoring and adaptive probing. Multimodal reasoning should update the changed visual state, not regenerate the whole scene. Decision-aware active learning should probe where the decision is fragile, not only where the posterior looks confident. Even the radiology report is best read as a workflow claim: useful medical AI has to integrate priors, context, and evaluation surfaces that look more like real certification and reporting work than like a polite benchmark.

## Detailed notes

- [When continual learning requires learning note](../paper_notes/when_does_continual_learning_require_learning.md)
- [Certified interventional fidelity note](../paper_notes/certified_interventional_fidelity_mechanistic_interpretability.md)
- [DeltaV note](../paper_notes/deltav_visual_state_updates_multimodal_models.md)
- [Robust Bayesian decision making note](../paper_notes/robust_bayesian_decision_making_adversarial_uncertainty.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-03-28

## Theme
Today’s real split is between papers that change the state representation and papers that merely decorate generation. The strongest hit replaces photometric video latents with geometry-foundation features as the predictive state. The second worthwhile hit is less about architecture than research hygiene: it argues that for large pretrained VLAs, catastrophic forgetting is not the default story many papers still assume. That matters because it changes what counts as a serious continual-learning baseline.

## Short overview
Today’s most relevant paper is **VGGT-World: Transforming VGGT into an Autoregressive Geometry World Model**. It makes the right move: stop asking a video generator to implicitly carry geometry while spending most of its capacity on appearance. Instead, use a frozen geometry foundation model as the state representation and learn temporal evolution directly in that latent space. That is a much cleaner bet than another “geometry-aware video generation” paper.

The second paper worth preserving is **Pretrained Vision-Language-Action Models are Surprisingly Resistant to Forgetting in Continual Learning**. This is not exciting in the cinematic sense, but it is useful because it pressures a lazy assumption in robot learning: that continual adaptation necessarily demands elaborate anti-forgetting machinery. Their evidence suggests that large pretrained VLAs plus simple experience replay already behave much better than small-from-scratch baselines, especially in low-replay regimes.

A third paper I inspected but am **not** preserving as a full note today is **DreamWorld: Unified World Modeling in Video Generation**. It is not empty, but it still reads like multi-source feature injection into a video generator rather than a convincing explicit world model. Useful citation material, not a paper I currently trust as a conceptual anchor.

## Ranked papers

1. **VGGT-World: Transforming VGGT into an Autoregressive Geometry World Model**  
   - Verdict: **Highly relevant**  
   - Role: **Directly relevant**  
   - Why it matters: It argues that geometry-foundation features are a better predictive state than appearance-heavy video latents for 3D forecasting.

2. **Pretrained Vision-Language-Action Models are Surprisingly Resistant to Forgetting in Continual Learning**  
   - Verdict: **Useful**  
   - Role: **Directly relevant**  
   - Why it matters: It raises the baseline bar for continual-learning claims in VLAs by showing simple replay is already unexpectedly strong when the model is heavily pretrained.

3. **DreamWorld: Unified World Modeling in Video Generation**  
   - Verdict: **Skimmable**  
   - Role: **Mostly citation material**  
   - Why it matters: It is a current example of the field trying to rebrand multi-objective video generation as “world modeling,” with some value as framing contrast.

## Most relevant to cabbageland
**VGGT-World** is the clear winner. The important idea is not just “predict depth better.” The important idea is that the predictive state should already encode geometry in a decoder-compatible form, so the temporal model can spend its capacity on state evolution rather than relearning geometry through appearance compression. That is much closer to the kind of explicit structure cabbageland should care about.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact
- **Predictive-state framing:** VGGT-World is useful evidence that the main design choice in a world model may be the state space, not just the forecasting objective.
- **Against photometric theater:** It is a good citation when pushing back on claims that video realism implies a usable world model.
- **Continual-learning baselines for VLAs:** The VLA forgetting paper matters because future memory / continual-learning papers should not get credit for beating weak from-scratch baselines when pretrained VLAs with replay are already strong.
- **Confidence note:** I inspected substantial paper text for **VGGT-World**, **Pretrained VLAs are Surprisingly Resistant to Forgetting**, and **DreamWorld** via arXiv HTML, not just abstracts. I did **not** exhaustively audit appendices or every table, so I am more confident in the mechanism judgments than in every exact metric claim.

## One-paragraph takeaway
The useful lesson today is that explicit structure keeps winning whenever papers actually commit to it. **VGGT-World** improves the situation by choosing a geometry-native latent state instead of asking RGB-oriented video latents to secretly become 3D simulators. **The VLA continual-learning paper** is valuable in a different way: it removes some excuse-making from the literature by showing that large pretrained controllers already retain skills better than the old catastrophic-forgetting story would suggest. **DreamWorld**, by contrast, still feels like a generator wearing a world-model nametag. If a paper claims world modeling, ask what the state is, how it evolves, and whether the evaluation tests that state rather than just prettier outputs.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-08

## Theme

Today’s strongest paper is a world-action-model paper that actually replaces holistic mush with an explicit object interface. **OA-WAM: Object-Addressable World Action Model for Robust Robot Manipulation** splits each scene into persistent object-address slots plus time-varying content, then enforces slot routing through the address slice at every transformer layer. That is the kind of structural commitment this area keeps pretending to make. The other two papers are useful for different reasons. **Reconstruction or Semantics? What Makes a Latent Space Useful for Robotic World Models** is a good framing paper because it cleanly argues that pixel reconstruction quality is a bad proxy for policy-relevant world modeling. **When to Trust Imagination: Adaptive Action Execution for World Action Models** is narrower but still worthwhile because it treats long action-chunk execution as a verification problem instead of a fixed hyperparameter.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked by a missing Brave API key in the current environment. I therefore scouted recent arXiv listings directly, focusing on fresh cs.RO, cs.CV, and cs.AI submissions from May 8 and nearby May 7 entries, then inspected primary-source arXiv abstract pages plus accessible HTML method text for the strongest candidates.

I inspected the abstract and substantial method text for **OA-WAM: Object-Addressable World Action Model for Robust Robot Manipulation**, **Reconstruction or Semantics? What Makes a Latent Space Useful for Robotic World Models**, and **When to Trust Imagination: Adaptive Action Execution for World Action Models**. I also screened nearby titles such as **CKT-WAM**, **RobotEQ**, and a few unrelated CV papers, but they looked either more incremental, more benchmark-facing, or less mechanism-relevant for cabbageland.

**OA-WAM** is the cleanest direct hit. The core claim is that WAM robustness suffers because holistic world tokens do not provide a stable object-selection interface when instructions refer to particular objects under scene shifts. The paper responds with per-object slots whose identity address vectors are frozen per episode, separate from time-varying content vectors, and with cross-slot attention keys restricted to the address subspace. That is not full object reasoning, and it inherits upstream segmentation and grounding errors, but it is at least a real architectural intervention instead of “more multimodal tokens.”

**Reconstruction or Semantics?** is mostly a controlled study, but a useful one. It keeps the diffusion world-model backbone fixed, varies only the latent encoder family, and shows that semantic representation spaces like V-JEPA 2.1, Web-DINO, and SigLIP 2 beat reconstruction-oriented VAE-style latents on planning, action recoverability, and policy evaluation, even when the reconstruction latents look better visually. That is exactly the kind of correction this literature needs.

**When to Trust Imagination** is a practical execution paper rather than a foundational one. The good part is that it uses the distinctive affordance of a WAM, predicted future observations, to decide when to keep executing a planned chunk and when to replan. The verifier is lightweight and apparently useful. The limitation is that this is still a patch around rollout reliability, not a deeper answer to memory, representation, or strategic planning.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **OA-WAM: Object-Addressable World Action Model for Robust Robot Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it replaces holistic future prediction with an explicitly addressable object-state interface and forces slot routing to depend on persistent identity vectors rather than drifting scene context.

### 2. **Reconstruction or Semantics? What Makes a Latent Space Useful for Robotic World Models**

**Verdict:** useful, with framing impact.

Why it matters: it makes a strong empirical case that semantic latent spaces are better for policy-relevant world modeling than reconstruction-first latents, which should affect how newer diffusion world-model papers are read and compared.

### 3. **When to Trust Imagination: Adaptive Action Execution for World Action Models**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent work.

Why it matters: it turns fixed action-chunk execution into a future-versus-reality verification problem and uses predicted world evolution for execution control, which is one of the more sensible ways to exploit WAM predictions at inference time.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** OA-WAM.

The reason is simple. It does not just say “object-centric” or “structured.” It makes the structure operational. Each slot is split into a persistent address vector and a changing content vector, and the transformer’s cross-slot key routing is forced to read only the address part while a per-layer reset prevents that address slice from drifting. So the model is trying to separate the question of which object is being targeted from the question of what that object currently looks like or what clutter surrounds it.

That is exactly the kind of distinction this area often handwaves and then fails to encode. If the method works as claimed, the useful idea is broader than this one benchmark family: give downstream control an interface to stable entities, not just a soup of future tokens. I also like that the paper includes a causal slot-intervention test rather than relying only on task success. A swap-binding cosine of 0.87 versus near-zero for holistic baselines is at least an attempt to show that the representation is doing the claimed routing work.

The caveat is important. I inspected the abstract, introduction, and substantial method text from the arXiv HTML, including the slot construction, address-only key projection, per-layer address reset, and the overall world-action architecture. I did not audit the entire appendix or every robustness table. So confidence is high on the mechanism and moderate on the full empirical story.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

OA-WAM raises the bar for papers that claim robustness from world modeling alone. If the real failure mode is target-object binding under perturbation, then holistic future prediction is not enough. A paper now has to say what interface lets action decoding reliably latch onto the right entity.

**Reconstruction or Semantics?** matters for baseline taste. If visual fidelity can look good while action recoverability, planning quality, and policy evaluation degrade, then image-quality metrics should stop being treated as primary evidence that a robotic world model is good. This is not glamorous, but it is corrective.

**When to Trust Imagination** mainly affects execution framing. It suggests that action chunk size in WAMs should be treated as a latent consistency question, not a single number chosen once. That is a useful operational idea, though still not a substitute for better representations.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today earns attention because it makes object structure do real computational work. **OA-WAM** builds a stable object-addressing interface into a world-action model instead of hoping holistic latents will somehow stay grounded under perturbation. **Reconstruction or Semantics?** is the strongest framing paper of the bunch, because it shows that policy-relevant world models want semantic latent spaces more than pretty reconstructions. **When to Trust Imagination** is a solid execution-side paper that uses imagined future observations to decide when to keep going and when to replan. The broad lesson is that world-model papers should be judged by whether their structure changes control-relevant computation, not by whether they have more future tokens and a nicer slogan.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-21

## Theme

The good papers today all refuse to confuse stored artifacts with live state. A memory system is not the same thing as the current world state it is supposed to preserve. A step-level credit score is not the same thing as causal contribution. A benchmark score is not the same thing as a real repository improvement unless integrity checks survive contact with the code. A compliant action filter is not the same thing as a workflow-level policy path. A monolithic predictive embedding is not the same thing as a structured latent state.

## Short overview

This Friday, August 21, 2026 run used arXiv HTML full-text inspection for all five ranked papers below. Four papers earn preserved notes. **Orthogonal JEPA** stays just below the preserve bar because the factorized predictive-state idea is real and useful, but the current evidence is still broad and cross-domain rather than anchored in one especially harsh planning or long-horizon setting. **Most relevant today:** **Can Agent Memory Systems Track Evolving State?**

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Can Agent Memory Systems Track Evolving State?**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the cleanest memory paper in the batch because it names the right target. Recall is not enough; the live problem is whether an agent can answer from the current state after earlier facts have been superseded. The paper builds **StateMemBench** with **234** multi-session scenarios and then shows a state-first memory design with explicit supersession and dependency tracking improves current-state accuracy from **0.205 -> 0.363** on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and from **0.149 -> 0.233** on Qwen-3.5-9B. The wrapper result is the sharp part: the same state structure lifts existing memory and retrieval backends by **+32 to +67** points, with a length- and cost-matched control attributing **+15 to +32** of that gain to state structure rather than extra context.

### 2. **Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the most severe evaluation paper in the batch because it stops grading credit signals against annotated step correctness and instead audits them against executed replay, meaning whether resampling the policy's own alternatives actually changes the outcome. Under that audit, the commonly used signals all collapse. Causal contribution is sparse at only **30.5%** of defined decision points, measurability differs sharply across policies (**13.1% vs. 26.8%** of points lack policy-supported counterfactuals), implicit credit mostly tracks fluency instead of causality (median rank correlation **+0.75**, replicated at **+0.70**), and outcome conditioning adds essentially no causal information (partial correlation **-0.004**). Even the training story gets punctured: no seven-arm training condition reliably beats the untrained policy once dose is matched.

### 3. **DeltaML-Bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Real-World Research Repositories**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This paper is strong because it makes autonomous ML experimentation pay the real repo tax instead of hiding inside toy harnesses. The benchmark uses **48** imperfect research repositories and asks agents to improve published baselines under compute budgets, with integrity checks explicitly built in so metric gains are not trusted by default. The scaffold result is large and concrete: under the **4 x 6h** allocation, ARG raises GPT-5 per-run success from **9.4%** to **33.9%**, and under **2 x 12h** it reaches **49.0%**. The more important systems result is negative: Modular configurations show specification gaming as high as **47.9%**, while the evaluated ARG setups show none.

### 4. **PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: Most compliance systems only swat down obviously bad actions. This paper does something better: compile domain policy into a workflow graph, persist graph state across turns, and use a proactive verifier that returns step-specific remediation before the agent drifts. On tau^2-bench airline, retail, and telecom tasks, mean **Pass^4** rises from **0.42** to **0.62**, with the biggest gain on the most workflow-shaped domain, telecom (**0.19 -> 0.61**). The transfer across GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 2.5 Pro is also a useful sign that the state machine is doing real work instead of just leaning on one model's prompt habits.

### 5. **Orthogonal JEPA: Factorized Predictive States for Latent World Models**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration, not yet preserve-worthy.

Why it matters: This is one of the better latent-world-model papers in the batch because it attacks a real representational problem rather than just changing branding. Instead of making one predictive embedding carry everything, it factorizes target state into learned orthogonal components, predicts each with its own branch, then synthesizes the full latent state back together. The mechanism is clean: learned basis matrices, orthogonality constraints, factor-activity regularization, and online variance regularization. It stays just below the preserve bar because the current read gives a broad multi-domain demonstration across vision, transcriptomics, health records, control, and molecular dynamics, but not yet one especially brutal long-horizon case that forces the factorization to prove its necessity.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **Can Agent Memory Systems Track Evolving State?**

It gets unusually close to the real failure mode. The useful move is not "more memory" but explicit handling of supersession and dependency so the system can keep the state that is still live rather than merely the state that was once said. The rest of the digest rhymes with that taste. **Credit Without Ground Truth** separates causal contribution from correctness proxies. **DeltaML-Bench** separates real improvement from scoreboard gaming. **PolicyGuide** separates policy-compliant workflow state from one-off action filtering. **Orthogonal JEPA** separates predictive factors instead of making one latent soak up everything.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**StateMem** matters because it turns state tracking into a separate benchmark axis rather than pretending recall scores already cover it.

**Credit Without Ground Truth** matters because it audits step credit against executed replay and forces training comparisons to control for dose rather than mystifying sparse credit signals.

**DeltaML-Bench** matters because it brings integrity verification and real repo heterogeneity into ML-agent evaluation instead of assuming a benchmark score is automatically a valid improvement.

**PolicyGuide** matters because it reframes policy compliance as a workflow-state problem, not merely a local action-guarding problem.

**Orthogonal JEPA** matters because it pushes latent world models toward explicit predictive factorization instead of monolithic target embeddings.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The August 21 lesson is that a system should be judged by whether it maintains and acts on the operative state, not by whether it stores a plausible proxy. StateMem keeps track of what is still active after revisions. Credit Without Ground Truth shows that fluent-looking credit signals do not track causal contribution. DeltaML-Bench shows that nominal improvements are not trustworthy without integrity checks inside messy real repositories. PolicyGuide shows that policy compliance requires a persistent workflow graph, not just local vetoes. Orthogonal JEPA argues that a predictive latent should expose separable factors instead of collapsing them into one undifferentiated state vector. Same rule all day: if the mechanism does not preserve the state that actually matters, the headline result is partly fake.

## Detailed notes

- [Credit audit note](../paper_notes/credit_without_ground_truth_auditing_step_level_credit_assignment_in_llm_agents_against_executed_replay.md)
- [DeltaML-Bench note](../paper_notes/deltaml_bench_evaluating_machine_learning_agents_on_real_world_research_repositories.md)
- [PolicyGuide note](../paper_notes/policyguide_from_guarding_one_action_to_guiding_the_whole_workflow_for_policy_compliant_llm_agents.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-11

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all attack the same lazy assumption: if the model saw the right context, then the right state must already be there. **SpecPath** says requirement history is not the active contract unless the agent resolves it explicitly. **Latent Dynamics Reasoning** says video prediction is not a world model unless the system models how the latent state evolves rather than just regressing frames. **MMDiff** says multimodal capability is not controllable unless the adapted features themselves become intervention targets. **MedPixel** says medical reasoning is not properly grounded unless the language path and the pixel path share a verifiable interface. **AMIE (Video)** says clinical competence is not text competence with a webcam attached; audio-visual evidence changes the task.

## Short overview

This run used the live Tuesday, August 11, 2026 arXiv batch, with explicit non-robotics passes across agent evaluation, interpretability/control, and medical/clinical lanes. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for all five ranked papers below.

Four papers earn preserved notes. **AMIE (Video)** is the strongest field-report runner-up: the evaluation is serious and the results are striking, but the preserve case is slightly weaker than the top four because the system details are less reusable and the evidence still depends on standardized patients rather than real deployment. **Most relevant today:** **SpecPath**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **SpecPath: Testing Coding Agents Across Contract-Equivalent Specification Histories**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It turns a vague complaint about agents getting confused by evolving requirements into a clean active-state problem. The useful move is to hold the repository, final contract, verifier, and budget fixed while varying only the path by which the contract is stated, then measure paired failures instead of average success.

### 2. **Learning How the World Evolves: Extrapolative Video World Models via Latent Dynamics Reasoning**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: It replaces "predict future frames" with explicit kinematic reasoning in a structured latent space. The useful move is to numerically integrate the lower-order dynamics and learn only the higher-order residual, which makes OOD extrapolation a real claim boundary instead of a slogan.

### 3. **Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It is one of the better recent multimodal interpretability papers because it makes feature discovery operational rather than decorative. The useful move is diffing a base-LM SAE against the multimodal-adapted model, then using task-specific contrastive firing to find causal features you can ablate or steer.

### 4. **MedPixel: A Unified Pixel-Language Model for Medical Reasoning and Segmentation**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It connects medical reasoning and dense grounding through a shared interface, then uses mask quality as an offline verifier for preference optimization. The useful move is not just unifying task formats, but aligning generated reasoning with actual pixel outcomes.

### 5. **Towards Expert-level Medical AI for Real-time Video Consultations**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: It is a serious multimodal clinical systems paper rather than a toy demo. The useful move is the asynchronous talker-planner-perception split plus a randomized video-OSCE evaluation against PCPs, but the preserve case is tempered by standardized-patient scope and less transferable underlying mechanism.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **SpecPath**.

This is the sharpest paper in the batch because it isolates a failure cabbageland should care about immediately: append-only conversational history is not the same thing as active state. The paper's central move, active-contract resolution, is exactly the kind of explicit-state framing that agent work keeps needing and evaluation keeps dodging. Aggregate accuracy barely changes across equivalent histories, but paired block analysis shows that more than a third of direct-success cases fail somewhere else once the same contract is expressed through revision history. That is a much better failure boundary than generic "long context" talk. It tells you what the agent must resolve before implementation even begins.

The rest of the batch reinforces the same broader taste. **LDR** makes latent dynamics explicit instead of hiding them inside frame regression. **MMDiff** treats multimodal capabilities as feature-level objects that can be isolated and intervened on. **MedPixel** turns medical grounding into a shared language-mask interface and uses pixel outcomes as real supervision for reasoning alignment. **AMIE (Video)** shows that clinically relevant perception is not just text chat with extra tokens.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**SpecPath** is strongest because it finds the right evaluation unit. Direct FCR is **78.8%** and the mean over alternate histories is **78.7%**, so a standard leaderboard would call the system stable. But among **100** complete blocks that succeed on the direct specification, **35** fail on at least one contract-equivalent history, giving a **36.4%** task-macro any-CPV estimate. That is the important framing result: average success hides state-resolution failures because it destroys the pairing.

**Latent Dynamics Reasoning** is strongest because it makes extrapolation the main object rather than an accidental byproduct. At **256^2**, LDR cuts the ID-OOD gap in position error by **23.9x** under single-task training and **27.7x** under joint five-task training. Under joint training, the DiT-S baseline jumps from **0.086** ID error to **0.592** OOD error, while LDR moves only from **0.050** to **0.068**. It also does this with **4.1M** parameters instead of **106.1M** and runs **143x** faster at **256^2**.

**MMDiff** is strongest because it makes multimodal SAEs do causal work instead of just post-hoc labeling work. Ablating top spatial features drops VSR by roughly **10-15%** on average with almost no VQA spillover. On multimodal safety, top unsafe features cut attack success rate by **17-28%** per category, and across **1,061** candidate safety features the mean effect is **-9.67%** ASR with essentially zero VQA loss. On OCR, top-feature ablation gives a **-16.9%** mean category drop with low spillover, and MMDiff-CAA steering improves spatial and OCR over vanilla CAA by **+3.6%** and **+1.8%** on average.

**MedPixel** is strongest because it uses the right verifier. MedPLG-440K repurposes segmentation masks into roughly **440K** pixel-language training samples, and PLPO turns ground-truth mask quality into offline response preferences. The result is not just a broader prompt interface. MedPixel-7B beats strong baselines by **29.2 Dice** on reasoning segmentation and **40.7 Dice** on explanatory segmentation, reaches **76.0 Dice** on the interactive setting, improves zero-shot MeCoVQA-G+ slice Dice by **5.3** over BiomedParse, and stays stable under imperfect box prompts. The catch is also useful: the language is still template-derived and the setup remains mostly 2D and single-turn.

**AMIE (Video)** is strongest as a field-report runner-up because the evaluation is serious and multimodal. In a randomized OSCE with **100** scenarios, AMIE (Video) gets an **83%** overall case-rubric score versus **68%** for PCPs, **91%** top-1 diagnostic accuracy versus **77%**, and much stronger use of live video for physical observation and guided exam maneuvers. But it is still a standardized-patient study, not real clinical deployment, and the paper itself is upfront that fine anatomical precision, affective nuance, and continuous turn-taking remain weak points.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that performance only becomes trustworthy when the operative state stops hiding in the margins. Requirement history has to be resolved into an active contract. Video prediction has to separate dynamics from appearance regression. Multimodal behavior has to become feature-addressable instead of just score-improvable. Medical reasoning has to ground itself in the pixels it claims to interpret. Even impressive clinical dialogue has to handle audio-visual evidence as something structurally different from text. The good papers are the ones that stop pretending more context is the same thing as better state.

## Detailed notes

- [LDR note](../paper_notes/latent_dynamics_reasoning_extrapolative_video_world_models.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-27

## Theme

Today’s strongest pattern is **structure that actually constrains reuse**, not structure as branding. The best direct paper is **SMoDP** because it tries to make expert routing respect semantically meaningful manipulation phases instead of letting sparse routing fragment similar behaviors arbitrarily. The most useful framing paper is **Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?** because it forces a basic but easy-to-ignore point: sequential real-world adaptation can collapse badly, and some reported continual-learning competence depends on implementation details that earlier setups made too easy. I also considered **Unified 3D Scene Understanding Through Physical World Modeling**, but only had abstract-level access in this environment, so I am not preserving it today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was unavailable in this environment because no Brave Search tool is configured for this run. AlphaXiv was also not available as a live tool surface here, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv API results, direct arXiv pages, and arXiv HTML when available.

I inspected full arXiv HTML for **Semantically Structured Mixture-of-Experts for Compositional Robotic Manipulation** and **Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?** Confidence is good on the main mechanism and headline evaluation story for both papers, and weaker on appendix-level hyperparameters and every implementation detail.

**SMoDP** is the most relevant paper today. Its core claim is that mixture-of-experts routing for manipulation should not be driven only by low-level latent statistics or diffusion noise level, because that tends to split semantically similar behaviors across different experts. The paper uses offline VLM-produced verb-noun skill labels, trains a lightweight skill predictor, and routes action chunks according to predicted skill phase. I like the underlying instinct: if expert modularity is supposed to help compositional reuse, then the routing interface should expose reusable behavioral structure instead of hoping the experts discover it accidentally. The main caveat is that the semantic structure is partly scaffolded by a VLM annotation pipeline, so some of the cleanliness comes from extra supervision rather than from a naturally emerging modular policy.

**Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?** is less architecturally exciting, but more important than it looks. The paper builds a four-task real-world sequential manipulation stream and shows that naive sequential fine-tuning of a π0.5-style policy catastrophically forgets earlier tasks. More interestingly, it argues that modest replay can help a lot, but only if practical details like replay frequency and action normalization are handled carefully. This is exactly the kind of paper that should affect how later continual-learning claims are read. If a method says it resists forgetting, the first question should now be whether it was tested in a heterogeneous real-world stream and whether the training protocol avoided future-information leakage.

I also briefly checked **Unified 3D Scene Understanding Through Physical World Modeling**. The abstract sounds potentially relevant because it frames multiple 3D tasks as inference paths through a shared probabilistic world model. But arXiv HTML was unavailable for that paper in this environment, and I did not do a deeper PDF audit today, so I am treating it as a possible follow-up rather than a preserved note.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Semantically Structured Mixture-of-Experts for Compositional Robotic Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it makes a clean demand on modularity. If experts are supposed to be reusable, routing should reflect reusable skill structure rather than arbitrary latent partitioning.

### 2. **Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?**

**Verdict:** useful and framing-important.

Why it matters: it raises the bar for continual VLA evaluation by moving the question into a heterogeneous real-world setting and showing that implementation details can dominate the outcome.

### 3. **Unified 3D Scene Understanding Through Physical World Modeling**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration, but not preserved today.

Why it matters: the framing is attractive, but today’s inspection stayed at abstract level only, so confidence is too low for a canonical note.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** SMoDP.

The useful part is not “mixture of experts” by itself. Plenty of MoE papers just add sparse routing and call the resulting fragmentation modularity. SMoDP at least tries to define what the reusable unit is supposed to be: a semantically meaningful manipulation phase, represented as a skill-like verb-noun chunk. That is closer to the right question for compositional control.

This matters for cabbageland because it sharpens a standard suspicion: pseudo-modularity often appears when the decomposition does not touch the interface where reuse decisions happen. Here the interface is routing. The paper’s answer is not fully satisfying, because VLM-generated skill labels do a lot of the structuring work, but it is still much better than pretending low-level routing statistics alone will recover human-legible behavior phases.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**SMoDP** is useful mainly as a challenge to lazy MoE framing in robotics. After this paper, it feels weaker to claim compositionality from sparse activation alone if the routing mechanism has no explicit notion of behavioral phase or skill compatibility.

The continual-learning paper has stronger baseline impact than novelty glamour. It says that real-world sequential VLA learning is brittle enough that protocol details, especially replay scheduling and action normalization, can decide whether the whole setup looks viable or hopeless. That should make future forgetting papers easier to interrogate.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **SMoDP** because it pushes modularity down to the routing decision instead of merely scaling an MoE policy and hoping experts self-organize into reusable skills. The most practically important paper is **Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?** because it shows that continual VLA learning in the real world is still fragile, and that small implementation decisions can dominate the conclusion. The shared lesson is that explicit structure matters most when it changes the actual computational bottleneck, either which expert gets activated or whether previously learned skills survive sequential updates at all.

## Detailed notes

- [SMoDP note](../paper_notes/semantically_structured_mixture_of_experts_for_compositional_robotic_manipulation.md)
- [Continual VLA forgetting note](../paper_notes/can_vla_models_learn_from_real_world_data_continually_without_forgetting.md)
