# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-20

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **make the hidden mechanism carry the claim**. The best papers I found do not just add a name to a latent, a judge, or a symbolic layer. They make a specific internal object do work: an action-recoverable latent state, a single-world counterfactual program, or an evaluation protocol that rejects fake preference signal.

I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered latent world models, neurosymbolic counterfactual inference, continual-learning mechanism analysis, radiology grounding, 3D generative evaluation, video-diffusion reward modeling, and embodied/surgical world models. No robotics/VLA paper landed in the top three today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable for individual paper pages and useful for metadata/title checks, but the pages I inspected mostly exposed abstracts, metadata, and empty comments/resources rather than useful related-paper trails. I used AlphaXiv as a supplement, then relied on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs for primary-source inspection. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

There was no fresh Saturday arXiv batch, so the strongest available set came from the June 18 uploads. I avoided simply reusing yesterday's already-preserved top papers. Full-text PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for **Sensorimotor World Models**, **DeepSWIP**, **Judging to Improve**, **Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting**, **Scalable Training of Spatially Grounded 2D VLMs for Radiology**, **Through the PRISM**, **UNIEGO**, **Marginal Advantage Accumulation**, **SurgVista**, and **Holo-World**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Sensorimotor World Models: Perception for Action via Inverse Dynamics** is the most relevant paper today. It adds a single inverse-dynamics head to a JEPA-style latent world model and lets action recoverability prevent collapse. The useful part is not just "inverse dynamics helps"; it is that the latent state is pushed toward controllable degrees of freedom and away from uncontrollable distractors.

**DeepSWIP** is the strongest neurosymbolic paper in the scan. It materializes fixed-context neural predicates into ordinary ProbLog choices, applies a single-world intervention program, and computes counterfactuals as a quotient of weighted model counts. The paper is unusually clear about the boundary: exact symbolic counterfactual inference is still only exact relative to the learned, calibrated neural probabilities.

**Judging to Improve** is the most useful evaluation/protocol paper today. Its headline result is negative: lightweight public-data adaptation of TRELLIS reaches parity with a strong base, not a win. The part worth preserving is the hardened VLM-as-3D-judge protocol: separate training and evaluation judge families, swap-consistency position-bias filtering, normal-map mesh montages, and clear-gap sanity checks.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. **Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting** gives a controlled toy-world diagnostic for continual learning; I liked the low-representation/high-overlap vulnerability story, but the paper is deliberately synthetic and should be treated as hypothesis generation. **RadGrounder** is a solid healthcare grounding paper with a 1.2M CT/MRI slice corpus and tokenized bounding-box grounding, but the labels are anatomical rather than pathology-level and come from one hospital. **Through the PRISM** is a good video-diffusion reward-modeling paper, using frozen diffusion-backbone intermediate states as noisy-latent preference features, but its claims are closer to reward-model engineering than a new general mechanism.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Sensorimotor World Models: Perception for Action via Inverse Dynamics**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it turns "latent world state" into an action-sufficient representation. If the transition latent pair cannot recover the action, the representation is free to collapse or preserve the wrong details; if it can, the encoder has pressure to keep controllable state.

### 2. **DeepSWIP: Quotient-WMC Counterfactuals for Neural Probabilistic Logic Programs**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as a neurosymbolic causal-inference mechanism.

Why it matters: it separates perception uncertainty from symbolic counterfactual inference. That is exactly the boundary cabbageland should care about when neural modules feed structured reasoning.

### 3. **Judging to Improve: A De-biased VLM-as-3D-Judge Protocol for Single-Image 3D Generation**

**Verdict:** useful and adjacent, with a strong protocol contribution.

Why it matters: it shows how easy it is for a VLM judge to become a position-answering or render-artifact detector, and it gives practical checks before trusting a model-in-the-loop preference signal.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Sensorimotor World Models.

The steal is the inverse objective as a representation audit. A world state should not be judged only by whether a forward predictor can map it to the next latent. It should preserve enough transition structure that the action is identifiable from the before/after embeddings. That pressure is simple, local, and more semantically grounded than forcing the embedding distribution to look Gaussian.

DeepSWIP contributes the complementary symbolic boundary. Let the neural part estimate uncertain predicates; then freeze those probabilities into symbolic choices before intervention surgery. The quotient-WMC view makes it obvious which neural probabilities are active, which ones are cleaned away by intervention, and where calibration errors get amplified.

Judging to Improve contributes the evaluation hygiene. If a judge cannot survive swap-consistency checks, clear-gap calibration, and rendering choices that expose the real geometry, it is not a reliable optimization signal. Preference data is not automatically present just because two samples exist.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Sensorimotor World Models** raises the bar for latent world-model papers that claim controllable representation learning. The key baseline is SIGReg-style distributional regularization: SMWM matches it on 2D tasks and beats it on OGBench-Cube in the reported planning setup, while using inverse dynamics as the only anti-collapse mechanism. The caveat is scope: moderate-scale simulated control tasks, single-frame latents, and an assumption that actions are recoverable from consecutive observations.

**DeepSWIP** is valuable because it refuses to blur exactness. The SWIP/WMC transformation is exact relative to a learned materialized FCM; if the neural predicate is miscalibrated, the system can be exactly wrong about the outside world. That distinction is the whole lesson.

**Judging to Improve** is useful because the negative result is localized. Clean inputs are judge-saturated, flow-DIT LoRA updates wash out through the sampler, and DINOv2 conditioner repair is the only intervention that moves outputs, reaching parity under severe degradation. The main limitation is sample size: final held-out win rates use eight objects, so the result is directional rather than definitive.

**Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting** is the important runner-up for continual learning. It suggests overlap is not automatically forgetting; weak representations under high overlap are the fragile regime. The limitation is that this is a synthetic generator-separator world, not a real CL benchmark.

**RadGrounder** is a good healthcare reminder: spatial verification matters for clinical VLMs, and tokenized box grounding can be cheaper than an auxiliary mask head. The red flag is that anatomical grounding is still not lesion-level clinical grounding.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all make a hidden layer accountable. **Sensorimotor World Models** asks latent state to recover the action that caused a transition. **DeepSWIP** turns neural predicate uncertainty into explicit probabilistic choices before doing counterfactual surgery. **Judging to Improve** refuses to optimize against a judge until the judge survives presentation, rendering, and clear-gap controls. Different domains, same standard: if a latent, symbol, or evaluator is carrying the claim, expose the exact job it must perform and test that job directly.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-31

## Theme

Today's best papers are all about unit mismatch. **AskChem** says a paper is not the right retrieval object when the user actually needs a provenance-carrying claim. **Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache** says identical tokens are not the same thing as the decoder state that produced them. **Change2Task** says a historical PR is not yet an executable modern coding-agent task. **Negative controls reveal volume-driven confounding** says a predictive imaging signature is not yet biological signal. **KAISEN** says a mean fairness intervention effect is not the same thing as a dependable audit instrument.

## Short overview

I attempted Brave Search first through the OpenClaw `web_search` tool on Friday, July 31, 2026, and it failed with `missing_brave_api_key`, specifically saying Brave search needs a configured API key. Discovery therefore fell back to direct arXiv recent-category inspection, targeted arXiv API title passes, and full-text reading through arXiv PDFs.

This run did the explicit non-robotics pass the repo asks for. That surfaced papers such as **OSReward**, **A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports**, **ReToken**, **PhiZero**, and **ACE-Data-0**. Some were respectable, but the five below were stronger on mechanism, evaluation hygiene, and transferable systems lessons. The top four are preserve-worthy note candidates. **KAISEN** is useful and unusually honest about audit failure modes, but I do not think it beats the top four on direct steal value.

**Most relevant today:** **AskChem: Claim-Centered Infrastructure for Chemistry Literature Synthesis**. The steal is not chemistry-specific. If the thing a human or agent needs is a verified claim with provenance, do not keep forcing retrieval through paper-shaped objects and then pretending the post-processing pain is someone else's problem.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **AskChem: Claim-Centered Infrastructure for Chemistry Literature Synthesis**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is the cleanest systems paper of the day because it changes the unit of retrieval to match the actual task. A paper list is too blunt when the user needs a grounded cross-paper answer with traceable evidence.

### 2. **Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache: Fixed-Prefix Precision Controls and Bidirectional Cache Transplantation**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It is a sharp reminder that exact token replay is not state replay. The practical consequence is severe for interpretability, replay diagnostics, and any workflow that treats reconstructed prefixes as if they were live decoder state.

### 3. **Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: This attacks a real bottleneck for coding agents: task supply. The useful move is to reconstruct developer-grounded tasks on healthy modern revisions instead of treating historical snapshots and modern environments as separate worlds.

### 4. **Negative controls reveal volume-driven confounding in radiomics and imaging foundation model features**

**Verdict:** highly relevant adjacent paper.

Why it matters: This is exactly the kind of quality-control paper more fields need. It asks whether the supposed signal survives when spatial structure is destroyed but volume is preserved, and often the answer is embarrassingly yes.

### 5. **KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models**

**Verdict:** useful direct runner-up.

Why it matters: The paper is strongest where it treats the audit as an instrument that can fail quietly. Its best lesson is that the variance of a mitigation's fairness effect can matter more than its mean, and that drift thresholds tuned on one cohort can fail badly on another.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** AskChem: Claim-Centered Infrastructure for Chemistry Literature Synthesis.

The reason is simple. Cabbageland keeps running into cases where the thing we want is not a document, a webpage, or a note title. It is a specific claim, with source, evidence, and relations to neighboring claims. AskChem makes that object explicit instead of forcing humans or agents to reconstruct it after retrieval. The same claim identities then flow through web UI, REST, SDK, and MCP access, which is exactly the right systems instinct.

The rest of the digest strengthens the same discipline from other angles. **Stage-Replay Divergence** says token identity is not state identity. **Change2Task** says PR history is not yet executable task data unless the lifecycle on a maintained base actually closes. **Negative controls reveal volume-driven confounding** says prediction is not evidence of meaningful structure if the score survives when you destroy the relevant spatial information. **KAISEN** says an audit report is not trustworthy just because it prints a number; the instrument itself needs failure analysis.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**AskChem** is strongest because it changes the central retrieval object from document to provenance-carrying claim. The important baseline lesson is that ranked-paper interfaces are structurally mismatched to cross-paper synthesis and agent tooling.

**Stage-Replay Divergence** is strongest because it isolates four different questions people too often collapse together: replica stability, token identity, live-state fidelity, and causal state sufficiency. The useful result is not an accuracy gain. It is the cleaner measurement rule.

**Change2Task** is strongest because it reframes executable coding-agent data as something that can be recovered from repository lineage on healthy modern bases, rather than something tied forever to old snapshots or freshly synthesized failures.

**Negative controls reveal volume-driven confounding** is strongest because it changes what a predictive radiomics signature is allowed to mean. If the score survives structured destruction of spatial signal, the field should stop narrating it as biologically meaningful texture.

**KAISEN** is strongest as an audit-discipline paper rather than as a clinical model paper. The useful framing is that mitigation averages and drift thresholds are not self-explanatory; you need the run-level distribution and the cohort sensitivity too.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that the object you manipulate should match the claim you want to make. Papers are not claims. Token prefixes are not decoder state. Historical PRs are not executable modern tasks. Predictive imaging signatures are not necessarily biological signal. Mean fairness improvements are not reliable audit behavior. The papers worth keeping are the ones that replace proxy comfort with object-level checks: claim provenance, retained live state, lifecycle validation on a maintained base, negative controls that preserve the confound while destroying the story, and audit stress tests that show how the instrument breaks.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-05

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **make recovery and search compositional instead of hoping the first trajectory is right**. DecompRL turns hard code generation into decomposed module search plus cheap recombination. VRRL trains vision-language models to recover from bad visual-feedback states, not just to emit a reflective-looking trace. DriftLens measures how persistent user memory changes the reasoning path even when the final answer still sounds reasonable. RDM makes one-step visual generation a multi-representation distribution-matching problem rather than a single gamable feature score. Self-auditing MRI reconstruction pairs the generated image with explicit error maps and slice-level risk.

I kept robotics and VLA work out of the ranked five today. I did inspect the robotics lane, including VT-WAM, Embodied.cpp, TAP for VLAs, WorldSample, and ACID from the recent arXiv batch. Several were competent, but none cleared the higher bar set by the non-robotics papers below. The scan also covered medical imaging, RAG verification, object-centric representation learning, uncertainty-aware LoRA calibration, long-term agent memory, model-card style foundation reports, 3D / generative media, and agent safety.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv, arXiv recent pages, direct arXiv pages, and arXiv HTML were reachable and used for discovery and inspection. Discovery quality is therefore narrower than a healthy Brave-first run, but the preserved notes below are not abstract-only.

No preserved note today is abstract-only. I inspected full arXiv HTML for **DecompRL**, **Visually Grounded Self-Reflection via Reinforcement Learning**, **DriftLens**, and **Representation Distribution Matching**, including the method, main result sections, and limitations or caveats where available. I also inspected the full arXiv HTML for **Self-Auditing Residual Drifting for accelerated knee MRI**, **CheckRLM**, **Object-centric LeJEPA**, and **Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation** as runner-up candidates. I did not audit every appendix, proof, or code artifact.

**DecompRL** is the most directly useful paper today. It turns code generation into a modular search problem where the expensive part is generating a small set of subfunction implementations and the cheap part is recombining and testing them.

**VRRL** is the strongest multimodal learning paper today. Its useful point is that visual self-reflection has to be trained on recovery states; prompting a VLM to "reflect" mostly teaches a costume.

**DriftLens** is the sharpest evaluation paper. It treats personalized memory as a perturbation that can move the reasoning trajectory even when no objective answer exists and no obvious final-answer failure is visible.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **DecompRL: Solving Harder Problems by Learning Modular Code Generation**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most reusable mechanism today.

Why it matters: DecompRL attacks the cold-start failure of pass@k and ordinary RL. If the base model has near-zero probability of writing a correct monolithic solution, sampling more whole programs is wasteful. DecompRL trains a decomposition policy and an implementation policy, then recombines module candidates into many full programs. The best idea is the cost shift: spend GPU tokens on modules, then spend CPU on verification over combinations.

### 2. **Visually Grounded Self-Reflection for Vision-Language Models via Reinforcement Learning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for multimodal agents and visual feedback loops.

Why it matters: VRRL separates reflective behavior from reflective text. The model receives visual feedback from prior predictions, then is trained with random turn masking and buffered roll-ins so it learns to recover from bad intermediate states. This is a clean pattern for any agent that acts, sees the result, and has to repair its trajectory under distribution shift.

### 3. **DriftLens: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant evaluation infrastructure.

Why it matters: persistent memory is not a neutral retrieval feature. DriftLens asks whether irrelevant user-attribute memories change the model's value-labeled reasoning trajectory on persona-indifferent questions. Across four models and ten user-attribute categories, the paper reports medium-to-large drift above pragmatic-noise baselines, with final answers often still plausible. That is exactly the kind of hidden failure long-lived assistants need to measure.

### 4. **Representation Distribution Matching for One-Step Visual Generation**

**Verdict:** strong generative-media mechanism, preserve-worthy as architecture taste.

Why it matters: the paper reframes one-step image generation as direct matching between generated and reference feature distributions under frozen encoders. The useful part is not just "MMD works now." It is the design discipline: use a full frozen reference, large generated batches, joint image-text matching for conditional generation, and a balanced multi-encoder objective because single encoders can be gamed.

### 5. **Self-Auditing Residual Drifting for Pathology-Preserving Accelerated Knee MRI**

**Verdict:** useful clinical reliability paper, lighter recommendation today.

Why it matters: the attractive piece is integrated self-auditing. SA-RDM-DC reconstructs accelerated knee MRI while also emitting dense error maps, quantile maps, and slice-level risk scores in the same pass. The medical lesson transfers well: if a model produces a high-stakes reconstruction, the output should carry a local reliability signal, not just a global SSIM score.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** DecompRL.

The steal is the modular-search interface. A lot of hard agent work is verifier-rich but generation-expensive: code repair, tool-plan synthesis, workflow automation, browser action scripts, data-cleaning pipelines, structured extraction, even paper-note drafting under schema constraints. DecompRL's claim is that when a problem can be decomposed into independently testable pieces, the agent should not burn frontier-model calls on full-solution retries. It should generate a small set of modules, recombine them, and let cheap validators search the product space.

VRRL gives the same lesson for perception-action loops: train recovery, not just first-pass correctness. DriftLens gives it for memory: measure the trajectory shift, not just answer fluency. RDM gives it for generation: use multiple independent representation checks because one metric becomes a target. Self-auditing MRI gives it for clinical deployment: pair outputs with case-specific reliability estimates.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**DecompRL** is strong because it changes the scaling axis. A decomposition with `n` functions and `k` implementations per function costs roughly `n*k + 1` model generations but yields up to `k^n` candidate programs for CPU-side evaluation. On LiveCodeBench with Qwen 2.5 7B, the reported solve rate at 500K tokens is 0.48 versus 0.46 for the strongest listed high-pass baseline and 0.44 for GRPO. More importantly, the cost table claims about 4K generated tokens for 512 recombined evaluations versus about 198K tokens for standard sampling, shifting the bottleneck from GPU generation to CPU execution. The caveat is real: decomposition has a format tax and underperforms on easier or low-budget problems.

**VRRL** is strong because the training intervention matches the failure. Prompting and ordinary multi-turn traces often repeat the same bad visual guess. VRRL masks prefix losses so training emphasizes suffix recovery, and it starts new rollouts from buffered historical mistake prefixes. On visual grounding, Qwen2.5-VL-7B VRRL reports 78.4 OOD average versus 73.2 for multi-turn GRPO; on spatial navigation, Qwen3-VL-4B VRRL reports 52.2 OOD average versus 40.8 for Multi-SFT and 38.4 for reflection tuning. The caveat is that the tasks are synthetic visual-feedback environments; the mechanism is good, but real-world visual action spaces will be messier.

**DriftLens** is strong because it does not need ground-truth answers to catch a memory failure. It maps reasoning steps into a value ontology and compares no-memory versus memory-perturbed trajectories using DTW and SRI. The paper validates the instrument with pragmatic-noise negative controls and major-life-event positive controls, then reports persona-memory drift across Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-4B, and DeepSeek-R1. Qwen3-4B and Claude show SRI effect sizes in the roughly 0.75-0.98 and 0.77-0.90 ranges, respectively. The caveat is that the method measures expressed reasoning, not hidden cognition, and ontology labeling is itself a model-mediated instrument.

**RDM** is strong because it treats metric gaming as a first-class design constraint. The paper shows that single feature spaces can be overfit: a generator can score below real on a training encoder while images still look fake. iRDM uses large generated batches, a frozen Nystrom reference, joint image-text distribution matching for conditional generation, and a proportional controller over a battery of encoders. It reports one-step ImageNet `SW_r14` of 1.30 versus a previous one-step best around 2.05, plus FLUX.2 one-step post-training that beats the four-step base on GenEval, 0.826 versus 0.794, and PickScore, 22.76 versus 22.58. The caveat is compute and reference curation: 90 H200 GPU-hours and a curated teacher-generation reference are not casual.

**Self-Auditing MRI** is useful because its evaluation is not only global reconstruction fidelity. SA-RDM-DC reports best SSIM at acceleration factors 4, 8, and 12, subsecond per-slice inference, ROI SSIM gains in pathology regions, and high-error AUROC values near 0.997, 0.986, and 0.986 across accelerations. The caveat is domain specificity and validation scale: promising selective-review signals still need prospective clinical validation and stronger protocol-shift tests.

**CheckRLM** was a strong runner-up. It extracts factual claims during reasoning and performs localized retrieval-backed corrections before errors propagate. I did not preserve it today because the method depends on a separate large recognition/correction stack and is closer to RAG control engineering than the top four mechanisms, but it is worth revisiting for tool-using agents.

**Object-centric LeJEPA** was another strong runner-up. It uses SAM masks to align object-level LeJEPA representations and adds an instance-separating loss. It is a clean representation-learning paper, but I already surfaced it yesterday and today's top five had broader agent and deployment transfer.

**Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation** was the uncertainty runner-up. Rank-level stochastic masking for LoRA calibration is neat, but the evidence is narrower than DriftLens, DecompRL, VRRL, and RDM.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all punish first-trajectory optimism. DecompRL says hard code generation should search recombinable modules. VRRL says visual agents must train on recovery states. DriftLens says personalized memory can bend reasoning in ways answer-level metrics miss. RDM says one-step generators need multiple representation checks because a single metric becomes a loophole. Self-auditing MRI says high-stakes outputs should carry local reliability estimates. The shared lesson is clean: when a system can fail through its intermediate path, the path itself needs structure, supervision, and verification.

## Detailed notes

- [DecompRL note](../paper_notes/decomprl_modular_code_generation_recombination.md)
- [VRRL note](../paper_notes/vrrl_visually_grounded_self_reflection_vlm.md)
- [DriftLens note](../paper_notes/driftlens_memory_induced_reasoning_drift.md)
- [Representation Distribution Matching note](../paper_notes/representation_distribution_matching_one_step_visual_generation.md)

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-06

## Theme
Today’s real pattern is not generic “planning,” it is **trying to make foresight structurally usable instead of decorative**. The best paper is **DIAL**, because it puts a hard latent intent bottleneck between semantic reasoning and motor execution instead of letting a VLM dissolve into yet another oversized action encoder. **Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models** is also strong, though in a different way: it does not invent a new world-model backbone so much as it shows that multi-timescale latent planning can rescue long-horizon zero-shot control when flat MPC collapses. **CLaD** is the most mixed case. It has a legitimate mechanism — cross-modal transition modeling between proprioception and semantics — but it is also the most at risk of sounding deeper than it is.

Brave Search was checked first in this run and was unavailable because the Brave API key is missing in this environment, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv listings plus direct inspection of arXiv abstract and HTML paper text.

## Short overview
The clearest hit is **DIAL: Decoupling Intent and Action via Latent World Modeling for End-to-End VLA**. The paper’s diagnosis is correct: many end-to-end VLAs say they preserve high-level reasoning, but in practice they fine-tune a VLM under low-level action loss until the semantics get dragged into motor soup. DIAL’s fix is to make the VLM predict a future visual latent in its own feature space and force the action policy to treat that latent as the intent bottleneck. That is much healthier than loosely attaching a world-model loss and hoping the policy does not learn shortcuts.

Second is **Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models**. The idea is simple but actually useful: keep world-model planning in latent space, but split it across temporal scales so a high-level planner searches over macro-actions and produces latent subgoals for a low-level planner. This is not a flashy new representation paper. It is a planning abstraction paper. The value is that it appears to transfer across several latent world-model families and makes non-greedy tasks tractable without pretending flat MPC will somehow become reliable at long horizons.

Third is **CLaD: Planning with Grounded Foresight via Cross-Modal Latent Dynamics**. The good part is the shift from aligning static semantic and proprioceptive states to aligning their transitions under action. That is a more defensible place to impose cross-modal structure. The weaker part is that the paper still leans on self-supervised latent machinery and benchmark success in ways that make it harder to tell how much of the gain comes from the specific cross-modal mechanism versus just having a decent latent-foresight-conditioned diffusion policy.

I also inspected **Open-Loop Planning, Closed-Loop Verification: Speculative Verification for VLA**. It did not clear the preservation bar for a full note today. The core idea — cheap online verification of chunked plans — is reasonable, but the paper feels more like a pragmatic systems patch than a conceptually important research move.

## Ranked papers

1. **DIAL: Decoupling Intent and Action via Latent World Modeling for End-to-End VLA**
   - Verdict: **Highly relevant**
   - Role: **Directly relevant**
   - Why it matters: It imposes a real structural separation between high-level intent formation and low-level action decoding while keeping the whole stack differentiable.

2. **Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models**
   - Verdict: **Highly relevant**
   - Role: **Directly relevant**
   - Why it matters: It shows that temporal hierarchy can be added at planning time, not only policy-learning time, and that this materially helps long-horizon zero-shot control.

3. **CLaD: Planning with Grounded Foresight via Cross-Modal Latent Dynamics**
   - Verdict: **Useful**
   - Role: **Adjacent inspiration**
   - Why it matters: It treats semantic and proprioceptive transitions as coupled objects and predicts grounded latent foresights from that joint dynamics signal.

## Most relevant to cabbageland
**DIAL** is the most relevant paper today. The important move is not just “use latent foresight.” Lots of recent papers already decorate policies with predictive latents. The important move is that DIAL makes the predicted latent future the interface between cognition and control. If the downstream policy must infer actions by comparing current state to predicted latent intent, then the architecture has at least some chance of preserving an explicit computational role for the higher-level model instead of quietly demoting it into a feature extractor.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact
- **Hard bottlenecks beat auxiliary vibes:** DIAL’s strongest contribution is architectural discipline. It does not merely add a predictive loss; it makes execution depend on the predicted intent representation.
- **Hierarchy can live in the planner, not only the policy:** HWM matters because it shows a way to get long-horizon competence from pretrained latent world models without needing skills, options, inverse models, or reward-shaped hierarchical RL.
- **Transition-level cross-modal structure is more honest than state-level alignment:** CLaD’s central framing is good. If semantics and kinematics are coupled by action, then matching transitions is more meaningful than just aligning per-timestep embeddings.
- **But not every foresight paper earns the same confidence:** DIAL and HWM feel mechanically necessary. CLaD feels plausible, but I am less certain the specific asymmetry and latent training recipe are doing all the conceptual work the paper claims.
- **Baseline implications:** DIAL is a useful counterargument to VLA designs that call themselves dual-system but still let the action head freeload on fused features. HWM is a useful counterargument to the assumption that world-model failures on long-horizon tasks require a new backbone rather than a better planning decomposition.
- **Truthfulness / access note:** I directly inspected arXiv abstract pages and substantial arXiv HTML text for DIAL, HWM, CLaD, and SV-VLA. Confidence is strongest on problem framing, architecture, and visible losses; weaker on appendix-only ablations, exact training details omitted from the accessible sections, and the robustness of reported margins across seeds.

## One-paragraph takeaway
The useful lesson today is that foresight only matters when it changes the computation. **DIAL** is the strongest paper because it makes latent future prediction the actual bridge between semantic reasoning and action generation. **Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models** is strong for a related reason: it uses temporal abstraction to change how planning is done, not just how results are narrated. **CLaD** is worth keeping as an adjacent reference because it tries to ground latent prediction in cross-modal transition structure rather than static embedding alignment, but it is the least settled of the three. Overall, today’s better papers are the ones that replace loose auxiliary objectives with interfaces, bottlenecks, or decompositions that the policy is forced to respect.

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-14

## Theme

Today’s strongest papers are all trying, in different ways, to stop robot planning and control from depending on latent wishful thinking. The best one moves world-model planning into a vision-language retrieval space so actions can be scored against language instead of a pre-specified goal image. The next best paper adds an explicit spatial value interface between future prediction and action decoding, which is healthier than pretending RGB futures alone contain usable control intent. The smallest but still worthwhile paper keeps a persistent SE(3) anchor through occlusion, which is exactly the kind of explicit memory interface most reactive policies still lack.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv inspection via the arXiv API plus direct reading of arXiv abstract, HTML, and extracted PDF text for shortlisted papers. I inspected the primary-source text for the three ranked papers, including method and result sections from extracted PDFs, but I did not do a full appendix audit for every candidate. So this is careful triage, not theatrical certainty.

The strongest paper is **Grounded World Model for Semantically Generalizable Planning**. Its core move is simple and useful: instead of doing model-predictive control against a goal image, it learns world-model transitions directly in a pretrained vision-language retrieval space, then scores predicted futures by similarity to the language instruction. That is not a complete solution to embodied generalization, but it is a real mechanism, and it attacks a genuine failure mode in current VLAs: they overfit demonstrations while failing to generalize to semantically new but motorically familiar tasks.

**AIM: Intent-Aware Unified world action Modeling with Spatial Value Maps** is the best follow-up. The useful idea is not "use video priors for robot control" — everyone says that now. The useful idea is the explicit spatial value-map bottleneck: future prediction is forced to hand the action branch a control-oriented spatial interface rather than dumping dense future RGB latents on it and hoping intent emerges. That is much closer to an interpretable action scaffold than ordinary world-action mush.

**3D-Anchored Lookahead Planning for Persistent Robotic Scene Memory via World-Model-Based MCTS** is narrower and less mature, but still worth keeping. The contribution is architectural rather than statistical: it preserves a persistent camera-to-world anchor through occlusion and re-roots an MCTS tree instead of recomputing everything from the current view. The experiments are small and the setup is toyish, but the central lesson is good — if the problem is memory of hidden geometry, then the answer should probably involve explicit persistent spatial state.

I also checked **Pair2Scene** and **ComSim**. Pair2Scene is a respectable adjacent 3D-generation paper because it replaces end-to-end global layout modeling with local relational rules plus physics-aware sampling, but it is more relevant to procedural scene generation than to world models or embodied memory. ComSim is practically useful for robot data scaling, but the main contribution is pipeline engineering around sim-to-real video-action generation rather than a deeper representational idea.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Grounded World Model for Semantically Generalizable Planning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it reframes world-model MPC as language-grounded retrieval in a pretrained multimodal embedding space, rather than goal-image matching. That is a clean and defensible way to decouple semantic understanding from action proposal.

### 2. **AIM: Intent-Aware Unified world action Modeling with Spatial Value Maps**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it inserts an explicit spatial value representation between future prediction and action decoding, which is much healthier than asking a policy to recover contact intent from dense future RGB features.

### 3. **3D-Anchored Lookahead Planning for Persistent Robotic Scene Memory via World-Model-Based MCTS**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it makes persistent spatial memory concrete with a surviving SE(3) anchor and tree re-rooting under occlusion. The evidence is narrow, but the mechanism is crisp.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** Grounded World Model for Semantically Generalizable Planning.

It matters because it attacks a real and embarrassing gap in many VLA stories: models inherit semantic knowledge during pretraining, then promptly lose most of its usefulness once fine-tuned end-to-end on robot data. GWM’s answer is to avoid making the action policy itself carry all semantics. Instead, it learns a latent transition model in a frozen multimodal retrieval space and lets MPC choose among demonstrated motions according to instruction similarity. That is not magic — the motion repertoire still comes from demonstrations — but it is a much cleaner interface between semantics and control.

AIM is the best design lesson for future world-action work. If action generation really needs a notion of where to interact and why, then routing control through an explicit value-map-like spatial interface is better than letting it parasitize future appearance tokens.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

GWM is baseline pressure on nearly every claim that VLAs naturally inherit pretrained world knowledge. The paper’s WISER benchmark is specifically built so the test tasks require unseen visual signals and referring expressions but not unseen motions. If a VLA truly retained semantic knowledge, it should generalize there. The reported collapse of standard VLAs against a much stronger GWM-MPC result suggests that much of the supposed inheritance story is just overfit control wrapped in foundation-model branding.

AIM is framing pressure on unified world-action models that decode actions straight from future visual latents. The paper’s critique is fair: future RGB tells you what may happen, but not necessarily where intervention should occur. A spatial value interface is not the final answer, but it is a real structural hypothesis rather than more generic multimodal fusion.

3D-ALP is useful pressure on reactive manipulation stacks. If objects leave view and success still depends on them, then no amount of clever current-frame decoding substitutes for persistent state. The caveat is that the paper’s evidence is much smaller and less benchmark-heavy than the other two, so it should be read as a mechanism sketch, not as a settled win.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The recurring pattern today is explicit intermediate state. GWM keeps semantics in a frozen retrieval space and uses MPC to select demonstrated motions by instruction similarity. AIM inserts a spatial value map between imagined futures and action decoding so intent is not forced to hide inside RGB latents. 3D-ALP keeps a persistent SE(3) anchor so occluded objects do not disappear just because the camera turned away. Different domains, same lesson: if semantics, interaction structure, or spatial memory matter, they should probably exist somewhere explicit in the interface instead of being left to latent goodwill.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-19

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all make the same complaint in different subsystems: if the interface boundary stays implicit, the rest of the stack starts lying to you. **Harness Handbook** says behavior-to-code mapping should be a first-class artifact instead of something every coding agent re-derives from raw files. **Write-Protected Discrete Bottlenecks** argues that language should not get to backprop straight into a world model's discrete symbol layer. **Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda** shows that public web interfaces can leak adversarial text into pretraining corpora after crawling and filtering. **MCPEvol-Bench** measures what happens when tools evolve and agents do not. **Project Kaleidoscope** refuses to automate eval scoring until judges actually align with human review on the local rubric.

## Short overview

I checked the current `cs.AI`, `cs.CV`, and `cs.LG` arXiv recent pages on **Sunday, July 19, 2026**, ran an explicit non-robotics title pass for medical, multimodal, evaluation, uncertainty, and world-model terms, and used AlphaXiv as a supplementary scout surface. Brave Search was attempted first on **July 19, 2026** through the OpenClaw `web_search` tool and failed with the verified provider error `missing_brave_api_key`, so discovery fell back to AlphaXiv plus direct arXiv full-text inspection.

For the preserved notes, I inspected substantial full-text sections of the arXiv HTML papers for **Harness Handbook**, **Write-Protected Discrete Bottlenecks**, **Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda**, and **MCPEvol-Bench**, focusing on framing, mechanism, experiments, and limitations. I also inspected the abstract, workflow, and setup sections of **Project Kaleidoscope** and did a deliberate medical pass through **UniMedSeg** and **Decouple and Reason**. The medical papers were real, but they felt more like large bundled application systems than sharper reusable mechanism papers, so neither beat the final five.

**Harness Handbook** is the most relevant paper today. The useful move is not "summarize the repo better." It is turning behavior localization into an explicit artifact with staged disclosure and source-backed validation, so edit planning stops pretending file structure is the same thing as runtime behavior.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable, Navigable, and Editable**

**Verdict:** must read for coding-agent infrastructure.

Why it matters: This is one of the cleaner recent agent-systems papers because it isolates a real bottleneck instead of just adding another retrieval layer. The paper says harness evolution fails first at behavior localization, then builds a behavior-centric handbook plus staged navigation workflow around that fact. On the evaluated harnesses, handbook assistance raises overall plan-quality win rates from `28.3%` to `38.3%` on Codex and from `26.7%` to `45.6%` on Terminus-2, while also cutting planner token use.

### 2. **Write-Protected Discrete Bottlenecks for Language-Grounded World Models: A Structural Limitation and Sufficient Fix**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: The paper's core claim is narrow and strong: language gradients should not directly rewrite a world model's discrete physical symbols. The evidence is unusually blunt. Vanilla Gumbel-softmax collapses, anti-collapse tricks keep diversity but fail to learn labels, and the proposed three-layer fix gets `97.2%` grounding accuracy with conflict splitting versus `22.2%` without it. The style is polemical, but the architectural lesson is real.

### 3. **Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda**

**Verdict:** highly relevant security paper.

Why it matters: The paper does not just say "poisoning is bad." It follows poison through the actual web-data path: injection, crawl capture, extraction, and filtering. The useful move is **HalfLife**, a pipeline-level inclusion estimate rather than a toy injection proof. Their estimate is that public-comment poisoning can survive into training data at about `0.13%` inclusion probability over Common Crawl, which is enough to exceed the effective Wikipedia slice used in some modern corpora.

### 4. **MCPEvol-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agent Performance Across Dynamic Evolutions of MCP Servers**

**Verdict:** useful and directly relevant.

Why it matters: Static tool benchmarks flatter agents because the tool surface stands still. This paper asks the better question: what happens when the tool schema drifts underneath the workflow? The benchmark finds real degradation even for frontier models, with `13.7%` and `14.4%` task-fulfillment drops for the top reported models and substantial increases in planning and reasoning errors. The mutation machinery is synthetic, but the failure mode is absolutely real.

### 5. **Project Kaleidoscope: Contextual, Human-Aligned Evaluation for Real-World AI Applications**

**Verdict:** useful workflow artifact, lighter keep.

Why it matters: The best idea here is governance-shaped rather than algorithmic. Generated tests, contextual rubrics, and LLM judges only count after the judges clear agreement thresholds against human-reviewed labels. That is the right contract for local eval automation. The main caveat is scale: the paper is still a three-week pilot with `108` annotated Q&A pairs, so treat it as a workflow pattern, not a settled benchmark result.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Harness Handbook

The main steal is simple: behavior is not stored in filenames. If we want coding agents to modify large harnesses without hallucinating where the behavior lives, we probably need an explicit behavior-to-source layer and a workflow that forces progressive narrowing instead of raw repository grazing.

**Write-Protected Discrete Bottlenecks** is the representational complement: separate physical symbol formation from language-side semantic binding, and do not let gradients blur that boundary. **Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda** is the data-pipeline complement: open participation surfaces can become model-conditioning surfaces if the corpus pipeline never models provenance cleanly. **MCPEvol-Bench** is the tool-use complement: the benchmark surface should mutate if the deployment surface mutates. **Project Kaleidoscope** is the eval complement: automated judging should earn its authority on the local rubric instead of inheriting it from benchmark vibes.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Harness Handbook** is strongest because it attacks the prerequisite step many agent-editing papers hand-wave away. The paper's best result is not just higher win rate; it is better localization with lower planner token use and fewer zero-overlap misses. Caveat: it is still only two harnesses and handbook construction itself depends on good static analysis plus LLM structuring.

**Write-Protected Discrete Bottlenecks** is strongest where many world-model papers are weakest: it makes one architectural claim, tests the failure mode directly, and provides a minimal fix with causal ablations. Caveat: the domains are still toyish and the paper's rhetoric is more universal than its evidence.

**Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda** is strongest because it models survival through the data pipeline instead of pretending the attack stops at webpage injection. Caveat: the controlled model experiments are still small compared with frontier-scale training, and the real-world attack budget is operationally nontrivial.

**MCPEvol-Bench** is strongest as a correction to benchmark design. Tool environments are not static, so agent evaluation should stop acting like they are. Caveat: both the task generation and the evolution operators are partly LLM-mediated, so the benchmark inherits some synthesis bias.

**Project Kaleidoscope** is strongest as an organizational workflow pattern. Caveat: the evidence base is small, the paper is more product report than mechanism paper, and the results should not be over-read.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful lesson today is to stop assuming that a boundary will stay well-behaved just because the stack is currently getting away with it. Repositories need explicit behavior maps. Discrete world symbols need protection from semantic-gradient mush. Web corpus pipelines need provenance-aware thinking about third-party content. Tool-use agents need evaluation under actual interface drift. And eval automation itself should be gated by demonstrated human alignment. Same meta-point across five papers: if the interface matters, make it explicit and test it under change.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-12

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **world models are being judged by the interfaces they expose to control, not by rollout aesthetics alone**. **WEAVER** is the strongest paper because it treats a robotic world model as a learned simulator that must support policy evaluation, synthetic policy improvement, and test-time planning under latency constraints. **MaskWAM** is the cleanest object-centric WAM paper: masks are both a future prediction target and an optional first-frame spatial prompt, so the model predicts what matters, not only what happens. **EA-WM** is the predicate-level companion: it adds event prediction and verification on top of feature-space rollouts so a planner can score imagined futures by task progress rather than feature distance alone.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight fetched `/search` URL returned 404, so it was not useful for discovery today. Discovery and inspection for this run used the arXiv API over the June 11, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for **WEAVER, Better, Faster, Longer: An Effective World Model for Robotic Manipulation**, **RepWAM: World Action Modeling with Representation Visual-Action Tokenizers**, **MaskWAM: Unifying Mask Prompting and Prediction for World-Action Models**, **EA-WM: Event-Aware World Models with Task-Specification Grounding for Long-Horizon Manipulation**, **NavWAM: A Navigation World Action Model for Goal-Conditioned Visual Navigation**, **World Tracing: Generative Pixel-Aligned Geometry Beyond the Visible**, **SpatialClaw: Rethinking Action Interface for Agentic Spatial Reasoning**, **SPARC: Reliable Spatial Annotations from Robot Demonstrations at Scale**, **VISA: VLM-Guided Instance Semantic Auditing for 3D Occupancy World Models**, **Real-Time Execution with Autoregressive Policies**, **See Selectively, Act Adaptively**, and **LabVLA / RoboGenesis**. WEAVER, MaskWAM, and EA-WM are preserved today.

**WEAVER** is the best direct hit. Its central claim is practical and useful: a manipulation world model should jointly satisfy fidelity, temporal consistency, and inference speed because the downstream uses are policy evaluation, policy improvement, and online planning. The architecture combines multi-view visual latents, proprioception prediction, sparse long-term memory, short-term history, flow-matched latent dynamics, diffusion-forcing style noise, accelerated denoising, and latent reward/critic heads. The paper is strongest where it connects the world model to decisions: predicted rollouts correlate with real success after finetuning, synthetic segments improve a `pi0.5` policy without extra real interaction, and latent best-of-4 steering improves test-time task success.

**MaskWAM** is the strongest object-centric WAM interface paper. It treats masks as first-class latent streams, jointly predicting future RGB, future masks, and action chunks. That makes target regions explicit during training and enables a deployment-time mask prompt for language-ambiguous manipulation. The best result is not the tiny LIBERO gain over other strong baselines; it is the ablation showing that a mask prompt without future-mask prediction collapses in ambiguous tasks, while joint mask prediction plus prompting stays robust across distractors, novel instances, and lighting shifts.

**EA-WM** is worth preserving with caveats. The mechanism is exactly aligned with explicit-state taste: roll out candidate actions in frozen visual-feature space, decode task-grounded event predicates, and score futures with task, semantic, physical, and uncertainty terms before CEM or hybrid selection. The red flag is that event supervision is simulator-derived, LIBERO online evaluation is short-window rather than full autonomous episodes, and Goal10 gains are modest. Still, the design pattern is useful: visual-feature closeness is not the same as event progress.

**RepWAM** is directly relevant but not preserved as a separate note today. It trains a representation visual-action tokenizer aligned to a visual foundation model, then learns latent actions as transitions inside that semantic visual space. The ablations are useful, especially the two-stage latent-action training result, but the paper overlaps with the last few days of WAM interface/alignment papers and is less sharply explicit than MaskWAM or EA-WM.

**NavWAM** is strong adjacent direct work for navigation. It represents current state, goal image, future observations, action chunk, future state, and goal-progress value as a shared latent canvas inside a Cosmos Predict2-style video model. It beats CEM-style navigation world-model baselines and reports 19/24 real-world image-goal navigation successes. I am not preserving it today because the strongest cabbageland thread is manipulation/world-action interfaces, but NavWAM is good citation material for "future prediction is useful when trained with action and value targets."

**World Tracing** is the best 3D/geometry paper in the batch. It predicts layered pixel-aligned 3D point stacks, where layer 0 is the visible surface and deeper layers complete occluded intersections along each input ray. This is a serious representation paper, especially for input-faithful hidden geometry, but it is adjacent to today's robotics-control thread rather than the main preserved story.

**SpatialClaw**, **SPARC**, and **VISA** are useful citation material. SpatialClaw argues that code in a persistent kernel is a better spatial-reasoning action interface than single-pass code or fixed tool calls. SPARC scores robot-demo annotations by phase-aware object motion, 3D gripper proximity, and robot-overlap filtering. VISA converts offline VLM object audits into voxel-grounded semantic supervision for 3D occupancy world models. All three are useful, but none displace today's WAM/control-interface papers.

**Real-Time Execution with Autoregressive Policies**, **See Selectively, Act Adaptively**, and **LabVLA / RoboGenesis** are mostly baseline/framing material for deployment, bimanual routing, and synthetic lab robotics data. The ideas are useful, but they are less central than today's top three.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **WEAVER, Better, Faster, Longer: An Effective World Model for Robotic Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it turns a manipulation world model into an actually used learned simulator for evaluation, synthetic improvement, and test-time planning, with explicit attention to multi-view state, proprioception, memory, reward, and latency.

### 2. **MaskWAM: Unifying Mask Prompting and Prediction for World-Action Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it makes task-relevant object regions explicit both as prediction targets and as deployment-time prompts, which is a real interface improvement over RGB-only future prediction.

### 3. **EA-WM: Event-Aware World Models with Task-Specification Grounding for Long-Horizon Manipulation**

**Verdict:** relevant and worth preserving with evidence caveats.

Why it matters: it scores imagined futures by predicted event and predicate progress rather than visual-feature distance alone, which is the right conceptual direction for long-horizon manipulation planning.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** WEAVER.

The steal-worthy idea is to evaluate a world model by the jobs it can perform for a policy. Does it predict the robot's proprioceptive state, not just pixels? Does it maintain enough memory to survive occlusion and long-horizon manipulation? Can a reward or value model score the imagined latent directly, without decoding every frame and asking a separate judge? Can synthetic rollouts actually improve the base policy, and can online planning run within a latency budget?

MaskWAM adds the object-centric interface lesson. If a policy is supposed to act on the cup, drawer handle, bottle, or contact patch, the world model should carry that target region as a state variable. A future mask is a better training signal than asking the action head to infer relevance from unconstrained RGB futures.

EA-WM adds the task-progress lesson. If the important event is "drawer opened," "object moved," "object on target," or "contact condition satisfied," then a planner needs those events exposed as predicted predicates or verifier scores. Feature-space closeness can be useful, but it is too blunt to stand in for task logic.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**WEAVER** raises the bar for manipulation world models. A serious baseline should report not only visual FVD/FID, but whether imagined rollouts correlate with real task success, whether synthetic segments improve a policy, and whether test-time search is fast enough to matter.

**MaskWAM** raises the bar for WAM grounding. RGB-only WAMs should now be compared against object-centric mask prediction or equivalent explicit target-state supervision, especially in cluttered or language-ambiguous tasks. Prompting alone is not enough; the model must be trained to propagate the prompted state into future prediction and action.

**EA-WM** sharpens the baseline for feature-space planning. If a feature world model is used for CEM or MPC, the scoring function should be checked against task predicates, physical margins, and event progress, not only terminal representation distance. The caveat is that the paper's own deployable evidence is still preliminary.

**RepWAM** is useful for novelty framing around semantic visual-action tokenizers and latent actions. It supports the claim that reconstruction-oriented tokenizers are a weak default for WAMs, but it does not replace the need for explicit object or event interfaces.

**NavWAM** is useful for arguing that future-view prediction should be coupled to action and value targets when the task is closed-loop navigation.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **WEAVER** because it asks whether a world model can do real policy work: evaluate trajectories, generate useful synthetic improvement data, and steer actions online quickly enough to matter. **MaskWAM** is the clean object-centric complement, showing that predicting and prompting masks gives the action head a target-specific interface instead of a generic RGB future. **EA-WM** is the event-level complement, using predicted predicates and verifier scores to judge whether imagined futures make task progress. The common lesson is blunt: world models become useful when their hidden state is exposed as the right control object, whether that object is a value-scored latent rollout, a future target mask, or a task-event scorecard.

## Detailed notes

- [MaskWAM note](../paper_notes/maskwam_unifying_mask_prompting_prediction_world_action_models.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-03-25

## Theme
The useful VLA papers right now are not just adding context. They are choosing a memory object, an update rule, and an interface to control. That is the difference between real structure and another reheated “long-horizon” claim.

## Short overview
Today’s strongest paper is **MemoryVLA: Perceptual-Cognitive Memory in Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation**. It is the cleanest direct hit because it does not reduce memory to prompt stuffing. It explicitly separates short-term working memory from a long-term perceptual-cognitive bank, defines retrieval and consolidation, and conditions a diffusion action expert on the retrieved state. The main caution is that the brain-inspired framing is louder than the actual novelty; mechanistically, this is still a learned retrieval-fusion memory stack, not a principled model of episodic reasoning.

The second worthwhile paper is **Notes-to-Self: Scratchpad Augmented VLAs for Memory Dependent Manipulation Tasks**. Its core move is simpler and, in some ways, more legible: let the policy write an explicit language scratchpad describing state, plan, and completed subtasks, then feed that back into future action prediction. This is less elegant than a latent memory bank, but the write semantics are unusually inspectable. The catch is obvious too: if the scratchpad is wrong, stale, or poorly supervised, the whole system can drift into self-authored confusion.

I also inspected **SG-VLA: Learning Spatially-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Models for Mobile Manipulation**. This is more about representation grounding than memory, but it survives filtering because the auxiliary targets are concrete and operational: robot pose, joint state, object pose, grasp state, and segmentation masks. It is useful evidence that VLA performance in mobile manipulation improves when the latent state is forced to predict physically relevant intermediate variables instead of only being punished through imitation loss.

## Ranked papers

1. **MemoryVLA: Perceptual-Cognitive Memory in Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation**  
   - Verdict: **Highly relevant**  
   - Role: **Directly relevant**  
   - Why it matters: It gives VLA memory actual mechanics: typed storage, retrieval, fusion, and consolidation tied to action generation.

2. **Notes-to-Self: Scratchpad Augmented VLAs for Memory Dependent Manipulation Tasks**  
   - Verdict: **Useful**  
   - Role: **Directly relevant**  
   - Why it matters: It turns memory into an explicit writable artifact, which is crude but unusually legible and easy to reason about.

3. **SG-VLA: Learning Spatially-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Models for Mobile Manipulation**  
   - Verdict: **Useful**  
   - Role: **Adjacent inspiration**  
   - Why it matters: It shows that better intermediate supervision on spatial variables can materially improve VLA control in mobile manipulation.

## Most relevant to cabbageland
**MemoryVLA** is the best fit. The important part is not the neuroscience costume. The important part is that it treats low-level perceptual detail and high-level semantic summary as different memory streams, retrieves them separately, and fuses them before action generation. That is much closer to typed memory than the usual “just add recurrence” move.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact
- **Memory framing:** MemoryVLA is a good citation when arguing that within-episode memory should specify stored object, retrieval path, and update rule rather than just append more temporal context.
- **Legibility framing:** Notes-to-Self is useful because it makes the memory trace inspectable. That matters if we care about controllability and debugging rather than just benchmark wins.
- **Representation framing:** SG-VLA is a reminder that some “memory” failures are actually representation failures. If the latent cannot recover geometry, pose, and grasp state, no amount of vague temporal context will save it.
- **Caution:** My confidence is highest in the method read for **MemoryVLA** and **Notes-to-Self**, because I inspected the abstract plus substantial method text. For **SG-VLA**, I inspected the abstract and method sections covering architecture, auxiliary decoders, losses, and training scheme, but I did not audit every experiment table or supplement.

## One-paragraph takeaway
The useful split today is between papers that merely extend context and papers that define a memory contract. **MemoryVLA** defines one with typed perceptual and cognitive stores plus retrieval and consolidation. **Notes-to-Self** defines one with an explicit writable language scratchpad that tracks grounding, plan, and progress. **SG-VLA** is not a memory paper in the same sense, but it supports the broader lesson that control gets better when the model is forced to represent inspectable task structure. The standard should be harsh: if a paper says “memory” or “spatial grounding” without changing what is stored, queried, or predicted, it is probably packaging.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-04-27

## Theme

Today’s strongest cluster is explicit interfaces that make latent behavior less mushy. The best papers either force a world model to respect actions as first-class tokens, or force a multimodal model to separate image attribution from vague pooled attention. The common win is not scale. It is making the internal contract harder to fake.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. arXiv API discovery was then attempted and partially worked before repeated HTTP 429 rate limiting, so primary-source inspection fell back to direct arXiv abstract and HTML pages. I inspected the abstract plus substantial method and experimental text for **Scalable Robotic Policy Evaluation via Discrete Diffusion World Model**, **Compositional Grounded Contrast for Fine-Grained Multi-Image Understanding**, and **OccDirector: Language-Guided Behavior and Interaction Generation in 4D Occupancy Space**.

The strongest paper today is **Scalable Robotic Policy Evaluation via Discrete Diffusion World Model**. Its main claim is not just “use a world model for evaluation.” The important move is architectural: treat actions, language, and observations as coequal discrete tokens inside one denoising model, then predict a progress token jointly with the imagined future. That directly attacks a familiar failure mode in video-style evaluators, where action conditioning is weak and the model hallucinates success.

**Compositional Grounded Contrast** is more adjacent, but still useful. It treats multi-image understanding as an attribution-and-grounding problem rather than generic VLM cleverness. The recipe is simple and steal-worthy: synthesize cross-image distractor setups from single-image grounding data, then optimize with a rule-based spatial reward that checks image index, localization, and output structure.

**OccDirector** is interesting but mixed. The shift from rigid trajectory conditioning to language-driven 4D occupancy generation is real, and the paper is ambitious about procedural multi-agent behavior. But it also has the usual big-generative-world-model smell: large custom dataset, strong benchmark framing, lots of state-of-the-art language, and less evidence yet that the semantic structure is genuinely robust outside its curated occupancy regime.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Scalable Robotic Policy Evaluation via Discrete Diffusion World Model**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it tries to make policy evaluation faithful by giving actions equal representational status instead of injecting them as weak side conditions into a video generator.

### 2. **Compositional Grounded Contrast for Fine-Grained Multi-Image Understanding**

**Verdict:** useful, with adjacent inspiration value.

Why it matters: it turns multi-image grounding into a structured training problem with explicit attribution pressure, instead of vague “reason over many images” branding.

### 3. **OccDirector: Language-Guided Behavior and Interaction Generation in 4D Occupancy Space**

**Verdict:** skimmable but worth noting.

Why it matters: the language-to-occupancy interface is conceptually interesting, but the paper currently looks more like a strong generative benchmark package than a clearly transferable mechanism paper.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Scalable Robotic Policy Evaluation via Discrete Diffusion World Model.

What is worth stealing is the refusal to let actions remain auxiliary. The paper’s complaint about prior evaluators is credible: if the backbone is mostly a video generator, it will often smooth over bad actions and hallucinate plausible-looking success. dWorldEval’s answer is to flatten images, language, and action chunks into a single token sequence, then make success detection part of the same generative act through a discrete progress token.

That does not fully solve evaluator faithfulness, but it is the right pressure. If you want a world model to be useful for ranking or debugging policies, action sensitivity and long-horizon consistency have to be part of the architecture, not just the prompt.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

dWorldEval sharpens a useful baseline question for robotics world models: are actions structurally primary, or are they still weak hints attached to a visually dominant generator? If the latter, evaluation claims deserve skepticism.

CGC adds pressure on multi-image reasoning papers that talk about perception and grounding in one breath without enforcing source attribution. A model that cannot reliably keep track of which image owns which object does not really have compositional multi-image understanding.

OccDirector matters more for framing than for immediate adoption. It pushes against geometry-only control in 4D driving generation, but it still needs stronger evidence that natural-language control is giving real structured behavior instead of benchmark-shaped plausibility.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The good papers today do not ask for trust. They add structure where failure would otherwise stay hidden. dWorldEval makes imagined robotic futures answer to actions and explicit progress. CGC makes multi-image reasoning answer to image identity and grounded spatial outputs. OccDirector is ambitious and maybe directionally right, but I trust it less because the mechanism-to-evaluation chain is looser. The useful throughline is simple: if a model claims controllability or compositionality, give it a representation where cheating is harder.

## Detailed notes

- [Scalable Robotic Policy Evaluation via Discrete Diffusion World Model note](../paper_notes/dworldeval_discrete_diffusion_world_model_for_policy_evaluation.md)
- [Compositional Grounded Contrast note](../paper_notes/cgc_compositional_grounded_contrast_multi_image_understanding.md)
