# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-13

## Theme

The good papers today all attack the same soft spot: hidden state that sounds useful but is not yet operationally legible. **Harnessing agent memory to build lifelong AI partners for materials scientists** says memory should survive the agent as inspectable facts and executable skills. **Detecting a Route Flip Is Easier Than Knowing Whether to Fix It** says a routing event is not yet an actionable intervention because occurrence and benefit are different questions. **LoongReflect** says reflection should be an explicit memory-control policy, not a vague self-critique monologue. **Mechanism Design for Generative Engines** says defense should reward verifiable substance rather than only punish spam. **ForeWAM** says action policies can expose predictive dynamics through latent state instead of paying full future-video cost.

## Short overview

This run used the live Thursday, August 13, 2026 arXiv batch with explicit non-robotics passes across agent memory, uncertainty/verification, and clinical/medical interpretation lanes. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for the three preserved papers below. I also inspected the arXiv HTML full text for **Mechanism Design for Generative Engines** and the abstract of **ForeWAM** as runner-ups. A clinical/medical pass surfaced papers like **COGENT** and **DD-CMD**, but both felt narrower and less transferable than today's top five.

Three papers earn preserved notes. **Mechanism Design for Generative Engines** is the strongest adjacent runner-up because the incentive framing is sharp and the repeated-game setup is useful, but it is more ecosystem-governance than core cabbageland architecture. **ForeWAM** is the one robotics/VLA paper worth keeping in the five because it actually changes how predictive state reaches the action pathway instead of just stapling "world model" branding onto a policy. **Most relevant today:** **Harnessing agent memory to build lifelong AI partners for materials scientists**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Harnessing agent memory to build lifelong AI partners for materials scientists**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the strongest paper in the batch because it treats memory as a durable scientific artifact instead of an agent-side residue. The useful move is the split into provenance-linked facts and executable skills that can transfer across models, prevent repeated failures, and compress repeat workflows without pretending memory is just a long chat log.

### 2. **Detecting a Route Flip Is Easier Than Knowing Whether to Fix It: Causal Route-Mediated Damage in Quantized Mixture-of-Experts**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It separates a real deployment question into two non-equivalent parts: did quantization flip the route, and would fixing that flip actually help? The useful move is the four-run causal decomposition and the ugly but important result that local router statistics can detect flips while staying at chance on harm direction.

### 3. **LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It turns reflection into explicit state control with `<reflect>` and `<backtrack>` actions over a reversible trajectory tree. The useful move is not "more self-reflection" but answer-masked teacher supervision on reflection tokens plus outcome-based GRPO to align local control with final success.

### 4. **Mechanism Design for Generative Engines: From Exploitation toward Win-Win Outcomes**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: It is one of the better recent papers on citation-governance incentives because it does not stop at spam filtering. The useful move is VCR, a platform-side reward for source-supported, pair-verifiable content, which shifts the attacker's profitable direction from manipulative phrasing toward actual checkable substance.

### 5. **Foresight Without Seeing: Latent Futures for World Action Models**

**Verdict:** direct robotics runner-up.

Why it matters: This is the one robotics paper in the top five because it has a real mechanism. The useful move is Future-KV plus dynamics registers, which feed predictive dynamics into the action pathway without having to decode future video at inference time.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **Harnessing agent memory to build lifelong AI partners for materials scientists**.

This paper has the right unit of progress. Instead of treating the current agent, model, or framework as the carrier of learning, it treats saved experience as the asset: facts for warnings, boundary conditions, and observations; skills for ordered procedures and executable workflows. That is the right direction if the point is to build systems that get better across sessions, models, and toolchain changes instead of relearning the same traps after every upgrade.

The results are also unusually concrete. On the real-world MatTools subset, memory raises GPT-5.2 task success from **44.2%** to **75.4%** over three rounds, and GPT-5.4 from **66.7%** to **88.4%**. A GPT-5.4 memory transfers to GPT-5.4-nano with a reported **50.8-point** gain over the nano model's own three-round memory. On Sol27LC, repeated wavefunction-initialization failures are turned into guardrails, improving aggregate outcomes from **22/1/4** to **25/2/0 Correct/Partial/Error** while avoiding **91.7%** of repeated failures. On 13 VASP and LAMMPS workflows, tokens drop from **17.90M** to **8.96M** and non-polling tool calls from **1,038** to **481** by round three.

The other papers reinforce the same broader lesson. **Route Flip** says a state perturbation is not yet an intervention policy. **LoongReflect** says reflection should explicitly rewrite working state rather than narrate about it. **VCR** says ecosystem incentives should point toward verifiable substance. **ForeWAM** says latent predictive state can be routed into action without paying the full rendering tax.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Harnessing agent memory** is strongest because it makes memory portable, inspectable, and transferable rather than embedding all progress inside a particular agent stack. The important framing result is that facts and skills can become a model-agnostic scientific asset. The benchmark story is strong too: GPT-5.2 rises from **44.2%** to **75.4%** task success on MatTools over three rounds, Sol27LC improves from **22/1/4** to **25/2/0**, and practical workflows cut tokens and tool calls by about half by round three.

**Route Flip** is strongest because it kills a lazy mitigation story before people build around it. On the OLMoE pilot, roughly a third of the quantization damage is routing-mediated with headline **RMF ~= 0.31**, but the deployable router margin only predicts whether a flip occurred (**AUC 0.772**), not whether fixing it helps (**harmful-flip AUC 0.490**, benefit-prediction **0.499**). That is a useful negative result: a repair channel can exist without a practical local decision rule for invoking it.

**LoongReflect** is strongest because it gives reflection an explicit control surface and trains it with the right separation of signals. On the seven QA benchmarks, average F1 reaches **46.15** on Qwen2.5-3B and **49.21** on Qwen2.5-7B, beating AgenticRAG-R1 by **12.60** and **12.61** points respectively. On math transfer, the 3B model reaches **56.0** on MATH and **82.4** on GSM8K. The important framing result is that local reflection supervision should live on reflection spans, not be diluted into generic trajectory imitation.

**Mechanism Design for Generative Engines** is useful because it recasts platform defense as incentive design instead of only detection. The reported headline is that VCR beats the strongest baseline by an average **12.1-point** Net defense-utility margin and is the only defense that stays in the positive Net region across repeated interaction rounds on the paper's main setup. The reason it stays a runner-up is that the problem is real and the mechanism is sharp, but the domain is one step further from the core memory/control problems than today's top three.

**ForeWAM** is a good robotics runner-up because it changes where predictive structure enters the policy. The standard and accelerated variants reach **96.7%** and **96.9%** on LIBERO, with the standard model at **61.6%** on LIBERO-Plus, without embodied-data pretraining. The main caveat is that this is still a robotics benchmark paper, so the transferable idea is the latent-future interface rather than the headline success rate.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful August 13 lesson is that state only becomes valuable when the system knows what kind of state it is, where it came from, and what decisions it can safely support. Durable memory should be readable and executable, not trapped inside a session. A route flip should not trigger repair unless the system can tell whether repair helps. Reflection should modify working state through explicit control actions. Platform defenses should reward checkable content, not only punish bad style. Predictive dynamics should reach policies through a cheap latent interface when full generative rollout is too expensive. Same taste everywhere: explicit state beats decorative state.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-26

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all say the same thing in different subsystems: memory, confidence, and evidence do not become trustworthy just because they exist somewhere in the stack. **Delivery, Not Storage** says a fact on disk is not operational memory unless the harness knows when to re-deliver it. **Dream Rehearsal** says retaining a world model is not the same as retaining behavior, because the actor can still forget. **ConfidenceBench** says answer accuracy is not a substitute for calibrated self-uncertainty. **Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis** says a correct diagnosis is not enough if the model got there through the wrong evidence. **ChronoStitch** says cached visual state is not reusable temporal memory unless the positional geometry and missing cross-chunk context are repaired explicitly.

## Short overview

I checked the live `cs.AI`, `cs.CV`, `cs.LG`, `cs.RO`, `q-bio.NC`, and `eess.IV` arXiv recent pages on Sunday, July 26, 2026. There was no newer arXiv day beyond the Friday, July 24 batch, so this is a deliberate second-pass scout rather than a fake "new release" digest. Brave Search was attempted first through the Brave API and failed with `HTTP 422` because the required `x-subscription-token` header is missing in this environment, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv category pages and primary-source paper inspection.

For the preserved set, I reused the repository's existing canonical full-text-based notes for **Delivery, Not Storage**, **Dream Rehearsal**, and **Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis**, and directly inspected the current arXiv sources for **ConfidenceBench** and **ChronoStitch** during this run. I also ran the explicit non-robotics scan the repo asks for. Robotics and VLA papers were present, but none beat the five below on mechanism, evaluation clarity, and future usefulness.

**Delivery, Not Storage** is the most relevant paper today. The useful move is not "have a memory file." It is making memory delivery a harness responsibility with explicit cues, provenance, and re-entry after compaction.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is still one of the cleanest recent papers on agent memory because it moves the responsibility to the right layer. The core result is rude in the right way: the seeded voluntary-memory arm performs `0` memory operations in `114` turns, while harness-delivered facts survive `138/138` compact-resume boundaries and deterministic cue delivery fires in every seeded injection run with zero logged false alarms.

### 2. **The World Model Remembers, the Actor Forgets: Dream Rehearsal for Continual Model-Based RL**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: The paper does the causal decomposition many continual-learning papers skip. In the replay-maintained Dreamer regime, the world model keeps much of the old-task structure while the actor still forgets the behavior. Dream rehearsal then uses graded imagined trajectories to repair the actual failing channel, yielding `3/3` successful four-task chains, `3/3` eight-task chains, and a paired gain of about `+0.13` over matched real-episode cloning.

### 3. **ConfidenceBench: Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant evaluation paper.

Why it matters: This paper is useful because it scores verbalized confidence directly instead of pretending accuracy will proxy for it. Across `15` frontier LLMs and `200` private multiple-choice questions, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview both reach a `0.103` Brier score, far better than the calibrated-random baseline of `0.1875`, while Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores `0.367`, which is severe miscalibration despite being a recent model.

### 4. **Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis**

**Verdict:** useful direct evaluation paper.

Why it matters: This is a good audit paper because it does not confuse "strong interaction" with "failure." It decomposes evidence into diagnosis-relative roles, mines interaction effects in diagnostic margins, and only then escalates stable suspicious cases for clinical review. In the enriched DDXPlus sample, `111/130` reviewed interactions are valid, `8/130` questionable, and `11/130` invalid or shortcut-like, mostly around negated or clinically local evidence.

### 5. **ChronoStitch: Training-Free Composition of Visual KV Memories for Long-Horizon Temporal Reasoning**

**Verdict:** useful direct paper.

Why it matters: The main negative result is the useful part: independently cached video chunks do not compose by naive concatenation because their local rotary phases collide and later chunks never attended to earlier ones. ChronoStitch fixes both errors with three-axis key re-basing plus selective token repair, improving TempCompass temporal-split accuracy by `4.8` points overall and `7.0` points on event ordering while running about `3.3x` faster than full joint re-prefilling.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Delivery, Not Storage.

The steal is simple and actionable. Memory is not "a note exists somewhere." Memory is "the system knows when the note becomes live again." That maps directly onto coding-agent harnesses, long-running assistants, compaction-heavy workflows, and any architecture where the model itself cannot be trusted to remember to remember.

The same boundary discipline shows up in the rest of the digest. **Dream Rehearsal** says stored world knowledge is useless if the actor-learning channel cannot reuse it. **ConfidenceBench** says uncertainty has to be scored on its own axis. **Auditing Evidence Use** says evaluation should test whether the right evidence moved the decision. **ChronoStitch** says cache reuse only counts as memory if temporal structure survives composition.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Delivery, Not Storage** is strongest because it attacks the actual failure boundary instead of merely adding another persistence surface. The useful novelty is not a memory database. It is cue-owned, harness-side delivery with auditability and compaction survival. Caveat: the study is still small, single-harness, and much stronger on delivery than on automated capture.

**Dream Rehearsal** is strongest because it localizes the continual-learning failure before proposing the fix. The world model is not the part that forgot most of the time; the actor is. Caveat: the evidence comes from MiniGrid chains with `n=3` seeds and a `17M`-parameter DreamerV3 setup, so the diagnosis is strong but still not fully general.

**ConfidenceBench** is strongest as a measurement correction. The paper uses a proper scoring rule, includes an unknowable category, and shows that calibration and accuracy diverge materially. Caveat: it evaluates prompted verbalized confidence, not latent logit confidence, so some of the behavior may reflect instruction following rather than pure epistemic state.

**Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis** is strongest because it keeps the interpretation layer disciplined. Many strong interactions are legitimate differential-diagnosis structure, not failures, and the paper forces clinical review before making stronger claims. Caveat: it is still prompt-conditioned behavior over fixed candidate sets rather than a direct readout of latent reasoning.

**ChronoStitch** is strongest because it shows why the obvious cache-composition trick fails and then repairs both the geometry error and the missing-content error. Caveat: the reader is only a `3B` VLM, the benchmark ceiling is only `63.9%`, and the paper itself admits that the scalar-versus-three-axis difference is more obvious in the representation diagnostic than in downstream QA unless selective repair is added.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that latent state is not automatically useful state. A stored note is not memory unless the harness can re-deliver it at the right cue. A retained world model is not retained competence unless the actor can still exploit it. A correct answer is not reliable if the model cannot state calibrated confidence. A medical diagnosis is not trustworthy if the evidence margin is being moved by the wrong clues. A cached video chunk is not reusable long-range memory if its temporal coordinates and missing attention history are broken. Same pattern everywhere: if a paper claims memory, confidence, or evidence, ask whether the interface that makes it usable is explicit and testable.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-30

## Theme

Today's best papers are all about refusing proxy confusion. **Scores Are Not Decisions** says a tool ranking is not yet a tool budget, because stopping depth has to price marginal value against heterogeneous cost. **What Can Latent World Models Know?** says fused input is not retained state unless the prediction target actually forces the latent to keep it. **Visual Credit Audit** says a correct multimodal answer is not evidence that the image carried the decision. **Prior Directions** says stale context is not harmless history if it recruits a compact recurrent control route. **Cost-Sensitive Conformal Prediction** says global coverage is not protection for rare costly cases unless the guarantee is conditioned on the class and coupled to a deferral policy.

## Short overview

I attempted Brave Search first through the OpenClaw `web_search` tool on Thursday, July 30, 2026, and it failed with `missing_brave_api_key`, specifically saying Brave search needs a configured API key. Discovery therefore fell back to direct arXiv recent-category inspection and full-text reading through arXiv PDFs.

This run did the explicit non-robotics pass the repo asks for. That surfaced papers such as **Anatomy Contextualized Adaption of CT Foundation Models**, **CalTwin: Towards Calibrated, Shift-Robust Medical World Models via Fisher-Information Regularisation**, and **The Art of Not Forgetting: A Local Learning Architecture for Continual Learning**. They were interesting, but the five below were stronger on mechanism, operational framing, and transferable systems lessons. The top four are preserve-worthy note candidates. **Cost-Sensitive Conformal Prediction** is a good direct runner-up with practical deployment value, but I do not think it beats the top four on conceptual sharpness.

**Most relevant today:** **Scores Are Not Decisions: Cost-Aware Stopping for Tool Acquisition in LLM Agents**. The steal is direct: stop pretending that ranking candidate tools and deciding how many to expose are the same problem. They are not, especially once cost, privacy, and context load differ across tools.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Scores Are Not Decisions: Cost-Aware Stopping for Tool Acquisition in LLM Agents**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is the cleanest direct paper of the day. It inserts the missing control layer between ranking and execution by learning when to stop acquiring tools from a ranked list, using downstream payoff rather than score folklore.

### 2. **What Can Latent World Models Know? Physical Parameter Identifiability in Multimodal Predictive Representations**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: The paper gives a sharp answer to a usually hand-wavy claim. A latent only keeps the physical quantities its targets force it to keep. Touch fused as input does nothing for stiffness; touch forecast as a target changes the latent.

### 3. **Visual Credit Audit for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: It attacks an embarrassing benchmark failure mode directly. A model can be correct on a spatial question while the image contributed little beyond text-only or blank controls. The audit decomposes correctness from image-supported correctness instead of treating them as the same thing.

### 4. **Prior Directions: Why GUI Grounding Gets Locked in the Past**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: This is a useful mechanistic account of stale-context failure in multimodal grounding. The paper argues that lock-in depends less on how much the representation moves and more on whether prior-induced movement concentrates along a recurrent low-dimensional route that can later dominate the decision.

### 5. **Cost-Sensitive Conformal Prediction and Human-in-the-Loop Abstention for Imbalanced High-Stakes Decision Support: A Multi-Domain Benchmark**

**Verdict:** useful direct runner-up.

Why it matters: It is a practical reminder that marginal coverage can be scientifically and operationally useless under class imbalance. The useful result is not just "use conformal prediction"; it is that Mondrian coverage plus explicit deferral economics can make minority-class uncertainty and human review budgets line up.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Scores Are Not Decisions: Cost-Aware Stopping for Tool Acquisition in LLM Agents.

The reason is blunt. Cabbageland keeps building agents in environments where exposing every plausible tool is not free. It burns context, latency, money, privacy surface, and error surface. This paper says the obvious thing that too many stacks still ignore: a ranking is only an ordering, not a deployment policy. Once costs differ, the right question is whether the next tool's marginal value clears its marginal cost.

The rest of the digest reinforces the same discipline from other angles. **What Can Latent World Models Know?** says representation claims should be target-gated, not narrated from vibes. **Visual Credit Audit** says benchmark wins should be evidence-qualified, not accepted at face value. **Prior Directions** says persistent context can become a structured override channel rather than a harmless reminder. **Cost-Sensitive Conformal Prediction** says uncertainty guarantees are only meaningful if they protect the cases that actually matter.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Scores Are Not Decisions** is strongest because it reframes tool acquisition as a stopping problem over ranked prefixes instead of a thresholding problem over raw scores. The important baseline lesson is that score-only rules become structurally wrong once costs are heterogeneous.

**What Can Latent World Models Know?** is strongest because it separates recoverability from retention. The useful novelty is the certificate-gated protocol: first prove a parameter is present in the observations, then ask whether the objective made the latent keep it.

**Visual Credit Audit** is strongest because it changes what benchmark accuracy is allowed to mean. Correctness without additional image support is not the same thing as multimodal reasoning, and the paper gives a post-hoc audit that makes that visible.

**Prior Directions** is strongest because it resists the lazy explanation that stale priors win simply by producing "more" internal movement. The paper's claim is tighter: stronger lock-in can come with smaller movement if that movement is organized along a compact recurrent route.

**Cost-Sensitive Conformal Prediction** is strongest as a deployment benchmark rather than as a deep new algorithmic idea. The useful lesson is that minority-class coverage, abstention policy, and human-review cost should be treated as one operational object rather than three separate dashboards.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that the object you score is not necessarily the object you control. Tool relevance scores are not acquisition decisions. Fused sensory channels are not retained state. Benchmark accuracy is not image-grounded evidence use. Persistent priors are not benign context. Marginal coverage is not protection for the cases you most care about. The papers worth keeping are the ones that force the operational object to match the claim: the right tool prefix, the right latent target, the right evidence audit, the right intervention direction, the right uncertainty contract.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-04

## Theme

Today's best papers refuse to hide the real support structure behind one neat score. **Why Does the Future Branch?** says predictive uncertainty is not one thing: some of it comes from hidden state, some from genuine process noise, and forecast calibration cannot tell you which is which. **PMMC** says long-term multimodal memory should not wait until query time to improvise an evidence plan. **Don't Offer What Can't Be Done** says semantic relevance is the wrong object if the current account state already makes a skill impossible to execute. **What Carries the Signal in Pathology Foundation-Model Atlases?** says patient-level evidence matters more than a glamorous manifold story, and the geometry in that pipeline mostly does no work. **Measurement Without Validity** pushes the same suspicion up one level: if task generation, simulation, and judging each distort the signal, the benchmark score compounds the distortion instead of averaging it away.

## Short overview

This run attempted Brave Search first on Tuesday, August 4, 2026 through the public Brave HTML surface. The surface was reachable, but it behaved more like a coarse index dump than a trustworthy fresh-paper filter, so the real scouting moved to direct arXiv recent-page inspection and arXiv HTML full-text reading. I also did the required non-robotics pass across pathology, radiology, calibration, memory, verification, and world-model terms in the August 4 batch, which is why the final list is not just another agent-memory heap.

I inspected arXiv HTML full text for the four preserved papers below and enough full text for the fifth to judge it honestly. The top four are preserve-worthy. **Measurement Without Validity** is useful and worth reading, but I see it more as a framing and audit memo than as a must-keep mechanism paper.

**Most relevant today:** **Why Does the Future Branch? Identifiable Closure Tests for Stochastic Physical World Models**. It sharpens a confusion that shows up constantly in world modeling and belief-state design: a broad predictive distribution does not tell you whether you need better state, better sensors, or genuine branching.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Why Does the Future Branch? Identifiable Closure Tests for Stochastic Physical World Models**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It turns a vague uncertainty complaint into an identifiable estimand. Forecast accuracy and calibration cannot tell whether branching comes from hidden state aliasing or real process noise; ClosurePairs can.

### 2. **PMMC: Prospective Multimodal Memory Compilation for Long-Term LVLM Agents**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: The useful move is compile-time memory planning. Instead of waiting for a future query and then doing expensive query-time search, PMMC predicts likely future information needs, compiles typed evidence programs, and verifies them before the query arrives.

### 3. **Don't Offer What Can't Be Done: Deterministic Executability Gating for LLM Skill Selection at Scale**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It isolates a real production failure mode that semantic retrieval does not solve. A skill can be topically relevant but impossible under the current account state, so the system should remove it before the LLM ever sees it.

### 4. **What Carries the Signal in Pathology Foundation-Model Atlases? A Patient-Level Controlled Benchmark in Breast Cancer**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: This is the rare pathology foundation-model paper that attacks its own glamour stack. It rebuilds the claim around held-out patients and shows the signal is real, but the fancy Riemannian geometry and graph decoder are mostly dead weight.

### 5. **Measurement Without Validity: The Compounding Reliability Problem in Agentic AI Evaluation**

**Verdict:** strong framing runner-up.

Why it matters: The paper's best contribution is not a new benchmark but a harsher measurement lens. If task generation, user simulation, and judgment each leak validity, the benchmark score compounds that damage instead of averaging it away.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **Why Does the Future Branch? Identifiable Closure Tests for Stochastic Physical World Models**.

The paper attacks a genuinely important ambiguity in world modeling. A stochastic predictor may look well calibrated while hiding two very different stories: either the observation is missing state that would make the future more determinate, or the declared state is already complete and the world really does branch. Those imply different interventions. One calls for refinement, memory, or sensing. The other calls for preserving multiple futures. ClosurePairs gives a protocol for separating the two, then shows that the distinction changes downstream routing decisions even when total predictive variance is matched. That is exactly the kind of explicit-state versus real-stochasticity distinction cabbageland keeps caring about.

The other strong papers reinforce the same taste from different angles. **PMMC** makes memory access plans explicit before the query arrives. **Don't Offer What Can't Be Done** makes state-feasibility checks deterministic instead of hoping the model remembers them. **What Carries the Signal** forces an overdecorated pathology pipeline to compete against simpler controls. **Measurement Without Validity** argues that benchmark pipelines need the same suspicion turned on themselves.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Why Does the Future Branch?** is strongest because it shows that good predictive likelihood is not enough. The baseline lesson is severe: two systems with identical predictive distributions can require opposite interventions.

**PMMC** is strongest because it does not just say "better memory." The useful framing move is to shift part of multimodal memory reasoning from online retrieval into offline compilation plus execution-backed verification.

**Don't Offer What Can't Be Done** is strongest because it separates topical relevance from executability. The baseline lesson is that semantic tool retrieval is not a safe proxy for whether a production skill can actually run.

**What Carries the Signal** is strongest because it puts a fashionable image-genomics story under held-out patient controls and shows exactly where the signal stops. The baseline lesson is that driver-count gene lists and geometric stories are cheap unless they beat composition, scanner, and simple linear alternatives on held-out patients.

**Measurement Without Validity** is strongest as framing. The baseline lesson is that IRR, simulation calibration, and construct validity are not paperwork; they determine whether the score means much at all.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that if a hidden support structure matters, it should be represented or audited directly. World models should separate hidden-state aliasing from true process noise. Memory systems should compile evidence-access strategies rather than leaving everything to last-minute retrieval. Tool agents should gate impossible actions before the model sees them. Foundation-model biology claims should be tested against held-out patients and brutal competing controls. Benchmarks should report how valid the measurement pipeline is, not only the final number. The papers worth keeping are the ones that stop treating these support structures as implementation details and make them legible enough to contest.

- [PMMC note](../paper_notes/pmmc_prospective_multimodal_memory_compilation_long_term_lvlm_agents.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-16

## Theme

Today’s signal is **explicit structure being used as an operational contract rather than a branding layer**. The strongest paper is **Pinductor** because it turns language-model priors into executable POMDP induction under real partial observability instead of relying on privileged hidden-state access. **OpenSGA** is the best adjacent paper because it treats object-level correspondence as a reusable mapping and memory primitive rather than as a narrow registration trick. **Closing the Motion Execution Gap** is useful mainly as a systems reference for explicit constraint execution across embodiments.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in the prior scouting pass for this digest and was unavailable because the current environment is missing a Brave API key. I therefore used direct arXiv discovery plus accessible arXiv HTML and abstract pages. I inspected substantial arXiv HTML for **Learning POMDP World Models from Observations with Language-Model Priors**, **OpenSGA: Efficient 3D Scene Graph Alignment in the Open World**, and **Closing the Motion Execution Gap: From Semantic Motion Task Constraints to Kinematic Control**. My confidence is strongest on the high-level mechanism and weaker on appendix-level empirical details.

**Pinductor** is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is simple and strong: ask an LLM to propose executable POMDP code from a small number of observation-action-reward trajectories, then iteratively repair that code using a belief-based likelihood objective that does not require hidden-state supervision. That matters because a lot of recent LLM-for-world-model work quietly keeps privileged latent state around during learning. This paper explicitly removes that crutch.

**OpenSGA** is strong adjacent inspiration. The paper frames scene-graph alignment as a practical primitive for relocalization, map fusion, and persistent object memory. The mechanism is less interesting as pure graph neural-network novelty than as a clean multimodal matching stack: fuse vision-language, text, and geometry features, aggregate local context with distance-gated spatial attention, then solve association with a minimum-cost-flow allocator. The accompanying dataset expansion also matters because most prior scene-graph alignment work looks tiny and closed-set.

**Closing the Motion Execution Gap** is not a learning-heavy paper, but it is still useful. Its main contribution is to keep semantic motion constraints explicit all the way down to execution by combining Motion Statecharts, a differentiable kinematic world model that includes the environment, and linear model predictive control with jerk bounds. I do not think this is a breakthrough architecture paper, but it is a respectable rebuttal to the idea that high-level semantic task structure must collapse into brittle pose primitives.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Learning POMDP World Models from Observations with Language-Model Priors**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it uses language-model priors to induce executable latent-state world models without cheating through hidden-state supervision.

### 2. **OpenSGA: Efficient 3D Scene Graph Alignment in the Open World**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it treats object correspondence as a scalable memory and relocalization primitive, not just a geometry-only matching problem.

### 3. **Closing the Motion Execution Gap: From Semantic Motion Task Constraints to Kinematic Control**

**Verdict:** mostly systems reference, but worthwhile systems reference.

Why it matters: it keeps semantic constraints explicit through execution and shows a world-centric constraint stack transferring across eight robot platforms.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Pinductor.

The reason is not just that it says "POMDP" out loud. It actually tries to learn an explicit executable latent-state model from partial observations alone, which is the point where a lot of world-model rhetoric usually gets mushy. The useful mechanism is the repair loop: propose symbolic probabilistic code with an LLM, score it using likelihood under the beliefs induced by its own filtering dynamics, and iteratively refine the program without ever observing the true hidden state.

That makes the paper more interesting than standard "LLM writes environment code" work. It narrows the gap between symbolic model induction and genuinely partially observed control. The main caveat is that the experiments are in MiniGrid-like domains with compact latent structure, so this is still far from messy embodied deployment. But as a proof that language priors can substitute for some interaction while staying inside an auditable model class, it is a real result.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update is that **LLM-assisted world-model induction should be judged by whether it still works after privileged state access is removed**. Pinductor is useful precisely because it survives that harder regime, at least in small environments.

OpenSGA sharpens a different point. If we want long-lived scene memory for embodied agents, object-level correspondence needs to become a first-class primitive, not an afterthought attached to geometry registration. The paper also pressures prior alignment work by scaling both task coverage and category diversity enough that open-world claims are harder to fake.

The Motion Execution Gap paper mainly affects systems framing. It is a reminder that explicit symbolic-to-kinematic bridges are still alive, and in some cases more honest than asking a giant policy to absorb every semantic motion constraint implicitly.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Pinductor** because it uses language-model priors to induce executable POMDP world models without relying on privileged hidden-state labels. **OpenSGA** is the most useful adjacent paper because it treats multimodal scene-graph alignment as a scalable object-memory primitive for relocalization and map fusion. **Closing the Motion Execution Gap** is more engineering than conceptual leap, but it is good engineering in the right direction, explicit semantic constraints, explicit world models, and smoother execution rather than end-to-end mush. The broader lesson is that structure starts to matter when it constrains learning, memory, or control under the actual hard information regime, not when it is just decorative taxonomy.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-04

## Theme

Today's strongest pattern is **world models are becoming useful as evaluation instruments, but only when the representation makes the evaluation contract sharper**. **OSCAR** is the most relevant paper because it asks whether generated rollouts can rank real robot policies and makes the action interface explicit through cross-embodiment skeleton conditioning. **Generalization of World Models under Environmental Variability** is the best reality check because it shows that simulation policy win rate can point at the wrong model, while cross-environment reconstruction during self-supervised pretraining predicted real deployment better. **A 3D Isovist World Model** is the best adjacent representation paper because it predicts navigable negative space instead of photometric appearance and adds a writable map for cross-path consistency.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first, but the OpenClaw web search provider returned `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable, but fetching the selected AlphaXiv pages exposed only the shell page text rather than useful related-paper content. The arXiv export API also rate-limited or timed out, so discovery used general web search plus direct arXiv pages, followed by arXiv HTML and PDF inspection. That makes the scouting narrower than an ideal Brave-plus-AlphaXiv pass, but the preserved notes are not abstract-only.

I inspected arXiv HTML and PDFs for **OSCAR: Omni-Embodiment Action-Conditioned World Model for Robotics**, **Generalization of World Models under Environmental Variability for Vision-based Quadrotor Navigation**, **A 3D Isovist World Model: Revealing a City's Unseen Geometry and Its Emergent Cross-City Signature**, **GeoSem-WAM: Geometry- and Semantic-Aware World Action Models**, and **3DThinkVLA: Endowing Vision-Language-Action Models with Latent 3D Priors via 3D-Thinking-Guided Co-training**. The first three are preserved today. GeoSem-WAM and 3DThinkVLA look useful, but their central moves are closer to incremental training-time structure injection, so I am treating them as citation/background material rather than full notes today.

**OSCAR** is the most directly relevant paper. It finetunes Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B as an action-conditioned video world model, using 2D kinematic skeleton renderings as a unified conditioning representation across four robot embodiments and human hands. The useful claim is not merely that generated robot videos look better. The useful claim is that a generated-world policy-evaluation protocol on RoboArena correlates with real-world policy ranking, while the skeleton condition gives a better generalization/precision trade-off than latent action or robot-specific mesh renders.

**The quadrotor generalization study** is less flashy and probably more important for keeping later world-model claims honest. It trains DreamerV3-style world models under different environmental-randomness regimes, evaluates cross-environment reconstruction during self-supervised pretraining and policy performance after RL, then deploys every model on a real quadrotor. The sharp result is that the model that looked best in simulation RL failed in the harder real deployment, while models with better cross-environment SSL reconstruction transferred.

**A 3D Isovist World Model** is adjacent rather than directly robotic manipulation work, but it has one of the cleaner representation arguments of the week. It predicts the geometry of open navigable volume as a spherical depth map, not RGB appearance or flattened occupancy. It also makes persistent spatial memory explicit through a writable latent BEV map. The empirical claims are still modest, especially the spatial-map ablation, but the representation is conceptually crisp.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **OSCAR: Omni-Embodiment Action-Conditioned World Model for Robotics**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it treats generated robot rollouts as a policy-evaluation substrate and makes the action-conditioning interface explicit enough to transfer across embodiments.

### 2. **Generalization of World Models under Environmental Variability for Vision-based Quadrotor Navigation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as deployment and evaluation discipline.

Why it matters: it shows that world-model quality should be judged by cross-environment predictive robustness, not just by the policy that wins inside the simulator.

### 3. **A 3D Isovist World Model: Revealing a City's Unseen Geometry and Its Emergent Cross-City Signature**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it reframes an embodied world model around action-conditioned negative-space geometry, with an explicit persistent map, instead of photometric frame prediction.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** OSCAR.

The steal-worthy idea is the evaluation contract. OSCAR is not claiming that generated worlds are now perfect robot simulators. It narrows the job: given the first frame and a candidate action trajectory, generate a rollout good enough to compare policies against real RoboArena rankings. Skeleton conditioning matters because it says what the action is in a spatially aligned, texture-free, embodiment-flexible form. That is much healthier than hiding action in a latent and hoping the video model learns what motion means.

The quadrotor paper is nearly as important because it attacks a failure mode that will keep recurring: a world model can look good under the wrong validation signal. Its result suggests that self-supervised predictive generalization across environments may be a better deployment predictor than simulated RL success. That is a serious baseline-framing lesson.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**OSCAR** raises the bar for action-conditioned robot world models. It is no longer enough to show plausible videos. A serious paper should say how action is represented, whether that representation transfers across embodiments, and whether generated rollouts correlate with real policy outcomes.

**The quadrotor paper** raises the bar for sim-to-real world-model validation. If a paper reports strong simulation policy returns but never stress-tests predictive robustness under environment shift, its deployment claim should be treated as weak.

**The isovist paper** is not a baseline reset for robotics, but it is a framing correction. For navigation, the right predictive target may be the geometry of reachable open space rather than appearance. The paper's own evidence is still early, but the representation choice is cleaner than most "world model" branding.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **OSCAR** because it makes generated robot worlds answer an evaluation question rather than just a visual-fidelity question. The most important cautionary paper is the **quadrotor generalization study**, which shows that the validation metric deciding model selection can matter more than the simulator leaderboard. The best adjacent representation paper is **A 3D Isovist World Model**, because it predicts the negative space an agent moves through and gives that geometry a persistent writable memory. The common lesson is simple: world models earn their name when their state or conditioning interface changes what can be tested, transferred, or trusted.

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-20

## Theme

Today’s best papers all replace a mushy interface with a grounded one. GWM replaces goal-image matching with language-grounded latent planning. 3D-ALP replaces reactive frame-only control with persistent anchored scene memory. LaviGen replaces text-as-layout with native-3D autoregressive scene updates. Different domains, same pattern: if the representation and objective actually live in the right space, the downstream system gets less fake and more controllable.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv search plus primary-source inspection. I inspected the abstract, introduction, method framing, and accessible early-results sections for **Grounded World Model for Semantically Generalizable Planning**, **3D-Anchored Lookahead Planning for Persistent Robotic Scene Memory via World-Model-Based MCTS**, and **Repurposing 3D Generative Model for Autoregressive Layout Generation**. For GWM and LaviGen I had access to the arXiv HTML text and enough method detail to be reasonably confident about the mechanism. For 3D-ALP I inspected the abstract plus PDF text extraction from the first several pages, so confidence is solid on the core architecture and headline ablations, but weaker on appendix-level implementation details.

The strongest paper today is **Grounded World Model for Semantically Generalizable Planning**. Its useful move is not just “language-condition the world model.” The sharper claim is that semantic understanding and action generation should stay factored: keep a pretrained retrieval model’s aligned vision-language space frozen, learn only the transition dynamics inside that space, and use MPC to pick demonstrated motions whose predicted future best matches the instruction embedding. That is a real mechanism, and it also doubles as an indictment of many VLA papers whose semantic generalization is mostly assumed rather than tested.

**3D-Anchored Lookahead Planning for Persistent Robotic Scene Memory via World-Model-Based MCTS** is narrower and less mature, but still genuinely useful. Its core contribution is simple and good: maintain a persistent camera-to-world anchor that survives occlusion, then plan in that anchored space with a world-model oracle instead of pretending the current frame is enough. The paper is a bit small and benchmark-light, but at least it attacks a real architectural failure mode rather than waving at “reasoning.”

**Repurposing 3D Generative Model for Autoregressive Layout Generation** is the adjacent graphics paper worth keeping. It is not a world model or robotics paper, but it does make a transferable representational point: if layout generation is fundamentally a 3D geometric process, stop routing it through text-like coordinate strings or 2D image optimization and use native 3D priors directly.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Grounded World Model for Semantically Generalizable Planning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it turns semantic instruction following into a planning-and-scoring problem inside a frozen multimodal retrieval space, instead of hoping an end-to-end VLA will keep its pretrained world knowledge after finetuning.

### 2. **3D-Anchored Lookahead Planning for Persistent Robotic Scene Memory via World-Model-Based MCTS**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it gives persistent spatial memory an explicit anchor in SE(3) rather than treating occlusion robustness as something a reactive policy should somehow absorb implicitly.

### 3. **Repurposing 3D Generative Model for Autoregressive Layout Generation**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it argues, correctly, that 3D layout generation should happen in native 3D space if we actually care about geometry and physical plausibility.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** Grounded World Model for Semantically Generalizable Planning.

The reason is that it cleanly separates three things that recent VLA work often tangles together: semantic grounding, action proposal, and dynamics prediction. The paper’s bet is that if you keep the pretrained multimodal embedding space intact and train only the transition model in that space, you preserve open-world semantics better than you do by finetuning a monolithic policy. Whether the exact benchmark is fully representative or not, that is a strong design pattern for cabbageland: use explicit interfaces between semantics, state prediction, and control, then test the claimed generalization directly.

3D-ALP is the more direct memory/planning paper. Its persistent anchor is mechanically simple but conceptually right, and it highlights how often “long-horizon reasoning” claims are really just missing persistent state. LaviGen is more adjacent, but the representational lesson is still useful: if the task is geometric, make the model allocate and update geometry rather than a lossy proxy language for geometry.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

GWM is framing pressure on standard VLA evaluation. Its WISER benchmark is basically asking a question many VLA papers avoid: do these systems actually inherit semantic world knowledge in a way that survives grounding to action, or do they mostly memorize language-task bindings and visual shortcuts? If the reported gap holds up, some current VLA success stories are less about semantic generalization than about closed-distribution competence.

3D-ALP is pressure on reactive-policy thinking in manipulation. It does not introduce a grand new foundation model, but it makes the architectural point that object permanence should be built into the planner rather than hoped for in the policy weights.

LaviGen is pressure on layout-as-language work that gets semantics but keeps failing basic physical plausibility. The novelty is not “use diffusion somewhere.” The novelty is using structure-level 3D priors as the actual workspace for autoregressive scene updates.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that explicit structure matters most when it is attached to the right interface. Put semantics in a language-aligned retrieval space and learn dynamics there, as GWM does. Put memory in a persistent spatial anchor, as 3D-ALP does. Put layout reasoning in native 3D geometry rather than proxy text or 2D heuristics, as LaviGen does. That is the version of structure worth caring about, not decorative modularity that leaves the real computation unchanged.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-09

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all attack the same flattering lie: a system can look evidence-grounded, calibrated, or realistic while the actual support path is fake, weak, or missing. **HERALD** says proof-of-retrieval rewards are not trustworthy unless they survive citation-laundering attacks, not just fake-ID checks. **The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use** says tool calls are not evidence use unless the gain survives causal intervention on what the model actually sees. **CalibForge** says terminal-task corpora should be calibrated against solver strength instead of mass-produced and prayed over. **Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks** says a benchmark that clears a utility threshold can still be structurally fake. **Does FLAIR super-resolution erase or hallucinate small white-matter lesions?** says a prettier reconstruction is not the same thing as lesion-faithful imaging.

## Short overview

This run used direct arXiv recent-page inspection on Sunday, August 9, 2026, focusing on the Friday, August 7, 2026 submission batch because arXiv had no newer Sunday batch to inspect. I did the required non-robotics pass across agent reliability, calibration, synthetic-clinical benchmarks, and neuro/medical-imaging papers rather than defaulting into another robotics pile. I inspected arXiv HTML full text for all five ranked papers below.

The top four are preserve-worthy and get notes. The FLAIR lesion paper is the best adjacent medical runner-up: the result is useful and the warning is real, but it is more of a sharp validation study than a reusable new mechanism. **Most relevant today:** **HERALD**. It has the right cabbageland instinct: do not reward a retrieval agent for looking grounded if a counterfactual citation swap can preserve the answer while severing the evidence path.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **HERALD: Counterfactual Audits and Minimal Repairs for Proof-of-Retrieval Rewards**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It turns retrieval-grounding rewards into something falsifiable. The useful move is a paired counterfactual audit that isolates citation laundering and then asks for the smallest repair that actually kills the exploit.

### 2. **The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It refuses to equate tool invocation with evidence use. The useful move is a three-level causal decomposition that separates policy choice, trajectory corruption, and step-level visual evidence gain.

### 3. **CalibForge: Adversarial Solver Calibration for Scaling Learnable Terminal Tasks**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It treats synthetic task generation as a calibration problem against solver ability, not a volume problem. The useful move is the author-solver revision loop with stronger/weaker and multi-solver retention criteria.

### 4. **Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks Under Utility Constraints**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It is a good benchmark-design paper because it refuses the lazy inference that "downstream utility passed, therefore the benchmark is realistic." The useful move is deterministic realism-targeted revision under an explicit utility floor, with a naive densification control to show what fake improvement looks like.

### 5. **Does FLAIR super-resolution erase or hallucinate small white-matter lesions?**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: It is a clean medical-imaging warning shot. The dominant SR failure is not hallucinating lesions out of nowhere but erasing small real ones, which is exactly the kind of upstream image-enhancement failure that can flatter downstream pipelines.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **HERALD**.

This is the sharpest direct paper in the batch because it attacks a failure mode agent people routinely wave away. A retrieval answer can look impeccably grounded while its citation path is fake in the only way that matters: the cited corpus item is real, but it was never retrieved, so the support chain is decorative. HERALD does not answer that with more vibes, more aggregate reward, or more heuristic overlap checks. It defines exact counterfactual edits on saved trajectories, measures attack success rate under paired scoring, and then identifies the observed inclusion-minimal repair: the single targeted strengthening `L` that kills isolated laundering where broader bundles were previously treated as necessary. That is good scientific hygiene and good agent taste. It separates scorer robustness from selection stability, and it shows why a verifier patch should be justified by the exploit class it actually closes.

The rest of the batch reinforces the same lesson from adjacent angles. **Visual Tool-Use** shows that a tool-use gain can be mostly non-visual shortcutting. **CalibForge** shows that a synthetic task set can look productive while being badly miscalibrated to the solver. **Utility-Constrained Clinical Benchmarks** shows that utility metrics can coexist with absurd templating and sparsity. **FLAIR super-resolution** shows that perceptual recovery can still destroy the clinically important small structures.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**HERALD** is strongest because it finds the real verifier gap instead of a straw-man one. Outcome-only rewards collapse completely, exact controls already kill some easy loopholes, but citation laundering still survives unless the reward explicitly checks whether cited evidence was actually retrieved. The important result is not just that `R[L]` reaches zero observed isolated-laundering success while broader hardening is non-monotone. It is that the paper explains why broader bundles can cancel under selection and why the targeted repair is the right one to keep.

**The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use** is strongest because it decomposes an accuracy bump into causal paths instead of calling the whole bump "evidence use." The result is ugly in a useful way: only 45.95% of the apparent tool-use gain comes from actual visual evidence, while 54.05% comes from correlated non-visual factors. The paper also gives two concrete miscalibration modes worth stealing as diagnostics: Calling Without Looking and Looking Without Planning.

**CalibForge** is strongest because it changes the unit of supervision quality. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, its 30B and 35B variants reach 32.58% and 47.57%, beating the strongest shared-protocol baselines by 6.36 and 6.75 points. That matters less as another leaderboard jump than as evidence that solver-relative task calibration produces better synthetic supervision than just scraping together more terminal tasks.

**Utility-Constrained Clinical Benchmarks** is strongest because the baseline pathology is embarrassingly concrete: 79.44% sampled-pair missingness, only 12.75% actionable rows, 38.94% zero-actionable patients, and 100% top-three token concentration. That is a benchmark that can pass utility checks while still barely resembling the stated domain. The deterministic revisions improve realism while the dense control shows how easy it is to preserve fake templating under superficial densification.

**FLAIR super-resolution** is strongest because it narrows the imaging question to the clinically relevant object. The main failure is lesion erasure, not hallucination, and ECLARE beats the INR plus cubic interpolation on recovering small-lesion signal. That is a better result than the usual perceptual-quality theater, even if the study is still simulated and segmenter-dependent.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that systems get overcredited when a visible artifact is allowed to impersonate the support path that supposedly produced it. A citation is not retrieval evidence unless the cited passage was actually retrieved. A tool trace is not visual reasoning unless causal interventions show the answer changed because of what was seen. A synthetic benchmark is not realistic because downstream utility cleared a threshold. A sharper-looking MRI is not lesion-faithful because it looks nicer. The useful papers are the ones that replace flattering end metrics with explicit path checks, targeted audits, or solver-relative calibration.

- [Visual Tool-Use note](../paper_notes/visual_tool_use_causal_audit.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-30

## Theme

Today’s useful pattern is **making memory or attribution explicit enough that you can inspect the failure mode instead of blaming “context length” or “generalization” in the abstract**. The strongest paper is **SAM** because it turns long-horizon agent history into a page-and-cue memory system with a concrete write/read contract and then optimizes that contract directly. **Embodied Interpretability** is the best adjacent paper because it gives a causal-ish diagnostic for whether a VLA policy is acting on the right pixels. **Context-Aligned Medical Reasoning** is interesting mainly as a safety-and-grounding protocol paper, but the mechanism is lighter and the gains are modest.

## Short overview

Brave Search was not available as a configured tool surface in this run, and AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable here, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv papers plus direct PDF inspection.

I inspected full paper PDFs for **SAM: State-Adaptive Memory for Long-Horizon Reasoning Agent**, **Embodied Interpretability: Linking Causal Understanding to Generalization in Vision-Language-Action Models**, and **Towards Responsible Multimodal Medical Reasoning via Context-Aligned Vision-Language Models**. Confidence is highest for SAM and Embodied Interpretability because the core mechanism and evaluation are easy to recover from the paper body. The medical paper is readable and directionally sensible, but I am less convinced that the method is strong enough to treat as a major mechanism paper.

**SAM** is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is simple and real: instead of compressing the past into one rolling summary or blindly retrieving old snippets, it stores trajectory history as raw pages plus lightweight memory cues that stay in context as handles. When the agent later needs something, it chooses cues based on its current intent, then the memory model reconstructs support from the corresponding raw pages. That is a cleaner contract than most “agent memory” work, because the summary is not pretending to be the memory itself.

The second useful part is that SAM is trained as a memory module rather than hand-waved as prompting. The authors supervise both page summarization and recall against stronger frontier models, then add a tree-structured RL objective so individual memory actions get credit instead of only the final task outcome. I do not love the dependence on frontier-model committees for supervision and reward, but the system at least knows what component is being optimized.

**Embodied Interpretability** is adjacent rather than central, but still worth keeping. It introduces the Interventional Significance Score, which estimates how much masking a visual region changes the action prediction, and then compresses that into a Nuisance Mass Ratio measuring how much causally significant saliency lands on irrelevant regions. The strongest result is not interpretability theater, it is that higher nuisance attribution predicts worse out-of-distribution task success.

I would not oversell the causal language here. The method is still an interventional proxy based on masking and action divergence under teacher forcing, not a full causal identification of what the robot “really reasons about.” But as a diagnostic for spurious visual dependence in VLA policies, it seems more serious than reading off attention maps and calling it understanding.

**Context-Aligned Medical Reasoning** is the day’s weaker keep-in-view paper. It wraps a frozen Qwen2-VL model with radiomic features, Grad-CAM statistics, vocabulary cues, and a structured safety-conscious output format. That is directionally aligned with explicit evidence checking, but the method looks more like tool-augmented protocol engineering than a deep representational advance. I would cite it as an example of forcing multi-evidence agreement, not as a breakthrough.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **SAM: State-Adaptive Memory for Long-Horizon Reasoning Agent**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives memory a concrete object model, raw pages plus compact cues, then trains the read/write behavior instead of pretending retrieval or summarization alone solved long-horizon reasoning.

### 2. **Embodied Interpretability: Linking Causal Understanding to Generalization in Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it offers a plausible diagnostic for whether a VLA policy is relying on nuisance visual evidence, and shows that this diagnostic tracks OOD performance.

### 3. **Towards Responsible Multimodal Medical Reasoning via Context-Aligned Vision-Language Models**

**Verdict:** mostly citation and framing material.

Why it matters: it is a decent example of enforcing evidence agreement and uncertainty structure around a frozen VLM, but the mechanism is lightweight and the empirical jump is not huge.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** SAM.

The useful part is not just “memory helps agents.” The useful part is the representation choice. Past interaction is split into raw pages that preserve detail and memory cues that remain in-context as durable handles. That means the system does not have to choose between full-history bloat and lossy rolling summaries. It can defer reconstruction until the current intent makes specific old evidence worth reviving.

That design also exposes a better decomposition boundary for future work. The agent backbone stays frozen. The memory module is the component that writes cues and reconstructs recall. So when performance changes, the paper can at least claim the gain came from memory behavior rather than yet another full-stack soup of prompting, retrieval, and backbone changes.

My confidence is fairly good because I inspected the paper body and main results table. My main uncertainty is practical: I have not independently stress-tested whether the gains would survive outside their benchmark mix, or how brittle the memory module becomes when the cue quality degrades.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**SAM** strengthens an argument we keep making: long-horizon agent failure is not only a context-window problem, it is an explicit memory-interface problem. A page-and-cue memory with intent-conditioned reconstruction is a stronger baseline than naive summarize-or-retrieve systems.

**Embodied Interpretability** is useful for baseline pressure in robotics. If nuisance-attribution scores reliably track OOD failure, then future VLA papers should not get away with reporting only task success while ignoring what visual evidence the policy actually uses.

**Context-Aligned Medical Reasoning** is mostly framing pressure. It says medical multimodal systems should justify outputs across multiple evidence channels and include explicit uncertainty and safety notes. That is a sensible protocol demand, but the current implementation does not look like a big mechanism leap.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The strongest paper today is **SAM** because it treats memory as a real interface with explicit write and read behavior: compress to cues, keep raw pages, reconstruct by current intent. **Embodied Interpretability** is the best adjacent paper because it turns spurious visual reliance into a measurable diagnostic that actually predicts generalization. **Context-Aligned Medical Reasoning** is worth remembering as a safety-oriented evidence-checking wrapper, but it feels more like disciplined scaffolding around a frozen VLM than a major new model idea. The common lesson is that explicit structure matters when it changes what gets stored, recalled, or causally attended to, not when it is just a nicer story wrapped around the same latent mush.

## Detailed notes

- [SAM note](../paper_notes/sam_state_adaptive_memory_for_long_horizon_reasoning_agent.md)
- [Embodied Interpretability note](../paper_notes/embodied_interpretability_linking_causal_understanding_to_generalization_in_vision_language_action_models.md)

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the cleanest terminal-agent synthesis paper in the batch because it makes a simple but usually hidden rule explicit: the instruction, initialized environment, reference solution, and verifier need to be generated from the same realized executable state, not from loosely aligned intermediate drafts. FACET validates **6,078** tasks with an average of **22.77** executable checks per task, then uses **1.2K** successful trajectories to fine-tune Qwen3.5 models. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, the resulting gains are real and data-efficient: **+7.12** for 4B, **+8.24** for 9B, and **+6.75** for 27B, with the 27B model reaching **47.57**, only **1.49** points below a **397B** Qwen row under the same evaluation setting.

### 2. **ReWEIGH the Evidence: Calibrating Token-Level Ordinal Visual Evidence to Mitigate Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This is one of the best hallucination-mitigation papers in the batch because it asks the right question at decode time: not whether the model is confident, and not where attention points, but whether the current candidate token has unusually weak support in the internal visual states. ReWEIGH uses rank-based evidence pooling plus token-specific calibration from unlabeled images, and it does so without retraining. Across four 7B backbones it cuts hallucinated object mentions by up to **21.3%** with only **1.33%** average added latency per token, and the reductions extend across **11** models spanning **6** architecture families up to **32B**.

### 3. **Bridge Graphical Models: Coupling, Projection, and Current-Preserving Dynamics for Generative Modeling**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: This paper is valuable because it isolates a structural bottleneck that continuous-time generative papers often blur away: the bridge used during training can condition on endpoints, but the deployed sampler only sees current state and time. The Markovization gap turns that compression loss into a measurable design object before training. On a CIFAR-10 proxy diagnostic computed in about **9 minutes** on CPU, straight independent coupling scores **3.25** while straight minibatch OT scores **2.34**; the lower-gap choice then also lowers downstream pilot train loss from **0.182** to **0.168** and FID from **50.48** to **49.17**. On Fashion-MNIST the same ranking is cleaner, with FID dropping from **30.14** to **21.96**.

### 4. **A Jagged Frontier: Evaluating Robustness of Code Agents to Semantics-Preserving Transformations**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the strongest code-agent robustness paper in the batch because it does not confuse stochastic variance with robustness loss. The authors build a library of **14** semantics-preserving transformations, evaluate **54** SWE-bench instances, and use paired repeated runs to isolate perturbation effects from normal agent randomness. The average resolve-rate degradation is modest but real, reaching **6.7** percentage points in the worst affected configurations, with statistically significant drops in **6 of 16** scaffold-model-dataset combinations. The more important result is structural: robustness rankings do not transfer across scaffolds, and even when solve rate barely moves, cost can still rise by up to **22.9%**.

### 5. **Harness Continual Learning: Continual Adaptation Beyond Model Parameters**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration, not yet preserve-worthy.

Why it matters: This paper makes the right conceptual move by treating prompts, memories, capability maps, and routers as an evolving agent state around a frozen model rather than pretending all continual learning lives in weights. Its guarded update-and-commit framing is also sensible. The results are nontrivial: textual-reasoning final average rises from **45.50%** zero-shot to **64.70%** under the plastic profile with only **0.07** average forgetting, and multimodal final average rises from **39.40%** to **68.92%** under the stability profile. It stays below the preserve bar because the abstraction is broad enough to hide many degrees of freedom, and the evidence still lives inside a fairly curated harness/task ecology rather than a harsher deployment setting.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **FACET**.

It makes the most reusable systems claim in the batch: if the artifact bundle does not share a realized executable state, then both training data and evaluation numbers get polluted by bookkeeping drift. The same severe taste echoes through the rest of the digest. **ReWEIGH** says candidate confidence is not the same thing as candidate evidence. **Bridge Graphical Models** says endpoint-conditioned bridge structure is not the same thing as what a Markov decoder can recover from current state. **Jagged Frontier** says semantic equivalence for a repository is not semantic equivalence for a scaffolded agent. Same lesson all day: use the operative state, not the decorative proxy.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**FACET** matters because it turns shared executable state into the controlled variable instead of leaving it as invisible synthetic-data plumbing.

**ReWEIGH** matters because it replaces generic confidence heuristics with candidate-specific ordinal evidence calibrated per token.

**Bridge Graphical Models** matters because it reframes continuous-time generative design around an irreducible bridge-to-Markov compression gap that can be estimated before training.

**A Jagged Frontier** matters because it shows robustness is jointly a property of model, scaffold, and workload, not a scalar trait of the model alone.

**Harness Continual Learning** matters because it formalizes harness-level forgetting and makes external-state retention an explicit deployment decision rather than an accidental side effect.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The August 20 lesson is that a system should be evaluated against the state it can actually act on, not against the larger object we casually say it is using. FACET grounds task artifacts in one realized container state. ReWEIGH grounds candidate tokens in token-specific visual evidence rather than uncalibrated confidence. Bridge Graphical Models grounds generative design in the information a Markov sampler can truly access after endpoint compression. Jagged Frontier grounds robustness in paired perturbation tests rather than headline benchmark rows. Harness Continual Learning grounds continual adaptation in mutable external state rather than frozen slogans about learning. Same underlying rule: stop awarding mechanism credit to proxies that do not survive contact with the actual operative state.
