# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-01

## Theme

Today’s useful pattern is explicit scene structure doing practical work instead of being left as decorative latent mush. The best paper builds occupancy as a layered map with explicit geometry and semantics, and the best adjacent paper reconstructs whole multi-object scenes by forcing shape and pose to be solved jointly rather than as a brittle handoff between modules.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. I then scouted recent arXiv category listings directly and inspected the abstract plus substantial method text from arXiv HTML pages for **FreeOcc: Training-Free Embodied Open-Vocabulary Occupancy Prediction**, **Reconstruction by Generation: 3D Multi-Object Scene Reconstruction from Sparse Observations**, **LaST-R1: Reinforcing Action via Adaptive Physical Latent Reasoning for VLA Models**, and **HERMES++: Toward a Unified Driving World Model for 3D Scene Understanding and Generation**.

**FreeOcc** is the strongest direct hit. It is not flashy, but it has a clean contract: SLAM for pose and sparse geometry, Gaussian mapping for dense structure, VLM features for open-vocabulary semantics, then probabilistic projection into occupancy. That is exactly the sort of explicit intermediate state that can matter for embodied systems.

**RecGen** is the best adjacent paper. It matters less as a world-model paper than as scene-construction infrastructure for robotics and simulation. The real contribution is not generic “3D generation,” but joint probabilistic estimation of shape and pose for occluded multi-object scenes, plus synthetic training that actually reflects partial visibility instead of pretending objects are always cleanly exposed.

**LaST-R1** is the most obviously on-topic VLA paper, but it survives only as a cautious mention. I inspected substantial method text, and there is a real algorithmic move in jointly optimizing latent reasoning tokens and actions with RL. Still, the framing is heavy on “latent chain of thought” rhetoric, and I am not yet convinced the latent reasoning variables are structurally clear enough to count as more than better hidden-state shaping.

**HERMES++** looks mostly like citation material today. It is an extended version of an earlier unified driving paper, and while the BEV-to-LLM bridge plus geometric regularization are respectable, the paper feels more like a competent integration pass than a fresh mechanism note I need to preserve right now.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **FreeOcc: Training-Free Embodied Open-Vocabulary Occupancy Prediction**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it replaces annotation-heavy occupancy learning with an explicit streaming stack that builds geometry and semantics incrementally, and it does so in a form that is actually legible enough to reason about.

### 2. **Reconstruction by Generation: 3D Multi-Object Scene Reconstruction from Sparse Observations**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it treats scene reconstruction as a joint shape-and-pose inference problem under occlusion, which is a more honest formulation than generating a pretty object first and hoping registration fixes the rest.

### 3. **LaST-R1: Reinforcing Action via Adaptive Physical Latent Reasoning for VLA Models**

**Verdict:** skimmable, with one idea worth tracking.

Why it matters: the LAPO training rule is a real design contribution, but the rest still feels too close to rewarding a hidden scratchpad and calling that physical reasoning.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** FreeOcc.

The useful thing here is not merely that it is training-free. The useful thing is the decomposition. FreeOcc does not pretend one learned blob should solve mapping, semantics, pose estimation, and occupancy completion all at once. It keeps a sequence of explicit intermediate representations: SLAM state, Gaussian map, language-aligned Gaussian semantics, then occupancy.

That interface discipline matters. Occupancy is not just a visualization target. It is directly tied to collision checking, navigation, and action feasibility. If a system claims to reason about embodied space, having an explicit occupancy-like state is often more actionable than another latent feature field whose geometric commitments are murky.

The main caveat is that FreeOcc is still a pipeline, not a learned integrated agent architecture. But as a design pattern, it is strong. It says some forms of generalization are better bought by explicit structure plus good priors than by yet another supervised occupancy network.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

FreeOcc is a useful challenge to the assumption that occupancy prediction must be a heavily supervised learning problem. If a learned occupancy model cannot clearly beat a well-assembled training-free pipeline with explicit geometry, semantics, and global consistency, that should lower our respect for the learned model’s claimed necessity.

RecGen sharpens a different baseline question. For digital-twin creation and robotics simulation assets, we should be suspicious of pipelines that separate shape generation from pose registration and then celebrate robustness. RecGen’s joint estimation framing is a stronger default baseline whenever occlusion and symmetry are central.

LaST-R1 mostly affects framing rather than conviction. It suggests RL for VLA systems might profit from optimizing hidden reasoning variables as well as actions. But it also highlights a recurring problem in this area: once “latent reasoning” becomes hard to inspect, papers can smuggle ordinary representation learning back in under a more glamorous name.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The strongest work today gets value by making internal structure more explicit and operational. FreeOcc builds a layered embodied map that stays close to actionable geometry. RecGen treats reconstruction as joint scene inference rather than staged cleanup. LaST-R1 contributes a potentially useful RL interface for hidden reasoning, but it still has not convinced me that latent thought is more than a better-trained internal workspace. The general lesson is simple: when a paper introduces structure, ask whether the structure carries real downstream obligations like occupancy, pose, or action conditioning. If not, it may just be renamed mush.

## Detailed notes

- [RecGen note](../paper_notes/recgen_multi_object_scene_reconstruction_from_sparse_observations.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-13

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **trust and memory need explicit budgets**. There does not appear to be a fresh Saturday arXiv batch in the scoped robotics/CV/AI categories, so today's scan widened across the current week and avoided papers already preserved in the June 10-12 digests. **Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon** is the strongest paper because it turns world-model trust into a predictable-horizon certificate rather than an average rollout score. **Action-Effect Memory Pretraining** is the best practical robotics note because it learns a compact action-conditioned history state before policy training. **Learning What to Remember** is adjacent but useful: it makes the forgetting decision blind to future queries and learns a multi-factor value for retention rather than leaning on recency or query similarity.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level. The arXiv API query for `submittedDate:[202606120000 TO 202606132359]` over the relevant AI/CV/robotics categories returned no entries, so discovery quality today is a current-week fallback rather than a true new-Saturday batch. I used arXiv API search plus direct arXiv PDFs, and inspected extracted full PDFs for **Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon: Certified Predictability for Equivariant World Models**, **Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory**, **Bounding Boxes as Goals: Language-Conditioned Grasping via Neuro-Symbolic Planning**, **Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation**, **ProPlay: Procedural World Models for Self-Evolving LLM Agents**, **TetherCache: Stabilizing Autoregressive Long-Form Video Generation with Gated Recall and Trusted Alignment**, and **MoVerse: Real-Time Video World Modeling with Panoramic Gaussian Scaffold**. Scale Buys and AEM are preserved today.

**Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon** is the strongest direct hit. The paper argues that an equivariant latent world model can certify how far a rollout remains trustworthy: exact equivariance makes rollout error constant over symmetry orbits, while approximate equivariance yields a finite per-channel horizon controlled by the latent predictor's Lyapunov spectrum. The best idea is the distinction between a universal audit and an a-priori guarantee. Any smooth latent loop can be spectrally audited, but exact structure is what makes the number trustworthy without a held-out divergence check. I did not independently verify the proofs, so the note preserves the framing and caveats rather than treating the theorem stack as settled law.

**Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation** is the best robot-memory note. AEM interleaves visual and action tokens, masks aligned action-effect timesteps, and trains a Mamba encoder to compress history into the encoded final vision token. That one vector is then concatenated with current perception inside Diffusion Policy or ManiFlow. The results are useful because the paper compares against no-history policies, direct DINOv2 feature stacking, randomized scenes, and memory-dependent tasks. The caveat is that the real-world result prose has inconsistent averages, so I trust the direction more than every exact margin.

**Learning What to Remember** is adjacent inspiration for long-running agents. Its useful point is methodological: if a retention policy scores memory relevance against the held-out future question, it is measuring retrieval with an oracle, not forgetting. In the blind consolidation regime, a learned multi-factor value over reliability, emotion, self/user relevance, and goal/session relevance beats recency and single-factor policies on LongMemEval gold-evidence retention. I am not preserving a separate note today because the evaluation is still retention-only, three of the seven factors are inert in the API-free setup, and final QA/task return is left for follow-up. Still, the oracle-vs-blind distinction is worth remembering.

**MoVerse** is the strongest 3D adjacent paper. It turns a single narrow-FOV image into a gravity-aligned panorama, lifts it into a persistent panoramic 3D Gaussian scaffold, and uses a distilled causal video renderer for interactive roaming. The representation lesson is excellent: keep long-range spatial memory in explicit geometry and let the video model repair local rendering quality. I am not preserving it today only because the paper is mostly a large staged system with qualitative-heavy evidence, while today's two kept papers are sharper for trust and robot-memory interfaces.

**TetherCache** is useful citation material for long-form video/world-model memory. Its sink/memory/recent cache split, attention-diversity recall, and trusted statistic alignment are sensible for drift-resistant autoregressive video. It is less central to cabbageland today because the mechanism is cache management for generation rather than embodied state or planning.

**ProPlay** is useful agent-memory/planning material. It builds a procedure graph with reliability records, preplays likely procedural trajectories, and updates the graph after environment feedback. The idea is aligned with procedural world models for LLM agents, but the abstraction remains natural-language procedural guidance over public text/game benchmarks, not a stronger direct hit than today's preserved papers.

**Bounding Boxes as Goals** is mostly citation material. It compiles language into bounding-box goal states and uses GroundingDINO plus closed-loop proportional control. The explicit goal-state interface is nice, but the evaluated robot task is still mostly grasp-and-lift; full end-to-end sorting and goal-similarity verification are left to future work.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon: Certified Predictability for Equivariant World Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it frames world-model trust as a local, horizon-priced certificate, with a clean separation between structure-backed guarantees and cross-validated audits.

### 2. **Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it makes robot memory a pretrained action-effect representation with a small downstream interface, instead of raw frame stacking or policy-time recurrence by hope.

### 3. **Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it correctly separates forgetting from retrieval by forbidding the consolidation policy from peeking at the future query, then learns a value signal for what survives memory budget pressure.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon.

The steal-worthy idea is to make trust an object in the model interface. A world model used for planning should expose when it is calibrated, when it is optimistic, when it should abstain, and how quickly its rollout horizon decays under the demanded tolerance. If that number is backed by exact structure, it may be usable a priori. If it comes from a generic dense latent loop, it needs cross-validation.

AEM adds the practical robot-memory companion. The action history should not be a pile of frames for the policy to sift through. If the robot needs temporal state, pretrain a compact action-effect representation and feed it to the policy as a deliberate interface.

Learning What to Remember adds the agent-memory companion. Forgetting policies should be evaluated under the information available at consolidation time. Anything that scores against a future query is measuring retrieval, not memory survival.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Scale Buys Interpolation** raises the bar for world-model trust claims. Average error, model size, and plausible rollouts are not enough; a serious planner-facing model should report a horizon, an abstention region, or at least a cross-validated latent audit.

**AEM** raises the baseline for manipulation-memory papers. Direct history stacking and single-frame visual pretraining are weak baselines when the claimed problem is partial observability or task phase. A better baseline should compress action-conditioned history under a comparable latency budget.

**Learning What to Remember** raises a useful evaluation warning for agent memory. Query-defined gold evidence can create an oracle retrieval ceiling that hides whether the memory system made a good forgetting decision earlier.

**MoVerse** is useful for 3D world-model framing: explicit geometry should carry persistent spatial memory, while generative video handles perceptual repair. That is a cleaner decomposition than asking a video model to remember the whole world in hidden state.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon** because it gives world-model trust a shape: a per-situation horizon that structure can certify and generic latents must cross-check. **Action-Effect Memory Pretraining** is the robot-memory note to keep because it compresses vision-action history into a small pretrained state that downstream policies can actually use. **Learning What to Remember** is the agent-memory warning label: do not evaluate forgetting with future-query information. The common lesson is that long-horizon systems need explicit budget interfaces, whether the budget is rollout trust, history length, or memory survival.

## Detailed notes

- [Action-Effect Memory Pretraining note](../paper_notes/action_effect_memory_pretraining_robot_manipulation.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-27

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all attack the same lie from different angles: a system claims to have state, safety, or planning competence, but the contract that makes that claim real is either missing or wrong. **Persistent Computational State** says some world-model "memory failures" are really serving failures caused by stateless request handling. **Self-Poisoning in Adaptive Out-of-Distribution Detection** says adaptive novelty detectors collapse unless the admission rule is certified against a frozen reference. **Learning on the Job** says deployment feedback only becomes capability if it is distilled into reusable rules instead of being discarded after each episode. **Securing Multimodal AI through Internal Information Decomposition** says multimodal safety should inspect the fusion process rather than just prompt surfaces. **On the Identifiability of Controlled World Models** says action-conditioned latent prediction is not enough if the learned transition is only valid on-policy and becomes untrustworthy off-support.

## Short overview

I checked the live `new` arXiv pages for `cs.AI`, `cs.CV`, `cs.LG`, `cs.RO`, `q-bio.NC`, and `eess.IV` on Monday, July 27, 2026. Brave Search was attempted first through the Brave API and failed with `HTTP 422` because the required `x-subscription-token` header is missing in this environment, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv browsing plus primary-source inspection through the arXiv abstract and HTML pages.

This run also did the explicit non-robotics pass the repo asks for. That surfaced papers like **Atlas 2** and the small-VLM confidence study, but the five below were stronger on mechanism, control-surface clarity, and future usefulness. All five are preserve-worthy notes. The top three are the clear keeps.

**Persistent Computational State** is the most relevant paper today. The useful insult is that several recent world-model papers blamed the model for losing state when the runtime was the thing throwing the state away.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Persistent Computational State: A Session-Centric Runtime for Generative World Models**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is one of the sharper recent world-model papers because it relocates the failure to the correct layer. The authors show byte-identical restore on three different model families, with checkpoint and restore costing `0.012 ms` against a `1.85 s` generation step, then show that once memory pressure matters the right eviction rule is relevance, not recency. If that result survives broader replication, a chunk of recent "persistent world model" work was diagnosing the runtime as if it were the model.

### 2. **Self-Poisoning in Adaptive Out-of-Distribution Detection: A Sharp-Threshold Theory and Certified Label-Free Calibration**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This paper is unusually good because it does not stop at "adaptive OOD detection can fail." It models the failure as a provable phase transition, predicts the collapse threshold across `96` settings, shows the ungated detector loses `0.163` mean AUROC while its OOD dictionary becomes more than `90%` ID contamination, and then gives a certified gate that removes the transition. The useful move is severing the feedback loop, not tuning another heuristic.

### 3. **Learning on the Job: Continual Learning from Deployment Feedback for Frozen-Weights Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: This is a clean frozen-agent learning paper because it uses the feedback deployments already produce instead of pretending every capability update needs weight changes. On `tau`-bench banking, instruction-style feedback lifts Mistral Large to `2.6x` the static-RAG baseline on `pass^1`, replicates on Claude Sonnet 5 at `1.6x`, and converts `22` of the `84` tasks the Mistral baseline never solves. The cross-model transfer result is the extra useful bit: one model's learned rules help another.

### 4. **Securing Multimodal AI through Internal Information Decomposition**

**Verdict:** useful direct paper.

Why it matters: FlowGuard is interesting because it monitors the fusion process instead of filtering the surface prompt harder. A four-dimensional FlowVector built from redundancy, synergy, and modality-dominance signals keeps average attack success at or below `14.2%` with overall AUROC `0.942`, preserves benign utility within about `2.4%` of the undefended model, and still works in a partial-logprob API setting on GPT-4.1-mini at `10.4%` average ASR. The paper is strongest where multimodal attacks really are multimodal; text-only attacks remain harder.

### 5. **On the Identifiability of Controlled World Models**

**Verdict:** useful theory paper.

Why it matters: This is a valuable corrective to lazy world-model evaluation. The paper shows that representation identifiability and transition identifiability are different problems, and that low on-policy prediction error can coexist with bad counterfactual control if conditional action coverage is weak. The theory is narrow, but the framing is exactly right: if the transition is only trustworthy along the behavior policy, planning claims are being overstated.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Persistent Computational State.

The steal is not "store more memory." The steal is "name the non-recomputable kernel, make it measurable, and move the serving unit from request to session." That matters for world models, long-horizon assistants, coding agents, and any system where the useful state is live runtime structure rather than a static artifact on disk.

The rest of the digest mostly reinforces the same boundary discipline. **Self-Poisoning** says adaptive memory should be treated as a feedback system with failure thresholds. **Learning on the Job** says post-episode feedback should become reusable rules rather than evaporating. **FlowGuard** says safety should monitor the internal coupling between modalities. **Identifiability** says planning claims need action-support guarantees, not just pretty rollout demos.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Persistent Computational State** is strongest because it makes a concrete counter-claim to the current world-model benchmarking mood: some excursion failures are not evidence that the model lacks persistent state, but evidence that the runtime discarded it. Caveat: the PCS fingerprint is still a measurement procedure over three model families, not a universality proof.

**Self-Poisoning** is strongest because it turns an anecdotal failure mode into a possibility and impossibility story. Caveat: the detector stack is still built on frozen features and reserve-based certification, so the result is more about safe adaptive decision rules than about full end-to-end novelty learning.

**Learning on the Job** is strongest because it measures learning between trials without touching weights, then shows the learned store transfers across models. Caveat: the evidence is one domain with reliable evaluator feedback, and the benchmark's `pass^4` metric is partly blind to learning-by-later-trial conversion.

**FlowGuard** is strongest because it uses process-level features rather than content heuristics or purification theater. Caveat: it needs logprob access and three forward passes, so it is not a pure black-box safety method.

**On the Identifiability of Controlled World Models** is strongest as a framing paper. It tells you which successes should stop impressing you: good behavior-policy prediction does not certify good counterfactual planning. Caveat: the theory assumes invertible observations and linear-Gaussian latent dynamics, so this is more a standards paper than a finished answer for realistic world models.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that state only counts if the interface that makes it usable is explicit. A world model does not "forget" if the runtime threw away the non-recomputable kernel. An adaptive detector is not robust if its own bank can poison the admission channel. A frozen agent is not static if deployment feedback is turned into retrievable rules. A multimodal safety stack is not serious if it never inspects whether the modalities agree inside the fused computation. A controlled world model is not planning-ready if it only learned the action responses that happened to appear under the behavior policy. Same pattern everywhere: stop praising latent capability in the abstract and inspect the contract that operationalizes it.

## Detailed notes

- [Self-poisoning note](../paper_notes/self_poisoning_adaptive_ood_detection.md)
- [Learning on the job note](../paper_notes/learning_on_the_job_deployment_feedback_frozen_agents.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-02

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **make the hidden state explicit before trusting the surface behavior**. Self-GC treats agent context as indexed runtime objects with lifecycles instead of a disposable text suffix. Prototype Language Models train the next-token path to expose sparse, data-grounded handles rather than asking post hoc attribution to recover everything from dense parameters. Theoria turns informal reasoning into licensed state transitions so hidden premises have somewhere visible to fail.

I kept robotics to one ranked slot. The scan deliberately covered agent context and memory, interpretability, verification, citation integrity, uncertainty / calibration, medical and scientific ML, 3D / generative media, and robotics. Fresh robotics papers were strong today, especially 3D Point World Models, but the best non-robotics mechanisms were cleaner and broader.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv candidate pages were reachable and used as a discovery supplement, but the preservation work below relies on arXiv PDFs / HTML rather than AlphaXiv summaries. arXiv list pages and direct PDFs were accessible.

No preserved note today is abstract-only. I acquired and inspected the arXiv PDFs for **Self-GC**, **Prototype Language Models**, **Theoria**, **AutoMem**, **Phantom References**, and **3D Point World Models**. I read the main method, evaluation, results, and limitations / conclusion where present; I did not audit every appendix table for the longer PRISM paper or every adversarial case in Theoria.

**Self-GC** is the most directly useful paper today. It gives a concrete runtime contract for agent context governance: index context as objects, plan fold / mask / prune actions in a side channel, rehearse edits deterministically, and preserve recoverable sidecars.

**Prototype Language Models** is the strongest interpretability / attribution paper. Its useful move is architectural: train prototypes into the prediction pathway so attribution and steering happen through sparse, data-grounded coordinates instead of fragile post hoc explanation.

**Theoria** is the strongest verification paper. It does not eliminate judge fallibility, but it makes the verifier's job more local: every rewrite between reasoning states needs an explicit citation, computation, or problem-given license.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Self-GC: Self-Governing Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the cleanest agent-systems mechanism today.

Why it matters: it names the right abstraction. Long-horizon agent context is not a linear chat buffer; it is a collection of user turns, tool spans, plans, file handles, evidence, and skill state with different future-dependency risks. Self-GC's object IDs, fold / mask / prune actions, sidecar recovery, and cache-aware commit policy are directly stealable for real agent harnesses.

### 2. **Prototype Language Models**

**Verdict:** must read for interpretable model design and training-data attribution.

Why it matters: PRISM asks the model to expose data-grounded prediction coordinates during training, not after the fact. Each next-token prediction is mediated by a sparse non-negative mixture of learned prototypes plus a residual. The evidence is still early by frontier-model standards, but the architectural idea is exactly the right kind of interpretability: causal, editable, and tied to training neighborhoods.

### 3. **Theoria: Rewrite-Acceptability Verification over Informal Reasoning States**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for verifier architecture.

Why it matters: Theoria separates answer correctness from certificate quality. A solver's answer is rewritten into state transitions, each licensed by a typed justification; hidden premises become unlicensed state mutations rather than vibes hidden inside prose. The caveat is sharp: the current system still uses LLM judges and one main benchmark, so the durable contribution is the witness format more than the headline precision number.

### 4. **AutoMem: Automated Learning of Memory as a Cognitive Skill**

**Verdict:** highly relevant but slightly behind Self-GC as today's preserved memory paper.

Why it matters: it treats memory use as a trainable skill, not a fixed retrieval module. File operations become first-class actions, a meta-LLM revises the memory scaffold from full trajectories, and a dedicated LoRA memory specialist is trained on selected good memory decisions while the gameplay/action model remains frozen. The result is a strong long-horizon-game story; the open question is whether the same scaffold optimization survives non-game workflows.

### 5. **3D Point World Models: Point Completion Enables More Accurate Dynamics Learning**

**Verdict:** the one robotics / world-model paper that cleared the balance bar today.

Why it matters: it argues that explicit completed 3D geometry makes action-conditioned dynamics easier to learn and plan with. The method completes partial RGB-D point clouds, predicts per-point velocities with a Point Transformer V3 dynamics model, and uses rollouts for MPPI planning. It is still modular and brittle to segmentation / completion failures, but the core lesson is clean: complete object geometry can be a better world-state substrate than partial sensory points.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Self-GC.

The steal is not "summarize context better." The steal is to promote context management into an object-lifecycle layer with deterministic harness checks. Context objects need stable IDs, lifecycle state, future-dependency categories, recovery pointers, safe commit boundaries, and measurable no-impact rates. That maps almost embarrassingly well onto OpenClaw-style sessions, skills, tool spans, files, browser traces, and memory notes.

Prototype Language Models gives the representation analogue: if you want traceability, expose traceable coordinates inside the prediction path. Theoria gives the verification analogue: if you want trust, require each state change to carry a local license. AutoMem gives the training analogue: memory competence is a behavior to optimize from trajectories, not just a directory you hand the model and hope it uses well.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Self-GC** is strong because the mechanism matches the failure. Chronological pruning and generic summarization destroy exact URLs, file paths, row values, task IDs, user corrections, and live handles because they do not represent future dependencies. Self-GC maps context into objects, asks a planner for fold / mask / prune actions, rehearses and validates edits in the harness, stores folded payloads in sidecars, and commits only at safe turn boundaries. On the Hard Set, it prunes less aggressively than heuristics but reports much higher no-impact; on the larger Production Suite, multiple planner backbones clear 90 percent no-impact. The caveat is that the traces are production-derived but not open, and the key offline metric is judge-based no-impact rather than full replay success.

**Prototype Language Models** is strong because it makes interpretability a modeling choice. PRISM keeps a standard decoder backbone but replaces the opaque output path with sparse prototype reconstruction: hidden states activate a small set of learned prototypes, prototypes contribute additively to logits through the shared LM head, and clustering losses keep them near real training-token neighborhoods. The paper reports competitive 130M-1.6B performance, about 97 percent training throughput of a dense XL GPT-style baseline in its setup, roughly 500x faster cached prototype attribution than EK-FAC under comparable memory, and test-time prototype suppression / controllers as causal handles. The caveat is scale: 1.6B and 50B tokens is serious research scale but not proof that this remains clean at frontier scale or inside deeper model circuits.

**Theoria** is strong because its formal story predicts its empirical advantage. Completeness-of-change says every semantic difference between consecutive reasoning states must be licensed; hidden premises should therefore appear as unlicensed mutations. In the paper's HLE-Verified Gold run, Theoria certifies 105 of 185 completed problems at 91.4 percent strict precision, similar to holistic judges at matched coverage, but with low error overlap and a stronger advantage on hidden premises / fabricated citations in poisoned proofs. The caveat is important: LLM judges still do the local checking, semantic diffing is not yet an explicit parser layer, and formal CAS / SMT / Lean backends are future work.

**AutoMem** is a strong runner-up because it treats memory actions as first-class behavior. Its two outer loops are useful: first revise the scaffold from full trajectory review, then train a dedicated memory specialist on selected good memory-operation traces. The 2x-4x gains across Crafter, MiniHack, and NetHack are compelling, but games are a favorable lab for episodic memory and the paper uses separate scaffolds / specialists per environment.

**3D Point World Models** is the strongest robotics item because it puts explicit completed geometry in the loop before dynamics prediction. The method has a real model definition and meaningful sim-to-real evidence, but its modular stack has obvious cascading-failure surfaces: SAM3 segmentation, point completion under occlusion/noisy depth, and slow rollout planning.

**Phantom References** was the best integrity / scholarly-record runner-up. RefChecker is valuable because citations are a narrow auditable surface for hallucination: resolve identity, authorship, and title compatibility before trusting a bibliography. I did not preserve it today because it is more audit infrastructure than a reusable model or agent mechanism, but the paper is worth citing in any discussion of AI-written scientific workflows.

**Bayesian Uncertainty Propagation for Agentic RAG Pipelines**, **PSCT-Net**, and **SchemaRAG** were useful scouting hits in uncertainty, medical imaging, and healthcare/e-commerce extraction, respectively. They did not beat the top five on mechanism reuse today.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all reject hidden mush. Self-GC says an agent trace must expose the objects whose future dependencies matter. PRISM says a language model should expose sparse, data-grounded prediction handles if we expect attribution to work. Theoria says a reasoning certificate should expose every state mutation and its license. AutoMem says memory quality lives in observable actions, not in the mere existence of a memory folder. 3DPWM says a robot world model needs completed geometry before long rollouts are worth trusting. Same lesson at five scales: explicit state is not decorative; it is the thing that lets systems be audited, adapted, and repaired.

## Detailed notes

- [Prototype Language Models note](../paper_notes/prototype_language_models_prism.md)
- [Theoria note](../paper_notes/theoria_rewrite_acceptability_verification.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-16

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **diagnostic interfaces beat aggregate success**. The strongest papers do not merely report higher task scores. They expose where a model thinks it is on track, whether an answer is grounded in the supplied context, and where a scientific evidence pipeline loses eligible studies. I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work as one lane rather than the center. The scan looked first at interpretability, agent grounding, healthcare/evidence synthesis, search-agent security, KV-cache context management, generative world models, representation learning, and medical imaging, then used the robotics papers as comparison cases.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight `/search` route returned a 404 page, so it was not useful for discovery today. I used the arXiv API plus direct arXiv PDFs. Full-text PDFs were available for the leading candidates. I inspected the method, result, and limitation sections for **The Value Axis: Language Models Encode Whether They're on the Right Track**, **Context-Aware RL for Agentic and Multimodal LLMs**, **Benchmarking LLM Agents on Meta-Analysis Articles from Nature Portfolio**, **How Much Can We Trust LLM Search Agents?**, and **KVEraser**. I did lighter full-text skims for **DreamX-World 1.0**, **Selection Without Signal, Recovery Through Expression**, **T-Rex**, and adjacent technical candidates including posterior-score inverse problems, urban inverse rendering, phase in neural representations, and non-contrast abdominal CT diagnosis.

**The Value Axis** is the most relevant paper today. It constructs a linear activation direction in Qwen3-8B from synthetic in-context RL conversations, then shows that the direction tracks and causally modulates confidence-like behavior across math, code, DPO word preferences, SFT domains, and evaluation-awareness settings. This should not be treated as a general truth detector: it is one model, one axis-construction recipe, and a set of selected validation domains. But it is exactly the right kind of interpretability object for cabbageland: an internal state variable that can be measured, steered, and audited against external behavior.

**Context-Aware RL** is the strongest training-method paper in the scan. The method adds a context-selection loss to GRPO: given a query, an answer, and two similar contexts, the policy is rewarded for identifying which context actually supports the answer. The important part is not the contrastive data by itself. The paper shows that supervised augmentation can collapse an agentic policy and outcome-only RL mostly fails to use the signal; the bounded auxiliary loss is what preserves the policy while improving grounding.

**MetaSyn** is the strongest healthcare/scientific-evidence evaluation paper today. It builds a benchmark from 442 Nature Portfolio meta-analyses, a PubMed-anchored corpus of 140,585 articles, 8,674 corpus-matched positives, hard negatives, and PI/ECO-structured inclusion criteria. The headline is sharp: retrieval can reach 90.9% Recall@200, but no end-to-end pipeline recovers more than 52.7% of included studies. The bottleneck is not "can it retrieve relevant papers?" but "can it screen topically similar distractors against protocol criteria?"

**SearchGEO** is a strong security/evaluation warning. It tests whether manipulated web evidence becomes user-facing endorsement in LLM search agents. The useful result is the source-diversity effect: distinct corroborating attacker pages move endorsement far more than repetition of one source. I did not preserve a detailed note because today's top two papers are more reusable as model-training and model-debugging mechanisms, but SearchGEO is worth revisiting for agent-search hardening.

**KVEraser** is a very relevant systems paper, but just below the preservation line today. It learns local KV-cache steering states to erase a harmful, stale, or retracted span without recomputing the entire suffix. The mechanism is attractive for long-running agents because "forget this tool observation" should be an actual cache edit, not a polite instruction appended after contamination. I did not write a note today because the two preserved papers were more central and the pipeline is already audio-heavy, but this one should stay in the follow-up queue.

The robotics lane had one genuinely strong candidate: **T-Rex: Tactile-Reactive Dexterous Manipulation**. It combines human egocentric pretraining, a 100-hour tactile-rich teleoperation dataset, a variable-rate Mixture-of-Transformers, and a temporal tactile VQ-VAE for high-frequency residual tactile refinement. On a robotics-only day it would likely deserve a note. Today it stays out of the top three because the non-robotics candidates are stronger for general mechanism transfer.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **The Value Axis: Language Models Encode Whether They're on the Right Track**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives "model confidence in its current trajectory" a measurable and steerable internal representation, then tests it against backtracking, coding coherence, DPO preference shifts, SFT domains, and evaluation awareness.

### 2. **Context-Aware RL for Agentic and Multimodal LLMs**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it turns context grounding into an auxiliary policy objective rather than hoping final-answer reward teaches the model which evidence mattered.

### 3. **Benchmarking LLM Agents on Meta-Analysis Articles from Nature Portfolio**

**Verdict:** useful, with healthcare/evidence-synthesis relevance.

Why it matters: it shows that scientific-agent failure is often a screening failure under explicit eligibility criteria, not a retrieval failure or a final prose-generation failure.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** The Value Axis.

The steal-worthy idea is an internal progress gauge, but with a hard caveat: it should be used as one diagnostic signal, not as a self-certifying truth oracle. A cabbageland agent could compare an internal "on track" signal against external checks: tests, citations, tool observations, contradiction detectors, or human-visible uncertainty. The danger is just as useful as the promise. DPO can make rewarded behaviors feel internally more valuable, so a model can become more confident around a preference even when the surrounding task has not become more justified.

ContextRL supplies the training-side companion. Instead of rewarding only final success, train the model to identify which piece of context justifies a fixed answer. That is exactly the shape of many agent failures: the right text or tool result is present, but the model fails to bind its next action to the decisive evidence.

MetaSyn supplies the evaluation-side companion. Scientific agents need stage-attributed failure metrics. An aggregate report-quality score hides whether the system failed to retrieve, failed to screen, failed to apply inclusion criteria, or synthesized from the wrong evidence base.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**The Value Axis** raises the bar for internal-state interpretability. Verbal confidence is cheap; a causal activation direction that changes backtracking and task persistence is more interesting. The paper still needs replication beyond Qwen3-8B, but it earns attention because the intervention moves behavior.

**Context-Aware RL** reframes context utilization as a process-level training target. The strongest baseline result is negative: the same contrastive data does not help unless the objective consumes it in the right way.

**MetaSyn** raises the baseline for scientific-agent evaluation. If a system cannot separate eligible studies from PI/ECO-failing distractors, fluent synthesis is premature.

**SearchGEO** is a deployment warning: source diversity can be adversarially manufactured, and a model's own self-audit is not enough to detect credibility loss.

**KVEraser** is a systems-design prompt: long-context agents need actual state-editing machinery for stale or harmful context, not only text instructions to ignore prior spans.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today are about making hidden interfaces visible. **The Value Axis** finds a candidate internal gauge for whether a model thinks its current trajectory will succeed. **Context-Aware RL** trains models to bind answers to the context that actually supports them. **MetaSyn** shows that scientific-agent pipelines fail at protocol screening even when retrieval is strong. The shared lesson is that end scores are too blunt: the useful object is the stage, span, head, cache state, or activation direction where the failure can actually be localized.

## Detailed notes

- [The Value Axis note](../paper_notes/value_axis_language_models_encode_whether_theyre_on_right_track.md)
- [Context-Aware RL note](../paper_notes/context_aware_rl_agentic_multimodal_llms.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-25

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **the interface decides what can be repaired**. A memory note that keeps a conclusion but drops the source becomes uncorrectable. A looped-model readout that hides scale cannot supervise scale, no matter how many loop losses you add. A relational benchmark that only measures known difficulty axes cannot reveal the structures that actually break the reasoner.

I deliberately kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered agent memory, looped language models, neural-symbolic evaluation, scientific ML, MoE interpretability, multimodal robustness, medical decision support, 3D/video generation, representation learning, tool-use RL, and robotics/VLA candidates. The strongest robotics/VLA candidates were **In-Context World Modeling for Robotic Control**, **Reflective VLA**, **FORCE**, **RAVEN**, and **Learning Action Priors for Cross-embodiment Robot Manipulation**, but none beat today's best non-robotics papers on mechanism clarity and future usefulness.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv pages were reachable for the three preserved arXiv IDs, but I used them only as supplemental reachability checks. Discovery therefore relied on arXiv new listings, arXiv abstract pages, and direct arXiv PDFs. The arXiv API was also checked, but a wider sweep hit rate limiting after the initial category pass, so discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on June 25, arXiv listed a large June 25 batch across AI, ML, CV, CL, robotics, medical imaging, statistics, and neuro/scientific lanes. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text with targeted reads through methods, experiments, results, and limitations for **Reclaim Evaluation**, **Dense Supervision Is Not Enough**, **Project Auto-World**, **LLM-ACES**, **How Modular Is a Frontier Mixture-of-Experts?**, **Holographic Memory for Zero-Shot Compositional Reasoning**, **Same Evidence, Different Answer**, **xAARA**, **Wan-Streamer**, **In-Context World Modeling for Robotic Control**, **Why Multi-Step Tool-Use Reinforcement Learning Collapses**, and **Disease-Centric Vision-Language Pretraining for 3D CT**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Reclaim Evaluation** is the most relevant paper today. It says memory should be tested by whether later correction can recover truth, not by whether a plausible summary survives.

**Dense Supervision Is Not Enough** is the sharpest mechanism paper. It shows that per-loop loss trains visible exits while leaving hidden recurrent scale uncontrolled when the readout normalizes scale away.

**Project Auto-World** is the strongest benchmark-generation paper. It uses LLM-written graph samplers to expose relational-reasoning difficulties not captured by the usual hand-designed metrics.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives a clean test for agent memory. If the memory keeps a stale conclusion and drops the answer-determining source, later correction can fail more dangerously than if the system had remembered nothing.

### 2. **Dense Supervision Is Not Enough: The Readout Blind Spot in Looped Language Models**

**Verdict:** must read for recurrent-depth and latent-state modeling.

Why it matters: it separates exit supervision from recurrent-state control. Dense cross-entropy can supervise every loop while still failing to control a state variable hidden by the readout.

### 3. **Project Auto-World: Towards Automated Benchmarking of Neural Relational Reasoners**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for evaluation, neurosymbolic reasoning, and benchmark design.

Why it matters: it treats hard-case generation as executable search over worlds, then turns discovered failures into interpretable difficulty axes. That is much better than static benchmark folklore.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Reclaim Evaluation.

The steal is the source-first memory rule plus the reclaim test. For any long-running agent, a memory note should preserve the observations needed to recompute or repair a conclusion. A conclusion-only note is cheap and often poisonous.

Dense Supervision adds the model-internal version of the same standard. A loss only controls what its interface exposes. If state variables matter later, make them visible to the objective or remove them from the recurrent path.

Auto-World adds the evaluation version: if known metrics do not predict failure, generate small controlled worlds that make the model fail, then reverse-engineer the hidden axis.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Reclaim Evaluation** raises the bar for memory systems. The right question is not "can the model recall the note?" but "can the model recover when the note's conclusion was wrong?" The paper's strongest result is the matched-budget contrast: lossy and lossy-padded memory wall at 0.00 Reclaim Rate when the source is gone, while source-first memory reaches roughly 0.99 to 1.00 on arithmetic wall cells. The caveat is important: source-first only works when the answer-determining source is compact and identifiable, and the deployable source-first-auto prompt is weaker than the oracle note.

**Dense Supervision Is Not Enough** is valuable because it names a precise visibility-activity mismatch. In the main ablation, per-loop RMSNorm readouts still let final hidden-state norms drift to about 39,207 at 44M and 56,051 at 129M, while raw readouts and norm penalties keep scale in the tens. This is not just an instability anecdote; radial-gradient diagnostics, scale clamps, and final-only normalization controls all support the same mechanism. The caveat is scale and scope: the main controlled evidence is WikiText-103 at 44M and 129M, with a 1.4B sanity check rather than a full large-scale ablation.

**Project Auto-World** is strong because it does not stop at "LLMs can generate benchmarks." It generates executable sampling functions over Datalog worlds, scores them by Edge Transformer failures, then analyzes the discovered failures. The inferred off-path edge metric is the key payoff: it is a new difficulty axis surfaced by the generator rather than assumed in advance. The caveat is transfer: this is still mostly NoRA-style relational reasoning with one main evaluator, so cross-model validation is the next bar.

**LLM-ACES** is the best scientific-ML runner-up. It couples LLM-induced operator priors with disagreement-based active trajectory acquisition for ODE discovery, reaching the best median NMSE and symbolic accuracy on ODEBench and ODEBase in the reported setup. I kept it below the note line because the setting assumes a queryable trajectory oracle and stays in autonomous ODE systems, but the closed-loop evidence-acquisition pattern is worth stealing.

**How Modular Is a Frontier Mixture-of-Experts?** is the strongest interpretability runner-up. It pre-registers expert families, ablates them against a random null, and shows that only the Arabic-language family is a robust selective module in Command A+. This is useful pressure against casual "expert equals module" stories. I kept it as a runner-up because the empirical scope is one model plus one positive control, but the measurement discipline is good.

**Same Evidence, Different Answer** is a useful multimodal evaluation runner-up. It audits order sensitivity across five ordering facets and 18 MLLMs, with panel-mean flip rates spanning 24 to 50 percent and the best model still flipping on 13.4 percent of trials. It is a strong reliability axis, but today the preserved notes went to papers with more reusable mechanisms.

**xAARA** is the strongest healthcare/deployment runner-up. Its useful move is not just multi-view stroke-rehab video scoring; it treats clinical scoring as uncertainty-aware, clinician-bounded inference and routes low-confidence cases back to review. I kept it below the line because the deployment evidence is promising but narrow and retrospective.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all punish a bad compression. **Reclaim Evaluation** says a memory that keeps the answer but drops the source can be worse than empty. **Dense Supervision** says a loop loss that sees the normalized readout does not necessarily control the recurrent state. **Auto-World** says a benchmark that keeps only known difficulty metrics misses the structures that actually break the reasoner. Different layers, same rule: preserve the variable the next step needs, not the proxy that looks nice in the current interface.

## Detailed notes

- [Reclaim Evaluation note](../paper_notes/reclaim_evaluation_lossy_memory_worse_than_empty.md)
- [Dense Supervision note](../paper_notes/dense_supervision_readout_blind_spot_looped_language_models.md)
- [Project Auto-World note](../paper_notes/project_auto_world_automated_benchmarking_relational_reasoners.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-04

## Theme

Today’s strongest paper is a clean structural move inside diffusion-policy imitation: force the denoising field to come from a scalar energy, then use that integrability both to recover a reward-like signal and to regularize generalization. The rest of the shortlist is weaker but still informative. One vision-language paper has a decent mechanism for preventing long textual rollouts from washing out visual evidence, while an affordance-agent paper is useful mostly as a systems diagnosis of why fixed skill pipelines are brittle, not as a deep new representational idea.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. I then scouted recent arXiv listings directly, especially cs.RO, cs.AI, cs.CV, cs.LG, and q-bio.NC, and inspected abstracts plus substantial method text from arXiv HTML pages for **Recovering Hidden Reward in Diffusion-Based Policies**, **Persistent Visual Memory: Sustaining Perception for Deep Generation in LVLMs**, **Affordance Agent Harness: Verification-Gated Skill Orchestration**, and **SIMON: Saliency-aware Integrative Multi-view Object-centric Neural Decoding**.

**Recovering Hidden Reward in Diffusion-Based Policies** is the clear direct hit. Its useful claim is not just that diffusion policies can be interpreted as energy-based models, but that forcing the denoising vector field to be the gradient of a scalar potential gives a principled route from imitation to recoverable soft-Q structure. I inspected the abstract and substantial theory and method text, including the score-to-soft-Q derivation, the conservative-field constraint, and the training objective framing.

**Persistent Visual Memory** is adjacent but worth noting. The paper’s diagnosis is simple and plausible: long autoregressive reasoning chains in large vision-language models dilute visual attention as textual context grows. The proposed fix, a lightweight retrieval branch that keeps raw visual embeddings available throughout generation, is more concrete than most “visual reasoning enhancement” work. I inspected the abstract and substantial method and results text from the arXiv HTML page, including the module placement and ablation summaries. My main caveat is that this is still a patch to a transformer’s information flow, not an explicit memory model in the stronger sense.

**Affordance Agent Harness** is useful mostly as systems-adjacent citation material. I inspected the abstract and substantial introduction and method text. The paper correctly frames open-world affordance grounding as budgeted evidence acquisition with verification-triggered retries, but the mechanism is still a fairly large runtime wrapper around existing skills, memory, and routing modules rather than a sharp new representation.

**SIMON** is the neuro-adjacent extra worth keeping in mind, but not worth a full note today. It improves EEG-to-image retrieval by replacing center-biased foveation with saliency-aware multi-view crops. That is sensible, but the contribution feels like a careful front-end alignment trick rather than a broader reusable mechanism for cabbageland’s main agenda.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Recovering Hidden Reward in Diffusion-Based Policies**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it turns a currently hand-wavy connection between diffusion policies and reward structure into an explicit modeling constraint, and the constraint might genuinely improve out-of-distribution behavior rather than just reinterpret the same policy after the fact.

### 2. **Persistent Visual Memory: Sustaining Perception for Deep Generation in LVLMs**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it treats long-horizon multimodal reasoning failure as a routing problem for visual evidence, not just a scaling problem.

### 3. **Affordance Agent Harness: Verification-Gated Skill Orchestration**

**Verdict:** skimmable citation material.

Why it matters: it is a reasonable systems argument for closed-loop evidence collection and retry policies in affordance grounding, but I do not think the core idea is as deep as the paper’s surface area suggests.

### 4. **SIMON: Saliency-aware Integrative Multi-view Object-centric Neural Decoding**

**Verdict:** mostly citation material.

Why it matters: it is a competent neuro-decoding improvement, but the transferable lesson is narrow.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Recovering Hidden Reward in Diffusion-Based Policies.

The important move is the conservative-field constraint. Standard diffusion policies learn a denoising vector field over actions, which is good for imitation but leaves the learned preference structure implicit and potentially non-integrable. This paper instead parameterizes a scalar energy and defines the denoising field as its action-gradient. Under a maximum-entropy-optimality assumption, that lets the score recover the gradient of the expert’s soft Q-function, so the same learned object can both generate actions and provide a reward-like shaping signal.

That matters for two reasons. First, it is structurally cleaner than bolting inverse-RL rhetoric onto an ordinary diffusion policy after the fact. Second, the integrability constraint may actually do useful work as an inductive bias in high-dimensional action spaces, because it rules out arbitrary vector fields and forces globally consistent preferences.

The caveat is that a lot depends on the strength of the theory-to-practice bridge. The score-to-reward equivalence leans on maximum-entropy assumptions, and the paper still lives in manipulation benchmarks rather than harsher long-horizon embodied settings. So I buy the direction more than I buy any universal claim that diffusion imitation has now “solved” reward recovery.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

EnergyFlow sharpens a baseline question for diffusion-policy papers. If a method claims better robustness, adaptation, or reward-awareness, we should now ask whether the model learns a generic denoising field or an explicitly integrable one. If there is no scalar potential behind the field, then any talk about recovered reward structure is much weaker.

Persistent Visual Memory matters more for framing than for baseline disruption. Its best contribution is the diagnosis that long textual rollouts can suppress visual evidence by construction, which means some multimodal reasoning failures are architectural bookkeeping failures rather than pure reasoning failures. That is a useful corrective to vague “needs more visual reasoning” narratives.

Affordance Agent Harness mostly affects evaluation taste. It usefully insists that test-time affordance systems should be judged on evidence acquisition, retry policy, and cost-aware routing rather than only final accuracy. But I would still treat it as a runtime-systems paper, not as proof that agent wrappers have discovered a new affordance representation.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today makes a real structural claim: diffusion-policy imitation becomes more legible and potentially more robust when the denoising field is forced to be the gradient of a scalar energy, because that links action generation to a recoverable preference landscape. The adjacent papers are more mixed. Persistent Visual Memory is a decent architectural fix for visual evidence decay in long multimodal rollouts, while Affordance Agent Harness is mostly a competent systems wrapper around routing, memory, and verification. The common lesson is that if a paper claims better reasoning, perception, or adaptation, the first question should be where the constraint actually lives. If the answer is “mostly in branding,” the paper is probably weak. If the answer is “in the learned field, memory path, or commitment rule,” it may be worth keeping.

## Detailed notes

- [EnergyFlow note](../paper_notes/energyflow_recovering_hidden_reward_in_diffusion_based_policies.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-25

## Theme

Today’s useful pattern is **explicit long-horizon state that stays decision-facing instead of decorative**. The strongest direct paper is **Point Tracking Improves World Action Models** because it replaces mushy pixel-only latent dynamics with an explicit point-track state that is actually used for robot control under occlusion and off-screen motion. **PathNavigate** is the best medical / agentic pick because it turns pathology VQA into a real search problem with slide-level surprise memory instead of pretending a frozen VLM can absorb a gigapixel slide in one shot. **HorizonStream** is the strongest adjacent systems paper because it treats long streaming 3D reconstruction as a memory-kernel design problem rather than a bigger-context problem.

## Short overview

Brave Search was unavailable in this environment because no Brave Search tool is configured for this run. AlphaXiv was also not used as a live discovery surface here, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv inspection plus direct arXiv HTML/PDF reads.

I inspected the full text for **Point Tracking Improves World Action Models**, **PathNavigate: A Training-Free Pathology Agent with Surprise-Guided Scan and Shared Slide Memory for Whole-Slide Image VQA**, and **HorizonStream: Long-Horizon Attention for Streaming 3D Reconstruction** through arXiv HTML and PDF text extraction. Confidence is good on mechanism, evaluation setup, and headline results, and weaker on appendix-level implementation details I did not audit line by line.

**Point Tracking Improves World Action Models** is the most relevant paper today. The central move is simple and strong: instead of letting a world-action model operate only on image latents, it jointly predicts future frames, point tracks, and visibility, then conditions action selection on both latent and explicit motion state. The paper calls the resulting controller JOPAT. This matters because it gives the policy a representation that can carry contact-induced motion, temporary occlusion, and off-screen displacement more legibly than pixel latents alone. The main caveat is that this is still a fairly engineered hybrid, not a clean general-purpose world model abstraction.

**PathNavigate** is the best non-robotics paper in the batch, and I’m glad it exists. It frames whole-slide pathology VQA as extreme-context evidence search, builds a low-magnification surprise map before question-conditioned reranking, then performs high-magnification readout only on selected regions. That is a much better decomposition than patch dumping or question-first guessing. It is still a frozen-stack agent rather than a learned memory system, but the structure does real work and the memory is tied to concrete evidence selection rather than branding.

**HorizonStream** is adjacent but worth preserving. It introduces Geometric Linear Attention, a recurrent O(1) geometric state with learned channel-wise retention, so evidence can decay smoothly across very long monocular sequences instead of being hard-reset or shoved into a contaminated KV cache. The paper’s value is not just benchmark placement. It gives a cleaner explanation for why streaming 3D systems break on long horizons and shows that memory shape matters as much as nominal context length.

I also inspected **SkillOpt** and **MemAudit** enough to triage them. SkillOpt has the right keywords but currently looks more like packaging around agent-skill optimization than a deep mechanism paper. MemAudit is directionally interesting for agent-memory security, but today’s preserved set felt stronger and more transferable.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Point Tracking Improves World Action Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it shows that explicit point-track state materially improves world-model-based robot control, especially when the hard part is motion grounding under occlusion, interaction, and long horizons.

### 2. **PathNavigate: A Training-Free Pathology Agent with Surprise-Guided Scan and Shared Slide Memory for Whole-Slide Image VQA**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it turns a giant-slide VQA problem into scan, search, and readout with shared slide memory, which is much closer to an actual evidence-gathering procedure than standard pathology VLM prompting.

### 3. **HorizonStream: Long-Horizon Attention for Streaming 3D Reconstruction**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it makes long-horizon memory an explicit geometric retention problem and avoids the usual refresh-or-drift trap in streaming reconstruction.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Point Tracking Improves World Action Models.

What I like here is that the explicit structure is not cosmetic. The model does not merely add a side head for tracks and keep acting from the same opaque state. It uses joint latent-plus-track prediction and then conditions action generation on that combined representation, with visibility modeling to handle when points disappear. That means the explicit motion state is in the control loop rather than just in the paper’s diagrams.

This is exactly the kind of paper that helps pressure-test broader world-model rhetoric. If the task depends on object displacement, contact, or temporary observability loss, then a world model that only compresses appearance may simply be exposing the wrong state to the policy. I would not overclaim generality, but as a concrete demonstration that explicit motion state can improve policy robustness, it is strong.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Point Tracking Improves World Action Models** sharpens a useful baseline question for robot world models: is the learned state actually good at carrying object motion and visibility through interaction, or is the policy mostly leaning on short-horizon appearance reconstruction? After this paper, pixel-latent-only baselines look less satisfying when the claimed target is robust long-horizon manipulation.

**PathNavigate** improves the framing of pathology agents. Instead of treating whole-slide reasoning as prompt engineering over a frozen perceptor, it makes search policy, memory, and answer-time evidence budget first-class system components. That is a stronger decomposition and a better baseline target for future pathology-agent papers.

**HorizonStream** makes a different but related point. Long-sequence competence is not just “more context.” The actual retention kernel matters. Hard refreshes and naive cache carryover now look like crude memory policies rather than neutral engineering choices.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Point Tracking Improves World Action Models** because it shows that explicit point-track state can improve world-model-based robot control where appearance-only latents start to blur away the motion structure that action really needs. **PathNavigate** is the strongest medical / agentic paper because it treats whole-slide pathology VQA as bounded evidence search with shared slide memory instead of giant-context prompting theater. **HorizonStream** is the best adjacent paper because it turns long-horizon streaming reconstruction into a principled retention problem with constant-memory recurrent state. The shared lesson is that persistent internal structure matters only when it stays tied to the actual decision interface, whether that interface is robot action, pathology evidence selection, or online geometric reconstruction.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-07

## Theme

Today's best papers all attack the same bad systems habit: treating a compressed proxy as if it were the real state. **Runtime Observability** says a memory guarantee only counts if the metric, failure budget, and certification tier compose mechanically at runtime. **MASS** says a multiplayer world model should roll one authoritative typed state, not a pile of camera-specific latent histories. **Beyond Top-K** says structured-document retrieval should expose deterministic line-level operations instead of hiding behind top-k chunk rankings. **When History Lies** says a tool agent needs reliable current task state, not whatever precedent happens to look plausible in the transcript. **Support x Operation Factorization** says compositional-readout metrics should bind where and what injectively instead of letting one slot impersonate several edits.

## Short overview

This run attempted Brave Search first on Friday, August 7, 2026 through the public Brave HTML surface. The surface was reachable, but the results were noisy and mixed fresh papers with older survey and keyword sludge, so it was useful only as a scout. Real filtering moved to direct arXiv recent-page inspection plus arXiv HTML full-text reading.

I did the required non-robotics pass across uncertainty, calibration, interpretability, and representation papers rather than defaulting into another VLA batch. I inspected arXiv HTML full text for all five ranked papers below. The top four are preserve-worthy and get notes. **Support x Operation Factorization** is the best adjacent runner-up: the evaluation idea is real, but it is more of a representation-analysis tool than an immediate system-design keep.

**Most relevant today:** **Runtime Observability for Heterogeneous Attention Memory**. It is the sharpest direct paper in the batch on a problem agent systems actually have right now: memory corruption and compression failure are not one bug class, so the guarantee object itself has to be typed, compositional, and machine-adjudicated.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Runtime Observability for Heterogeneous Attention Memory**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It turns "memory seems fine" into an executable claim object with typed metrics, certification tiers, and a request-level risk ledger. The useful move is not more probing. It is refusing to let unlike metrics compose unless a proved bridge exists.

### 2. **MASS: Multiplayer World Models with Authoritative Shared State**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It cleanly separates shared world dynamics from camera rendering. The useful move is a learned authoritative typed state that becomes the recurrent memory, synchronization object, and source of every rendered client view.

### 3. **Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It is a strong attack on chunk-and-embed retrieval for exactness-critical structured documents. The useful move is not "agentic" in the vague sense. It is exposing deterministic lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads as replayable evidence operations.

### 4. **When History Lies: Evaluating and Improving Tool Use under Misleading Multi-Turn Histories**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It isolates a real failure mode in tool agents: a model can already know the right policy and still get redirected by stale but plausible precedent in the history. The useful move is Oracle-conditioned policy transfer onto polluted-context student rollouts.

### 5. **Support x Operation Factorization: Compositional Readout of Frozen Vision Encoders under Controlled Interventions**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: It exposes a specific evaluation cheat, operation laundering, where a readout gets credit for several edits through the same slot. The injective support-operation scoring idea is the part worth stealing.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **Runtime Observability for Heterogeneous Attention Memory**.

It fits cabbageland unusually well because it refuses the two laziest failure modes around model memory: pretending all caches are the same object, and pretending an end-to-end guarantee exists because each local piece sounds reasonable on its own. The paper writes heterogeneous attention memory as update, select, and read operators, makes the error metric part of the type, and lets composition inherit the weakest certified tier automatically. That is exactly the right instinct for systems that mix compressed memory, probes, fallbacks, and production claims. The DeepSeek-V4 case study is less important than the contract discipline underneath it. If a chain needs an empirical bridge, the paper says so. If a regime is only safe under zero eviction and identity isolation, the paper says so. That refusal to blur the guarantee boundary is the real contribution.

The rest of the batch reinforces the same taste from other angles. **MASS** replaces view-coupled latent mush with a typed shared world state. **Beyond Top-K** replaces opaque similarity ranking with deterministic evidence operations. **When History Lies** separates current task state from misleading historical precedent. **Support x Operation Factorization** separates support binding from operation identity and then uses injective scoring to stop a metric from flattering the model.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Runtime Observability** is strongest because it makes the guarantee object itself explicit. The type checker rejected the authors' own first composition chain, the replay covered 12.4M entry reads with zero budget violations, and the final claim boundary is strict: the clean certified regime is zero-eviction and identity-isolated, while every observed failure lands in an eviction or slot-reuse regime.

**MASS** is strongest because it stops pretending multiplayer consistency can emerge from synchronized camera histories. On matched multiplayer Snake it reaches 0.76 state recovery versus 0.128 for the strongest video-based baseline, and it advances 1,024 concurrent player entities for 10,000 recurrent steps.

**Beyond Top-K** is strongest because it measures the retrieval failure instead of hand-waving it. Dense retrieval scores 15.7% in the default setting and 35.3% after honest tuning, while READ reaches 58.8%. The key caveat matters too: BM25 gets 51.0%, so the paper separates embedding-based retrieval from embedding-free retrieval more clearly than it separates "agentic" from lexical.

**When History Lies** is strongest because it isolates a failure mode many tool-agent papers blur away. On Qwen3-1.7B, misleading history flips 32.14% of decisions that are correct under the original context. Oracle-OPD lifts Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy to 87.0%, ahead of Gold-SFT at 66.3%, Oracle sequence distillation at 82.3%, and off-policy token distillation at 85.0%, with the same 1.7B student reaching 91.9% when trained with an 8B teacher.

**Support x Operation Factorization** is strongest because it attacks the metric boundary, not just the probe architecture. Under matched axis-aware supervision on Shapes3D, the factored carrier improves learned-assignment injective accuracy from 0.653 to 0.841 over a dense carrier, while the MuJoCo rebuild exposes the failure boundary with learned-assignment scores dropping to 0.569 for DINOv3 and 0.484 for SigLIP2 after injective scoring.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that a system gets brittle when a proxy is allowed to masquerade as the state transition, evidence object, or guarantee object it came from. Memory claims should carry typed metrics and certification tiers. World models should separate shared state from camera rendering. Retrieval should surface deterministic evidence operations when the document's structure matters more than semantic nearness. Tool agents should distinguish reliable current state from stale precedent in the transcript. Representation probes should bind edits injectively instead of letting one slot collect fake credit. The good papers are the ones that replace a flattering summary with an explicit object you can inspect, revoke, or route on.
