# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-25

## Theme

Today's stronger papers all move the real claim to an inspectable interface. **OpenForgeRL** says agent training should happen in the deployed harness, not in a toy loop that only resembles deployment from far away. **Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction** says compression damage is unmonitorable unless the eviction design itself makes the missing mass statistically identifiable. **Sparse Concept Channels in Frozen 3D CT Vision Encoders** says clinically useful findings do not have to stay smeared across a giant latent soup; many live in a small, ablatable coordinate set. **Self-Supervised Learning of Structured Dynamics from Videos** says motion gets more usable once dominant change and residual change stop sharing a single token. **Do Pathology Vision-Language Models Truly See Pathology?** says a correct answer is not evidence of visual grounding if the benchmark lets text priors do the work.

## Short overview

I checked the fresh `cs.AI`, `cs.CV`, `cs.LG`, `cs.RO`, `q-bio.NC`, and `eess.IV` arXiv recent pages on Saturday, July 25, 2026. Because it was a weekend run with no newer arXiv day beyond the Friday batch, I did a second-pass scout over that fresh batch instead of pretending a nonexistent release had appeared. Brave Search was unavailable because an unauthenticated request to the Brave API returned `HTTP 422` and explicitly reported a missing `x-subscription-token` header. AlphaXiv was reachable, so I used it for candidate sanity checks and then read the primary arXiv abstracts / HTML for the keepers. I also ran an explicit non-robotics title pass over terms like `medical`, `clinical`, `pathology`, `radiology`, `brain`, `memory`, `world`, `3D`, `4D`, `calibr`, `uncert`, `reason`, and `planning`, so the digest would not collapse into another robotics-only lane.

The strongest papers today are not about bigger models looking impressive. They are about forcing a vague claim to expose its control surface. If you say you can train agents, train them in the actual harness. If you say cache compression is safe, make its damage identifiable online. If you say a medical encoder knows a finding, show which channels carry it and what breaks when you zero them. If you say a video representation understands motion, separate the dominant motion source from the leftovers. If you say a pathology VLM understands images, show that it actually needs the image and binds the queried concept to the right tissue. No robotics or VLA paper cleared today's top five.

**OpenForgeRL** is the most relevant paper today. The central lesson is simple and useful: if the harness is where agent behavior is actually made, then training outside the harness is training the wrong object.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is one of the clearest current attempts to close the train-deploy mismatch for agents. Instead of reimplementing a toy imitation of a real harness, it records real harness interactions through a lightweight proxy and couples them to standard RL infrastructure. The resulting models reach `31.7` `pass^3` and `55.9` `pass@3` on ClawEval, `33.7` on QwenClawBench, and strong GUI scores too, while also exposing a more interesting result: harness choice itself changes what is learnable.

### 2. **Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: The useful move here is not another eviction heuristic. It is the impossibility result plus the repair: deterministic top-`k` eviction cannot consistently know the error it caused, while a known randomized design can. The paper gets a per-step certificate with about `0.97` empirical coverage, strong certificate-error correlation, and a cleaner practical conclusion than the headline might suggest: randomization buys attribution, not generic failure prediction.

### 3. **Sparse Concept Channels in Frozen 3D CT Vision Encoders**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: This is a rare medical-foundation-model paper that makes interpretability do real work instead of decorative post-hoc heatmaps. The claim is concrete: many radiological findings can be recovered from roughly `10` sparse channels, ablating those channels selectively collapses the target finding, and the same probe idea transfers across a second 3D abdominal VLM. The report-generation angle is also practical, beating CT-CHAT on clinical and NLG metrics at much lower latency.

### 4. **Self-Supervised Learning of Structured Dynamics from Videos**

**Verdict:** keep.

Why it matters: The paper's useful bet is that video dynamics should not be represented as one entangled transition blob. A recurrent model over frozen image features separates primary motion from residual motion and then probes better than naive global-feature baselines across the new ProbeMotion suite, even beating VGGT-style probes on `3/7` tasks despite much weaker supervision.

### 5. **Do Pathology Vision-Language Models Truly See Pathology?**

**Verdict:** useful direct evaluation paper.

Why it matters: This paper attacks a recurring multimodal lie: benchmark accuracy can go up while image dependence and grounding stay bad. Its best result is embarrassing in the right way: Gemini-3-Pro gets `53.5%` average accuracy across five pathology VQA benchmarks without visual input, and pathology-specific tuning can improve answer accuracy while reducing multimodal gain and attention IoU.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** OpenForgeRL.

The steal is not just "do RL on agents." It is to treat the harness as part of the model, because that is where tool use, context policy, branching, and state management actually live. The same control-surface lesson shows up in the other keepers too. **Error Certificates** says monitoring requires a design that preserves identifiability. **Sparse Concept Channels** says useful internal structure often lives in a small explicit subspace if you look correctly. **SDM** says motion becomes more usable when you split the dominant driver from the residue. **PathBind** says multimodal evaluation should test whether the evidence channel is causally necessary, not merely whether the answer string is right.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**OpenForgeRL** is strongest because it refuses the convenient fiction that agent training on simplified loops is "close enough." Caveat: the framework still inherits the quality limits of the chosen harnesses, synthesized tasks, and benchmark mix, and the behavioral analysis shows error recovery is still stubbornly weak.

**Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction** is strongest because it starts with a negative theorem rather than a new score. Caveat: the certificate is loose as an absolute bound, helps more with attribution than with generic failure prediction, and is most useful when cache damage is a real part of the error budget.

**Sparse Concept Channels** is strongest because it couples sparse probing to causal ablation and cross-backbone transfer instead of stopping at readout accuracy. Caveat: linear channel probes are not a full mechanistic story, and the report-generation win still depends on a fixed template verbalizer rather than richer open-ended generation.

**SDM** is strongest because it gives structure to temporal change without demanding a fully supervised 3D stack. Caveat: it still relies on weak synthetic supervision and probe-based evaluation, so this is more a representation paper than a full control-ready world-model result.

**PathBind** is strongest because it measures whether visual evidence is necessary and whether concept-to-region binding survives evaluation, not just whether a model says the right pathology word. Caveat: attention overlap is an imperfect proxy for grounding, and some of the strongest benchmark content depends on private atlas material.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that systems look smarter when the decisive variable stays hidden. Agents look trainable when you ignore the harness. Cache compression looks safe when you cannot identify the damage channel. Medical encoders look mysterious when you never ask which coordinates carry a finding. Video dynamics look learned when camera motion and object motion stay entangled. Pathology VLMs look grounded when the benchmark never checks whether the image mattered. The better papers expose the hidden interface directly and then ask whether the claim still survives there.

- [KV eviction certificate note](../paper_notes/error_certificates_for_kv_cache_eviction_via_randomized_design.md)
- [Sparse concept channels note](../paper_notes/sparse_concept_channels_in_frozen_3d_ct_vision_encoders.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-10

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **predictive structure is being pushed closer to the hidden state that actually matters for action**. **Next Forcing** is the strongest paper because it changes the training target for autoregressive video world models: instead of denoising only the current chunk, it asks lightweight auxiliary heads to predict multiple future chunks and backpropagate longer-range temporal pressure into the main model. **TacForeSight** is the strongest contact-world-model paper because it uses force/torque as a leading signal to forecast tactile latent dynamics before local contact changes fully appear. **LIBERO-Occ** is the best VLA robustness paper because it turns occlusion into a controlled partial-observability benchmark, then tests whether generated complementary views can recover task-relevant evidence.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable at the site level, but discovery and inspection for this run used arXiv API search over the June 9, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for **Next Forcing: Causal World Modeling with Multi-Chunk Prediction**, **TacForeSight: Force-Guided Tactile World Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation**, **LIBERO-Occ: Evaluating and Improving Vision-Language-Action Models under Scene-Induced Occlusion via Viewpoint Imagination**, **MV-Actor: Aligning Multi-View Semantics and Spatial Awareness for Bimanual Manipulation**, **IMPACT: Learning Internal-Model Predictive Control for Forceful Robotic Manipulation**, **WorldOlympiad: Can Your World Model Survive a Triathlon?**, **P3D-Bench: Benchmarking MLLMs for Parametric 3D Generation and Structural Reasoning**, and **Bridging Semantics and Physical Execution: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Multi-Pair Robotic Assembly**. Next Forcing, TacForeSight, and LIBERO-Occ are preserved today.

**Next Forcing** is the strongest direct hit. Its claim is simple and useful: teacher-forced next-chunk denoising lets high-frame-rate video world models lean on appearance copying, so the model needs a denser target that makes dynamics unavoidable. The method adds multi-chunk prediction modules for next1, next2, and next3 chunks, chains them causally, fuses intermediate main-model layers, and optionally keeps the depth-1 module at inference to generate the next video chunk in parallel. The results are strong on RoboTwin, PhyWorld, and a general video pretraining setting, though the training scale and proprietary data mean I trust the mechanism more than any single headline number.

**TacForeSight** is the best contact-rich manipulation note. It treats wrist force/torque as a high-frequency global cue that can precede local tactile deformation, then predicts future tactile latents and feeds them into a flow-based policy through current-future tactile cross-attention and adaptive visuo-tactile gating. The real-robot results are much stronger than the baselines across five contact tasks and three perturbation settings. The caveat is that the system assumes force and tactile hardware, and the evaluation is specialized, but the mechanism is exactly the kind of explicit physical foresight worth remembering.

**LIBERO-Occ** is the strongest VLA evaluation/framing note. The benchmark physically instantiates occluders in LIBERO scenes, verifies visibility/validity/executability, and separates manipulated-object, receptacle, and dual occlusion. The main empirical point is blunt: models that look strong on standard LIBERO collapse under scene-induced occlusion. VIM then imagines a complementary viewpoint from the occluded primary view and conditions action prediction on both observed and generated evidence. It improves substantially, but the paper is honest that this is a simulation benchmark and generated views remain bounded by learned priors.

**IMPACT** is strong adjacent inspiration and may deserve a later control note. It decouples high-level diffusion-policy planning from low-level force compensation by learning an online internal model from joint torque residuals, then applying feedforward wrench compensation. It is not a VLA/world-model paper in the narrow sense, but it is a very clean example of putting hidden physical state into a control interface instead of expecting imitation learning to absorb payload dynamics implicitly.

**MV-Actor** is useful citation material for multi-view bimanual perception. It aligns semantic tokens across physically corresponding camera regions, injects feed-forward reconstruction features for spatial awareness, and repairs noisy depth. I am not preserving it as a top note because it is mostly a perception-front-end improvement, while today's stronger thread is predictive hidden-state completion for action.

**WorldOlympiad** and **P3D-Bench** are good benchmark papers, not today's core preserved mechanisms. WorldOlympiad is useful for evaluating whether video world models preserve physics, 3D consistency, and interaction state. P3D-Bench is useful for checking whether code-generating MLLMs recover parametric 3D structure rather than merely producing plausible shapes. Both may be worth citing when framing evaluation, but they do not change the architecture/control story as directly as today's top three.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Next Forcing: Causal World Modeling with Multi-Chunk Prediction**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it makes an autoregressive video world model learn beyond local appearance copying by supervising multiple future chunks, and it can reuse that auxiliary structure for faster rollout.

### 2. **TacForeSight: Force-Guided Tactile World Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for contact-rich embodied world models.

Why it matters: it turns force/torque into a predictive condition for future tactile state, giving the policy an anticipatory contact prior rather than reactive sensor fusion.

### 3. **LIBERO-Occ: Evaluating and Improving Vision-Language-Action Models under Scene-Induced Occlusion via Viewpoint Imagination**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as VLA partial-observability evaluation and perception-completion mechanism.

Why it matters: it exposes that standard VLA benchmark success can depend on full visibility, then tests generated complementary views as an intermediate hidden-evidence representation.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Next Forcing.

The steal-worthy idea is to attack the supervision target, not only the context window or the sampling schedule. If a world model can solve the training task by copying adjacent appearance, the objective is under-specifying dynamics. Multi-chunk prediction makes the model answer "what keeps changing?" across several horizons, which is closer to the representation needed for planning and rollout.

TacForeSight is the physical-sensing companion. It is not enough to concatenate contact sensors and hope the policy sorts it out. If one signal reliably leads another, make that temporal asymmetry explicit and predict the hidden local state the controller will soon need.

LIBERO-Occ is the robustness companion. A VLA that performs well when all task evidence is visible may not be learning a recoverable state representation. Viewpoint imagination is not magic, but it is a clean intermediate object: an explicit guess about missing evidence that can be trained and inspected.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Next Forcing** raises the baseline for autoregressive video world models and WAMs. Papers should now say whether their objective creates pressure for multi-horizon dynamics or mostly rewards near-frame reconstruction. It also gives a practical ablation checklist: timestep shift, multi-layer feature fusion, auxiliary horizon depth, and whether the auxiliary heads can accelerate inference.

**TacForeSight** raises the baseline for contact-rich manipulation policies using force/tactile sensing. Reactive multimodal fusion is a weak baseline if the claimed problem is contact transition. A stronger method should model how global force cues anticipate future local tactile state and show perturbation recovery, not just nominal success.

**LIBERO-Occ** raises the baseline for VLA robustness. Occlusion should be physically instantiated and task-executability checked, not simulated as cosmetic image corruption. It also sharpens the evaluation question: does the model infer missing task evidence, or only exploit currently visible objects?

**WorldOlympiad** is useful evaluation pressure for generative world models: video quality is not enough if physics, geometry, and interaction continuity fail separately.

**P3D-Bench** is useful evaluation pressure for 3D/code-generation systems: executable and visually plausible parametric code can still fail the real structural target, especially dimensions, topology, and part-level decomposition.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Next Forcing** because it changes what a causal video world model is forced to learn: multi-horizon dynamics rather than local chunk copying. **TacForeSight** is the tactile/contact note to remember because it predicts future tactile latents from force/torque, giving the policy physical foresight instead of reactive fusion. **LIBERO-Occ** is the VLA robustness note because it turns occlusion into a real partial-observability test and uses imagined complementary views as inspectable missing evidence. The common lesson is that hidden state should not be left as a hope inside a giant latent. Make the missing future, contact, or view into an explicit interface.

- [TacForeSight note](../paper_notes/tacforesight_force_guided_tactile_world_model.md)
- [LIBERO-Occ note](../paper_notes/libero_occ_viewpoint_imagination_scene_induced_occlusion.md)

# Daily Digest — 2026-03-31

## Theme
Today’s useful pattern is not raw novelty volume. It is about interfaces: how planning gets coupled to prediction, and how evaluation gets coupled to reality. I found two papers worth preserving as mechanism notes and one benchmark paper worth keeping because better evaluation is becoming a hard bottleneck for robotics work. Brave Search was unavailable in this environment because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery for this run used arXiv queries plus direct inspection of arXiv abstract/HTML pages.

## Short overview
The strongest paper today is **PiJEPA: Policy-Guided World Model Planning for Language-Conditioned Visual Navigation**. It is not trying to invent a whole new ontology. It just fixes a real weakness: latent world-model planning is bad when action search starts from nowhere. Using a learned policy as the proposal distribution for MPPI is a sensible, steal-worthy interface choice.

Second is **Uni-World VLA: Interleaved World Modeling and Planning for Autonomous Driving**. This one is useful because it forces prediction and planning to interact step by step instead of letting a planner consume a stale precomputed rollout. I do not think it escapes the limitations of tokenized video world models, but the temporal ordering is materially better than decorative joint training.

Third is **ManipArena: Comprehensive Real-world Evaluation of Reasoning-Oriented Generalist Robot Manipulation**. This is not a model paper. It is worth keeping because real-world evaluation quality is now constraining what counts as believable progress in VLA and world-model robotics.

## Ranked papers

1. **PiJEPA: Policy-Guided World Model Planning for Language-Conditioned Visual Navigation**
   - Verdict: **Useful**
   - Role: **Directly relevant**
   - Why it matters: It gives policy and world model distinct jobs instead of pretending one of them should do everything.

2. **Uni-World VLA: Interleaved World Modeling and Planning for Autonomous Driving**
   - Verdict: **Useful**
   - Role: **Adjacent inspiration**
   - Why it matters: Its alternating frame/action generation is a real attempt to stop predicted futures from going stale before planning finishes using them.

3. **ManipArena: Comprehensive Real-world Evaluation of Reasoning-Oriented Generalist Robot Manipulation**
   - Verdict: **Useful**
   - Role: **Mostly citation material**
   - Why it matters: It offers a stronger evaluation target for claims about generalist manipulation than another simulator-only benchmark.

## Most relevant to cabbageland
**PiJEPA** is the most relevant paper today. The main idea is modest but good: policy as proposal, world model as evaluator/refiner. That division of labor is more useful than another monolithic "reasoning agent" stack where the internal roles stay blurry.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact
- **Planner initialization matters:** PiJEPA is good evidence that some world-model failures are really search-interface failures. Bad initialization is not a footnote.
- **Coupling must change the computation:** Uni-World VLA is useful mostly because it actually interleaves prediction and planning, rather than merely co-training them.
- **Evaluation pressure shapes architectures:** ManipArena is good framing material when arguing that benchmark design determines whether the field rewards memorized visuomotor shortcuts or more general reasoning.
- **Truthfulness / access note:** I inspected the arXiv abstract pages and substantial HTML method/introduction text for PiJEPA, Uni-World VLA, and ManipArena. I did not fully audit appendices, supplementary videos, or every results table, so the confidence here is higher on mechanism and framing than on exact numeric gains.

## One-paragraph takeaway
The day’s lesson is that explicit interfaces matter. **PiJEPA** is useful because it treats a policy as a proposal mechanism for planning rather than as the final answer. **Uni-World VLA** is useful because it treats the ordering of prediction and action as part of the method rather than an afterthought. **ManipArena** is useful because better evaluation can force these models to become less mushy. None of these papers is a grand slam. But all three are better than generic scale-and-branding work because they make some part of the computation or the evaluation contract more explicit.

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-16

## Theme

Today’s strongest pattern is selective explicitness. The worthwhile papers are not just adding “memory” or “geometry” as branding. They each pick a specific place where explicit structure earns its keep: ESCAPE uses persistent spatial memory plus an execution policy that can interrupt itself when the world changes, SpatialEvo turns geometry into a deterministic supervisory signal instead of a noisy pseudo-labeling game, and H2-EMV treats forgetting as a first-class design problem rather than pretending infinite memory is free.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv API queries, recent arXiv listings, and primary-source reading on arXiv abstract, HTML, and PDF text. I inspected the abstract plus substantive method/introduction text for ESCAPE and SpatialEvo, and the abstract plus PDF introduction/results framing for H2-EMV. I did not audit appendices or every quantitative table, so the judgments below are strongest on mechanism and framing, and a bit softer on exact empirical margins.

The strongest paper today is **SpatialEvo: Self-Evolving Spatial Intelligence via Deterministic Geometric Environments**. The useful move is not “self-evolving” branding. It is the observation that 3D spatial reasoning has something many self-improvement settings lack: exact answers can often be computed directly from geometry. Instead of letting a model vote on its own homework, the paper builds a deterministic geometric environment that validates questions and computes ground truth from point clouds and camera poses. That is a real conceptual upgrade over consensus-based pseudo-labeling.

**ESCAPE: Episodic Spatial Memory and Adaptive Execution Policy for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation** is the most directly relevant robot systems paper in the batch. Its good idea is a narrow one: keep a persistent 3D memory for long-horizon search, ground manipulation masks by querying current images with memory-derived object features, and let a reactive local monitor interrupt the global plan when an opportunistic target appears. The claimed depth-free memory construction is slightly oversold because camera geometry is still doing heavy lifting, but the routing logic is useful.

**Learning to Forget -- Hierarchical Episodic Memory for Lifelong Robot Deployment** is less flashy but worth keeping. Most robot memory papers act as if more memory is automatically better. This one faces the more annoying truth: if a robot is meant to answer questions about its past over long deployments, selective forgetting and relevance adaptation are part of the system design, not an afterthought. I inspected the PDF intro and result framing, not the full method section, so confidence is lower than for the top two papers, but the problem choice is good.

A nearby paper worth mentioning but not worth a full note today is **Feed-Forward 3D Scene Modeling: A Problem-Driven Perspective**. It looks like a useful survey and citation map rather than a mechanism paper.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **SpatialEvo: Self-Evolving Spatial Intelligence via Deterministic Geometric Environments**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it replaces model-consensus self-training with exact geometry-derived supervision in a domain where that replacement is actually justified.

### 2. **ESCAPE: Episodic Spatial Memory and Adaptive Execution Policy for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it couples persistent spatial memory with an execution policy that can switch from long-horizon search to opportunistic local action instead of sleepwalking through a fixed plan.

### 3. **Learning to Forget -- Hierarchical Episodic Memory for Lifelong Robot Deployment**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it treats forgetting as an adaptive systems problem for long-term robot memory, which is more realistic than pretending lifelong storage and retrieval are free.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** SpatialEvo.

The reason is not just “spatial reasoning.” It is that the paper notices a rare opportunity for exact supervision inside a domain currently infected by self-evolving vibe language. If the answer is computable from geometry, then using model consensus as a noisy proxy is just self-inflicted damage. That is a good cabbageland standard: when structure gives you an exact judge, use it.

ESCAPE is the better immediate robotics reference, especially for long-horizon embodied systems that need memory and opportunistic replanning rather than a single monolithic policy.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

SpatialEvo is framing pressure on a lot of self-improving VLM work. In domains with exact physical structure, consensus pseudo-labels should stop being treated as the default. The paper’s strongest baseline argument is not that its model is magically better, but that its supervision source is cleaner.

ESCAPE is useful baseline pressure on embodied memory papers that either ignore persistent state or hard-code rigid execution logic. Its best contribution is the combination of persistent memory with a planner that can be interrupted by reactive local evidence.

H2-EMV is framing pressure on robot-memory papers that optimize retrieval while silently assuming memory can grow forever. Forgetting is not a bug here. It is the resource-management problem.

## One-paragraph takeaway

Today’s shared lesson is that explicit structure is best used selectively and honestly. SpatialEvo uses geometry as a deterministic teacher instead of a decorative prior. ESCAPE uses persistent memory and reactive interruption to make long-horizon embodied behavior less brittle. H2-EMV treats forgetting as part of intelligence under resource limits, not as an embarrassing failure mode. Different papers, same basic standard: explicitness is valuable when it removes ambiguity, cleans supervision, or preserves useful state under real constraints.

## Detailed notes

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-15

## Theme

The useful papers today all attack the same operational lie: that possessing the right information is the same thing as using it correctly. **Beyond Retrieval** says memory is not retrieval but target-bound reuse. **The Objective Is the Bottleneck** says a world model can encode what its planner still cannot value. **Agent Behavioral Contracts II** says redundant agents are not independent just because the diagram says so. **TRAPSBench** says VLMs can internally know they should abstain and still blurt out an answer. **Diagnosing JEPA World Models** says robustness is a rollout property, not a one-step encoder-distance property.

## Short overview

This run used the live recent arXiv pages on Saturday, August 15, 2026, with deliberate non-robotics passes across agent memory, reliability certification, calibration, world-model planning, and medical world models. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for the five ranked papers below. I also inspected the arXiv HTML full text for **Intervention-Aware Clinical World Model for Post-Op Outcome Forecasting in Cardiology** as the medical-world-model check.

Three papers earn preserved notes. **TRAPSBench** is the strongest runner-up because the benchmark and the representation-to-output diagnosis are real, but the paper is more about output-stage restraint than about reusable system structure. **Diagnosing JEPA World Models** is useful because the diagnostic target is right, though it remains a diagnostic rather than a control improvement. The clinical world-model paper has a real structured-state design, but the evidence is internal to DECAAF-II and workshop-scale. **Most relevant today:** **Beyond Retrieval**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Beyond Retrieval: Query-Conditioned Reuse of Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the strongest paper today because it isolates the missing middle in agent memory. On **2,391** target tasks across WebArena, WorkArena, and AppWorld, its query-conditioned reuse note lifts average success to **62.3%**, which is **10.7 points** above full raw-trajectory injection while using **48.9% fewer** online tokens. The useful move is not "better retrieval" but a sharper post-retrieval support object: reusable workflow, bindings to recover, applicability conditions, and verification guardrails.

### 2. **The Objective Is the Bottleneck: Latent World Models Encode What Their Planners Cannot Use**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This paper does the right kind of humiliation to latent world-model folklore. It shows that LeWorldModel's predictor is still informative **75 environment steps** out, while the planner only imagines **25**, and the real failure is the squared-latent-distance objective that saturates and then inverts. Replacing only the planning cost lifts offset-100 success from **26.0%** to **98.0%** on the reproduced checkpoint and from **14.0%** to **70.0%** on the original authors' released weights.

### 3. **Agent Behavioral Contracts II: Certifying Compositional Reliability Without Assuming Independence**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This paper attacks a bad but common systems habit: multiplying component reliabilities as if redundant agents fail independently. In a preregistered **18,000-mission** confirmatory evaluation, two instances of one model co-fail on **90.0%** of the missions on which either fails, with log OR **6.66**. The repair is not hand-wavy copula theater but a dependence-free LP certificate over measured co-execution moments, which raises the certified floor from **0.2455** to **0.4116** when the moment family is enriched from **10** to **14** functionals.

### 4. **TRAPSBench: Vision-Language Models Encode but Fail to Express Epistemic Restraint**

**Verdict:** strong direct runner-up.

Why it matters: The benchmark is sharp and the mechanistic finding is better than the usual calibration sermon. On **1,404** matched physics video pairs, the best spontaneous PECS is only **0.292**, yet linear probes read answerability from hidden states at up to **0.91 AUROC** and single-layer steering can causally induce abstention. The useful claim is that the bottleneck is expressive, not perceptual.

### 5. **Diagnosing JEPA World Models with Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency**

**Verdict:** useful direct runner-up.

Why it matters: The paper asks the right robustness question for JEPA-like world models. Instead of relying on encoder distance, it rolls clean and perturbed histories forward under the same action sequence and measures divergence in predicted trajectories. The IR-SR diagnostic tracks planning recovery under perturbation well, including **22 of 24** relative blur/resize comparisons and a pooled Spearman **0.835** between diagnostic improvement and success improvement, but the paper stops at diagnosis rather than using the measure to improve control.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **Beyond Retrieval**.

It is the cleanest systems paper in the set because it refuses to treat memory access as memory usefulness. A retrieved long trajectory is not help by default. It is a contaminated object containing workflow, stale bindings, irrelevant branches, and obsolete local state. The paper's support schema says the right thing explicitly: store the rich trace offline, but hand the actor only the transferable procedure, the values it must re-ground, the applicability constraints, and the verification obligations. That is exactly the distinction cabbageland keeps needing across agent memory, tool traces, and operational reuse.

The next-most relevant paper, **The Objective Is the Bottleneck**, sharpens the same taste in a world-model form. The latent state can contain the right information and still fail operationally if the decision objective measures the wrong geometry. **Agent Behavioral Contracts II** makes the parallel point for multi-agent reliability: composing local competence scores under the wrong dependence assumption yields a fake system guarantee.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Beyond Retrieval** matters because it changes the baseline. Raw trajectory injection is not the natural strong memory baseline once bindings can move. The right comparison boundary is after candidate retrieval and after single-memory selection.

**The Objective Is the Bottleneck** matters because it turns a long-horizon planning failure from "maybe the predictor degrades" into "measure the planner's metric first." That is a framing correction likely to matter beyond this one reproduction.

**Agent Behavioral Contracts II** matters because it makes a signed operational claim, not a vague warning. Under positive dependence, multiplying reliabilities overstates safety exactly when redundant components share a model.

**TRAPSBench** matters because it separates internal epistemic signal from verbalized restraint. That shifts part of the abstention problem from representation learning toward output-stage control.

**Diagnosing JEPA World Models** matters because it evaluates perturbation robustness at the rollout level under action conditioning, which is closer to what planners actually consume than encoder-only diagnostics.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The August 15 lesson is that stored, encoded, or latent competence does not cash out automatically as reliable action. A retrieved trajectory can still inject stale bindings. A predictive latent state can still be scored by a useless planner objective. Two reliable-looking agents can still fail together because their errors are correlated. A VLM can still know it should abstain and say the wrong thing anyway. A robust encoder can still hide a fragile rollout. Same taste everywhere: inspect the boundary where representation becomes action, because that is where the real failures accumulate.

## Detailed notes

- [The Objective Is the Bottleneck note](../paper_notes/objective_is_the_bottleneck_latent_world_models.md)
- [Agent Behavioral Contracts II note](../paper_notes/agent_behavioral_contracts_ii_compositional_reliability.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-05

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all reject the same lazy systems habit: letting a coarse proxy stand in for the real state transition. **TraceCompiler** says adjacency is not dependency, so recurring agent traces should only compile edges backed by attributable values. **Uncertainty Is Not Enough** says uncertainty is not itself a spending rule; the right question is whether the next expert is expected to remove risk. **TARL** says write versus hold is too blunt for long-term agent memory because revise, reject, and defer create different future worlds. **Preferred, Not Safer** says pairwise preference is not a safety signal, even when clinicians are casting the votes. **Cross-Anesthetic ECoG State Decoding Fails at the Decision Threshold, Not the Representation** says transfer failure can live in the threshold rather than in the representation, which means the fix is recalibration rather than feature worship.

## Short overview

This run attempted Brave Search first on Wednesday, August 5, 2026 through the public Brave HTML surface. The surface was reachable, but it still behaved more like a coarse web index than a trustworthy fresh-paper scout, so the real filtering moved to direct arXiv recent-page inspection and arXiv HTML full-text reading. I also did the required non-robotics pass across clinical, neuro, pathology, calibration, memory, verification, and evaluation terms instead of lazily collapsing back into another robot-heavy batch.

I inspected arXiv HTML full text for the five papers below. The top four are preserve-worthy. **Cross-Anesthetic ECoG State Decoding Fails at the Decision Threshold, Not the Representation** is a strong adjacent runner-up. The lesson is sharp and reusable, but the empirical scope is smaller and the key ketamine result is still within-subject cross-drug transfer rather than a population-level transfer claim.

**Most relevant today:** **TraceCompiler: Skill-Guided Mining and Compilation of LLM Agent Traces into Mostly Deterministic Workflows**. It is the cleanest direct paper in the batch on a problem agent builders actually have: traces contain reusable structure, but if you compile them with naive ordering heuristics you fossilize retries, accidents, and false dependencies into the workflow.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **TraceCompiler: Skill-Guided Mining and Compilation of LLM Agent Traces into Mostly Deterministic Workflows**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It stops workflow compilation from confusing order with causality. A hard edge only survives when a consumer argument can be uniquely attributed to an earlier producer, with an auditable evidence tuple and abstention when exclusion fails.

### 2. **Uncertainty Is Not Enough: Value-of-Information Routing for Mixtures of LoRA Experts**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It asks the right routing question. High uncertainty does not mean more experts are useful; the system should buy the next expert only when certified residual risk is expected to drop.

### 3. **TARL: Transaction-Aware Reliable Ledgers for Executable Memory Management in Long-Term Agents**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It replaces binary write-versus-hold memory updates with executable transaction semantics that can revise, reject, or defer instead of quietly polluting accepted memory.

### 4. **Preferred, Not Safer: Pairwise Preference Is a Poor Proxy for Clinical Safety**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It is a direct audit of a dangerous evaluation habit. Clinician pairwise preference leaderboards can reward surface plausibility while still hiding substantial harmlessness and accuracy failures.

### 5. **Cross-Anesthetic ECoG State Decoding Fails at the Decision Threshold, Not the Representation**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: It is a very clean failure decomposition. The decoder keeps the awake-versus-anesthetized ranking under ketamine, but the inherited threshold collapses, so the actionable bug is calibration rather than representation transfer.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **TraceCompiler: Skill-Guided Mining and Compilation of LLM Agent Traces into Mostly Deterministic Workflows**.

This paper is aimed right at a recurring agent-systems problem that cabbageland keeps circling: agents rediscover procedures they have already executed, but blindly replaying or summarizing old traces preserves too much accidental garbage. TraceCompiler treats reuse as a compilation problem under partial observability. It clusters recurring intents, strips retries and exploratory clutter, verifies dependencies at the argument level rather than by adjacency, types remaining bindings, and leaves only genuinely open choices as residual LLM nodes. The best case study is honest and useful: a Venmo money-request intent shrinks from 34 observed API calls to 11 runtime calls, while the bad case study is even more important because the compiler refuses to compile an irreversible Spotify and Todoist workflow whose branching logic was never observed. That refusal instinct is exactly the right standard.

The other strong papers reinforce the same deeper taste from different angles. **Uncertainty Is Not Enough** says a routing policy should estimate the value of the next computation, not just its confidence deficit. **TARL** says memory updates should be treated as typed state transitions, not as one binary commit bit. **Preferred, Not Safer** says evaluation needs to separate what humans like from what is safe enough to deploy. **Cross-Anesthetic ECoG** says a transfer failure diagnosis should tell you whether to learn new features or simply move the threshold.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**TraceCompiler** is strongest because it refuses the default event-log lie that "next in time" means "depends on." The baseline lesson is severe: adjacency and directly-follows statistics are weak proxies for executable structure when arguments, retries, and missing outputs are all in play.

**Uncertainty Is Not Enough** is strongest because it separates uncertainty from recoverable uncertainty. At matched compute it improves the average commonsense score from 77.5 for CARE to 78.1, while also lowering ECE from 0.051 to 0.042 and AURC from 0.099 to 0.087. The useful framing move is that the routing state should estimate marginal risk reduction, not just entropy.

**TARL** is strongest because it turns memory updating into an executable semantics problem instead of a retrieval embellishment problem. The baseline lesson is brutal: even gold binary Write/Hold supervision plus heuristics only reaches 0.4539 next-state accuracy and 0.1059 conflict preservation, while TARL reaches 0.6521 and 0.5376 by predicting the finer transaction directly.

**Preferred, Not Safer** is strongest because it does not merely complain about leaderboards. It quantifies the failure. In the paper's snapshot, the most preferred model still shows 18.0% harmlessness failures and 18.4% accuracy failures, while cardiology ECG reaches an 89.9% dangerous rate. The baseline lesson is that preference can be a style score wearing a safety costume.

**Cross-Anesthetic ECoG** is strongest because it localizes the failure. Ketamine keeps a session AUROC of 0.98, but the inherited threshold sits at chance and a baseline-anchored threshold lifts balanced accuracy from 0.50 to 0.85. The baseline lesson is that richer representation and domain adaptation are the wrong reflex if the real bug is threshold drift.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that a system should not be allowed to hide its real state transition behind a convenient scalar or binary proxy. Recurring traces need evidence-backed dependency structure, not event order. Modular expert routers need value-of-information estimates, not generic uncertainty panic. Long-term memory needs executable update types, not a write bit. Clinical evaluation needs direct failure accounting, not preference worship. Cross-domain decoding needs threshold diagnosis, not automatic representation escalation. The papers worth keeping are the ones that replace a mushy proxy with a more explicit object you can inspect, contest, and route on.

## Detailed notes

- [VI-MoLE note](../paper_notes/value_of_information_routing_mixtures_lora_experts.md)
- [TARL note](../paper_notes/tarl_transaction_aware_reliable_ledgers_memory_updates.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-10

## Theme

Today's useful papers all attack the same lazy assumption: if a system has more context, more code execution, or more structure-shaped outputs, then it must be using state correctly. **Addressable Memory for Video World Models** says long-horizon failure is often an addressability problem, not just a capacity problem. **Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling** says calibration under shift is not a scalar afterthought but a constrained training problem. **DocMemo** says iterative retrieval is still mostly fake state unless page beliefs actually get updated across rounds. **Fisher-R1** says executable analysis is not reliable statistical inference unless the method choice and p-value stay grounded. **Scenix** says sparse-view 3D reconstruction becomes much more useful when the representation is an executable scene program instead of an asset pile.

## Short overview

This run used the live Monday, August 10, 2026 arXiv batch, with direct inspection of the arXiv HTML full text for all five ranked papers below. I deliberately checked calibration, long-document evidence reasoning, and structured 3D reconstruction alongside world-model memory so the digest would not collapse into a single lane.

The top four are preserve-worthy and get notes. **Scenix** is the best structured-3D runner-up: the representation is real and the supervision design is good, but the stronger preserve case today belongs to the papers that make hidden state or reliability explicitly testable. **Most relevant today:** **Addressable Memory for Video World Models**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Addressable Memory for Video World Models**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It identifies the real long-horizon failure mode in autoregressive video world models: stored memory becomes unreadable once RoPE offsets leave the training range. The useful move is slot-rank virtual positioning plus canonical-space key storage, which keeps compressed memory both distinct and retrievable without retraining.

### 2. **Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling: Bilevel Optimization for LLM Calibration**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It treats calibration as a constrained training-time optimization problem instead of a scalar patch on top of a frozen model. The useful move is the bilevel framing: entropy pushes against overconfidence while the lower-level task objective prevents the system from becoming uniformly mushy.

### 3. **DocMemo: Dynamic Evidence Discovery via Probabilistic Memory-Guided Retrieval for Multi-Modal Document Understanding**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It turns long-document retrieval into an explicit evolving belief state instead of repeated stateless re-querying. The useful move is the tri-level memory plus Bayesian page-belief updates with Thompson sampling, which makes evidence search genuinely stateful.

### 4. **Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It is one of the better recent agent-reliability papers because it evaluates inferential correctness rather than just runnable code or plausible language. The useful move is a benchmark and RL signal grounded in p-value accuracy and decision correctness on real scientific data.

### 5. **Scenix: Sparse-View 3D Scene Reconstruction via Executable Scene Programs**

**Verdict:** strong direct runner-up.

Why it matters: It treats sparse-view scene reconstruction as structured program induction instead of texture-first geometry soup. The useful move is executable scene programs plus observation-consistent supervision that only asks the model to explain what the selected views actually support.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **Addressable Memory for Video World Models**.

This is the sharpest direct paper in the batch because it replaces a vague complaint about long-context forgetting with a specific mechanism failure and a clean fix. The paper argues that long-horizon video generation breaks not merely because the cache is too small, but because old memory becomes positionally unreadable once temporal RoPE offsets move outside the training distribution. That distinction matters. A bigger cache does not help if attention cannot address what is already stored. WorldTrace fixes that by assigning each compressed slot a distinct in-distribution virtual position and by unrotating keys into canonical space before compression, so the model can later re-encode them at the correct slot position without phase corruption. That is exactly the kind of explicit-state move cabbageland should care about: separate the memory representation from the addressing scheme, then make both testable.

The rest of the batch reinforces the same broader taste. **CALM** says uncertainty calibration should be trained under a constraint, not bolted on post hoc. **DocMemo** says retrieval should maintain an explicit evolving belief state. **Fisher-R1** says scientific agents should be rewarded for inferential validity, not just polished code traces. **Scenix** says scene structure should be represented as editable executable state rather than latent mush.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Addressable Memory for Video World Models** is strongest because it finds the right failure boundary. The paper does not merely say long rollouts drift. It shows that two different things break: old entries become hard to address because RoPE offsets go out of range, and naive compression destroys content because rotated keys from incompatible phases cancel. WorldTrace addresses both with slot-rank virtual positions and canonical-space memory writers. On long rollouts, **WorldTrace-Field** gives a **+15.5%** relative temporal-consistency gain, and on controlled revisits **WorldTrace-Landmark** gives a **+19.5%** episodic-recall gain on LoopBench, all without retraining.

**Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling** is strongest because it cleanly shows why naive calibration tricks do not survive shift. In the out-of-domain multiple-choice setting, CALM gets the best confidence ECE on three of four aligned models; on Llama-3.1 it cuts conf-ECE from **0.1784** to **0.1050**. In cross-domain generative QA it gets the best mean Sem-ECE, **0.0671**, beating both the uncalibrated baseline (**0.0846**) and tuned training-time baselines. The most useful result is conceptual: the flat entropy-regularization ablation fails, so the win is not "more entropy," it is the bilevel constraint that preserves task competence while pushing against overconfidence.

**DocMemo** is strongest because it turns memory from a slogan into a concrete retrieval state. The tri-level design separates document priors, page beliefs, and question-specific trajectory, then updates page confidence with Bayesian feedback instead of reconstructing context from scratch every round. On the three long-document benchmarks, it beats the strongest agentic baselines by **3.7** points on MMLongBench-Doc, **8.8** on LongDocURL, and **15.0** on PaperTab. The process metrics are even better: cumulative evidence recall rises from **28.32%** to **69.56%**, All-Hit Rate from **12.90%** to **58.05%**, and the system uses only **1.24** rounds on average, about **2.4x** more efficient than the fixed-three-round baseline.

**Fisher-R1** is strongest because it exposes the gap between looking statistically competent and actually being statistically reliable. P-Bench evaluates open-ended method choice, p-value computation, and reject/fail-to-reject decisions on 425 real scientific tasks. The paper shows that strong coding agents often get the direction right while missing the actual inferential target. Fisher-R1-14B beats GPT-5.4 on three of four strict metrics and outperforms DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with a reported **21%** average relative single-trial gain over DeepSeek and up to **26%** on the hardest tasks. The important framing result is that conclusion-only scoring flatters models too much; the raw-versus-strict gap is the real diagnostic.

**Scenix** is strongest because it replaces image-conditioned asset soup with structured executable state. The paper builds **XScene** with about **110,179** cases and **560,184** images, uses observation-consistent supervision, and predicts room-level scene programs before asset grounding and critic-editor-verify refinement. The catch is also useful: on raw out-of-domain SpatialGen evaluation, the model still over-generates inventory badly, predicting around **12.2** or **14.1** objects against a **6.3** ground-truth mean. That makes it a good runner-up rather than a preserve-over-everything note.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that systems only become trustworthy when their hidden state is made explicit enough to be checked, revised, and addressed correctly. A cache is not memory if the model cannot retrieve it at long horizons. A calibrated confidence number is not robust if it only works after fitting a domain-specific scalar. Iterative retrieval is not stateful if nothing like a belief state survives across rounds. Executable code is not scientific reliability if the inferential method is wrong. A 3D reconstruction is not structurally useful if it is just an opaque pile of assets. The good papers are the ones that force the support path itself to become a first-class object.

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-19

## Theme

Today’s useful papers are all about refusing the default coupling. TokenGS decouples Gaussian allocation from input pixels and camera rays, which matters because feed-forward 3D reconstruction has been tolerating huge representational waste as if it were an unavoidable tax. HiST-AT decouples action abstraction into a hierarchy and adds temporal reconstruction, which is a reasonable corrective to flat action tokenizers that treat smooth control as an afterthought. SpecGuard decouples speculative decoding from token-level acceptance alone and instead verifies whole reasoning steps using model-internal confidence and grounding signals.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing. arXiv API and search endpoints were also rate-limited during this run, so discovery fell back to direct inspection of recent arXiv category pages, then primary-source reading on shortlisted papers. I inspected the abstract, introduction, method framing, and early results sections for **TokenGS**, **A Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Action Tokenizer for In-Context Imitation Learning in Robotics**, and **From Tokens to Steps: Verification-Aware Speculative Decoding for Efficient Multi-Step Reasoning**. I did not fully audit appendices, supplements, or all implementation details, so the judgments below are strongest on mechanism and framing, moderately confident on headline results, and weaker on edge-case empirical claims.

The strongest paper today is **TokenGS: Decoupling 3D Gaussian Prediction from Pixels with Learnable Tokens**. The useful move is not merely “use tokens for 3DGS.” It is that the paper finally treats feed-forward Gaussian prediction as an allocation problem instead of a per-pixel dumping problem. Direct 3D mean regression plus learnable Gaussian tokens lets the model choose a compact scene representation that is not hard-tied to view count and image resolution.

**A Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Action Tokenizer for In-Context Imitation Learning in Robotics** is more modest, but still worth keeping. Its main contribution is not a new robot policy paradigm; it is a cleaner tokenizer for in-context imitation learning that uses two-level vector quantization and reconstructs both actions and timestamps. That sounds incremental, and it is incremental, but it is the right kind of increment: action discretization in robotics is often too flat and too indifferent to temporal smoothness.

**From Tokens to Steps: Verification-Aware Speculative Decoding for Efficient Multi-Step Reasoning** is the most adjacent paper in the batch. I would not overstate it as a reasoning breakthrough. But the paper does make one sensible systems point: if speculative decoding is meant to accelerate multi-step reasoning, token-level acceptance is the wrong unit of trust. Step-level verification with grounding and confidence signals is a more plausible control surface than yet another free-floating verifier stack.

A nearby paper I considered but did not keep for a full note is **Vision-Based Safe Human-Robot Collaboration with Uncertainty Guarantees**. It looks respectable, but from the accessible text it reads more like a safety-wrapper paper than a mechanism shift relevant to cabbageland’s main interests.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **TokenGS: Decoupling 3D Gaussian Prediction from Pixels with Learnable Tokens**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it replaces per-pixel Gaussian sprawl with explicit learnable scene tokens and makes compactness a first-class modeling choice rather than an accidental byproduct.

### 2. **A Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Action Tokenizer for In-Context Imitation Learning in Robotics**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it treats action tokenization as a structured hierarchy with temporal reconstruction instead of a flat codebook with vibes about smoothness.

### 3. **From Tokens to Steps: Verification-Aware Speculative Decoding for Efficient Multi-Step Reasoning**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it argues that reasoning-oriented speculative decoding should verify semantically coherent steps, not just locally plausible tokens.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** TokenGS.

The reason is that it attacks a failure mode cabbageland keeps circling around in other forms: the representation is technically explicit but still wastefully coupled to the observation surface. TokenGS makes the number of scene primitives a modeling choice, not a direct echo of pixel count. That is a useful pattern well beyond Gaussian splatting: allocate explicit state according to scene complexity, not according to whatever grid or tokenization the sensor happened to emit.

HiST-AT is the most useful robotics-adjacent paper if we care about learned action abstractions that are more structured than flat token bins. SpecGuard is mostly framing material, but it does reinforce a broader design taste: when a system reasons in chunks, verify chunks instead of pretending token-level local checks are enough.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

TokenGS is framing pressure on feed-forward 3DGS work that still treats one-pixel-ish primitive allocation as natural. If its results hold up, then some prior gains from large Gaussian counts may just be paying for a bad parameterization.

HiST-AT is baseline pressure on action-tokenizer papers that report gains from discretization without really modeling action hierarchy or temporal continuity. The gains are not enormous, but they are consistent enough to matter.

SpecGuard is framing pressure on speculative-decoding-for-reasoning papers that still optimize around token acceptance and bolt on heavy verifiers later. Its strongest claim is not the exact accuracy number; it is that the unit of verification should match the unit of reasoning.

## One-paragraph takeaway

Today’s lesson is that explicit structure becomes more useful when it breaks an unnecessary coupling. TokenGS breaks the coupling between scene complexity and pixel count. HiST-AT breaks the coupling between action abstraction and a single flat codebook. SpecGuard breaks the coupling between speculative decoding and token-level trust. Different domains, same standard: do not just add structure words — change what the model is forced to allocate, remember, or verify.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-02

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all attack the hidden interface where sloppy proxies quietly become the real system bottleneck. **Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late?** says computer-use agents do not mainly fail because they misunderstand the screen; they fail because expensive decoding sits on the decision-time critical path. **Tycho** says explicit world models only help if the agent can decide when building, testing, using, or bypassing them is worth the action budget. **KAISEN** says a fairness audit is not trustworthy just because it runs end to end; the audit instrument itself can fail silently. **When Derived Measurements Mislead** says upstream measurements should not become downstream facts unless instance-level reliability survives the semantic handoff. **QuantWAMs** says WAM quantization should be calibrated against deployment structure and rollout behavior instead of open-loop convenience losses.

## Short overview

This run started with Brave title discovery, but the live Brave HTML surface was too JS-heavy to use as a serious reading surface, so the real filtering happened on direct arXiv recent pages plus full-text arXiv HTML reads. I also kept the explicit non-robotics pass alive instead of lazily collapsing back into another all-world-model digest. That is why the final list mixes computer-use agents, explicit model induction, clinical fairness auditing, interface reliability, and deployment-oriented compression.

The five below are the most worth attention from the July 30-31 batch. The top four are preserve-worthy note candidates. **QuantWAMs** is useful and technically cleaner than the average deployment paper, but I think it is still more adjacent than the top four unless WAM deployment becomes an immediate priority.

**Most relevant today:** **Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees**. It isolates a very practical agent failure mode and fixes it with a systems move that does not require retraining the base model.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is the sharpest direct systems paper in the batch. It shows that a meaningful slice of GUI-agent failure is not bad reasoning but bad timing, then fixes it by moving generation off the critical path.

### 2. **Tycho: Active Abstraction with Programmatic World Models for ARC-AGI-3**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: The useful move is not merely "build a simulator." The paper treats world-model use itself as a metareasoning problem and shows that better transition matching does not automatically buy better action efficiency.

### 3. **KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It stress-tests the audit instrument instead of worshipping the audit output. Silent failure in mechanism diagnostics and cohort-sensitive drift alarms are exactly the kind of trap a serious measurement paper should expose.

### 4. **When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It names and operationalizes a real interface bug in modular AI systems: downstream language models over-trust upstream derived features unless reliability evidence survives the handoff.

### 5. **QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: This is one of the cleaner WAM deployment papers because it calibrates quantization around structure, rollout distribution, and joint video-action objectives instead of pretending open-loop losses are enough.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees**.

The core lesson is brutally practical: if a correct action arrives after the GUI window closes, that is not "almost correct." It is a systems failure caused by where the computation sits. AAPT fixes this by using idle time to precompile a bounded conditional policy tree with guards and deadlines, then routing cheaply at event time. That general pattern should transfer far beyond transient GUI windows: precompute when the environment is quiet, keep runtime routing cheap, and test whether a proposed bottleneck is actually causal instead of hand-waving about anticipation.

The other papers reinforce the same deeper instinct. **Tycho** says explicit world models matter only if the agent knows when they are worth using. **KAISEN** says evaluation pipelines need their own failure analysis. **When Derived Measurements Mislead** says uncertainty must survive the module boundary or the downstream model will canonize the wrong fact. **QuantWAMs** says deployment calibration should respect the structure of the actual closed-loop system.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late?** is strongest because it turns a vague complaint about agent latency into a controlled causal test. The framing move is that anticipation is not enough if decoding still happens on the decision-time critical path.

**Tycho** is strongest because it refuses the usual simulator fetish. The important framing move is that world-model quality and world-model usefulness are different objects, and action-efficient interaction depends on metareasoning over both.

**KAISEN** is strongest because it treats fairness auditing as an instrument with failure modes, not a moral incantation. The baseline lesson is that averages and nominal significance hide variance, proxy misspecification, and cohort-specific monitoring collapse.

**When Derived Measurements Mislead** is strongest because it defines a concrete downstream failure target rather than vaguely asking for "better uncertainty awareness." The matched-versus-shuffled evidence design is the paper's best methodological move.

**QuantWAMs** is strongest because it calibrates quantization against the closed-loop deployment object instead of against static proxy distributions. The useful baseline lesson is that WAM compression cannot be treated as ordinary homogeneous transformer quantization.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all punish the same lazy habit: treating a hidden intermediate as if it were already solved. GUI decoding latency is not solved just because the model can name the right action eventually. A world model is not useful just because it can replay observed transitions. A fairness audit is not informative just because it outputs a table. A derived measurement is not a fact just because it appears in structured text. Quantization is not deployment-ready just because an open-loop loss stays low. The papers worth keeping are the ones that drag these intermediates into the open, specify what they are supposed to do, and then test the failure modes directly.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-12

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all attack the same lazy assumption: if a model has state, then the system already knows what that state means and how to trust it. **Rollback Repair** says a bad memory is not a bad row; it is a contaminated dependency graph that needs explicit repair. **ReTree** says search state is not a transcript; it has to remember where evidence entered and what downstream reasoning depends on it. **ConfTriage** says confidence is not deployable just because a model can say a number; it has to be calibrated and attached to a deferral policy. **VidForensics-M1** says evidence supervision should come from verifiable temporal intervals rather than model-written rationales. **MAP-Graph** says shared memory is not governance unless provenance can filter, rerank, and gate actions.

## Short overview

This run used the live Wednesday, August 12, 2026 arXiv batch, with explicit non-robotics passes across agent memory/governance, medical calibration, and evidence/verification lanes. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for the four preserved papers below, and also inspected the full text of **MAP-Graph** as a strong direct runner-up.

Four papers earn preserved notes. **MAP-Graph** is the strongest direct runner-up: the typed provenance and gating story is useful, but the benchmark is synthetic and the paper overlaps enough with the stronger memory-repair pair that it loses the preserve slot today. **Most relevant today:** **From Faulty Memories to Corrected Actions: Dependency-Guided Rollback Repair for Memory-Augmented Agents**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **From Faulty Memories to Corrected Actions: Dependency-Guided Rollback Repair for Memory-Augmented Agents**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: It treats bad memory as contaminated downstream state rather than a bad record to delete. The useful move is explicit dependency tracing, independent-support checking, and answer-relevant replay, which turns repair into a state-management problem instead of a "please be more careful" ritual.

### 2. **Self-Correcting Long-Horizon Search Agents via Tree-Structured Memory**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: It turns search memory into an editable evidence tree with source-bound facts and contradiction-triggered pruning. The useful move is locating where a refuted claim entered the state, then rebuilding only the descendants that actually depended on it.

### 3. **ConfTriage: A Calibration-Aware LLM Triage Framework for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy with Selective Specialist Deferral**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It gives a cleaner deployment recipe for medical LLM triage than most clinical multimodal work. The useful move is not just asking an LLM for a diagnosis, but calibrating the model's verbalized confidence in logit space and routing low-margin cases to a specialist backstop with explicit guarantees.

### 4. **VidForensics-M1: Meta-Detection Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Temporal Grounding for AI-Generated Video Forensics**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It replaces model-written explanation rewards with verifiable temporal evidence. The useful move is Evidence-Guided Reward Redistribution, which redistributes label reward according to temporal-grounding quality rather than trusting a synthetic rationale just because it sounds forensic.

### 5. **MAP-Graph: Provenance-Aware Shared Memory for Multi-Agent Workflows**

**Verdict:** strong direct runner-up.

Why it matters: It separates permission, trust, and action risk inside a typed provenance graph. The useful move is recursive ancestry evaluation plus risk-sensitive gating, but the benchmark is synthetic and the exact-decision story is weaker than the task-success headline.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **From Faulty Memories to Corrected Actions: Dependency-Guided Rollback Repair for Memory-Augmented Agents**.

This is the sharpest paper in the batch because it attacks the place persistent-memory systems actually rot: not at retrieval time alone, and not at answer time alone, but in the propagated state between them. A poisoned or stale memory can alter claims, tool plans, answers, and later writes. The paper's central move is to stop pretending that deleting the source or rewriting the last answer solves that. Instead it builds a typed memory-to-action graph, traces downstream dependencies, preserves nodes with independent trusted support, and selectively replays only the answer-relevant affected computation.

That is exactly the kind of state discipline cabbageland keeps needing. On the controlled benchmark, the method reaches **85.3%** recovery versus **77.3%** for the strongest competing repair baseline, while removing all diagnosed faulty memories, preserving all benign memories, and replaying much less than the judge-style repair baseline. On the adapted LongMemEval-V2 subset, it reaches **68.0%** recovery versus **54.0%** for the next best method, while also posting the strongest claim-invalidation F1. The paper is not claiming perfect trace reconstruction, and the benchmark still assumes an upstream fault diagnosis. But the framing is right: fault removal is not state recovery.

The rest of the batch reinforces the same broader taste. **ReTree** makes search memory source-addressable and revisable at the claim-introduction point. **ConfTriage** makes model confidence operational by calibrating it and attaching it to a deferral policy. **VidForensics-M1** uses evidence the system can actually verify instead of explanations it merely likes. **MAP-Graph** pushes shared memory toward policy-governed provenance rather than semantic retrieval alone.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Rollback Repair** is strongest because it chooses the right repair unit. On the controlled benchmark it reaches **85.3%** recovery versus **77.3%** for LLM-judge repair, while cutting replay ratio from **0.217** to **0.123** and LLM calls from **9.80** to **5.70**. On the adapted LongMemEval-V2 subset it reaches **68.0%** recovery versus **54.0%** for the next best baseline. The main framing result is simple and useful: once faulty memory has already propagated, deleting the bad source is not the same thing as repairing system state.

**ReTree** is strongest because it turns contradiction repair into a state edit rather than a context-compression side effect. Across **2,149** questions, it reaches **44.0%** overall judge accuracy and **28.0%** EM, beating Full-Trajectory ReAct by **13.9** judge-accuracy points and the strongest aggregate bounded baseline by **3.0** points. On the FRAMES attribution diagnostic it reaches **42.8** CiteF1 with **14.8%** uncited claims, versus **31.5** and **33.1%** for Full-Trajectory ReAct. The important lesson is that bounded context only works if the system preserves where facts came from and what later reasoning depends on them.

**ConfTriage** is strongest because it turns LLM confidence into a real routing policy instead of a pretty side channel. The paper calibrates verbalized confidence in logit space, cuts ECE from **0.085** to **0.042**, and at threshold **tau = 0.28** lets the LLM resolve **76.5%** of cases while deferring **23.5%** to the specialist backstop. It reports **88.22%** F1 and **0.92** AUC. The sharper framing result is the ablation: natural-language radiology descriptions carry the signal, while low-level image statistics are basically diagnostically useless for the tested LLM setup.

**VidForensics-M1** is strongest because it makes evidence supervision verifiable. On ViF-Bench, the temporal-grounding version reaches **82.83%** accuracy, **73.16%** recall, and **81.00%** F1, improving over plain label RL by **10.30**, **9.74**, and **11.21** points respectively. It also beats explanation-based RL by **6.25**, **6.38**, and **6.96** on the same metrics. On the fake-only GenBuster subset, temporal grounding improves recall by **10.1** and **19.2** points on the OOD and Wild evaluations over label-only RL. The real contribution is not "better video forensics" in the abstract; it is the demonstration that reward should depend on evidence quality when the evidence is checkable.

**MAP-Graph** is a useful runner-up because it pushes provenance from audit metadata into runtime control. It reaches **94.96%** task success, **72.70%** exact decision accuracy, **90.22%** clean success, and **0%** attack success, leakage, and revocation violation inside its benchmark. The reason it stays a runner-up is that the benchmark is fully synthetic and the exact-decision story is less overwhelming than the task-success headline. It is still a good design paper, just not the one to preserve over today's sharper repair and evidence papers.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful August 12 lesson is that state only becomes trustworthy when the system can name where it came from, what depends on it, and what to do when it turns out to be wrong. Bad memories need dependency-aware rollback, not cosmetic rewriting. Search state needs introducers and descendants, not just summaries. Clinical confidence needs calibration plus a deferral boundary, not vibes. Evidence-aware reward works better when the evidence is a verifiable interval rather than a plausible story. Shared memory needs provenance that governs action, not just retrieval. Same lesson everywhere: stop treating state as text that happens to be lying around.

## Detailed notes

- [Rollback Repair note](../paper_notes/dependency_guided_rollback_repair_memory_augmented_agents.md)
- [ReTree note](../paper_notes/retree_tree_structured_memory_search_agents.md)
- [ConfTriage note](../paper_notes/conftriage_calibrated_llm_triage_pulmonary_nodules.md)
- [VidForensics-M1 note](../paper_notes/vidforensics_m1_verifiable_temporal_grounding_video_forensics.md)
