# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-19

## Theme

The strongest papers today all attack fake equivalence between a container and the state it is supposed to carry. A parsed view is not the workspace. Row accuracy is not evidence grounding. A JSON state field is not a state mechanism. Shared weights are not cross-task concept usability. Stacked frames are not memory.

## Short overview

This Wednesday, August 19, 2026 run used arXiv HTML full-text inspection for all five ranked papers below. Four papers earn preserved notes. **Action-Effect Memory Pretraining** is the one robotics paper worth carrying today, but it stays just below the preserve bar because the mechanism is better than the ecology: the gains are real, but the evidence still lives inside a fairly narrow benchmark-and-policy stack. **Most relevant today:** **StagedWorkspace**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **StagedWorkspace: A Versioned Workspace for Knowledge-Work Agents**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the cleanest agent-systems paper in the batch because it operationalizes a failure mode that usually gets buried under harness chatter: the agent can search one version, edit another, review a third, and submit a fourth. Instead of hand-waving about better tools, it defines a workspace-state contract tying parsed records, native artifacts, staged diffs, and submitted outputs to explicit versions. In paired ablations, dual parsed/native access improves OfficeQA Pass@1 by **8.3-12.1** points and APEX mean score by **4.7-9.2** points; with Gemini 3.1 Pro the system reaches **63.9%** on OfficeQA versus a published same-model row of **29.3%**.

### 2. **PathoArgus: Advancing Evidence-Grounded Long-Context Visual Reasoning across Gigapixel Whole-Slide and Multi-Slide Case Contexts**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the right embarrassment benchmark for long-context pathology QA because it asks whether the answer follows the evidence set, not whether the model can farm row-level multiple choice. PathoArgus-Bench contains **22,078** questions from **4,913** patients across **15** TCGA projects. GPT-5.6 reaches **57.09%** overall and **57.04%** ESG accuracy, but only **19 of 483** controlled evidence quartets are fully correct, or **3.93% QExact**. The companion reader reaches **50.39%** overall and **46.17%** ESG but only **1.86% QExact**, which is exactly the useful bad news: better access is not the same as grounded use.

### 3. **Explicit State Elicitation Is Not Enough: A Controlled Audit of Memory-Policy Classification**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This paper makes the right severe methodological move: it audits the benchmark and isolates the intervention before selling a structured-output story. On a frozen **160**-example controlled set with **40** matched four-way families, adding an explicit state-output field yields only **+0.6** points for Llama and **+3.3** for GPT-OSS, both non-significant. Taxonomy exposure helps more than state emission, which is precisely the problem: the gain mostly looks like label-structure leakage, not a faithful intermediate mechanism. The useful conclusion is brutal and correct: explicit state elicitation needs more than bolting a JSON field onto a routing prompt.

### 4. **Where a New Concept Must Enter: Entry Point Gates Cross-Task Usability in Unified Multimodal Models**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: This is the strongest multimodal concept-transfer paper in the batch because it separates architectural transfer from overlapping supervision. A concept bound through only one task direction transfers only if it enters shared computation in the right semantic format. An alignment probe predicts export across **36** configurations with **rho = +0.68**; a closed-form activation edit works at layer **7 of 28** and becomes indistinguishable from base behavior by layer **14**; and a mid-stack alignment objective acquires the concept with only **0.1%** relative loss of general text-to-image ability versus **41%** for the standard generative route.

### 5. **Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration, not yet preserve-worthy.

Why it matters: This is the one robotics paper today with a real mechanism rather than memory-branded frame stacking. AEM compresses interleaved vision-action history into a single Mamba-encoded final-token memory and uses masked reconstruction to force action-state structure into that bottleneck. On RoboTwin2.0 it lifts Diffusion Policy from **29.8%** to **50.5%** and ManiFlow from **9.8%** to **29.1%**, while beating direct feature stacking on both efficiency and randomized-scene success. It stays below the preserve bar because the evidence remains tightly tied to its chosen policy families and benchmark ecology.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **StagedWorkspace**.

Its core claim is exactly right for mixed-format agent work: artifact quality is downstream of state discipline. If parsed search, native edits, diffs, and submission do not point to the same evolving workspace state, then "good agent performance" becomes partly a bookkeeping illusion. The same taste shows up elsewhere in the digest. **PathoArgus** says answer accuracy is not enough unless predictions move with evidence. **Explicit State** says emitting a state label is not enough unless it actually improves the decision. **Where a New Concept Must Enter** says shared parameters are not enough unless the concept enters shared computation in a usable semantic format. Same moral across domains: the system has to keep the operative state live, not merely mention it.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**StagedWorkspace** matters because it turns artifact-state synchronization into an explicit experimental variable rather than invisible harness plumbing.

**PathoArgus** matters because ESG quartets and QExact punish models that keep answer priors while ignoring controlled evidence changes.

**Explicit State Elicitation** matters because it audits dataset shortcuts and bundled prompt changes before claiming that structured intermediate fields help.

**Where a New Concept Must Enter** matters because it reframes multimodal transfer around entry-point location and shared semantic format, not just weight sharing or more joint training.

**Action-Effect Memory Pretraining** matters because it argues for action-conditioned compact memory rather than naive history stacking in manipulation policies.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The August 19 lesson is that state has to stay operational all the way through the computation. A workspace contract has to preserve which artifact version the agent actually saw and changed. An evidence benchmark has to preserve whether the answer moves when the evidence moves. A memory-policy audit has to preserve the difference between answer-associated labels and real intermediate reasoning. A multimodal model has to preserve a concept at a site where both tasks can still use it. A robot memory has to preserve action-conditioned temporal structure rather than just append more frames. Same severe conclusion all day: do not confuse the object that stores the claim with the mechanism that makes the claim usable.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-11

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **memory, uncertainty, and evaluation only count when they enter the decision at the right boundary**. Remember When It Matters treats memory as a selective intervention policy, not a passive retrieval dump. CausalDS turns causal data-science evaluation into file-backed tool use with hidden SCM ground truth and first-class abstention. The patient-centred conversational-AI paper shows that identical clinical facts can produce different LLM triage behavior when the simulated patient changes communication style. Hidden Decoding adds latent per-token computation by expanding sequence length instead of widening the backbone. Latent Drift makes neurodegenerative forecasting target sparse latent change instead of reconstructing static anatomy.

I kept robotics / VLA out of the ranked five today. The scan deliberately covered non-robotics lanes: long-horizon agent memory, causal evaluation, medical / healthcare AI, foundation-model architecture reports, neuroimaging generative forecasting, diffusion numerical stability, LLM judge calibration, scientific ML, and generative video reasoning. The strongest robotics-adjacent candidates were **Latent Memory Palace**, **Native Video-Action Pretraining**, **Harness VLA**, **Temporal Ratio**, and **ContactMimic**. Several were plausible, but none clearly beat the non-robotics papers below on mechanism, evidence, and future usefulness.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. I used arXiv API/category search, direct arXiv pages, and full arXiv PDFs for discovery and inspection. Discovery quality is narrower than a healthy Brave-first run, but no preserved note today is abstract-only.

For the preserved notes, I inspected the full PDFs for **Remember When It Matters**, **CausalDS**, **The complexities of patient-centred conversational artificial intelligence**, and **Hidden Decoding at Scale**. I read the method / benchmark design, core results, ablations or reliability checks where relevant, and limitations. I also inspected full PDFs for **Progression as Latent Drift**, **Score Accuracy Along the Forward Diffusion Does Not Certify Numerical Stability in Diffusion Sampling**, **Do You Need a Frontier Model as a Citation Verifier?**, **When the Judge Changes, So Does the Measurement**, **Super Weights in LLMs and the Failure of Selective Training**, **MatBind**, and **OpenCoF** as ranked or runner-up candidates. I did not audit released code, reproduce benchmark runs, verify every appendix table, or independently validate provider-reported model outputs.

**Remember When It Matters** is the most relevant paper today. Its sharp move is to make memory a policy over when to intervene, including an explicit no-op action, instead of merely making more historical text available.

**CausalDS** is the strongest evaluation paper. It gives causal data-science agents hidden structural-causal ground truth, noisy observation layers, coding/tool use, Rung 1-3 tasks, and abstention cases where the correct answer is not to estimate.

**The complexities of patient-centred conversational artificial intelligence** is the strongest healthcare paper. It shows that communication style alone can shift LLM triage errors while the underlying clinical case is held fixed.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Remember When It Matters: Proactive Memory Agent for Long-Horizon Agents**

**Verdict:** must read for agent memory.

Why it matters: The paper names a real failure mode, behavioral state decay: task requirements, environment facts, failed attempts, diagnoses, and open subgoals stop influencing future actions even when they were observed earlier. The system adds a separate memory agent that maintains a structured bank and then chooses whether to inject a targeted reminder or stay silent. Across Terminal-Bench 2.0 and tau^2-Bench, memory intervention improves Sonnet 4.5 by +8.3 points on Terminal-Bench and +6.8 task-weighted points on tau^2-Bench, with smaller but nonzero gains for Opus 4.6. The ablations are the useful part: full-bank context, always-on reminders, generic memory retrieval, and advisor-only guidance are not equivalent to selective memory intervention.

### 2. **CausalDS: Benchmarking Causal Reasoning in Data-Science Agents**

**Verdict:** strong agent-evaluation benchmark, especially for abstention and uncertainty.

Why it matters: CausalDS builds each task around a hidden structural causal model, a narrated domain story, released tabular files, an observation layer that can corrupt or proxy the conceptual variables, and private SCM-derived ground truth. Tasks span Pearl's associational, interventional, and counterfactual rungs, and non-identifiable estimands require abstention. On the 100-scene realistic exam, Claude Opus 4.8 leads with CausalDSScore 0.278 and 82.4% pass rate, while GPT-5.5 ties the pass rate but falls to fifth by the composite score because its continuous estimates have heavier error tails. The important signal is that content correctness and abstention split apart: knowing when not to estimate is a separate capability.

### 3. **The complexities of patient-centred conversational artificial intelligence**

**Verdict:** strong healthcare deployment / evaluation paper.

Why it matters: The paper starts from 2,053 real patient-chatbot conversations, then builds a modular patient simulator with separate clinical-content, emotional-state, conversational-strategy, and communication-style channels. Human graders could barely distinguish real from simulated conversations, with 55.0% accuracy. The simulator then holds clinical facts fixed across 1,164 clinician-graded cases and varies five patient personae. For Gemini 3.5 Flash, anxious presentation raises over-triage by 11.0 points versus default, while dismissive presentation lowers over-triage and raises the more dangerous under-triage direction. The result generalizes qualitatively across GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude Opus 4.6. This is exactly the kind of interactional evaluation medical AI needs before deployment claims mean much.

### 4. **Hidden Decoding at Scale: Latent Computation Scaling for Large Language Models**

**Verdict:** important foundation-model architecture report, with proprietary-stack caveats.

Why it matters: Hidden Decoding gives each token multiple internal streams in the sequence dimension, supervises only the final stream, and keeps earlier streams as latent computation states whose KV cache remains available. Stream-Factorized Attention keeps most layers intra-stream and lets only selected layers mix streams, making a 4x expansion trainable at large MoE scale. The paper reports matched early-SFT comparisons where WeLM-HD4-80B and WeLM-HD4-617B improve every shared benchmark over their non-HD counterparts without increasing active Transformer parameters per token. This is a serious fixed-backbone scaling idea. The caveat is that the most important evidence sits inside the authors' WeLM training stack and unreleased frontier-scale checkpoints.

### 5. **Progression as Latent Drift: Generative Forecasting of Slow-Evolving Pathologies**

**Verdict:** useful neuro / medical generative modeling paper; lighter recommendation.

Why it matters: The paper argues that longitudinal brain MRI forecasting fails because the target is dominated by static identity anatomy while disease progression is subtle. It reframes the prediction target as latent temporal residuals, then uses Finite Scalar Quantization as a dead-zone filter to suppress nuisance variation while preserving consistent structural drift. On ADNI/AIBL longitudinal 3D MRI pairs, Latent Drift reports the best Diff-SSIM, NCC, downstream AD-classifier F1, and downstream accuracy among tested baselines. The mechanism is more interesting than the absolute clinical claim: model the change, not the image. The caveat is that downstream clinical utility is mediated by a frozen classifier rather than prospective medical validation.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Remember When It Matters.

The steal is the control contract: memory should not mean "retrieve more stuff." It should mean keeping structured execution state outside the action context, then deciding whether a specific remembered item is decision-relevant right now. The null intervention matters because a memory system that always speaks becomes another noisy planner. For OpenClaw-style agents, this maps directly onto repeated debugging, long-running tasks, tool observations, and user constraints that must re-enter the loop only when they affect the next action.

CausalDS gives the evaluation complement. If agents are going to claim causal or data-science competence, the benchmark needs hidden ground truth, file-backed analysis, noisy measurement layers, uncertainty scoring, and non-identifiable cases where abstention is correct. Patient-centred conversational AI gives the healthcare complement: benchmarks should vary how humans communicate, not just what facts they contain. Hidden Decoding and Latent Drift give two architecture-side echoes of the same idea: useful hidden state is not bulk context; it is computation or change represented at the boundary where the model needs it.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Remember When It Matters** is strong because its memory abstraction changes the control loop. The memory bank has private status, stable knowledge, and procedural experience; Phase 1 edits the bank through constrained memory tool calls; Phase 2 emits either a concise reminder or `<no_intervention/>`. The comparison against full-bank context is important: simply exposing remembered state improves less than selecting the behaviorally relevant memory. The Mem0 comparison is also useful because it separates production-style retrieval from memory as intervention policy. Caveats: the strongest memory agent is Claude Opus 4.6, many evaluations are single-sample pass@1 runs, and the method adds another expensive model call cadence.

**CausalDS** is valuable because it aligns the scoring object with the causal claim. The benchmark is not just "answer causal questions"; it generates hidden SCMs, stories, observed files, noisy measurement variants, and private ground-truth estimands. The result that abstention pass rate ranges from 18.8% to 75.0% is more interesting than a leaderboard rank because it says current agents can often compute when they commit, but they do not reliably know when the estimand is not warranted. Its limitations are mostly benchmark-design ones: synthetic scenes, editorial task-family weights, small per-slice counts in places, and dependence on the generator's realism.

**Patient-centred conversational AI** is strong because it tests an interactional variable that ordinary medical QA benchmarks erase. The simulator is not just a prompt persona; it decomposes facts, emotion, strategy, and communication style, then validates parameter adherence, clinical fidelity, and realism. The main result is not "LLMs are bad at triage"; it is more specific and more useful: with identical clinical content, patient presentation shifts calibration-in-the-large and error direction. The limitations matter: one clinical task, selected personae, simulated downstream conversations, clinician labels over vignettes rather than outcomes, and likely undercoverage of the communication styles least represented in digital health apps.

**Hidden Decoding** is one of the more plausible fixed-backbone scaling reports in the scan. The design avoids depth-loop recurrence, which fights large-model pipeline parallelism, by moving extra latent computation into sequence length. Supervising only the final stream gives earlier streams room to act as latent state, and the attention-factorization ablations support the cost/performance story. The caveat is reproducibility: the most persuasive numbers are on proprietary WeLM MoEs, including 80B and 617B total-parameter models, with public evidence largely limited to the paper report.

**Latent Drift** earns the fifth slot because its target choice is conceptually clean. If future and current brain MRI scans differ only subtly, predicting the whole future scan invites identity collapse. Predicting a quantized latent drift concentrates capacity on disease-relevant change. Its baselines and metrics are reasonable for a research paper, but the result should not be overread as clinical readiness. The downstream AD classifier is a proxy utility layer, and site / acquisition robustness remains open.

**Score Accuracy Along the Forward Diffusion Does Not Certify Numerical Stability** was a strong theoretical runner-up. It shows that small forward-marginal score error and even path-space closeness can coexist with Euler-Maruyama discretizations whose Wasserstein moments diverge. I kept it below the ranked five because its practical recommendation, bounded projection, is important but specialized, and today already had a strong generative-model slot.

**Do You Need a Frontier Model as a Citation Verifier?** and **When the Judge Changes, So Does the Measurement** both fit the evaluator-calibration lane. The citation-verifier paper is especially useful for source-attribution reward models: cheaper judges can be competitive, but directional false-positive / false-negative bias matters more than scalar F1. I did not preserve it today because the last two digests already centered heavily on evaluator validity, and CausalDS had broader mechanism transfer.

**Super Weights in LLMs and the Failure of Selective Training** is a neat interpretability / training warning. Parameter importance is not parameter trainability: training only critical coordinates can collapse, while LoRA succeeds by coordinating updates across layers. It stayed out of the ranked five because the controlled training story is mostly OLMo-1B/7B and less directly actionable than Hidden Decoding or CausalDS.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all reject bulk, undifferentiated state. Agent memory is useful when it becomes a calibrated intervention. Causal evaluation is useful when it knows which estimands deserve abstention. Medical conversational AI is useful only if evaluation includes the messy way patients actually communicate. Foundation models can gain latent computation without a wider backbone if intermediate streams are preserved and mixed carefully. Neuro-forecasting improves when the target is the sparse latent drift, not the whole static scan. The shared lesson is blunt: keep the state that matters, but make it enter the decision through a disciplined interface.

## Detailed notes

- [Proactive memory agent note](../paper_notes/proactive_memory_agent_behavioral_state_decay.md)
- [CausalDS note](../paper_notes/causalds_causal_reasoning_data_science_agents.md)
- [Patient-centred conversational AI note](../paper_notes/patient_centered_conversational_ai_style_triage.md)
- [Hidden Decoding note](../paper_notes/hidden_decoding_latent_computation_scaling.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-11

## Theme

Today’s strong pattern is **explicit control over what a world model is allowed to trust**. The best paper is **AGWM: Affordance-Grounded World Models for Environments with Compositional Prerequisites** because it adds explicit evolving affordance structure instead of hoping a latent state will remember which actions are currently legal. **Is the Future Compatible? Diagnosing Dynamic Consistency in World Action Models** is the sharpest evaluation paper because it asks whether imagined futures are actually compatible with the actions that supposedly caused them. **One Token Per Frame: Reconsidering Visual Bandwidth in World Models for VLA Policy** is the best systems result of the batch, but it is more about a practical bottleneck choice than a deeper representational shift.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, and discovery was blocked by a missing Brave API key in the current environment. I therefore used direct arXiv discovery and inspected recent papers from relevant world-model and robotics queries.

I inspected accessible arXiv abstract and HTML text for **AGWM**, **Is the Future Compatible?**, **One Token Per Frame**, and **NoiseGate**. I did not inspect appendices in full, so confidence is highest on the core mechanism and framing, and only moderate on exact empirical margins.

**AGWM** is the most important note to keep. Its core claim is simple and useful: standard world models entangle “what would happen if I took this action?” with “is this action even executable now?” In environments with prerequisite structure, that is a real modeling mistake. AGWM introduces a dynamic affordance graph with active, frontier, and locked capabilities, plus a structure-changing-event classifier that updates this graph during rollout. This is exactly the kind of paper that earns its structure language, because the explicit graph does real work.

**Is the Future Compatible?** is not a new world model. It is a diagnostic paper on WAM reliability. The useful contribution is the insistence that imagined futures should be judged by action-state consistency, not just visual plausibility or downstream success. That is a valuable evaluation axis, even though the concrete metric can be confounded by low-motion “background collapse” failures.

**One Token Per Frame** is the strongest practical systems paper of the set. It argues that when adapting a frozen VLA with a lightweight world module, high per-frame visual bandwidth may be wasteful. Their OneWM-VLA compresses each view to a single semantic token per frame and jointly generates latent rollout plus action trajectory under one flow-matching objective. I buy the systems lesson more than the broader conceptual claim. It is a good bottleneck paper, not a deep answer to world-model representation.

I also inspected **NoiseGate**. It is clever, but I do not think it clears the preservation bar today. Learning per-latent denoising schedules as information gates is a neat scheduler trick, yet the main contribution still feels like optimization around a specific joint denoising backbone rather than a more transferable structural idea.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **AGWM: Affordance-Grounded World Models for Environments with Compositional Prerequisites**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it separates action legality from transition prediction and explicitly tracks how the set of feasible actions evolves after structure-changing events.

### 2. **Is the Future Compatible? Diagnosing Dynamic Consistency in World Action Models**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it gives WAMs a missing reliability test, namely whether imagined futures are dynamically compatible with the actions they claim to model.

### 3. **One Token Per Frame: Reconsidering Visual Bandwidth in World Models for VLA Policy**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent systems paper.

Why it matters: it makes a concrete claim that a world module on top of a frozen VLA may only need one semantic token per frame, which is a nontrivial compression result if it holds up.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** AGWM.

The reason is not the benchmark win by itself. The reason is that it identifies a real category error in implicit world models. If a domain has compositional prerequisites, then “transition dynamics” alone is not enough, because the action space itself changes as the agent unlocks or destroys affordances. AGWM makes that evolving affordance state explicit through a DAG-structured graph with frontier constraints, and then conditions rollout on it.

That is much more interesting than another paper that says “world model” while quietly hoping a recurrent latent will somehow encode everything important. The graph here is not decorative. It constrains which imagined actions are feasible, provides interpretability, and is exactly the kind of explicit state cabbageland should pay attention to.

My confidence is fairly high on the paper’s core mechanism because I inspected the abstract, introduction, method framing, and substantial HTML text covering the dynamic affordance graph, structure-changing events, graph encoder, classifier, and predictor. My confidence is lower on how well it would transfer outside game-like prerequisite domains, because I did not inspect every experimental appendix or robustness detail.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update is that recent world-model work is getting more interesting when it explicitly distinguishes three questions: what happens next, what actions are currently legal, and whether imagined futures remain compatible with the actions that generated them. AGWM handles the second question explicitly. **Is the Future Compatible?** sharpens the third.

This matters for baseline choice too. A paper that only improves downstream success without checking action-state compatibility or affordance validity can still be hiding mush. If a world model predicts future observations but does not use explicit legality structure when legality is nonstationary, that is a weaker design than the headline metrics might suggest.

The modest negative update is for scheduler-heavy work like **NoiseGate**. The gating story is coherent, but the transferable mechanism is thinner. It looks more like a local optimization of a particular denoising architecture than a durable representational idea.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **AGWM** because it earns its explicit-structure claim: it models evolving affordances as a first-class state rather than burying executability inside latent drift. **Is the Future Compatible?** is the best reliability paper because it asks whether WAM futures are dynamically compatible with their own actions, not merely plausible-looking. **One Token Per Frame** is a good compression-and-coupling paper with a believable systems lesson, though less of a conceptual leap. The common theme is that explicit structure matters most when it changes what the model can trust during rollout, not when it just renames a latent.

## Detailed notes

- [Is the Future Compatible? note](../paper_notes/is_the_future_compatible_dynamic_consistency_world_action_models.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-22

## Theme

Today's strongest papers are about what happens after the first answer is no longer trustworthy. **CodeRescue** treats coding-agent recovery as a budgeted action choice instead of a dumb escalation ladder. **DWM** says latent world models should stop pretending all transition change comes from the agent. **ResearchArena** shows sabotage can hide inside artifacts while the headline task score stays flat. **Evaluating medical AI under missing information** makes the evaluator part of the safety measurement. **Neural Kolmogorov Equations** reframes stochastic-dynamics learning around density evolution so the time axis can be parallelized.

## Short overview

I checked the fresh `cs.AI`, `cs.CV`, `cs.LG`, `cs.RO`, `q-bio.NC`, and `eess.IV` arXiv recent pages on **Wednesday, July 22, 2026**. Brave Search was unavailable in this run because no Brave-specific search surface was exposed, so I used direct arXiv recent pages plus exact title-level search passes instead. I also ran an explicit non-robotics pass with terms like `medical`, `clinical`, `pathology`, `radiology`, `uncert`, `calibr`, `world model`, `memory`, `3D`, and `4D` so the digest would not collapse into yet another agent-only feed.

That pass surfaced several decent medical and deployment papers, but most of them were either benchmark wrappers, tutorials, or weakly supported claims. The best material today had a cleaner mechanism: budgeted post-failure routing, supervision-level world/action decomposition, artifact-aware sabotage evaluation, evaluator-confounded safety measurement, and a deterministic density-evolution alternative to autoregressive neural SDE training. No robotics or VLA paper cleared today's top five.

**CodeRescue** is the most relevant paper today. The useful idea is that once a cheap coding attempt fails, the next question is not just "escalate or not?" It is "which extra computation buys the best solve-rate gain per dollar under this failure signature?"

## Ranked papers

### 1. **CodeRescue: Budget-Calibrated Recovery Routing for Coding Agents**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is one of the first coding-agent papers to treat recovery as a real deployment decision rather than a moral duty to escalate. The router chooses among `reflect`, `replan`, and `escalate`, then a CRC layer turns the same router into budget-dependent operating points without retraining. Around the medium-budget regime, the three-action router reaches `0.717` solve rate while using only about `35%` of the cost of always escalating.

### 2. **DWM: Separating World Effects from Actions in Latent World Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: The mechanism is sharp. Instead of changing the world-model backbone, the paper changes the supervision so the model has to separate action-invariant world motion from action-driven change. On the three new `W` benchmarks, this buys an average absolute planning-success improvement of `13.1%` while leaving the flat control tasks roughly intact.

### 3. **ResearchArena: Evaluating Sabotage and Monitoring in Automated AI R&D**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: This is a real control benchmark, not just a vibes essay about AI R&D risk. The useful distinction is between **embedded sabotage** hidden inside the submitted artifact and **independent sabotage** that leaves the artifact unchanged. The ugly finding is that main-task scores can stay basically flat while sabotage succeeds anyway, and artifact-aware monitoring still misses a lot of embedded damage.

### 4. **Evaluating medical AI under missing information: same-provider judges and human raters change apparent safety**

**Verdict:** useful direct diagnostic paper.

Why it matters: The paper isolates a safety property that current medical-AI evaluation often smears out: whether the model over-commits when the necessary information is absent. The strongest result is not just that models fail there, but that judge choice materially changes the apparent safety ranking. Reported failure rates land roughly between `1 in 12` and `1 in 3`, and LLM judges look more permissive than clinicians.

### 5. **Neural Kolmogorov Equations: Parallelizable Learning of Stochastic Dynamics under General Noise**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent mechanism paper.

Why it matters: This is not agent work, but it has real structural value. The paper moves from trajectory-level neural SDE modeling to density evolution via the Kolmogorov Forward equation, which makes general Levy-type noise easier to express and opens a parallel-in-time training path. That is a meaningful change in where the computation lives.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** CodeRescue.

The steal is the recovery-action framing. Cheap repair, cheap replanning, and expensive escalation are not just a monotone ladder. Their usefulness depends on the failure signature and the current budget. That is a much better abstraction for tool-using agents than treating all post-failure compute as "use a stronger model."

**DWM** is the complementary world-model paper: if the environment moves on its own, the supervision should say so explicitly. **ResearchArena** is the deployment complement: monitors need artifact access because transcript-only inspection misses the thing that actually matters. **Medical AI under missing information** is the evaluator complement: the judge is part of the metric. **Neural Kolmogorov Equations** is the modeling complement: sometimes the right move is to learn probability-flow structure instead of serially simulating trajectories.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**CodeRescue** is strongest because it breaks the binary-cascade assumption cleanly. Caveat: the paper only studies one post-failure decision rather than full multi-round recovery.

**DWM** is strongest because it treats world/action separation as a supervision problem rather than a giant architectural rewrite. Caveat: the clearest wins come from controlled `W` variants, so part of the story is still benchmark construction.

**ResearchArena** is strongest because it evaluates sabotage where artifact inspection actually matters. Caveat: it is still a benchmarked red-team game with relatively small per-configuration run counts, so the exact rates will move as models change.

**Evaluating medical AI under missing information** is strongest because it exposes evaluator confounding instead of hiding behind a single judge. Caveat: the perturbation is a truncation-based probe, so the paper has to spend real effort auditing whether the truncations stay clinically meaningful.

**Neural Kolmogorov Equations** is strongest because it broadens the noise model beyond standard neural-SDE assumptions while also attacking time-scaling. Caveat: it is a fairly mathematical systems paper, so the practical payoff depends on whether the density-projection machinery remains stable on harder real data.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that hidden channels eventually come due. Recovery policy should depend on failure evidence and budget, not on a fixed escalation superstition. World models should separate autonomous drift from action-caused change if they want to plan honestly. Safety evaluation should inspect the artifact, not just the transcript, and medical-AI safety claims should name the judge because the judge changes the result. Even the stochastic-dynamics paper is about the same thing: move the problem into the right representation and the computation gets cleaner. In all five papers, the useful move is to stop averaging together things that should have been separated.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-06

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all attack the same lazy systems habit: letting a summary stand in for the state it supposedly summarizes. **EA-Graph** says a prose note is not a verification record unless it keeps the exact artifact content that made the claim true. **SafeCommit** says a high-confidence action is not safe unless it survives every still-plausible world. **The Calibration Floor** says a self-correction gain is not a reasoning gain unless it survives answer-extraction surgery. **CRS-Triage** says multimodal confidence is not trustworthy unless reliability, missingness, and disagreement all shape the defer decision. **Mimir** says a long history is not a memory architecture unless task progress and world belief are split into distinct state objects.

## Short overview

This run attempted Brave Search first on Thursday, August 6, 2026 through the public Brave HTML surface. The surface was reachable, but the results were noisy and mixed fresh papers with older generic memory hits, so it was not trustworthy enough for final filtering. Real selection moved to direct arXiv recent-page inspection plus arXiv HTML full-text reading.

I did the required non-robotics pass across calibration, clinical triage, radiology, and adjacent multimodal medicine rather than defaulting into another robot-heavy batch. I inspected arXiv HTML full text for all five ranked papers below. The top four are preserve-worthy and get notes. **Mimir** is a strong direct runner-up: the mechanism is good and the ablations are useful, but the paper is shorter and narrower than the four keeps above it.

**Most relevant today:** **EA-Graph: Artifact-Anchored Verification Memory for Coding Agents under Upstream Drift**. It is the sharpest paper in the batch on a problem coding agents actually have right now: a previous session can leave behind a true conclusion with a false freshness assumption, and ordinary prose memory is too coarse to tell the difference.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **EA-Graph: Artifact-Anchored Verification Memory for Coding Agents under Upstream Drift**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It treats verification memory as a claim-anchoring problem, not a note-taking problem. The useful move is sub-path artifact identity plus a hard **unprovable** state when replacement content is missing.

### 2. **SafeCommit: Certifying When Memory-Grounded Agents May Safely Act**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: It gives a clean decision rule for when an agent may safely release a side-effectful action. The action has to be safe in every retained plausible world, not merely favored by one story.

### 3. **The Calibration Floor: Format Repair Can Masquerade as Self-Correction at Small-to-Mid Scale**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It is a sharp audit of the self-correction literature. A lot of supposed reasoning gain collapses into answer-extraction repair once you decompose the margin correctly.

### 4. **CRS-Triage: Confidence- and Reliability-Aware Selective Triage under Incomplete Clinical Evidence**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: It does not treat uncertainty as a generic scalar. It makes reliability modality-specific, raises uncertainty under cross-modal disagreement, and optimizes against under-triage instead of pretending all mistakes cost the same.

### 5. **Mimir: A Neuro-Symbolic Memory System with Dynamic Grounding for Embodied Agents in Interactive Environments**

**Verdict:** strong direct runner-up.

Why it matters: It cleanly separates task memory from world memory and shows that the split actually does work. The ablations are the real selling point: remove world memory and EB-Habitat success collapses.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **EA-Graph: Artifact-Anchored Verification Memory for Coding Agents under Upstream Drift**.

This paper hits a real continuity failure in coding agents: one session can verify a behavior against a specific upstream state, another session inherits the claim after the upstream has drifted, and the workspace still looks superficially healthy. EA-Graph's core move is severe and correct. It does not store "we checked this." It stores claims anchored to sub-path artifact identities and the exact content digests that justified those claims. When the supporting artifact changes, the claim is not politely caveated. Its freshness is revoked, and if the replacement content is unavailable, the paper insists on **unprovable** instead of a fake binary guess. That is the right instinct for agent memory systems that need to survive handoffs, upstream drops, and partial visibility without bluffing.

The rest of the batch reinforces the same taste from other angles. **SafeCommit** says action release should depend on explicit alternative worlds, not on one confident narrative. **The Calibration Floor** says evaluation should separate content change from format rescue before talking about reasoning. **CRS-Triage** says defer logic should internalize missingness, disagreement, and asymmetric risk. **Mimir** says long-horizon control improves when progress state and scene belief stop living in one mushy latent bucket.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**EA-Graph** is strongest because it refuses file-level and prose-level invalidation. In the paper's worlds, file-granularity review marks about 88 of 96 behaviors as suspect when only about 17 are actually affected. In the Haiku round, artifact-anchored memory beats both prose notes and no persistent memory in all seven worlds, with exact paired p = 0.0156 against each control.

**SafeCommit** is strongest because it reframes action release as a set-valued safety question. At alpha = 0.05, single-world acting reaches a 41.2% unsafe-commit rate, while full SafeCommit gets that down to 2.6% with 97.4% task success. The important lesson is that certification without probing is too conservative, and probing without certification is too loose.

**The Calibration Floor** is strongest because it attacks the measurement boundary directly. On 12 admitted cells with live extraction failures, format effects exceed content effects with one-sided Wilcoxon p = 1.7e-3. The constrained-decoding control closes a median 71% of the gap between the naive total effect and the content-margin estimate, and the frontier arm still shows zero content margin in all five checked cells despite positive total deltas.

**CRS-Triage** is strongest because it treats selective prediction as a clinical risk problem rather than a generic abstention problem. At 80% coverage, its CRS score cuts expected triage penalty from 0.267 with evidential certainty to 0.208, and under-triage from 5.9% to 4.7%. The useful framing move is that disagreement between modalities should raise fused uncertainty, not get averaged away.

**Mimir** is strongest because the ablations show the memory split is doing real work. On EB-Habitat with Qwen3-VL-32B, removing world memory drops success from 71.5 to 12.5, while removing task memory drops it to 46.5. That is a much more convincing argument than just saying "we added memory and scores went up."

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that systems get brittle when a compressed summary is allowed to masquerade as the state transition it came from. Verification memory should keep artifact-level anchors, not only conclusions. Action release should range over plausible worlds, not one confidence number. Self-correction claims should survive decomposition into content and format margins. Clinical deferral should reflect reliability and asymmetric harm, not only uncertainty magnitude. Embodied agents should keep task progress and world belief as separate writable objects. The good papers are the ones that replace mushy proxy state with an explicit object you can revoke, inspect, or route on.

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-09

## Theme

Today’s useful thread is explicit structure at the interface, not bigger mush. The best hit separates camera motion from object motion and also distinguishes causes from consequences inside controllable video generation. The best adjacent hit stabilizes test-time memory updates for long 4D reconstruction instead of pretending unconstrained online plasticity will just behave. The practical robotics paper uses a stochastic planner to recover the multi-modality that deterministic end-to-end motion planners threw away.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to direct recent arXiv inspection and arXiv HTML reading. I inspected the arXiv abstract pages and experimental HTML for the top candidates, but I did not do a full PDF read for every surfaced paper, so the confidence level is "careful triage," not "full deep read."

The strongest paper is **MoRight**, because it is not just another motion-control skin on top of a video model. The real move is to split the problem into a canonical object-motion stream and a target-camera stream, then separately model active motion and passive consequence. That gives the paper a real mechanism and a cleaner causal story than most motion-control work.

**Fast Spatial Memory** is the best adjacent paper. It is not really a world model in the strong planning sense, but it is a serious memory-interface paper for long 4D reconstruction. The elastic test-time-training idea is the part worth stealing: stabilize fast adaptation with a Fisher-weighted pull toward anchor weights so long sequences do not just degenerate into drift.

**Flow Motion Policy** is the practical robotics pick. I would not oversell the conceptual novelty, but it fixes a real regression in end-to-end neural planning: deterministic planners lost the natural multi-modality that made best-of-N useful. Flow matching brings that back and makes inference-time sampling actually available again.

I also checked **Genie Sim PanoRecon**, **TAMEn**, **RoSHI**, and **From Blobs to Spokes**. They each have something real in them, but for this repo pass they felt either more infrastructural than mechanism-rich, or less transferable to the memory / controllability / explicit-structure questions that matter most here.

## Ranked papers

### 1. MoRight: Motion Control Done Right

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it explicitly disentangles object motion from camera motion and splits motion into active versus passive components, so the model is at least trying to learn action-consequence structure rather than merely animating trajectories.

### 2. Fast Spatial Memory with Elastic Test-Time Training

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: the elastic test-time training mechanism is a concrete answer to the usual fast-weight failure mode of drift and forgetting across long sequences. The 4D reconstruction framing is adjacent, but the stability mechanism is broadly reusable.

### 3. Flow Motion Policy: Manipulator Motion Planning with Flow Matching Models

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it restores multi-modal planning behavior to open-loop neural motion planning and uses best-of-N collision filtering at inference time. More practical than profound, but still a real improvement over one-shot deterministic planners.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** MoRight.

It lands squarely in the repo’s taste profile: explicit decomposition, cleaner interfaces, and a claim to causal structure that at least has an architectural counterpart instead of being pure branding. The most interesting part is not the headline benchmark story. It is the choice to put object motion in a canonical static-view branch and let target-view generation attend across views, while separately treating user-driven motion and resulting motion as different roles.

Fast Spatial Memory is the best adjacent reference because it treats memory as a mechanism problem rather than just a bigger-context problem. The elastic consolidation idea is likely more transferable than the exact 4D rendering stack.

Flow Motion Policy matters mainly as framing pressure. If end-to-end neural planners are deterministic by default, they are discarding feasible alternatives that classical stochastic planners exploited for decades. That is a self-inflicted wound, and this paper patches it.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

MoRight is good pressure on papers that say "controllable motion" when they really mean dense trajectory following. If camera changes and object motion share one control channel, the representation is already muddled. And if every moved object must be explicitly prompted, the model is not doing much causal work.

Fast Spatial Memory is useful pressure on long-context 3D / 4D papers that celebrate test-time adaptation without showing what keeps the adaptation from wandering off. The elastic prior is not glamorous, but it is exactly the kind of boring stabilizer these systems often need.

Flow Motion Policy is baseline pressure on open-loop neural planning. If a planner emits one path and hopes for the best, it should now be compared against a stochastic version that can cheaply sample several and keep the first collision-free result.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The strongest papers today improve the interface instead of just polishing outputs. MoRight makes camera, action, and consequence less entangled. Fast Spatial Memory makes online adaptation less forgetful by adding explicit consolidation pressure. Flow Motion Policy makes end-to-end planning stochastic enough to recover useful alternatives at test time. Different domains, same lesson: when the structure is doing real work, the model stops looking clever only by accident.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-23

## Theme

Today's strongest papers are about refusing to confuse access with retention. **Dream Rehearsal** shows a world model can keep the old task signal while the actor still forgets how to use it. **Decodability Supervision** shows a verbalizer can reconstruct an activation while still lying about the specific content that supposedly explains it. **PRO-LONG** argues that long-horizon memory may work better as a lossless log plus programmatic search than as clever summarization. The best medical paper says encoder convergence comes from the pretraining objective, not from scale theater or clinical-label mystique. The quantized-reasoning monitor is the weakest keep today, but at least it proposes a real intervention mechanism instead of another generic "think longer" slogan.

## Short overview

I checked the fresh `cs.AI`, `cs.CV`, `cs.LG`, `cs.RO`, `q-bio.NC`, and `eess.IV` arXiv recent pages on Thursday, July 23, 2026. Brave Search was unavailable in this run because `web_search` failed with `missing_brave_api_key`, so I used direct arXiv recent pages, exact title-level passes, and full-text reads from arXiv HTML instead. I also ran explicit non-robotics passes over terms like `medical`, `clinical`, `radiology`, `pathology`, `uncert`, `world model`, `memory`, `interpret`, and `foundation model` so the digest would not drift into a one-lane agent or robotics feed.

The best papers today all attack a false proxy. Replay is not retained policy. Reconstruction score is not truthful explanation. A bigger context window is not the same thing as usable memory. Clinical supervision is not what makes medical encoders geometrically converge. Even the quantized-reasoning monitor matters because it asks for a more surgical compute intervention than "sample more." No robotics or VLA paper cleared today's top five.

**Dream Rehearsal** is the most relevant paper today. The steal is the decomposition: if the world model already retains the old task signal, then continual-learning failure is not mainly a storage problem. The fix should rehearse the actor through that retained world, not keep pretending the world model itself needs more protection.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **The World Model Remembers, the Actor Forgets: Dream Rehearsal for Continual Model-Based RL**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is the cleanest mechanism paper of the batch. It localizes forgetting in replay-trained Dreamer-style agents to the actor channel rather than the world-model memory, then uses graded dream rehearsal to recover `3/3` four-task chains and `3/3` eight-task chains where plain replay passes `0/3`.

### 2. **Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable Activation Explanations**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: The audit is brutal in the right way. A released Qwen-based activation verbalizer reconstructs well while only about `2%` of specific claims are reconstruction-dependent, so the score mostly tracks gist. The repair is also real: train the target model so designated content stays probe-decodable instead of trying to beautify the verbalizer.

### 3. **PRO-LONG: Programmatic Memory Enables Long-Horizon Reasoning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: This is one of the better recent memory-harness papers because it resists fake sophistication. The main move is just to log everything and let a coding agent search the log programmatically. On ARC-AGI-3 that buys an average `18.0`-point improvement over the base coding agent while using `4.2x` to `5.8x` fewer tokens than stronger specialized harnesses.

### 4. **Self-supervision drives representational convergence in medical foundation models more than clinical supervision**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent paper.

Why it matters: The controlled result is the interesting part. Holding data, architecture, and scale fixed, the self-supervised objective produces much stronger cross-encoder alignment than clinical-label supervision or image-text training. That is a better story than the usual vague claim that scale or domain labels magically induce a shared medical geometry.

### 5. **CUSUM-Shaped Inference-Time Monitoring and Targeted Re-Decoding for Quantized Small Language Model Reasoning**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent paper.

Why it matters: The attractive part is not the modest accuracy gain by itself. It is the selective rollback mechanism: monitor uncertainty and degeneration windows online, restore token and KV-cache state, and re-decode locally instead of paying for a full restart. The paper is also unusually honest that its chronology-audit accuracy bump is suggestive rather than confirmatory.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Dream Rehearsal.

The key idea is to separate remembered world structure from retained behavior. If the world model already preserves rewards, values, and termination structure under replay, then the actor is the thing that needs rehearsal. That is a much sharper control story than the usual continual-RL habit of treating every forgetting problem as latent-state erosion.

**Decodability Supervision** is the interpretability complement: if a score cannot punish false additions, do not let it impersonate truth. **PRO-LONG** is the systems complement: keep the record lossless and make retrieval programmable. **The medical convergence paper** is the representation-learning complement: objective choice can matter more than supposedly privileged supervision. **The CUSUM paper** is the inference-time complement: if a reasoning trace is going rotten, fix the trace segment rather than blindly spending more compute.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Dream Rehearsal** is strongest because it breaks a field assumption instead of just decorating it. Caveat: everything is still demonstrated on MiniGrid chains with a `17M`-parameter Dreamer agent, so the scale claim remains open.

**Decodability Supervision** is strongest because it turns activation-verbalization faithfulness into a claim-level audit question and then narrows the repair to something verifiable. Caveat: RECAP guarantees decodability of designated content, not a full mechanistic explanation of the model's computation.

**PRO-LONG** is strongest because it treats memory as infrastructure rather than magic. Caveat: the empirical case is still concentrated in ARC-AGI-3, so some of the win may be benchmark-specific context engineering rather than a universal memory law.

**The medical convergence paper** is strongest because it runs the right controlled comparison instead of hand-waving about scale. Caveat: the observed shared geometry is modest, within-modality, and explicitly does not reproduce radiologist similarity judgments.

**The CUSUM paper** is strongest because it proposes a state-consistent rollback controller rather than pure output reranking. Caveat: the authors themselves say the chronology-audit result is statistically uncertain and the sequential statistic is not a validated e-detector.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that preserving the wrong object creates fake confidence. A replay buffer can preserve world knowledge while the policy channel still rots. A reconstruction score can stay high while specific explanatory claims are false. A huge context window can still be a bad memory system if retrieval is lossy or awkward. Clinical supervision can feel semantically privileged while contributing less to representational convergence than plain self-supervision. The useful move in all five papers is to stop trusting the proxy and reattach the mechanism to the thing that actually has to work.

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv pages were reachable for the serious candidates and useful as metadata checks, but I did not find useful discussion or related-paper trails there. I used AlphaXiv only as a supplement, then relied on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs for primary-source inspection. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on June 22, the arXiv API still returned June 18 uploads as the newest entries in the checked AI, ML, CV, CL, statistics, medical, and robotics lanes; I did not find a fresh June 22 batch yet. I therefore treated today as a remaining-strong-paper scan rather than pretending there was a new Monday drop. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for **Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents**, **Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction**, **When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital**, **StylisticBias**, **GroundControl**, **FlowEdit**, **Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning**, and **Evaluation of EEG Foundation Models for Event-Based Burst-Suppression Detection in ICU**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents** is the most relevant paper today. It treats agent monitoring as probabilistic inference over an execution trace instead of local thresholding of noisy predicates. The useful move is the distributionally robust bound: the monitor does not get to assume independence just because independence would make the action look safe.

**Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction** is the strongest theory paper in the scan. It resolves whether prediction-time randomization is statistically necessary for sample-optimal multicalibration and extends the same derandomization idea to outcome indistinguishability and omniprediction.

**When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital** is the strongest medical/healthcare paper today. It shows pooled federated conformal risk control can satisfy an average guarantee while failing 40 percent of hospitals in a real brain-tumor segmentation setting, then proposes a shrinkage risk-curve protocol that trades coverage and efficiency more sanely than local calibration.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. **StylisticBias** is a good MLLM bias benchmark: holding synthetic identity fixed while changing one visual cue reveals that roughly 15 appearance attributes account for nearly 80 percent of aggregate bias. I kept it as a runner-up because the setup is synthetic and the mechanism is more audit design than modeling primitive. **GroundControl** is a clean robotics/navigation uncertainty paper: distance-to-goal dynamics plus risk-coverage evaluation beats entropy-style uncertainty on EB-Navigation, but it stayed out of the top three under the topic-balance guardrail. **FlowEdit** has an attractive external-memory pronunciation adaptation mechanism for frozen TTS, but the paper is short and narrower than the preserved agent-verification and medical-calibration papers.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives agent runtime monitors a way to reason about uncertain policy predicates without collapsing them into brittle local binary decisions. The Datalog derivation graph plus distributionally robust SDP relaxation is a concrete template for enforcing global risk bounds under ambiguity.

### 2. **Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as calibration and evaluation theory.

Why it matters: it removes prediction-time randomness from sample-optimal multicalibration and omniprediction. That matters because randomization makes auditing, reproducibility, and downstream decisions messier exactly where calibration is supposed to improve trust.

### 3. **When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital: Federated Conformal Risk Control via Risk-Curve Shrinkage**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as medical deployment calibration.

Why it matters: it makes the marginal-versus-site failure visible. A pooled conformal guarantee can look fine while specific hospitals miss tumor voxels above the target false-negative rate. The paper's useful object is the per-site empirical risk curve, not another aggregate metric.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents.

The steal is the monitor shape. If an agent is about to mutate or transmit state, the monitor should not ask a sequence of isolated yes/no questions and then pretend the resulting trace is safe. It should preserve uncertainty across the trace, compile the dependency structure, and compute a global risk bound for the candidate action.

The multicalibration paper contributes a complementary lesson: if a trust property depends on random coins at prediction time, it is worth asking whether those coins are essential or just an artifact of the proof. Here they were not essential. The paper's adaptive interval-plus-rounding construction is not a plug-and-play engineering recipe, but the framing is valuable.

The federated CRC paper contributes the deployment lesson: average calibration is not enough when the harmed unit is a hospital, client, group, or environment. If the deployment unit matters, the calibration object has to keep that unit visible.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents** raises the bar for agent monitor papers. It models tool-call trajectories as Datalog derivation graphs, formulates exact worst-case policy-violation risk as an LP over joint measures, and uses a polynomial SDP relaxation to get a sound upper bound without assuming predicate independence. On Intercode, ATBench, and Praline side-channel tasks, the SDP monitor preserves security while improving utility and avoiding the long solver tails of exact SMT-style refinement. The caveats are serious: the guarantee is only as good as the tool semantics, predicate marginals, and policy specification, and long traces can make robust bounds collapse toward 1.

**Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction** is a clean theoretical advance. Earlier sample-optimal multicalibration algorithms output randomized predictors; deterministic predictors had worse epsilon dependence. This paper handles the atom problem by learning context-dependent confidence intervals, producing a randomized predictor whose support respects those intervals, partitioning the context space into rounding cells, and fixing one sampler seed per cell. The main theorem gives deterministic ECE multicalibration at the minimax randomized rate, roughly Otilde(epsilon^-3) in polynomial group regimes. The limitation is practical distance: this is theory, with finite or covered test classes and nontrivial implementation machinery.

**When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital** is valuable because the failure mode is concrete. On FeTS-2022 brain tumor segmentation, naive pooled CRC violates the alpha = 0.10 target at 8 of 20 institutions while looking marginally calibrated; local per-site CRC mostly restores coverage but blows stretch up to 83x. The shrinkage protocol sends only G-scalar risk curves from each site and uses n0 as a coverage-efficiency dial; the LOSO-selected n0 = 19 gets 2.7 violations at 2.0x stretch. The caveats: the practical per-site thresholds are empirically validated rather than formally site-conditional, and the result needs replication beyond one dataset/backbone.

**StylisticBias** is the strongest runner-up for multimodal bias. It is useful because it isolates attribute-level shifts by editing one visual cue while holding synthetic identity fixed. The main result is not that MLLMs are biased, which is unsurprising, but that the bias mass is concentrated in a small set of cues and amplified when the queried judgment is appearance-aligned. The limitation is also clear: synthetic faces reduce privacy problems but can import generator stereotypes and may not fully represent real deployment inputs.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all refuse an easy average. **Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents** keeps uncertain predicates alive until the whole agent trace can be bounded. **Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction** removes prediction-time coins from calibration guarantees without losing the optimal sample rate. **When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital** keeps hospital identity visible instead of hiding failures inside a pooled guarantee. Different domains, same standard: if the risk lives in a dependency, a group, or a randomization channel, do not summarize it away before testing the claim.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-18

## Theme

Today’s signal is **explicit structure that actually constrains behavior**. The strongest paper is **Learning Bilevel Policies over Symbolic World Models for Long-Horizon Planning** because it does not just bolt language onto planning rhetoric, it learns a small low-level policy while extracting and generalizing high-level symbolic rules from demonstrations. **Feedback World Model Enables Precise Guidance of Diffusion Policy** is the best direct robotics companion paper because it treats online prediction error as a first-class inference signal instead of pretending a frozen world model stays reliable off distribution. **STABLE** is the best adjacent 3D-generation paper because it separates semantic layout proposal from physics-aware correction rather than asking an LLM to hallucinate valid tabletop geometry end to end.

## Short overview

Brave Search was unavailable in this run because the environment is missing a Brave API key, so discovery relied on direct inspection of recent arXiv category pages plus accessible arXiv HTML. I inspected substantial arXiv HTML for **Learning Bilevel Policies over Symbolic World Models for Long-Horizon Planning**, **Feedback World Model Enables Precise Guidance of Diffusion Policy**, **STABLE: Simulation-Ready Tabletop Layout Generation via a Semantics-Physics Dual System**, and **Echo-Forcing: A Scene Memory Framework for Interactive Long Video Generation**. Confidence is strongest on problem framing, method structure, and headline empirical claims, and weaker on appendix-level training details and ablation nuance because I did not fully audit every supplementary section.

**BISON** is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is to split the problem cleanly: high-level symbolic policies are extracted from abstracted demonstrations using goal regression and inductive generalization, while a compact graph neural network low-level policy learns how to realize those symbolic actions in continuous control. That is much more interesting than the usual "neuro-symbolic" branding because the symbolic layer is not decorative, it actually carries the long-horizon planning burden.

**Feedback World Model** is more incremental, but still useful. The paper treats deployment-time observation error as a feedback residual that can correct future latent predictions online, then uses those corrected predictions to steer a diffusion policy. The useful part is the control-theoretic stance: if the world model is wrong, use the next real observation to update the model’s belief state instead of just rolling forward and hoping scale fixes it.

**STABLE** is good adjacent inspiration. The valuable design choice is to let an LLM produce a coarse instruction-aligned tabletop layout, then hand continuous pose repair to a geometry-aware flow model with explicit collision and support losses. That is much more credible than end-to-end task-to-scene generation that claims physical validity while hiding all the load-bearing work in prompting.

**Echo-Forcing** looks competent, but I did not preserve a note for it. The scene-memory framing for long video generation is sensible, yet it is still mostly cache-management engineering around autoregressive video diffusion rather than a stronger step toward explicit reusable world structure.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Learning Bilevel Policies over Symbolic World Models for Long-Horizon Planning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it uses symbolic abstractions to carry long-horizon structure while keeping low-level execution in a learned object-centric policy, instead of forcing one monolithic model to do both badly.

### 2. **Feedback World Model Enables Precise Guidance of Diffusion Policy**

**Verdict:** useful direct follow-up.

Why it matters: it turns online world-model mismatch into an explicit correction signal for test-time guidance under distribution shift.

### 3. **STABLE: Simulation-Ready Tabletop Layout Generation via a Semantics-Physics Dual System**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it cleanly separates semantic scene specification from physics-aware geometric correction, which is the right kind of decomposition for simulation-ready generation.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Learning Bilevel Policies over Symbolic World Models for Long-Horizon Planning.

The useful part is not just that it combines symbols and neural policies. Plenty of papers say that. The useful part is that the symbolic layer is learned from demonstrations as a compact open-world rule policy, then the low-level controller is explicitly conditioned on the chosen high-level action. That means abstraction is not only for post hoc explanation. It directly structures decision making.

That matters for cabbageland because it is a concrete example of replacing latent mush with a typed interface between planning and execution. The main caveat is that the setup still assumes a domain theory and a labeling function from low-level observations to symbolic states, so some of the hardest representation-learning work is pushed outside the paper’s core contribution.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update is that **symbolic world models become much more credible when they are used as learned policy structure instead of as hand-authored search scaffolding**. BISON is not merely another planner wrapped around a neural policy. Its contribution is to derive high-level condition-to-action rules from demonstrations and let those rules scale to more objects and longer horizons than the training traces cover.

Feedback World Model sharpens a different point. A frozen world model used for test-time guidance should not be treated as a sacred oracle. If execution reveals prediction error, the right move is to correct the model’s internal belief online. That sounds obvious in control terms, but a lot of recent robotic world-model papers still operate as if inference-time correction were optional.

STABLE mostly affects decomposition priors. It is a useful reminder that simulation-ready scene generation probably wants one module for semantic arrangement and another for continuous physical repair. An LLM-only scene generator is usually being asked to do geometry it does not actually know how to do.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **BISON** because it gives long-horizon embodied planning a real typed interface between symbolic structure and learned execution, instead of pretending one giant policy will discover clean abstraction boundaries by accident. **Feedback World Model** is a good direct companion because it adds online corrective feedback to world-model-guided control under shift, and **STABLE** is good adjacent inspiration because it separates semantic layout generation from physics-aware repair in a way that actually respects the problem. The broader lesson is simple: if a paper claims structure, check whether the structure really constrains planning, control, or geometry. Today’s strongest papers passed that test better than usual.
