# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-15

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **failure localization needs explicit interfaces, not aggregate comfort metrics**. There was no fresh Monday arXiv wave visible at the 08:00 Pacific scan time; the recent API/category surface was still dominated by the June 12 batch. I deliberately kept robotics out of the center today and inspected non-robotics lanes first: production agent reliability, VLM interpretability, medical hallucination diagnosis, self-improvement evaluation, diffusion language-model behavior, agent scaffolds, visual part representations, and generative-model memorization. **When Errors Become Narratives** is the strongest paper because it turns long-running LLM-agent failure into a mechanism taxonomy with real postmortems. **Gaze Heads** is the strongest mechanistic ML paper because it finds a small causal attention-head control surface for what a VLM describes. **ClinHallu** is the best healthcare/evaluation note because it asks where a medical MLLM hallucination enters the reasoning chain, not only whether the final answer is wrong.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight fetched `/search` URL returned 404, so it was not useful for discovery. I used the arXiv API plus direct arXiv PDFs. Full arXiv PDFs were inspected for **When Errors Become Narratives: A Longitudinal Taxonomy of Silent Failures in a Production LLM Agent Runtime**, **Gaze Heads: How VLMs Look at What They Describe**, **ClinHallu: A Benchmark for Diagnosing Stage-Wise Hallucinations in Medical MLLM Reasoning**, **When Good Verifiers Go Bad: Self-Improving VLMs Can Regress on New Tasks**, **Neither Parallel Nor Sequential: How DiffusionGemma Actually Commits Tokens**, **AgentSpec: Understanding Embodied Agent Scaffolds Through Controlled Composition**, **RATS! Patches Talk Through Registers**, **Local Coverage Governs Memorization in Diffusion Models**, **Memento: Reconstruct to Remember for Consistent Long Video Generation**, **A Low-Rank Subspace Analysis of LLM Interventions**, and **Compressed Computation is (probably) not Computation in Superposition**. I preserved detailed notes for When Errors Become Narratives and Gaze Heads.

**When Errors Become Narratives** is the most relevant paper today. It is a single-system case study, so the frequencies should not be generalized casually, but the mechanism taxonomy is exactly the right object: environment quirks, design-assumption mismatches, swallowed/diluted errors, fail-plausible fabrication, and operational/forensic blind spots. The strongest idea is the trigger/amplifier/concealer decomposition. Fixing the trigger is usually cosmetic; the durable work is removing the amplifier and making the concealer impossible. The paper is unusually close to cabbageland's own agent-runtime concerns, but that is not why it wins. It wins because the observed failures are concrete, longitudinal, and architecturally reusable.

**Gaze Heads** is the cleanest mechanistic model paper in the scan. In Qwen3-VL-8B, fewer than 9% of attention heads track the image region currently being described, and forcing those heads to attend to a chosen region steers the VLM's answer toward that region at 83.1% accuracy on six-panel comics. The intervention also works dynamically mid-generation and transfers imperfectly to natural COCO images and several VLM families. The caveat is that the testbed is heavily shaped by comics and the mechanism is not universal: some frozen-encoder architectures show no comparable head set. Still, this is real causal interpretability, not merely heatmap poetry.

**ClinHallu** is the strongest medical/evaluation paper today. It builds 7,031 validated medical VQA instances with structured traces split into Visual Recognition, Knowledge Recall, and Reasoning Integration, then uses stage-replacement interventions to diagnose where hallucinations enter. That decomposition is more useful than a final-answer hallucination score because it says whether the model is seeing wrong, remembering wrong, or combining evidence badly. The limitation is that the benchmark leans on generated traces, LLM-as-judge filtering/evaluation, and VQA-style tasks, so it is a diagnostic testbed rather than clinical deployment evidence.

**When Good Verifiers Go Bad** is the best deployment warning. It shows verifier-driven self-DPO can silently regress VLM students on MMMU even while DPO loss decreases, and argues that task-rubric verifier accuracy should be measured before running the loop. The single-family Qwen ladder and small verifier scale limit the claim, but the warning is practical: a verifier is not a moral authority. If it is confidently wrong on the target task, preference optimization can amplify the wrong direction.

**Neither Parallel Nor Sequential** is a useful foundation-model behavior audit. By hooking DiffusionGemma's own commit mechanism, it finds partial, granularity-dependent left-to-right token commitment rather than clean parallel or block-autoregressive decoding. The paper's most portable contribution is methodological: commit-order studies need to handle EOS padding artifacts, same-call ties, non-monotonic commits, pooling traps, and block-size sensitivity.

**AgentSpec** is aligned but broader and less decisive. It treats embodied LLM agents as typed compositions of perception, memory, reasoning, reflection, action, and learning modules, then compares scaffold combinations across interactive benchmarks. The useful lesson is that scaffold compatibility matters: memory helps only when matched to the reasoner and task, and policy optimization should train against the scaffold expected at deployment. I did not preserve it today because it is more framework-plus-sweep than sharp mechanism.

**RATS** and **Local Coverage Governs Memorization** are strong adjacent representation papers. RATS turns register tokens into a bottleneck that surfaces unsupervised part-level visual structure under a DINO objective. Local Coverage reframes diffusion memorization as a local data-coverage phenomenon rather than a global model property. Both are useful, but today's preserved notes are more directly actionable for agent reliability and multimodal control.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **When Errors Become Narratives: A Longitudinal Taxonomy of Silent Failures in a Production LLM Agent Runtime**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives long-running LLM-agent reliability a mechanism taxonomy built from production postmortems, with an especially useful account of fail-plausible fabrication.

### 2. **Gaze Heads: How VLMs Look at What They Describe**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it identifies a small causal attention-head interface that controls which image region a VLM grounds into language at inference time.

### 3. **ClinHallu: A Benchmark for Diagnosing Stage-Wise Hallucinations in Medical MLLM Reasoning**

**Verdict:** useful, with healthcare/evaluation relevance.

Why it matters: it decomposes medical hallucination into visual, knowledge, and reasoning stages, then uses replacement interventions to test which stage actually bottlenecks final-answer reliability.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** When Errors Become Narratives.

The steal-worthy idea is the failure chain contract. Every serious agent incident should be written as trigger, amplifier, and concealer. The trigger is often unbounded noise from the world. The amplifier is the architectural choice that lets it spread. The concealer is the missing observation path that lets it stay quiet. Cabbageland should care most about the last two, because those are the pieces we can design away.

Gaze Heads adds the model-facing companion: if a VLM has a small causal channel for "what visual region is being spoken about," that channel can become a steering and debugging interface. The point is not that every VLM has gaze heads. The point is that mechanistic localization can sometimes produce a practical inference-time lever.

ClinHallu adds the evaluation companion. A final hallucination score is too late and too coarse. Stage-level replacement turns the question into diagnosis: what exact sub-interface failed?

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**When Errors Become Narratives** raises the baseline for agent reliability writing. It is not enough to report failures as anecdotes or stack traces; the useful unit is the mechanism class plus the observation path that failed.

**Gaze Heads** raises the bar for VLM interpretability. Attention maps are weak evidence by themselves. This paper makes the head set causal by redirecting attention and measuring whether output follows.

**ClinHallu** sharpens medical MLLM hallucination evaluation. Benchmarks should expose whether failure came from perception, knowledge recall, or reasoning integration; aggregate answer correctness hides the repair target.

**When Good Verifiers Go Bad** is a baseline warning for self-improvement loops. DPO loss is not a reliability metric, and verifier scale is not verifier correctness on the target task.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **When Errors Become Narratives** because it treats production agent failures as mechanism classes, not embarrassing one-offs. **Gaze Heads** is the mechanistic ML note to keep because it finds a small causal control surface for VLM grounding. **ClinHallu** is the healthcare/evaluation reminder that hallucination diagnosis needs stage-local interventions, not just final-answer scoring. The common thread is diagnostic resolution: systems get better when they expose where the failure entered, how it propagated, and which interface can actually be repaired.

## Detailed notes

- [Gaze Heads note](../paper_notes/gaze_heads_how_vlms_look_at_what_they_describe.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-31

## Theme

Today’s strongest pattern is **explicit structure only matters when it changes what gets stored, updated, or decomposed**, not when it just renames a latent soup. **3D-Belief** is the best paper because it really does reframe embodied world modeling as online 3D belief maintenance under partial observability. **WEM** is interesting because it tries to split persistent scene evolution from robot-centric interaction, but I am more skeptical there because some of the benefit may come from benchmark design plus a heavy video-generation stack. **Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?** is not a mechanism breakthrough, but it is the best reality check of the set.

## Short overview

Brave Search was not available as a configured tool surface in this run, and AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable here, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv papers plus direct arXiv inspection.

I inspected substantial arXiv HTML full text for **3D-Belief: Embodied Belief Inference via Generative 3D World Modeling**, **World-Ego Modeling for Long-Horizon Evolution in Hybrid Embodied Tasks**, and **Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?** Confidence is highest for 3D-Belief and the continual-VLA paper. For WEM, I inspected the abstract, introduction, formulation, architecture, and visible experimental framing, but I did not fully recover every result table cleanly enough to claim the same level of confidence on the empirical margins.

**3D-Belief** is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is to treat world modeling as belief-state inference in explicit 3D space rather than as pixel rollout. The state is a 3D Gaussian-splat scene with semantic embeddings, split into observed structure and imagined unseen structure. New observations update the belief by preserving observed content, replacing stale imagined content, and keeping the result queryable for semantics and planning. That is a much healthier contract than “generate plausible future video and hope the planner can somehow use it.”

The main reason this matters is that the paper is trying to make uncertainty, memory, and semantics live in the same explicit state. Most recent visual world-model papers are still basically rendering systems with nicer branding. This one at least makes a serious attempt to represent what the agent knows, what it has only hypothesized, and how that changes after new evidence arrives.

**WEM** is a more mixed case. The motivating distinction, world as persistent instruction-agnostic scene structure and ego as robot-centric instruction-conditioned dynamics, is genuinely useful. Hybrid navigation-manipulation tasks probably do want something like that separation. The question is whether the paper’s proposed decomposition is buying real mechanism or mostly wrapping a large video-diffusion system in a better story. My read is that there is some real structure here, especially in assigning different predictive roles, but the implementation is still heavy enough that I would treat it as adjacent inspiration, not as clean evidence that “world-ego disentanglement” is now a solved design principle.

**Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?** is the least glamorous but maybe the most useful for keeping later claims honest. It shows that sequential real-world adaptation can collapse badly under naive fine-tuning, and that replay only looks robust when details like action normalization and replay cadence are handled carefully. That is less exciting than a shiny memory module, but it is exactly the kind of paper that should change how later continual-VLA claims are evaluated.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **3D-Belief: Embodied Belief Inference via Generative 3D World Modeling**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it treats the world model as an explicit evolving 3D belief state with memory, uncertainty, and semantics in one representation instead of collapsing everything into image realism.

### 2. **Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?**

**Verdict:** useful, mainly as a framing and evaluation paper.

Why it matters: it gives a more causally honest picture of forgetting in real-world sequential robot learning and shows that implementation details can decide whether replay helps or fails.

### 3. **World-Ego Modeling for Long-Horizon Evolution in Hybrid Embodied Tasks**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration with real ideas, but not yet a fully convincing mechanism paper.

Why it matters: it tries to separate persistent scene evolution from robot-centric interaction dynamics in long-horizon embodied video prediction, which is the right kind of decomposition question even if the current answer still feels somewhat entangled with benchmark and generator design.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** 3D-Belief.

The useful part is not just that it is explicit 3D. The useful part is the belief contract. The paper distinguishes what has actually been observed from what is still imagined, then updates those differently as evidence arrives. That is much closer to the kind of state an embodied agent should carry than a smooth latent that only becomes meaningful after downstream probing.

This also gives a cleaner research standard for future “world model” claims. If a paper says it supports planning under partial observability, the obvious question should be: where is the belief state, what part of it is explicit, how does it preserve old evidence, and how does it revise uncertainty after new observations? 3D-Belief does not solve everything, but it at least makes those questions answerable.

My confidence is fairly good because I inspected substantial full text. The main uncertainty is practical rather than conceptual: the whole stack is still heavy, and I am not yet convinced that the representation would scale cleanly to more dynamic or contact-rich manipulation settings.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**3D-Belief** raises the bar for embodied world-model framing. If a system only predicts plausible views but does not maintain explicit scene belief with inspectable uncertainty, it should probably stop claiming to be a serious belief-state world model.

**The continual-VLA paper** raises the bar for evaluation protocol. Later continual-learning claims in robotics should not get away with forgiving simulation-only streams or normalization setups that leak future information.

**WEM** is more of a framing nudge than a baseline reset. It usefully argues that long-horizon embodied prediction mixes at least two different responsibilities, persistent world evolution and instruction-conditioned ego dynamics. But I would want cleaner causal evidence before treating the specific decomposition recipe as a strong new default.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **3D-Belief** because it actually turns embodied world modeling into explicit 3D belief maintenance instead of prettier video prediction. **Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?** is the best reality check, showing that continual embodied learning is still fragile enough that protocol details matter as much as algorithm branding. **WEM** is worth remembering because the world-versus-ego split is a sensible decomposition target for hybrid long-horizon tasks, but the current implementation still feels too generator-heavy to count as decisive evidence. The common lesson is that explicit structure only earns the name when it changes the computational contract, memory update, or evaluation burden in a way you can actually inspect.

## Detailed notes

- [Continual VLA note](../paper_notes/can_vla_models_learn_from_real_world_data_continually_without_forgetting.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-04-30

## Theme

Today’s strongest pattern is that the better papers do not merely bolt a world model onto something. They force the world-model signal into a more explicit contract: geometry that modulates action attention, asynchronous schedules that admit action and video have different inference needs, or teacher-generated transitions that get distilled into the student instead of dragged around at test time.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. I then scouted recent arXiv category listings directly and inspected the abstract plus substantial method text from arXiv HTML pages for **STARRY: Spatial-Temporal Action-Centric World Modeling for Robotic Manipulation**, **Unified 4D World Action Modeling from Video Priors with Asynchronous Denoising**, **World2VLM: Distilling World Model Imagination into VLMs for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning**, **Atomic-Probe Governance for Skill Updates in Compositional Robot Policies**, and **ProcFunc: Function-Oriented Abstractions for Procedural 3D Generation in Python**.

The first three survive the bar. **Atomic-Probe Governance** is thoughtful and unusually concrete about post-deployment skill-library maintenance, but it is more evaluation-governance than core cabbageland architecture. **ProcFunc** looks genuinely useful as infrastructure for procedural 3D data generation, but today it reads more like a good systems library than a mechanism paper I need to preserve in note form right now.

The strongest direct hit is **STARRY**. Its central move is not just predicting futures, but converting predicted geometry into token-level weights that bias the action branch toward metric interaction regions near the future end effector. That is a real mechanism, not just generic “better spatial reasoning” language.

**X-WAM** is broader and messier, but still useful. The paper tries to unify video generation, depth reconstruction, and robot action in one diffusion-style stack, then makes a practical argument that action tokens and video tokens should not share the same denoising schedule. The main idea worth keeping is the asynchronous contract, not the grand unification rhetoric.

**World2VLM** is the best adjacent paper. It is not an embodied control paper, but it makes a clean training-time-teacher argument: use a world model to synthesize motion-conditioned view transitions offline, then distill that supervision into a plain vision-language model so deployment does not need expensive imagination loops.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **STARRY: Spatial-Temporal Action-Centric World Modeling for Robotic Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to make future prediction action-relevant by explicitly routing predicted geometry into action attention instead of hoping shared latent foresight will somehow do the job.

### 2. **Unified 4D World Action Modeling from Video Priors with Asynchronous Denoising**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it makes a defensible case that unified video-action models should acknowledge that actions want fast decoding while future video wants many denoising steps, then trains for that mismatch instead of pretending one schedule fits all.

### 3. **World2VLM: Distilling World Model Imagination into VLMs for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it treats the world model as a training-time teacher rather than an inference-time crutch, which is a much cleaner answer to the usual cost explosion in imagination-based spatial reasoning.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** STARRY.

The paper’s best contribution is not that it predicts future latent structure. Plenty of papers already do that and then act surprised when the control gain is modest. The sharper move is to ask how predicted future geometry should change the action computation itself. STARRY answers by predicting future depth and end-effector geometry, turning that into token-aligned geometry-aware weights, and applying those weights only inside the action attention branch.

That selective routing is the useful part. It admits that not every world-model feature deserves equal access to every branch. If the geometry signal is supposed to help control, make it enter as an explicit modulation path tied to action-relevant regions. Even if the current implementation is still benchmark-shaped, the interface discipline is good.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

STARRY is a useful baseline challenge to generic world-model-enhanced policies. If a paper claims future prediction helps action, it should increasingly be asked what action-relevant signal is actually transferred and where in the policy it enters.

X-WAM sharpens a different baseline question: unified world-action models should not be judged only on whether one big stack can do everything eventually. They should also be judged on whether the coupling between modalities respects their different inference requirements. The asynchronous denoising idea is more interesting than the 4D branding by itself.

World2VLM matters mostly for framing. It is a reminder that world models do not need to stay in the deployed loop to be useful. Distilling motion-conditioned supervision into a cheaper student is often the cleaner design, especially when the expensive teacher mostly exists to provide structured transition targets.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The good papers today are all trying to turn world-model power into a narrower, more explicit interface. STARRY turns predicted geometry into action-branch modulation. X-WAM turns a muddled unified diffusion stack into a clearer contract where actions decode early and videos decode longer. World2VLM turns inference-time imagination into offline teacher supervision. None of these fully solve long-horizon memory or planning, and some of the empirical claims still live inside benchmark comfort zones. But the direction is right: stop treating “has a world model” as the result, and specify what exact signal the world model contributes, where it enters, and whether it really has to survive at inference time.

- [X-WAM note](../paper_notes/x_wam_unified_4d_world_action_modeling.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-23

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **state management should be keyed to structure, not surface thresholds**. The strongest papers all reject a cheap proxy: token count is not a good trigger for agent memory compaction, a single evaluation-awareness score is not a safety claim, and a single document vector is too blunt for long-context retrieval.

I deliberately kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered agent memory, evaluation validity, long-context retrieval, enterprise-agent benchmarking, causal-discovery tooling, knowledge editing, medical representation learning, latent-group robustness, 3D / 4D generation, and VLA safety. **LIBERO-Safety** was the strongest robotics/VLA candidate, but it did not beat the best non-robotics papers on transferable mechanism today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable with a browser user-agent for specific paper pages, but the guessed search route returned 404, so it was useful only as a light metadata reachability check. Discovery therefore relied mainly on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs; discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on June 23, the arXiv API returned June 22 uploads as the newest batch in the checked AI, ML, CV, CL, IR, medical, statistics, and robotics lanes. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially methods, experiments, results, and limitations, for **Self-Compacting Language Model Agents**, **Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability**, **Improving Long-Context Retrieval with Multi-Prefix Embedding**, **EnterpriseClawBench**, **Causal Discovery in the Era of Agents**, **Exposing the Illusion of Erasure in Knowledge Editing**, **Patient-Aware Contrastive Learning**, **Discovering Latent Groups for Robust Classification**, **Semantic Browsing**, **Lift4D**, and **LIBERO-Safety**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Self-Compacting Language Model Agents** is the most relevant paper today. It treats compaction timing as a trajectory-state decision rather than a token-budget reflex, using a rubric-gated summary tool that fires after closed reasoning units and suppresses compaction mid-derivation or while stuck.

**Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability** is the strongest evaluation and interpretability paper in the scan. Its useful move is to split evaluation awareness into behavioral detection, safety-framing sensitivity, latent representation, and causal controllability instead of pretending one awareness score carries deployment validity.

**Improving Long-Context Retrieval with Multi-Prefix Embedding** is the strongest retrieval/infrastructure paper today. It extracts multiple EOS prefix embeddings from one causal forward pass, giving long documents chunk-level matching and evidence localization without token-level late interaction or chunk-level labels.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. **EnterpriseClawBench** has good deployment-evaluation taste: it reports harness-model pairs, artifact quality, cost, runtime, and skill-transfer behavior, and its unreleased proprietary data makes the reusable contribution mostly protocol. **Causal Discovery in the Era of Agents** is aligned with the house standard that agents assist while formal algorithms discover, but it is closer to a design manifesto plus platform description than a preserved mechanism paper. **Patient-Aware Contrastive Learning** is a clean medical representation note candidate, especially for the same-patient/same-class positive construction, but it is single-dataset and narrower than the retrieval paper. **Discovering Latent Groups for Robust Classification** is good structural robustness work, but its worst-group gains are competitive rather than dominant and its assumptions around difficulty routing need care.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Self-Compacting Language Model Agents**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives long-horizon agents an inspectable compaction policy that respects reasoning boundaries. The key idea is simple and stealable: expose summarization as a tool, then gate it with an explicit rubric about when the current trajectory is safe to compress.

### 2. **Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability: Evidence from Open Language Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for evaluation validity and deployment safety.

Why it matters: it shows that evaluation awareness is not one scalar property. A model can detect benchmark format, encode an eval/deploy distinction internally, shift safety behavior under framing, and respond to steering in partially independent ways. Benchmark claims need to name which axis they tested.

### 3. **Improving Long-Context Retrieval with Multi-Prefix Embedding**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for retrieval-augmented agents and evidence-grounded search.

Why it matters: it gives a compact way to make long-document embeddings less mushy. One document can expose multiple prefix embeddings for MaxSim matching, while keeping causal cross-chunk context and producing a candidate evidence location.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Self-Compacting Language Model Agents.

The steal is not "summarize more." The steal is "summarize only when the state of the trajectory says the current unit is closed." For agents that use files, tools, searches, or multi-step reasoning, compaction should not be a dumb context-window emergency. It should be a state transition with an explicit precondition.

The evaluation-awareness paper adds the complementary warning: if the system behaves differently under visible testing cues, a benchmark score is not a deployment guarantee. Measure cue sensitivity directly, keep benign null controls, and report signed behavior deltas rather than a single awareness score.

The multi-prefix retrieval paper contributes the infrastructure lesson: long context should not be forced through one vector when the evidence is localized. Prefix-level document embeddings are a pragmatic middle ground between one-vector mush and expensive token-level late interaction.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Self-Compacting Language Model Agents** raises the bar for context-management papers because it tests timing, not just compression quality. SELF COMPACT pairs an inline summarization tool with a rubric that asks whether a subtask has resolved or the trajectory is converging, and suppresses compaction mid-derivation or when the agent is stuck. Across competition math and agentic search, it beats fixed-interval summarization in 11 of 12 math settings and improves BrowseComp-Plus by 5.3 to 9.2 absolute points across three deployed search agents, while often lowering per-question cost. The caveats: it is still a scaffold over open-weight models, frontier systems may already have better internal timing, and the work does not train a compaction policy.

**Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability** is valuable because it refuses the headline metric. Across 37 open-weight models and eight experiments, the paper finds moderate evaluation-context detection, safety behavior shifts under framing, strong hidden-state decodability in some settings, and sparse correlations across the measured axes. The practical consequence is the "benchmark illusion": benchmark behavior can be an optimistic upper bound if deployment cues differ. The caveats are real: the Hawthorne framing study is deep on one model, larger-model coverage is partial, and the mechanistic steering work is exploratory.

**Improving Long-Context Retrieval with Multi-Prefix Embedding** gives retrieval a useful representation object. Instead of independently encoding chunks or collapsing a whole document into one vector, MPE inserts EOS boundaries, encodes the full document once with a causal embedding model, extracts hidden states at prefix boundaries, and scores with MaxSim. On MLDR-en, MPE Fixed-64 reaches 0.783 nDCG@10, while MPE-Rand improves out-of-domain BrowseComp-Plus retrieval and QMSum. In a BrowseComp-Plus search-agent setting, MPE-Rand improves answer accuracy from 42.29 percent to 51.45 percent over a single-vector retriever. Limitations: the experiments use one 0.6B embedding model, English benchmarks, LLM-derived span labels for attribution, and more storage than single-vector retrieval.

**LIBERO-Safety** is the strongest robotics runner-up. It contributes a parametric VLA safety benchmark, keypose-driven data generation, and a 19.7K-episode collision-free dataset. I kept it out of the top three because today's stronger papers had more direct cross-domain mechanism value, and the digest should not drift back into VLA-by-default mode.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all make the same demand in different systems: keep the unit of state visible. **Self-Compacting Language Model Agents** says the unit is a closed reasoning subtask, not a token count. **Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability** says the unit is a measured eval/deploy axis, not a single safety score. **Improving Long-Context Retrieval with Multi-Prefix Embedding** says the unit is a local evidence-bearing prefix, not the whole document squeezed into one vector. If the claim depends on state, do not flatten the state before evaluating it.

- [Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability note](../paper_notes/evaluation_awareness_not_one_capability.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-23

## Theme

Today’s useful pattern is **explicit structure that anchors perception across missing views or missing geometry**. The strongest direct paper is **SOMA** because it gives a vision-language-action system a persistent spatial memory that is allowed to matter operationally when the target leaves the camera frustum. **Cambrian-P** is the best adjacent paper because it treats camera pose as a first-class supervisory signal for video understanding instead of pretending frame-wise semantics are enough for spatial reasoning. **Vector Policy Optimization** is farther from the embodied stack, but it is still relevant as a mechanism paper about preserving structured diversity for downstream search rather than collapsing everything into one reward weighting.

## Short overview

Brave Search and AlphaXiv were not available in this run, so discovery fell back to direct recent arXiv inspection. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for **SOMA**, **Cambrian-P**, and **Vector Policy Optimization**, which is enough for decent confidence about their central mechanisms and evaluation stories, but not full appendix-level confidence.

**SOMA: Spatial Memory for Out-of-Vision Manipulation in Vision-Language-Action** is the most relevant paper today. Its core claim is simple and concrete: most VLA systems are reactively view-bound, so when the target leaves the current field of view they effectively lose the world. SOMA responds by having a movable head camera actively scan the scene, fuse multi-view detections and geometry into a global spatial-semantic memory, refine that memory during interaction, and retrieve instruction-relevant regions back into a DiT-based action decoder. This is not radically elegant, and it leans heavily on existing detectors and geometry priors, but at least the structure is explicit and the failure mode is real.

**Cambrian-P: Pose-Grounded Video Understanding** is adjacent rather than directly embodied, but it is a clean mechanism paper. The useful move is to append per-frame pose tokens to a video MLLM and jointly supervise next-token prediction with camera pose estimation. The paper’s argument is that pose is a lightweight way to force a shared spatial frame across views, which then improves spatial reasoning benchmarks and even some general video QA. I buy the core point more than I buy the paper’s broader rhetoric. Pose supervision is doing real work, but the method is still mostly a training-time geometric bias rather than a richer explicit world representation.

**Vector Policy Optimization** is the furthest from cabbageland’s main lane, but it earns a mention because the mechanism is sharper than most RL-for-LLM papers. Instead of optimizing one scalar reward and getting one collapsed mode, it trains policies to emit sets of answers that specialize to different reward trade-offs, then lets downstream search exploit that diversity. It matters less as an architectural ingredient for world models than as a framing correction for search-heavy systems.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **SOMA: Spatial Memory for Out-of-Vision Manipulation in Vision-Language-Action**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it targets a real VLA failure mode with explicit persistent spatial memory instead of pretending that more generic VLM reasoning can recover unseen objects from nothing.

### 2. **Cambrian-P: Pose-Grounded Video Understanding**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it uses pose as a cheap but meaningful geometric scaffold for video reasoning, which is a cleaner inductive bias than most vague “spatially aware” video-language claims.

### 3. **Vector Policy Optimization: Training for Diversity Improves Test-Time Search**

**Verdict:** useful, mostly for framing and training objective design.

Why it matters: it makes the case that if downstream search will do exploitation, post-training should preserve competent diversity rather than optimize a single scalarized mode into mush.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** SOMA: Spatial Memory for Out-of-Vision Manipulation in Vision-Language-Action.

What makes SOMA useful is not that it says “memory” in the title. It gives memory an actual job contract. The system scans with a movable head camera, lifts detections into a shared scene frame with geometry priors, merges instances across views into object-level memory tokens, keeps refining those tokens as interaction proceeds, and retrieves instruction-relevant regions back into the action model. That is a much more defensible story than the common VLA pattern where memory just means a short stack of recent frames or a language scratchpad.

The main caveat is that SOMA is still fairly baroque and somewhat tool-dependent. The memory is assembled from YOLO, DINOv3, and VGGT-style geometry rather than learned as one crisp endogenous representation. So I would not read this as a final architectural answer. I would read it as evidence that **persistent scene memory for out-of-view manipulation is real enough to pay for its complexity**, and that future cleaner systems should probably preserve the same contract.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**SOMA** sharpens a useful baseline question for future VLA work: when the target leaves view, does the policy still have a world, or does it merely have a prompt plus the current image? Papers that claim spatial reasoning without a persistent scene substrate should now be treated more skeptically.

**Cambrian-P** pushes a different framing correction. If a model is supposed to reason over video as a physical scene rather than a slideshow, then some shared geometric anchor should probably be explicit during training. Pose is not a full world model, but it is a concrete anchor that seems to improve both spatial QA and streaming pose estimation. That makes “we added a generic video MLLM and hoped attention would infer the geometry” look increasingly flimsy.

**Vector Policy Optimization** mostly matters at the objective level. It suggests that search-augmented systems may want training targets that preserve specialized alternatives instead of collapsing immediately to one scalar optimum. That is relevant anywhere later planning, verification, or evolutionary search is expected to do actual work.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **SOMA** because it addresses a real embodied failure mode with explicit spatial memory that stays tied to perception and action, even if the current implementation is modular and heavy. **Cambrian-P** is the best adjacent paper because it uses camera pose as a lightweight geometric scaffold for video reasoning instead of hand-waving about spatial understanding. **Vector Policy Optimization** is not directly a world-model paper, but it is a good reminder that if downstream search matters, training should preserve structured option diversity rather than hammer everything into one preferred response mode. The shared lesson is that explicit anchors, whether spatial memory, pose, or reward structure, are most useful when they actually constrain computation instead of merely decorating the narrative.

## Detailed notes

- [Cambrian-P note](../paper_notes/cambrian_p_pose_grounded_video_understanding.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-22

## Theme

Today’s strongest signal is **explicit intermediate structure that actually constrains generation or control**. The best paper is **DiLA: Disentangled Latent Action World Models** because it turns the vague goal of “abstract yet predictive latent actions” into a concrete architectural split between structure and content, then tests whether that split buys transfer and planning. **SceneCode** is the most interesting adjacent systems paper because it treats indoor scenes as executable programs with articulated object structure rather than static mesh soup. **Pelican-Unify 1.0** is ambitious and worth watching, but right now it reads more like a giant integration claim than a sharply isolating mechanism paper.

## Short overview

Brave Search and AlphaXiv were unavailable in this run, so discovery fell back to direct inspection of recent arXiv category listings and full-text arXiv HTML reads where accessible. I fully inspected arXiv HTML for **DiLA**, **SceneCode**, and **Pelican-Unify 1.0**. Confidence is good on their central mechanisms, task setup, and headline numbers, and weaker on appendix-level implementation details I did not independently reconstruct.

**DiLA** is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is to stop asking one latent pathway to carry both controllable dynamics and high-frequency appearance. Instead, it predicts future structural state through a bottlenecked latent action pathway while maintaining a separate content-memory pathway for visual detail, then fuses them for reconstruction. That is a much cleaner story than the usual LAM pattern where abstraction is purchased by wrecking generation quality or by discarding the learned forward model and handing rendering to a separate pretrained video model.

**SceneCode** is adjacent but genuinely useful. It compiles scene prompts into a room plan plus per-object executable Blender programs, then validates and repairs those programs before exporting simulation-ready assets with articulation metadata. The paper matters because it replaces opaque retrieved meshes with editable object programs and a persistent scene-state registry. The part I am less certain about is how far this scales beyond the relatively curated prompt set and the dominant hinged or sliding articulation patterns it targets.

**Pelican-Unify 1.0** makes the broadest claim, namely that understanding, reasoning, imagination, and action should be trained as one shared loop. I buy the direction more than the current evidence. The paper clearly has scale, and the shared latent interface between reasoning and joint video-plus-action generation is a real design choice, but the mechanism is not isolated as cleanly as DiLA’s and much of the story is still benchmark aggregation.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **DiLA: Disentangled Latent Action World Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it proposes an explicit structure-content split that seems to do real work for action abstraction, generation fidelity, and planning instead of treating those goals as magically compatible.

### 2. **SceneCode: Executable World Programs for Editable Indoor Scenes with Articulated Objects**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it treats scene generation as editable world construction with articulated object programs and persistent scene state, which is much closer to reusable simulation structure than static asset retrieval.

### 3. **Pelican-Unify 1.0: A Unified Embodied Intelligence Model for Understanding, Reasoning, Imagination and Action**

**Verdict:** interesting, but mostly framing pressure for now.

Why it matters: it is a serious large-scale attempt to put reasoning, future video generation, and action generation into one shared loop, even if the paper currently proves breadth more clearly than mechanism.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** DiLA: Disentangled Latent Action World Models.

The useful part of DiLA is not just that it says “disentanglement.” The useful part is the specific contract it imposes: latent actions are only allowed to model structural dynamics, while appearance and static detail are maintained in a separate content pathway with memory. That means the model is not forced to choose between an abstract action bottleneck and a visually competent forward model in the same way older LAMs often are.

This matters for cabbageland because it is exactly the kind of paper that tries to replace latent mush with **typed internal structure that changes what different parts of the model are allowed to represent**. The evaluation is also more aligned with the claim than usual. The paper checks not just reconstruction metrics, but action transfer, latent manifold behavior, and model-predictive visual planning. I am still somewhat uncertain how much of the gain comes from the disentanglement idea itself versus the entire decoder-and-memory package around it, but the architecture is at least making a falsifiable representation claim.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The framing update from **DiLA** is that latent action papers should probably be judged by whether they cleanly separate *what must stay controllable* from *what must stay reconstructable*. A lot of recent latent action work quietly escapes this problem by either weakening the forward model target or outsourcing generation to a separate pretrained model. DiLA is more interesting because it keeps a single-stage story and tries to solve the trade-off inside the model.

**SceneCode** sharpens a different point. If a generated world is supposed to support interaction, then editable object structure and motion metadata should be first-class outputs, not afterthought annotations on top of static meshes. That is a good novelty lens for future 3D and simulation papers: ask whether the representation really exposes state, parts, and mechanisms.

**Pelican-Unify 1.0** mostly affects framing rather than immediate design choice. It is a reminder that shared latent interfaces between reasoning, imagination, and action are becoming a live target. But the paper does not isolate enough ablations yet to tell which parts of the unification claim are necessary rather than merely co-present.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **DiLA** because it offers a concrete, legible answer to a real world-model problem: how to keep latent actions abstract without trashing generation quality. **SceneCode** is the best adjacent paper because it treats 3D scene synthesis as executable world construction with articulated structure and editable state, which is much closer to the kinds of reusable representations embodied work actually wants. **Pelican-Unify 1.0** is ambitious and maybe important, but I would currently treat it more as evidence that unified embodied foundation-model training is being seriously attempted than as a clean mechanism paper. The shared lesson is that explicit structural separation helps most when it meaningfully constrains what a subsystem is allowed to represent or output.

## Detailed notes

- [SceneCode note](../paper_notes/scenecode_executable_world_programs_for_editable_indoor_scenes_with_articulated_objects.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-03

## Theme

Today’s best paper is trying to make VLA post-training touch the model’s internal physical-reasoning process instead of only rewarding emitted actions. That is a real idea, even if the paper still leans on opaque latent reasoning. The broader pattern is mixed: one useful memory paper argues, correctly, that persistent agent memory should behave more like a validated system of record than a vector-store scrapbook, while a driving world-model paper looks competent but still feels more like ambitious unification than a genuinely clarifying abstraction.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. I then scouted recent arXiv category listings directly and inspected abstracts plus substantial method text from arXiv HTML pages for **LaST-R1: Reinforcing Action via Adaptive Physical Latent Reasoning for VLA Models**, **From Unstructured Recall to Schema-Grounded Memory: Reliable AI Memory via Iterative, Schema-Aware Extraction**, and **HERMES++: Toward a Unified Driving World Model for 3D Scene Understanding and Generation**.

**LaST-R1** is the strongest direct hit. Its useful move is not “reasoning” in the generic fashionable sense, but the RL formulation: LAPO explicitly lets reward shape both latent reasoning tokens and action generation, rather than treating hidden reasoning as frozen scaffolding around an action-only policy update. I inspected the abstract and substantial method text, including the model definition, latent-token construction, and the core LAPO optimization setup. The main caveat is that the latent CoT story is still mostly hidden-state engineering, so the paper earns credit for changing the training target, not for making reasoning legible.

**Schema-Grounded Memory** is adjacent rather than robotic, but the mechanism is worth saving. The paper argues that persistent memory for agents should shift interpretation cost from read time to write time by extracting validated schema-aligned records instead of repeatedly inferring facts from retrieved prose. I inspected the abstract and substantial early method / framing text from the arXiv HTML page, enough to verify the architecture claim, but not the full benchmark appendix.

**HERMES++** looks serious but lands mostly as framing and citation material. I inspected the abstract and substantial introduction / method text. The paper has a coherent integration story, BEV tokenization, LLM-enhanced world queries, a Current-to-Future Link, and joint geometric optimization, but the overall feeling is still “large unified stack with several glue modules” rather than a crisp new internal computational principle.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **LaST-R1: Reinforcing Action via Adaptive Physical Latent Reasoning for VLA Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to make VLA post-training optimize an internal progress-and-physics workspace instead of only the visible action channel.

### 2. **From Unstructured Recall to Schema-Grounded Memory: Reliable AI Memory via Iterative, Schema-Aware Extraction**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it states, more bluntly than most memory papers, that retrieval is not enough when the job is exact state, updates, relations, and explicit unknowns.

### 3. **HERMES++: Toward a Unified Driving World Model for 3D Scene Understanding and Generation**

**Verdict:** skimmable citation material.

Why it matters: it is a decent example of current unified-driving-world-model ambition, but I do not think the paper yet sharpens the notion of explicit state enough to preserve as a design note.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** LaST-R1.

The important part is LAPO, not the phrase “latent CoT.” The paper notices that recent VLA RL work usually improves the action head while leaving the internal reasoning process outside the optimization target. LaST-R1 instead treats latent reasoning tokens as part of the policy and defines a joint step-level likelihood ratio so reward can reshape both the latent sequence and the emitted action chunk.

That matters because it is at least a principled answer to a real problem. If a policy supposedly reasons about physical dynamics before acting, then training only on final actions is a weak form of supervision. LaST-R1’s fix is to make the hidden workspace part of what RL updates. I also like the adaptive latent-end mechanism in principle, because a variable reasoning horizon is more honest than forcing every task through the same fixed internal loop.

The caveat is equally important. The paper does not really make the reasoning state interpretable. It anchors latent targets with DINOv3-derived future representations and optimizes them with an RL surrogate, but this is still mostly better-shaped hidden state, not explicit symbolic or object-centric structure. So I buy the training contribution more than the rhetoric of “reasoning.”

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

LaST-R1 sharpens a useful baseline question for VLA post-training. If a method claims robust long-horizon improvement through “reasoning,” we should now ask whether reward actually touches the internal reasoning variables or only the final action distribution. If it is only action-space RL, that is a weaker story.

The schema-grounded memory paper affects framing in a different direction. It argues that persistent agent memory should not be judged mainly as retrieval quality, but as write-path discipline, validation, state updates, and exact query support. That is a healthy corrective to the current habit of calling vector recall “memory” and pretending the mismatch is just an embedding problem.

HERMES++ mostly affects citation framing. It is another reminder that “unified world model” often means bundling understanding and prediction into one backbone with several bridge modules. Sometimes that is fine, but it raises the bar for what should count as genuine representational unification rather than multitask packaging.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today improves VLA post-training in a real way: reward is allowed to shape the internal latent workspace as well as the action output. That is more meaningful than another action-only RL wrapper. The most useful adjacent paper is on agent memory, and its core point is right: durable memory for exact facts and state should be built as validated records, not as semantic-retrieval hope. HERMES++ is capable work, but mostly as a broad integration example, not as a sharp mechanism note. The common lesson is that if a paper claims better reasoning, memory, or world modeling, we should ask where the explicit computational commitment actually lives. If it only lives in branding, the paper is probably weaker than it sounds.

## Detailed notes

- [LaST-R1 note](../paper_notes/last_r1_reinforcing_action_via_adaptive_physical_latent_reasoning_for_vla_models.md)

I inspected the full arXiv HTML papers for **Can a Language Model Learn Facts Continually in Its Weights?**, **Inside the Unfair Judge**, **Think Through a Bottleneck**, **HASTE**, **Read It Back**, **ZendoWorld**, **LaGuadia**, and **Feature-Space Guided Diffusion**. For the preserved notes, I read the abstract, framing, method, main results, and limitation or discussion sections. I did not reproduce code or audit every appendix table.

**Can a Language Model Learn Facts Continually in Its Weights?** is the strongest paper today. The useful move is the access-versus-storage split: later writes do not have to erase a fact to make it operationally gone.

The most directly relevant paper to cabbageland is also **Can a Language Model Learn Facts Continually in Its Weights?**. If a long-lived agent needs knowledge that survives future updates and composes on demand, the paper's answer is blunt: context is still the reliable system of record, not the weights.

**Inside the Unfair Judge** is the sharpest evaluation and interpretability paper in the batch. It makes judge bias something you can localize, steer, and predict across unseen benchmarks rather than merely complain about at the prompt layer.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Can a Language Model Learn Facts Continually in Its Weights?**

**Verdict:** must read for agent memory, continual learning, and long-lived knowledge systems.

Why it matters: This paper asks the right unpleasant question. If you keep writing facts into a model's weights, do they really accumulate in a usable way? The answer is mostly no. Broad study-style data helps create more usable facts than bare statements, but later writes still break reachability. After twenty later writes, bare-statement facts retain only `1%` strict accuracy while broader study-trained facts retain `46%`, and forgotten facts often recover to `77-80%` once the fact is supplied in context. That is exactly the sort of result that should make anyone building weight-updated agent memory much less romantic.

### 2. **Inside the Unfair Judge: A Mechanistic Interpretability Account of LLM-as-Judge Bias**

**Verdict:** strong direct-relevance interpretability paper.

Why it matters: The paper's core claim is that LLM-as-judge bias is not just a prompt artifact. It lives in a low-dimensional hidden-state displacement that sharpens with depth, can be steered in both directions, and generalizes well enough to predict failures on unseen benchmarks. The strongest practical result is the cross-domain detector: a simple linear projection onto bias-direction features gets `0.82` AUC on three unseen benchmarks, while matched-norm random directions produce an order-of-magnitude smaller steering effect. That is a much cleaner story than "judges are unreliable, be careful."

### 3. **Think Through a Bottleneck: Hourglass Reasoning for Rigorous Induction**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent inspiration with very high direct relevance.

Why it matters: The paper argues that self-refinement often fails because the model keeps dragging too much unstructured state between reasoning stages. Its fix is a physically enforced bottleneck: induction, deduction, implementation, and refinement run in separate contexts, and only a compressed symbolic state crosses boundaries. The gains are not tiny. On ARC-AGI-2 it improves best-of-5 accuracy by up to `14` points over an iterative-refinement baseline, and on ChipBench it raises GPT-5.5 Verilog synthesis accuracy from `31%` to `58%`. More importantly, the ablations say the lift comes from the boundary itself, not from nicer prompt wording.

### 4. **HASTE: A Platform for Rapid Post-Disaster Building Damage Assessment**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy field-deployment systems paper.

Why it matters: HASTE is refreshingly non-theatrical. It starts from the actual disaster-response constraint that matched pre-event imagery and large in-domain training sets are often unavailable in the first day. The platform then offers two usable fallback paths: single-scene segmentation from quick polygon labels, and post-event-only footprint embeddings with in-browser logistic regression. The embedding route reaches about `0.82` macro ROC-AUC from `1%` of labels and around `0.92` by `50%`, while the broader system has already supported more than thirty real responses since 2023. This is exactly the sort of field-deployment documentation most model papers carefully avoid being compared against.

### 5. **Read It Back: Pretrained MLLMs Are Zero-Shot Reward Models for Text-to-Image Generation**

**Verdict:** strong lighter recommendation.

Why it matters: The mechanism is cleaner than most reward-modeling papers in this lane. Instead of asking a multimodal judge to output a score or answer decomposed verification questions, it uses image-conditioned prompt log-likelihood as the reward itself. That reuses the model's native image-text alignment objective and also gives a natural self-reward variant for unified multimodal models. I kept it fifth because the paper is narrower than the top four and still lives inside text-to-image RL, but the reward-policy alignment lesson is real and reusable.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Can a Language Model Learn Facts Continually in Its Weights?

The main steal is the separation between storage and access. A model can keep the log-probability trace of an earlier fact and still fail to retrieve it once later writes redirect the question pathways that used to reach it. That is the right warning for any agent stack tempted to treat fine-tuning as durable memory. If a fact must be composed, survive later updates, and remain queryable on demand, the paper's conclusion is severe but useful: weights are not the system of record.

**Think Through a Bottleneck** gives the complementary pipeline lesson: if reasoning stages leak too much latent sludge across boundaries, self-refinement does not stay anchored to the rule. **Inside the Unfair Judge** supplies the evaluator lesson: if a judge can be displaced along low-dimensional bias directions, then evaluation stacks need judge-health checks rather than faith. **HASTE** adds the deployment lesson: when distribution shift is real, per-scene adaptation and operator-facing simplicity can beat bigger offline assumptions.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Can a Language Model Learn Facts Continually in Its Weights?** is strong because it refuses to score continual learning only by whether a model can still recite a fact after writing it. The real distinction is between knowledge creation, long-horizon reachability, and general capability preservation. Broad study-style data narrows the recitation-to-use gap and improves later retention, but no tested intervention keeps earlier facts reliably reachable after many subsequent writes. The paper's framing, "stored but question-keyed," is the useful part. Caveat: the study is mostly on Qwen3 with invented facts and mostly LoRA writes, so this is a sharp boundary probe rather than the final word on all continual learning.

**Inside the Unfair Judge** is strong because it turns bias into something measurable in representation space rather than leaving it as prompt folklore. Geometry, causal steering, and failure prediction all point at the same hidden-state story. The cross-domain detector result matters because it survives unseen benchmarks instead of only working on the papers' own perturbation templates. Caveat: the activation-level claims depend on white-box access to three open-source judges, and controlled bias constructions are not the whole space of real evaluator failure.

**Think Through a Bottleneck** is strong because it isolates the causal variable that many multi-agent or structured-reasoning papers blur: not role labels, but context boundaries. The ablations are the best part. Remove physical isolation and the structured intermediate can actively hurt. Caveat: the bottleneck is still soft and prompt-enforced rather than architectural, the method is expensive in calls and tokens, and the current task suite is tilted toward deterministic rule induction rather than messy probabilistic reasoning.

**HASTE** is strong because it documents a system that has to work under the actual constraints the benchmark culture prefers to ignore. The key move is not a new giant model, but a pair of fast, operator-facing adaptation routes that assume only post-event imagery and a small labeling budget. Caveat: the xBD experiments are preliminary, binary, and cleaner than real disaster imagery, while the live system still misses damage invisible from overhead and inherits footprint registration problems.

**Read It Back** is strong because it extracts a reward directly from image-conditioned prompt recovery rather than from extra annotation or hand-built verification scaffolds. The self-reward case for unified multimodal models is especially interesting because it says alignment between reward source and generator may matter more than brute reward-model scale. Caveat: this is still a text-to-image RL paper with limited direct evidence about human preference, safety, or cross-domain reward robustness.

**ZendoWorld** was the closest runner-up. I like the benchmark because it tests hypothesis formation plus experiment design instead of passive pattern matching, and it clearly shows current VLM agents propose bad experiments. I left it out because today's final five had sharper direct design lessons. **LaGuadia** was another good runner-up: clinical language as a semantic anchor for multi-teacher pathology distillation is a real idea, but the deployment and transfer story felt narrower than the papers above.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all reject the idea that storing more stuff is the same as making a system more capable. Weight writes do not guarantee later access. Judge outputs do not explain judge bias unless you inspect the activation routes underneath them. Self-refinement does not become rigorous until the boundary between stages is physically enforced. Reward models do not need to be separate critics if prompt recoverability already exposes the right alignment signal. Fielded damage-assessment systems do not need huge global assumptions if they can adapt locally with a small operator loop. Same lesson in five costumes: the important part is not just where the information lives, but what interface still lets the system use it correctly later.

- [Inside the unfair judge note](../paper_notes/inside_the_unfair_judge_llm_as_judge_bias.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-13

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **structure only matters if the system preserves the right state and exposes the right boundary**. **Interference and Retention in Continual Learning** turns forgetting into explicit overlap geometry, so protection happens before damage rather than after. **Workflow as Knowledge** argues that workflows, inference records, context snapshots, and approvals should persist as typed objects rather than disposable traces. **MultiView-Bench** shows frontier VLMs still fail when they must anchor multiple views into a fixed allocentric coordinate frame. **ALICE** demonstrates that pathology expertise at different scales can be distilled into one backbone instead of kept in separate specialist silos. **GeoTrace** keeps exact skeleton tokens plus traceable residual event tokens, which is much cleaner than saliency-heavy video-token mush.

I deliberately kept robotics / VLA to one runner-up lane after checking the fresh `cs.RO` batch visible on **Monday, July 13, 2026**. The strongest robotics-adjacent candidates were **B-spline Policy**, **PAC-ACT**, **SplatCtrl**, and **GenVid2Robot**. Some were good engineering papers, but none clearly beat the non-robotics papers below on transferable mechanism, evidence quality, and future usefulness.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first on **July 13, 2026** via the Brave web API and failed with **HTTP 422** because the required `x-subscription-token` header was missing in this environment. I therefore used live arXiv category pages, arXiv API title resolution, arXiv HTML full text, and one PDF fallback. At scout time, the latest visible batches were **Monday, July 13, 2026** for `cs.RO`, **Friday, July 10, 2026** for `cs.AI` and `cs.LG`, and **Wednesday, July 8, 2026** for `cs.CV`.

No preserved note today is abstract-only. I inspected the full arXiv HTML papers for **Workflow as Knowledge**, **Interference and Retention in Continual Learning**, **MultiView-Bench**, **ALICE**, **All Explanations are Wrong, But Many Are Useful**, and **Video Generation Models are General-Purpose Vision Learners**, and the full arXiv PDF for **GeoTrace** because its HTML view returned `404`. For the preserved notes, I read the abstract, framing, method, main results, and discussion or limitation sections. I did not audit released code, reproduce experiments, or verify every appendix table.

**Interference and Retention in Continual Learning** is the strongest paper today. The useful move is to stop treating forgetting as a mysterious after-effect and instead model it as explicit task interference geometry, with a removable-versus-irreducible split.

**Workflow as Knowledge** is the most directly relevant paper to cabbageland. It is less proven than the top empirical papers, but the `derive` versus `infer` boundary and typed persistence of workflow instances, context snapshots, approvals, and panel records are exactly the sort of interface discipline long-lived agents need.

**MultiView-Bench** is the sharpest evaluation paper. It reveals that strong frontier VLMs still collapse on world-centric 3D reasoning, especially axis-direction identification, and that even a budget-matched agentic wrapper can materially help.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Interference and Retention in Continual Learning**

**Verdict:** must read for continual learning and adaptive agent systems.

Why it matters: The paper replaces the usual replay-versus-regularizer framing with a cleaner one: forgetting is interference geometry. In the frozen-feature regime, forgetting from learning task B is exactly the interference energy imposed on task A, and when supports overlap in conflicting directions there is a real distortion floor that no clever policy removes. That is a better mental model than "catastrophic forgetting happened somehow." The derived IGFA rule is also useful: share directions when tasks align, protect them when they conflict, and treat capacity, incompatibility, and control as separate costs instead of one blurry retention metric.

### 2. **Workflow as Knowledge: Semantic Persistence for LLM-Mediated Workflows**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent inspiration with very high direct relevance.

Why it matters: This is a conceptual paper, not a benchmark win, but it is unusually aligned with durable agent runtime design. The key claim is that workflow definitions, running instances, inference records, approvals, context snapshots, and dependency relations should live as typed objects in a shared knowledge substrate rather than as source code plus logs plus half-semantic traces. The `derive` versus `infer` split is load-bearing: deterministic computation and model-mediated judgment should not pretend to be the same thing.

### 3. **MultiView-Bench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for World-Centric Multi-View Integration in VLMs**

**Verdict:** strong direct-relevance benchmark paper.

Why it matters: The benchmark asks a question many multimodal papers dodge: can a model integrate multiple views into a fixed global 3D frame, rather than merely describe one image at a time? On the hardest tasks, most frontier models are near random chance, and the failure analysis is concrete rather than theatrical: models are decent at 2D local relations but fail at axis-direction identification and multi-view aggregation. The budget-matched ViewNavigator result is also informative because it shows structured viewpoint selection and belief aggregation help even when test-time image budget is held fixed.

### 4. **ALICE: Learning a General-Purpose Pathology Foundation Model from Vision, Vision-Language, and Slide-Level Experts**

**Verdict:** strong healthcare foundation-model paper.

Why it matters: ALICE is not just another "bigger medical model" report. The important move is staged agglomerative distillation across distinct types of pathology expertise: morphology-heavy vision models, vision-language models, and slide-level clinical-context models. The evaluation breadth is serious too: 21 task scenarios, 96 downstream tasks, and 48 data sources. The paper is useful less as a generic leaderboard item and more as evidence that multi-scale specialist knowledge can be consolidated into one reusable backbone without fully flattening the differences between local tissue features, semantic alignment, and whole-slide reasoning.

### 5. **GeoTrace: Geometry-Aware Trajectory Token Compression for Video Large Language Models**

**Verdict:** strong lighter recommendation.

Why it matters: GeoTrace is a training-free token compression paper, but the mechanism is cleaner than the usual prune-by-saliency story. It preserves exact skeleton tokens for scene structure and compresses the residual through traceable one-to-one temporal trajectories instead of vague clustering mush. The reported tradeoff is strong enough to matter: on LLaVA-OneVision at 10 percent token retention, it cuts TFLOPs by `12.99x`, improves time-to-first-token substantially, and still preserves `99.1%` of baseline accuracy.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Workflow as Knowledge.

The steal is the boundary design. Long-lived agent systems should not blur deterministic computation, model judgment, human approval, and resumable workflow state into one log stream. This paper proposes explicit workflow definitions, workflow instances, inference records, context snapshots, and dependency relations as typed persistent objects, plus a clean `derive` / `infer` split. It is still a conceptual paper, but the framing is unusually aligned with durable tool-using assistants, provenance, reviewability, and agent runtime design.

**Interference and Retention in Continual Learning** gives the complementary learning story: protect geometry before forgetting happens. **MultiView-Bench** supplies the evaluation lesson: do not trust a multimodal agent in 3D software or embodied settings until it can aggregate views into a fixed global frame rather than parroting coordinate priors. **ALICE** supplies the domain-transfer lesson: multi-scale expertise can be consolidated if the distillation pipeline respects the differences between local morphology, language semantics, and whole-slide context.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Interference and Retention in Continual Learning** is strong because it turns forgetting from a symptom into a measurable object. The important ideas are the interference identity, the removability dichotomy, and the distortion floor. The diagnostic split between incompatibility, capacity, and control is more useful than the usual retention scoreboard because it tells you which kind of intervention could possibly help. Caveat: the exact claims are strongest in the frozen-feature or function-space regime, and the broader language-model evidence is still thinner than the theory.

**Workflow as Knowledge** is strong because it refuses the lazy assumption that "we have logs" is equivalent to semantic persistence. The paper introduces a concrete object vocabulary and a real boundary between deterministic `derive` steps and mediated `infer` judgments. The caveat is obvious and the paper admits it: formal transition semantics, lifecycle policy, governance, and empirical validation are all future work, so this is a design lens rather than a demonstrated runtime win.

**MultiView-Bench** is strong because it exposes a specific multimodal weakness that normal VLM benchmarks mostly wash away. The benchmark is about allocentric integration into a fixed coordinate frame, not generic "spatial reasoning" branding. The failure analysis is particularly useful: single-view narration is not the same thing as cross-view 3D grounding, and many models quietly default to conventional coordinate priors instead of reading the axes in front of them. The caveat is that the proposed ViewNavigator help still does not solve the task cleanly, especially on the hardest settings.

**ALICE** is strong because it treats specialization across pathology models as something to be integrated structurally rather than averaged away. The staged distillation setup makes the claim more believable than a vague multimodal mashup. The caveat is that the evaluation is still mostly retrospective, and the authors themselves point to missing prospective multi-institutional validation, broader cohort diversity, and more efficient deployment structure.

**GeoTrace** is strong because it identifies the actual failure of many token-compression methods: they over-focus on local saliency and then fuse the remainder into ambiguous features. The skeleton-plus-event decomposition is a cleaner representation interface. I kept it fifth because the claim is narrower than the top four and mainly about efficient inference rather than broader representational or evaluation framing, but it is still a useful mechanism paper.

**All Explanations are Wrong, But Many Are Useful** was a strong runner-up. I like the attempt to replace one canonical explanation with a set of faithful explanations plus a prediction-linked workflow, but the paper felt more over-claimed and less cleanly transferable than the final five.

**Video Generation Models are General-Purpose Vision Learners** was another strong runner-up. The pretraining thesis is interesting and the results are large, but the paper also admits important regressions in some joint-training settings and leans a bit too hard on the "generalist world model" rhetoric for where the evidence currently is.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all reject flat, undifferentiated state. Continual learning should preserve or protect the geometry that actually causes interference. Agent workflows should retain typed records at the `infer` / `derive` boundary instead of dumping everything into traces. Multi-view VLM evaluation should ask whether the model can build a global coordinate frame rather than whether it can narrate a single image. Pathology foundation models should integrate local, semantic, and slide-level expertise instead of forcing users to pick one siloed backbone. Video token compression should preserve exact skeleton structure and traceable residual events rather than merge tokens into opaque mush. Same lesson at five scales: keep the state that carries the claim, and make its boundary inspectable.
