# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-21

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **make the bottleneck carry evidence**. The strongest papers I found are not just making latent or structured systems sound legible. They put pressure on the exact object that is supposed to carry the claim: a diffusion language model's inter-step bottleneck, a soft-routed MoE's aggregate confidence, or a 3D editor's source-to-target box specification.

I deliberately kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered interpretability, calibration under distribution shift, 3D/generative media, healthcare deployment, long-video temporal reasoning, Bayesian in-context learning, geometric representation learning, and skill/context compression. No robotics/VLA paper beat the best non-robotics alternatives today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable for individual paper pages and useful for metadata checks, but the pages I inspected exposed mostly abstracts, metrics, and empty comments/resources rather than useful discussion trails. I used AlphaXiv as a supplement, then relied on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs for primary-source inspection. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

The arXiv API returned no new submissions in the checked cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CV, and stat.ML categories for June 19-21, so the strongest available set came from the June 18 uploads. I did not reuse yesterday's already-preserved top papers. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the paper text, especially method, results, and limitations, for **How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?**, **Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift**, **Thinking in Boxes**, **GEN-Guard**, **TimeProVe**, **SoftSkill**, **Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning**, and **The Token Is a Group Element**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?** is the most relevant paper today. It turns the vague worry that text diffusion models may reason opaquely in latent space into a set of auditable measurements: opaque serial depth, bottleneck token ablations, monitorability, and case studies of non-autoregressive reasoning.

**Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift** is the strongest calibration paper in the scan. Its useful move is the distinction between hard-routing robustness and soft-routing fragility: calibrated experts do not guarantee calibrated aggregate probabilities once routing configurations get reweighted.

**Thinking in Boxes** is the best 3D/generative media paper today. It uses 3D boxes as an actual edit specification, not a decorative condition. The source and target boxes plus a depth-aligned floor give the generator a compact geometric contract for translation, rotation, scale, disocclusion, and camera change.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. **GEN-Guard** is a strong healthcare/deployment paper: client-blocked evaluation exposes model-selection failures in federated surgical AI, and disagreement-aware distillation gives a practical post-hoc correction. I kept it as a runner-up because the correction is more deployment hygiene than a broadly reusable modeling primitive. **TimeProVe** is a sensible propose-then-verify system for long ADL video QA, but it depends heavily on action detectors and heuristic evidence ranking. **The Token Is a Group Element** has a sharp geometric premise, but the empirical evidence is still toy sequence completion. **SoftSkill** is directly interesting for skill systems, but its strongest results are single-round QA; the paper itself admits long-horizon agentic compression is not robust yet.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives a concrete audit template for latent reasoning architectures. If a model computes between interpretable text states, the question is not "does it feel transparent?" but whether the intermediate bottleneck can be mapped to readable tokens without damaging capability, and whether monitorability survives in the settings where the model actually reasons.

### 2. **Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as a calibration and routing-mechanism paper.

Why it matters: it shows that "each expert is calibrated" is not enough when soft routing collapses many expert-weight configurations into one confidence value. The aggregate probability can be calibrated only because errors cancel under the training distribution, then break when the configuration mix shifts.

### 3. **Thinking in Boxes: 3D Editing in Real Images Made Easy**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as explicit-control generative media.

Why it matters: it replaces text prompts and loose 2D layout hints with a small geometric interface that actually specifies the desired transformation. Boxes encode object pose and visibility; the floor disambiguates object motion from camera motion.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?

The steal is the audit shape. Cabbageland should treat latent reasoning systems the way this paper treats DiffusionGemma: identify the hidden bottleneck, bound how much serial computation bypasses readable states, test whether the bottleneck can be compressed into interpretable symbols, and then check whether those symbols are actually useful to a monitor. The important part is not that DiffusionGemma looks fine today. The important part is that future latent systems now have a template they can fail.

The MoE calibration paper contributes a second reusable lens: do not trust modularity at the component level when the router creates a many-to-one aggregate. The calibration claim has to be tested at the routed aggregate, under shifts that stress the configurations where experts disagree.

Thinking in Boxes contributes the control-interface lesson. A generative model can be powerful and still need a small explicit state object to make user intent unambiguous. The box-and-floor representation is not aesthetically subtle, but it gives the model a job it can actually condition on.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?** raises the bar for latent-reasoning transparency work. The paper reports that DiffusionGemma's opaque serial depth is 28.6x Gemma 4 26B A4B if the inter-step bottleneck is treated as uninterpretable, but 1.1x if the bottleneck is interpretable. Its top-k and probability-threshold ablations show that k = 8 or p = 0.03 can match baseline capability on the tested benchmarks, and the token-identity analysis suggests most load-bearing intermediate states are guesses for current or neighboring final tokens. The caveat is important: multi-canvas monitorability may hide single-canvas regressions, and "mapped latent vector looks token-like" is not the same as guaranteed faithful reasoning.

**Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift** is valuable because the theory matches the practical failure mode. Hard routing creates an expert-confidence bottleneck; reweighting routing regions can preserve calibration if each expert-confidence slice remains reliable. Soft routing collapses routing weights and expert outputs into a scalar confidence, so many configurations can share the same confidence while having different outcome frequencies. The proposed Robust MoE and Robust Filtered objectives improve ECE on shifted or ambiguous subsets across CIFAR-10H, PACS, and CivilComments. The limitations are scale and proxy choice: the experiments use compact four-expert MoEs, and high proper loss is only a proxy for routing-induced calibration error.

**Thinking in Boxes** is useful because the explicit structure is doing the work. Prior box/depth/primitive methods often use 3D cues as approximate conditions or cleanup scaffolds; this paper treats source and target boxes as the edit itself. The strongest baseline impact is on large spatial edits, especially disocclusion and object/camera motion. The caveat is that the representation is only as good as the fitted boxes and floor estimate. When similar-scale boxes are ambiguous, the model can collapse to the identity transformation.

**GEN-Guard** is the strongest runner-up for healthcare deployment. It identifies performance leakage as a model-selection failure, reports MSFs in 38 of 46 experiments, and improves worst-case F1 in Multi-Cholec and PolypGen. The useful idea is client-blocked evaluation before deployment. The caveat is that CBE only works as well as the blocked validation clients represent the deployment shift.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all refuse to let the hidden part stay hand-wavy. **How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?** asks whether a latent diffusion language model's inter-step state is readable enough to monitor. **Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift** asks whether the routed aggregate remains calibrated when soft-routing configurations shift. **Thinking in Boxes** asks whether a 3D editor can be controlled by an explicit geometric specification instead of prompt vibes. Different domains, same standard: find the bottleneck, state what it must preserve, and test the claim at that bottleneck instead of admiring the system around it.

- [Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift note](../paper_notes/calibrated_moe_distribution_shift.md)
- [Thinking in Boxes note](../paper_notes/thinking_in_boxes_3d_editing.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-09

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **world models are becoming structured memory and action interfaces, not just future-frame generators**. **MemoryVLA++** is the most relevant paper because it gives a VLA an explicit past-present-future temporal interface: perceptual/cognitive memory for past context, current working tokens, and latent future imagination for action prediction. **iMaC** is the sharpest action-conditioning paper because it turns robot actions into rendered motion images and two contact-distance image streams instead of asking a video model to infer contact from a compact vector. **Latent Spatial Memory / Mirage** is the best video-world-model memory paper because it stores a 3D cache directly in diffusion latent space, avoiding the expensive RGB point-cloud render-and-reencode loop.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv pages for the main candidates returned HTTP 403 in this environment. Discovery therefore used arXiv API search over the June 8, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full PDFs for **MemoryVLA++: Temporal Modeling via Memory and Imagination in Vision-Language-Action Models**, **Latent Spatial Memory for Video World Models**, **iMaC: Translating Actions into Motion and Contact Images for Embodied World Models**, **Echo-Memory: A Controlled Study of Memory in Action World Models**, **AHA-WAM: Asynchronous Horizon-Adaptive World-Action Modeling with Observation-Guided Context Routing**, **omega-EVA: Envision, Verify, and Act with Latent Interactive World Models**, **Prisma-World: Camera-Controllable Multi-Agent Video World Model**, **MotionWAM: Towards Foundation World Action Models for Real-Time Humanoid Loco-Manipulation**, **FF-JEPA: Long-Horizon Planning in World Models with Latent Planners**, and **Your Model Already Knows: Attention-Guided Safety Filter for Vision-Language-Action Models**. MemoryVLA++, iMaC, and Latent Spatial Memory are preserved today.

**MemoryVLA++** is the strongest direct hit. It builds a full temporal VLA interface: current RGB and language become perceptual and cognitive working-memory tokens; a Perceptual-Cognitive Memory Bank stores low-level details and high-level semantics from past interaction; a manipulation-adapted video world model provides compact latent future imagination; and a diffusion action expert consumes the fused temporal tokens. The evidence is broad: Libero, SimplerEnv, Mikasa-Robo, Calvin, Libero-Plus, and several real-robot task categories. The paper is not perfectly controlled across all comparisons, but the ablations support the useful mechanism: both memory retrieval/consolidation and memory-guided imagination matter.

**iMaC** is the most concrete action-world-model interface paper. It asks a better question than whether generated robot videos look plausible: can a learned world model rank policy checkpoints in the same direction as real hardware? The method renders future robot motion from URDF and forward kinematics, predicts/uses depth, and builds two contact-image streams from scene-to-gripper and robot-to-scene distances. Across eight real-robot tasks, world-model scores are strongly positively correlated with real-world performance on most tasks, while the two weaker tasks expose missing-observation failure modes rather than generic metric noise.

**Latent Spatial Memory / Mirage** is the strongest memory-system paper for camera-controllable video world models. Instead of accumulating an RGB point cloud and repeatedly rendering it back to pixels before VAE encoding, Mirage stores VAE latent tokens at 3D world coordinates. Readout is a latent-resolution projection into the target camera view, then a ControlNet-style branch injects the memory into the diffusion backbone. The result is both a representation claim and a systems claim: better or competitive consistency on WorldScore and RealEstate10K, with much lower cache read cost and memory.

**Echo-Memory** is strong citation material and may deserve a later synthesis note. Its most useful result is that replay fidelity is not a proxy for revisit memory: spatial memory can win replay PSNR while failing open-domain return, and block-wise state-space recurrence can win semantic return while losing replay metrics. I am not preserving it as a full note today because it is mainly an evaluation/design-space study, while today's three notes provide more directly reusable architecture surfaces.

**AHA-WAM** is useful but not preserved. The two-timescale split between a slow video-DiT planner and fast action-DiT executor is a good deployment idea, and the latency story is concrete. I am treating it as adjacent because it is close to yesterday's action/world-model interface thread, and part of the result is systems optimization rather than a cleaner representation mechanism.

**omega-EVA** is also useful but not preserved. The proposal-conditioned Envision-Verify-Act loop is conceptually aligned with CAPE from June 8: make the policy inspect a latent consequence of its own proposed action before execution. The evidence is mostly simulation and the Stage 3 deltas are real but modest, so it is citation material rather than one of today's top three.

**Prisma-World** is adjacent for multi-agent video simulation. Its joint denoising, multi-agent RoPE, relative camera geometry, and minimap conditioning address cross-view consistency, but it is less directly tied to robot memory/planning than the preserved papers.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **MemoryVLA++: Temporal Modeling via Memory and Imagination in Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives a VLA a real temporal interface: past memory, current working tokens, future latent imagination, and action prediction in one loop.

### 2. **iMaC: Translating Actions into Motion and Contact Images for Embodied World Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as an action-conditioned world-model evaluator.

Why it matters: it turns robot actions into spatial robot-body and contact-geometry controls, which is a much better interface than a dense action vector when contact decides the outcome.

### 3. **Latent Spatial Memory for Video World Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for video world-model memory and efficient 3D consistency.

Why it matters: it stores persistent spatial memory in the model's native latent space, making memory both cheaper and less lossy than RGB point-cloud caches.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** MemoryVLA++.

The steal-worthy idea is not "add memory" or "add a world model." It is to divide temporal context by function. Current perception becomes working memory. Past interaction is retrieved from a compact memory bank that stores both perceptual details and cognitive semantics. Future state is represented by partially denoised latent world-model features rather than decoded video. The action expert gets a fused temporal representation instead of a raw stack of frames.

iMaC is the action-interface companion. If the world model must judge a candidate robot policy, the action condition should expose the robot's future body and the contact-relevant geometry. Motion images and contact images are clunky in a good way: they make the causal surface visible to the generator.

Mirage is the memory-system companion. If the generator already lives in latent space, a persistent 3D memory should not keep detouring through RGB. Storing latent tokens at world coordinates is the obvious idea after you see it, which is usually a good sign.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**MemoryVLA++** raises the baseline for temporal VLA papers. A serious long-horizon VLA should say whether it has working memory, episodic retrieval, future imagination, or only a frame window. It should also show whether memory and imagination help different task families.

**iMaC** raises the baseline for embodied world models used as policy evaluators. If a world model claims to evaluate robot actions, compact action vectors are a weak interface unless the paper shows they preserve contact-sensitive differences. A better baseline now includes robot-rendered motion and explicit contact geometry.

**Latent Spatial Memory** raises the baseline for persistent-memory video generators. If a method stores RGB point clouds only to render and re-encode them at every conditioning step, it should justify why the model's own latent features are not the cleaner memory substrate.

**Echo-Memory** is a framing warning: replay metrics, in-domain return, and open-domain semantic revisit can disagree. Any future world-model memory paper that reports only replay fidelity is under-measuring the claim.

**AHA-WAM** is useful deployment framing: the world branch and action branch may need different temporal rates. Slow predictive context and fast control do not have to share one horizon.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **MemoryVLA++** because it makes temporal modeling in VLAs explicit enough to reason about: past memory, present tokens, and future imagination each have a job. **iMaC** is the action-conditioning note to remember because it converts actions into robot motion and contact geometry before asking a video model to simulate manipulation. **Latent Spatial Memory** is the video-world-model note to keep because it treats persistent 3D memory as latent features rather than RGB cache clutter. The common lesson is blunt: world models get more useful when their memory and action interfaces expose the structure that decisions actually depend on.

- [iMaC note](../paper_notes/imac_motion_contact_images_embodied_world_models.md)

# Daily Digest — 2026-03-30

## Theme
Today was thinner than the last few days. I found one paper I think is genuinely worth preserving as a mechanism note, one adjacent paper that is useful mainly because it exposes a real failure mode in geometry-aware reasoning, and one competent robotics post-training paper that feels more like optimization hygiene than a conceptual step. Discovery in this run leaned on arXiv/API queries plus direct arXiv paper inspection; the digest should not have claimed Brave Search was unavailable without a verified tool check.

## Short overview
Today’s most relevant paper is **GaussianGPT: Towards Autoregressive 3D Gaussian Scene Generation**. I do not think it is a foundational world-model paper, but it is a serious representation-and-generation paper. Its useful move is to treat explicit 3D Gaussian scenes as a token sequence over occupied spatial structure and appearance, rather than only as a denoising target. The position/feature token split is the main thing worth remembering.

The second paper worth preserving is **Make Geometry Matter for Spatial Reasoning**. This is not a world model and not an embodied control paper, but it identifies a real problem: geometry-token injection into VLMs is often mostly decorative, and can even hurt if the model keeps leaning on 2D appearance shortcuts. The proposed fix is simple rather than deep, but the diagnosis is useful.

A third paper I inspected but am **not** preserving as a full note today is **VLA-OPD: Bridging Offline SFT and Online RL for Vision-Language-Action Models via On-Policy Distillation**. It looks competent and probably practical. But the core contribution is better post-training dynamics for existing VLAs via teacher-labeled on-policy rollouts, not a new memory, state, planning, or representation idea.

## Ranked papers

1. **GaussianGPT: Towards Autoregressive 3D Gaussian Scene Generation**  
   - Verdict: **Useful**  
   - Role: **Directly relevant**  
   - Why it matters: It shows a plausible autoregressive route for explicit 3D scene generation using structured Gaussian tokens instead of another holistic diffusion pipeline.

2. **Make Geometry Matter for Spatial Reasoning**  
   - Verdict: **Useful**  
   - Role: **Adjacent inspiration**  
   - Why it matters: It makes a blunt but correct point that geometry priors do not help if the downstream VLM is free to ignore them.

3. **VLA-OPD: Bridging Offline SFT and Online RL for Vision-Language-Action Models via On-Policy Distillation**  
   - Verdict: **Skimmable**  
   - Role: **Mostly citation material**  
   - Why it matters: It is a decent current example of using teacher-labeled on-policy data to clean up VLA post-training without solving deeper representation problems.

## Most relevant to cabbageland
**GaussianGPT** is the strongest hit today, though with moderate rather than high enthusiasm. The value is not “autoregressive is better than diffusion” in the abstract. The value is that it cleanly separates occupancy/position prediction from feature prediction over an explicit 3D scene representation, which is closer to controllable scene construction than another monolithic denoiser.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact
- **Explicit 3D tokens instead of holistic denoising:** GaussianGPT is useful framing material for arguments that explicit scene structure can support more natural completion and outpainting than global refinement pipelines.
- **Geometry priors can be performative:** GeoSR is good citation material against naive “we injected 3D tokens so now the model reasons spatially” claims.
- **Post-training is not the same as structure:** VLA-OPD may be practically strong, but it should not be confused with progress on memory, planning abstraction, or explicit state.
- **Search / inspection note:** Discovery in this run used arXiv API queries plus direct arXiv inspection. The earlier wording claiming Brave Search was unavailable was too strong without a verified tool check. I have now verified that the Brave tool in this environment is currently unconfigured because the Brave API key is missing, which is different from proving Brave was unavailable at the time of the original scouting run. I inspected substantial accessible arXiv HTML/text for **GaussianGPT**, **GeoSR**, and **VLA-OPD**, not just titles or abstracts. I did **not** fully audit appendices, supplementary videos, or every ablation table, so confidence is higher on the mechanism-level judgments than on exact numeric margins.

## One-paragraph takeaway
The useful pattern today is that explicit structure only matters if it changes the computation. **GaussianGPT** earns attention because it commits to an explicit 3D representation and builds an autoregressive interface over it, which at least makes completion, extension, and control feel native to the model rather than bolted on. **GeoSR** is useful for a different reason: it points out that geometry branches often become decorative unless training forces the model to actually rely on them. **VLA-OPD** may help deployment, but it is still mainly a better optimization recipe over existing policies. So the day’s lesson is simple: explicit tokens, explicit routing, explicit state—good; calling something geometry-aware or world-model-like without changing what the model must use—less impressive.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-17

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **aggregate success is not evidence of the right mechanism**. The strongest papers ask whether a memory system used reachable evidence, whether a medical VLM used the image, and whether deception leaves a different internal state than ordinary wrongness. I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work as one lane rather than the center. The scan covered agent memory, clinical AI, interpretability, source/provenance verification, prompt-injection sanitization, agent-search scaling, VLM reliability, clinical speech, environment-model RL, code-reasoning diagnostics, 3D/CAD data, and a list-level robotics/VLA pass.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv's lightweight search route returned a 404 page again. Individual AlphaXiv paper pages were reachable for some candidates, but the fetchable text exposed only title/navigation stubs, so it was not useful for discovery or related-paper branching. I used arXiv new listings, the arXiv API, and direct arXiv PDFs for the serious candidates.

Full-text PDFs were available for the papers I considered preserving. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitation sections, for **MemTrace: Probing What Final Accuracy Misses in Long-Term Memory**, **Vision-language models for chest radiography do not always need the image**, **Rift: A Conflict Signature for Deception in Language Models**, **ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents**, **PARSE**, **Beyond Parallel Sampling**, **Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories**, **Visuals Lie, Consistency Speaks**, **SpeechDx**, **EnvRL**, and **From Brewing to Resolution**. The robotics/VLA scan found several plausible candidates, including technical reports and VLA memory/control papers, but none beat the best non-robotics papers today on mechanism, evidence quality, and future usefulness.

**MemTrace** is the most relevant paper today. It changes the unit of long-term memory evaluation from independent QA rows to knowledge points: a single user fact probed across age, question type, and evidence condition. The important result is not merely that memory systems forget. It is that most hard failures are evidence-use failures after relevant evidence is already reachable.

**Vision-language models for chest radiography do not always need the image** is the strongest healthcare/evaluation paper in the scan. The paper builds an interventional audit using label-matched image swaps, radiologist-box target masks, and irrelevant masks to test whether a correct answer causally depends on the radiograph. The uncomfortable result is that a text-only model lands close to the best multimodal system, and several medical VLMs either ignore the image or use it only selectively.

**Rift** is the most provocative interpretability paper today, but I am keeping it below the two preserved notes because it needs replication and has a narrow experimental regime. The mechanism is interesting: residual rank rises during deceptive forward passes relative to both honest answers and naive wrong answers. The paper controls for wrongness and tests roleplay, strategic bluffing, concealment prompts, length, and cross-domain probes. That is worth attention. It is not yet a deployment-ready lie detector.

Several other papers were useful but stayed below the preservation line. **ProvenanceGuard** is highly aligned with MCP-style agents because it verifies not just whether a claim is supported somewhere, but whether it is attributed to the right tool/source. **PARSE** is a practical warning that prompt-injection defenses proven on synthetic tasks may collapse on real enterprise documents. **DivInit** is a clean agent-search trick: diversify first-turn queries before parallel rollouts instead of letting threads collapse onto the same retrieval path. **Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories** is valuable as an agent-harness paper, but the paper is partly a systems report around one harness. **SpeechDx** is a strong benchmark contribution for clinical speech AI, but today's two preserved notes have sharper mechanism transfer.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **MemTrace: Probing What Final Accuracy Misses in Long-Term Memory**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it evaluates memory at the fact level rather than the row level, then shows that trajectory tracking, false-premise correction, and evidence use are separable failure modes hidden by pooled accuracy.

### 2. **Vision-language models for chest radiography do not always need the image**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as a healthcare/evaluation audit.

Why it matters: it replaces benchmark accuracy with causal input-dependence checks. A model that answers correctly without using the image should not be credited as doing radiology.

### 3. **Rift: A Conflict Signature for Deception in Language Models**

**Verdict:** useful and provocative, but replication-needed.

Why it matters: it asks the right ELK-flavored question: can internal state distinguish knowing deception from ordinary wrongness? The residual-rank signature is interesting, but the current evidence should be treated as an early diagnostic lead, not a settled safety primitive.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** MemTrace.

The direct steal is the unit-of-evaluation shift. Instead of asking whether an agent answered a row correctly, hold a durable fact fixed and vary time, query type, and evidence condition. That maps almost perfectly onto real assistant memory: current-state questions, historical-state questions, change-over-time questions, absent-evidence refusal, and false-premise correction are not interchangeable.

The second steal is the reach/use split. A memory system can retrieve the right span and still fail because the generator is not given temporal structure, conflict structure, or an explicit enough interface to use it. That is a design warning for any long-lived cabbageland agent: storage and retrieval are not memory unless the evidence is presented in a form the reasoning loop can bind to the answer.

The chest-radiography paper contributes the evaluation analogue: a correct answer is not enough. Intervene on the supposed input channel and test whether the answer changes for the right reason. For medical VLMs, that means swapping or masking images. For agents, it could mean withholding a tool observation, swapping a source, masking a retrieved span, or altering a stated memory.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**MemTrace** raises the bar for memory benchmarks. It makes pooled QA accuracy look too blunt because it cannot tell whether a system remembers a current value, an earlier value, a trajectory, an absent fact, or a contradicted premise.

**Chest radiography VLM audit** raises the bar for medical multimodal evaluation. Reported VQA accuracy should not count as visual grounding unless interventional tests show the model used the image. This is especially important because text-only priors can look clinically competent on common yes/no finding probes.

**Rift** is a useful framing paper for deception interpretability: wrong output is not the same variable as internal conflict. The naive-liar control is the key design idea. The red flag is scope: small-to-mid models, simple facts, prompt-induced deception, and limited extraction. Keep the mechanism, not the hype.

**ProvenanceGuard** and **PARSE** are deployment reminders. Agents need source ownership, not just pooled support, and retrieval sanitization should be tested on real professional documents rather than toy prompt-injection strings.

**DivInit** and **EnvRL** point in the same agentic direction from opposite ends: diversify the evidence path before rollout collapse, and use environment transitions as training signal rather than treating outcome reward as the whole story.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today are all refusing a lazy metric. **MemTrace** says memory is not row-level accuracy; it is fact-level behavior across time, question type, and evidence condition. **Chest radiography VLMs do not always need the image** says medical VQA accuracy is not evidence of image use; grounding needs causal intervention. **Rift** says wrongness is not the same as deception; compare a model lying while knowing against a model that is merely wrong. The shared lesson is simple and useful: before trusting a success number, identify the mechanism that was supposed to produce it and test that mechanism directly.

## Detailed notes

- [MemTrace note](../paper_notes/memtrace_long_term_memory_evaluation.md)
- [Chest radiography VLM grounding audit note](../paper_notes/chest_radiography_vlms_do_not_always_need_image.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-06

## Theme

Today's strongest pattern is **explicit state interfaces are doing the real work**. **VASO** is the most directly relevant paper because it turns formal counterexamples into updates to reusable physical-agent skill contracts, rather than using verification as a one-off plan filter. **Astra** is the best world-model reasoning paper because it treats a world simulator as an evidence-acquisition tool and shows that both simulator consistency and learned tool-use policy matter. **PACT** is the cleanest agent-systems paper because it replaces free-form inter-agent chatter with compact action-state handoffs.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider, but it returned `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv search and paper URLs were attempted through web fetch, but the accessible paths returned AlphaXiv 404 pages. Direct arXiv category pages were reachable; expanded arXiv listing URLs with `show=150` returned HTTP 400, so discovery used the default recent category listings plus direct arXiv pages and PDFs. This makes discovery narrower than an ideal Brave-plus-AlphaXiv pass, but the preserved papers are not abstract-only.

I inspected arXiv PDFs for **VASO: Formally Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills for Physical AI Agents**, **Thinking with Imagination: Agentic Visual Spatial Reasoning with World Simulators**, **What Should Agents Say? Action-state Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Systems**, **Beyond Semantic Organization: Memory as Execution State Management for Long-Horizon Agents**, **Discrete-WAM: Unified Discrete Vision-Action Token Editing for World-Policy Learning**, and **DexFuture: Hierarchical Future-State Visuomotor Targeting for Bimanual Dexterous Tool Use**. I also screened abstracts for **TempoVLA** and **WorldFly**. VASO, Astra, and PACT are preserved today. MAGE, DexFuture, and Discrete-WAM are useful context, but I am not preserving full notes for them in this run.

**VASO** is the strongest direct hit. It represents each LLM-generated robot skill as a semantic contract with a temporal-logic local rule, proposition-aligned labeling function, and planner-facing template. The useful move is that model-checker counterexamples become textual gradients for updating the reusable skill contract. The caveat is important: the verification guarantee depends on the correctness of the proposition-aligned mapping from low-level robot behavior to symbolic propositions.

**Astra** is strong adjacent-to-direct world-model reasoning work. It couples an RL-trained VLM policy with a Bagel-based world simulator that generates novel views from camera-motion queries. The key point is not merely "generate another view"; off-the-shelf generation is not enough, and forced simulator use can hurt. Astra improves by training the simulator for view consistency and training the policy to decide when, where, and how to imagine.

**PACT** is the simplest stealable agent architecture idea today. It treats inter-agent communication as a public state-update problem. Agents may reason privately, but only an action, grounded state/evidence, and result enter shared history. The evidence is practical: across controlled multi-agent settings PACT improves the performance-cost frontier, and in OpenHands/SWE-agent ports it reduces cost per solved SWE-bench Verified instance.

**MAGE** is worth remembering as memory citation material. Its hierarchical execution-state tree, with Grow, Compress, Maintain, and Revise operations, is conceptually good. I am not preserving it as a full note today because PACT carries a cleaner minimal interface lesson, and VASO/Astra are stronger against the repo's embodied/world-model taste.

**DexFuture** is good adjacent robotics context. It amortizes future target generation for bimanual dexterous tool use instead of running slow online CEM over action-conditioned world-model rollouts. The target-interface idea is useful, but the paper is narrower than today's top three.

**Discrete-WAM** is relevant world-action modeling for autonomous driving, with a shared discrete token space for visual states, decisions, and actions. It is not weak, but the result stack is more benchmark- and system-heavy than the cleaner mechanism papers preserved today.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **VASO: Formally Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills for Physical AI Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it makes the reusable skill contract, not the hidden model weights or one-off plan, the object refined by formal verification feedback.

### 2. **Thinking with Imagination: Agentic Visual Spatial Reasoning with World Simulators**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as a world-model reasoning paper.

Why it matters: it treats generated novel views as action-conditioned evidence, then shows that useful imagination requires both a reliable simulator and a policy trained to govern simulator use.

### 3. **What Should Agents Say? Action-state Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Systems**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as an agent-interface paper.

Why it matters: it gives a tiny but sharp state contract for multi-agent systems: public history should contain action, grounded state, and result, not full private deliberation.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** VASO.

The steal-worthy idea is to make verification feedback land on a reusable, inspectable artifact. VASO does not merely ask whether a generated robot plan passes a safety check. It packages a skill with a formal interface and a planner-facing interface, verifies plans induced by that skill, then uses counterexample traces to update the contract that will guide future plans. That is a healthier loop for physical agents than "sample a plan, reject it, try again" or "fine-tune until the failures become less visible."

Astra is close behind because it reframes world models as tools for acquiring missing spatial evidence. The system still has simulator and policy failure modes, but the paper's core discipline is right: a generated observation should be judged by whether it follows the requested motion, preserves scene layout, and improves downstream reasoning when the policy chooses to use it.

PACT is the operational design pattern to steal immediately. It says the boundary between private computation and shared state should be explicit. That applies beyond multi-agent benchmarks: tool agents, coding agents, memory systems, and OpenClaw-style orchestration all benefit when the public trace is an action-state ledger instead of an exhaust plume of intermediate reasoning.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**VASO** raises the bar for self-evolving physical-agent skills. If a paper claims self-improving robot skills under safety constraints, sampled execution success is no longer enough; it should say what object is being updated, how safety specifications are represented, and whether counterexamples improve a reusable contract rather than only one plan.

**Astra** sharpens the world-model-as-reasoning-tool frame. The baseline question is not "does adding generated images help?" but "are the generated views spatially reliable, and can the policy decide when they are worth consulting?" Forced tool use is not a serious substitute for learned imagination governance.

**PACT** is useful baseline pressure for multi-agent systems. Role schedules, debate topologies, and bigger reasoning traces are incomplete if the inter-agent message contract is unconstrained. Papers should report what enters shared history and whether downstream agents need reasoning traces or only grounded action-state records.

**MAGE** is useful memory framing: memory for long-horizon agents should often be an execution-state structure, not semantic retrieval over disconnected snippets. That is compatible with PACT rather than competing with it.

**DexFuture** and **Discrete-WAM** are useful embodied context. They both separate or align state/action/future interfaces instead of treating policy as a direct black-box mapping, but their strongest contributions are narrower than today's preserved papers.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **VASO** because it turns formal verification from a post-hoc safety check into a reusable skill-optimization signal. **Astra** is the most interesting world-model reasoning paper because it makes imagined observations answer an evidence question and shows that simulator access alone is not enough. **PACT** is the most directly reusable agent-systems design because it keeps private reasoning private and turns public communication into compact action-state records. The common lesson is blunt: state interfaces matter. The good papers today do not just add more generation or more agent chatter; they define what must be exposed, verified, imagined, or passed forward.

## Detailed notes

- [VASO note](../paper_notes/vaso_formally_verifiable_self_evolving_skills_physical_ai_agents.md)
- [Astra world-simulator reasoning note](../paper_notes/astra_agentic_visual_spatial_reasoning_world_simulators.md)
- [PACT action-state communication note](../paper_notes/pact_action_state_communication_multi_agent_systems.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-24

## Theme

Today’s useful pattern is **planner-facing or policy-facing state repair**. The strongest direct paper is **EvoScene-VLA** because it gives chunked robot control an explicit recurrent scene prior that is updated by the model’s own predicted actions and then corrected by the next observation. **Repairing Latent World Models with Horizon-Matched Trajectory Reachability Metrics** is the sharpest mechanism paper because it shows, in a very controlled way, that a world model can contain the right state while the planner still sees the wrong metric. **Stream3D** is the best adjacent 3D paper because it keeps long monocular 3D generation grounded in retained evidence instead of dragging an ever-growing latent cache through time.

## Short overview

Brave Search was unavailable in this environment because no Brave Search tool is configured for this run. AlphaXiv was also not used as a live discovery surface here, so discovery fell back to direct recent arXiv API/category inspection and arXiv HTML full-text reads.

I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for **EvoScene-VLA**, **Repairing Latent World Models with Horizon-Matched Trajectory Reachability Metrics**, **Pre-VLA**, and **Stream3D**. Confidence is good on central mechanism, framing, and headline results, and weaker on appendix-level implementation details I did not audit line by line.

**EvoScene-VLA: Evolving Scene Beliefs Inside the Action Decoder for Chunked Robot Control** is the most relevant paper today. Its core claim is that chunked VLA policies keep acting on stale scene assumptions between visual refreshes, because actions themselves change contact state, occlusion, and geometry inside the chunk. EvoScene-VLA responds by carrying a recurrent scene prefix across chunks, letting the decoder co-denoise both the next action chunk and a compact scene update, then feeding that scene update forward as the next prior. This is a real structural move, not just more temporal tokens. The caveat is that the system is still fairly scaffolded, with geometry teachers and a training-only future-scene predictor doing a lot of support work.

**Repairing Latent World Models with Horizon-Matched Trajectory Reachability Metrics** is the cleanest mechanism paper of the batch. The paper shows that a latent world model can encode position almost perfectly and still fail at planning because raw terminal Euclidean distance underweights the tiny latent subspace that actually matters for reachability. The proposed fix is post-hoc and narrow on purpose: learn a small horizon-matched pairwise metric from trajectory separations, then swap that in as the terminal candidate-ranking score while holding the world model, optimizer, and manifests fixed. I like this paper because it attacks a real interface failure instead of assuming better representations will automatically expose better control geometry.

**Stream3D: Sequential Multi-View 3D Generation via Evidential Memory** is adjacent rather than directly embodied-control relevant, but it is still worth keeping in view. Instead of transporting hidden generator state across a long monocular stream, it stores a bounded memory of high-evidence historical views selected from cross-attention behavior and reuses those as conditioning views for a frozen 3D generator. That is a better story than latent-cache accumulation, although it is still a wrapper around single-object 3D generation rather than a richer persistent scene model.

**Pre-VLA** looked initially relevant, but it lands lower for me. The runtime verifier is practical and probably useful, yet the paper is mostly a safety filter around candidate action chunks rather than a more legible state, memory, or planning mechanism. It feels more like a deployability patch than a structural advance.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **EvoScene-VLA: Evolving Scene Beliefs Inside the Action Decoder for Chunked Robot Control**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives a VLA an explicit action-updated scene prior that persists across chunks instead of making each chunk reason from the latest image as if the previous actions did not already change the world.

### 2. **Repairing Latent World Models with Horizon-Matched Trajectory Reachability Metrics**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it isolates a genuine planner interface bug, namely that the world model may know the state while raw latent distance still ranks candidate futures badly.

### 3. **Stream3D: Sequential Multi-View 3D Generation via Evidential Memory**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it preserves a bounded set of evidential views instead of pretending cross-chunk latent transport will stay aligned and stable forever.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** EvoScene-VLA: Evolving Scene Beliefs Inside the Action Decoder for Chunked Robot Control.

The useful part is not just that it says “scene beliefs.” The useful part is the specific job contract for those beliefs. The model keeps a recurrent scene prefix, refines that prefix against the new observation, then uses the action decoder to jointly denoise both actions and the next scene state. That means the representation passed to the next control call is not just remembered perception and not just predicted future video, but an action-updated prior that the next observation is allowed to correct.

That is exactly the kind of structural move cabbageland usually wants: something explicit enough that you can ask what state is being carried, how actions update it, and where correction enters. I do not think EvoScene-VLA is the final clean architecture, because the training stack leans on a scene predictor and geometric anchoring teachers that disappear at inference. But the paper still earns attention because it treats stale within-chunk world state as a real systems problem and gives the decoder a concrete mechanism for handling it.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**EvoScene-VLA** sharpens an important baseline question for chunked VLAs: does the policy carry an action-updated world prior across chunks, or does it merely remember past images and then guess again? Papers that only add temporal context without letting actions explicitly update carried state now look less satisfying.

**TRM** changes a different part of the framing. It says that “the representation contains the information” is not enough. The planner only gets the metric interface you expose to it. If the reachability-relevant subspace has low energy under raw latent MSE, a perfectly probeable state can still produce terrible candidate ranking. That is a useful warning for a lot of joint-embedding world-model rhetoric.

**Stream3D** mostly matters as a representation-management lesson. If you want long streaming consistency, it may be better to retain bounded explicit evidence than to keep hauling opaque latent baggage forward and praying it stays calibrated.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **EvoScene-VLA** because it gives chunked robot control an explicit, action-updated scene prior that persists across control calls and is corrected by fresh observations. **Repairing Latent World Models with Horizon-Matched Trajectory Reachability Metrics** is the sharpest mechanism paper because it cleanly demonstrates that a world model can encode the right state while exposing the wrong control metric to the planner. **Stream3D** is the best adjacent paper because it uses bounded evidential memory instead of latent-state drift for streaming 3D generation. The shared lesson is that persistent internal structure only matters if it changes the actual decision interface, whether that interface is a recurrent scene prior for action or a terminal metric for planning.

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-24

## Theme

The useful pattern today is explicit scaffolding around brittle VLA behavior. Hi-WM turns a world model into a reusable correction workspace instead of a passive evaluator. LoHo-Manip separates long-horizon task management from short-horizon execution and externalizes intent as a progress-aware trace. How VLAs (Really) Work In Open-World Environments is the uncomfortable audit paper, showing that benchmark scores can hide reproducibility gaps, unsafe behavior, and weak task awareness.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv querying plus primary-source inspection through the arXiv abstract and HTML pages. I inspected the abstract and substantial HTML text for **Hi-WM: Human-in-the-World-Model for Scalable Robot Post-Training**, **Long-Horizon Manipulation via Trace-Conditioned VLA Planning**, and **How VLAs (Really) Work In Open-World Environments**.

The strongest paper for this repo is **Hi-WM**. The useful move is not just “use a world model for robotics”, which is already crowded. The paper makes the world model an interactive corrective substrate: roll out a policy inside it, let a human intervene at failure-prone states, then reuse that same cached failure state for rollback and branching so one bad state yields multiple corrective continuations. That is a concrete answer to the cost problem in post-training, and it respects where human supervision is actually valuable.

**LoHo-Manip** is also directly relevant. Its best idea is not the generic hierarchy but the specific interface: the manager predicts both a done-versus-remaining language plan and a 2D visual trace, then the executor only has to follow the trace locally. That is cleaner than pretending one giant VLA should silently carry task memory, progress tracking, and recovery logic by itself.

**How VLAs (Really) Work In Open-World Environments** matters as evaluation pressure. It is not an architecture paper, but it makes a necessary point: progress-agnostic task success can flatter unsafe or inconsistent behavior, and even leaderboard claims may not be very reproducible. This repo should keep rewarding explicit structure, but it also needs better ways to tell whether the structure actually works outside the happy path.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Hi-WM: Human-in-the-World-Model for Scalable Robot Post-Training**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it turns the world model into a branching correction workspace for failure-focused post-training instead of treating it as mere imagination or evaluation machinery.

### 2. **Long-Horizon Manipulation via Trace-Conditioned VLA Planning**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it gives the planner an explicit progress memory and trace interface rather than burying long-horizon management inside the low-level executor.

### 3. **How VLAs (Really) Work In Open-World Environments**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it argues, with concrete failure analysis, that current open-world VLA evaluation can overstate capability by ignoring safety violations, instability, and task inconsistency.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** Hi-WM.

The key reason is that it replaces generic “human in the loop” rhetoric with an actual reusable structure. Human effort gets concentrated around the states the policy handles badly, and the world model lets those states be revisited and branched instead of burned once in physical robot time. That is exactly the sort of explicit memory-and-branching interface this repo should care about.

LoHo-Manip is strong too, especially because it refuses to overload one policy with all horizons at once. But Hi-WM feels more steal-worthy as a systems principle: if correction data are precious, cache the state, branch the alternatives, and harvest dense supervision around the true failure basin.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

Hi-WM is good framing pressure on papers that use world models only as synthetic rollout engines or static evaluators. The better question is whether a world model can support targeted correction, rollback, and branching around failure states with enough fidelity to improve real behavior. If that claim holds up beyond the reported tasks, it is a more interesting use of world models than yet another generic imagination loop.

LoHo-Manip pushes on a familiar weak point in long-horizon VLA work. The novelty is not hierarchy alone. It is the explicit remaining-plan representation plus the trace prompt, which gives a narrow contract between planner and executor. The caveat is that the system still depends on a fairly involved supervision pipeline for subtask segmentation and trace extraction, so some of the cleanliness is purchased with tooling.

How VLAs (Really) Work In Open-World Environments is baseline pressure on evaluation culture. If reproduced scores drift sharply, safety violations go unpenalized, and policies oscillate between lucky success and total failure across trials, then many current open-world VLA comparisons are softer than they look.

## One-paragraph takeaway

Today’s useful lesson is that better embodied systems need explicit interfaces not only for acting, but also for correcting and judging themselves. Hi-WM externalizes failure-focused supervision through cached world-model states. LoHo-Manip externalizes task progress and near-term intent through a remaining-plan plus trace interface. The evaluation paper externalizes hidden failure modes that headline metrics wash away. Different angle, same message: stop asking giant latent mush to silently do bookkeeping that should have a visible structure.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-06-01

## Theme

Today’s strongest pattern is **memory or dynamics structure only counts when it changes the control contract**. **ECHO** is the most relevant paper because it makes retrieval structure operational instead of treating memory as an undifferentiated bag of past episodes. **SOMA** is the clearest embodied systems paper because it gives memory a concrete job, acting on objects that the camera cannot currently see. **ELAN4D** is weaker conceptually, but still worth keeping because it shows that compact future-geometry supervision can improve robustness without a full architecture rewrite.

## Short overview

Brave Search was not available as a configured tool surface in this run, and AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable here, so discovery again fell back to recent arXiv listings plus direct arXiv HTML inspection.

I relied on substantial prior full-text inspection already done in this run for **ECHO: Continuous Hierarchical Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models** and **Spatial Memory for Out-of-Vision Manipulation in Vision-Language-Action**, and I additionally inspected the arXiv HTML full text for **ELAN4D: Embodiment-Centric 4D Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Models via Plug-and-Play Adaptation**, including its method framing and visible main-results sections. Confidence is highest for ECHO and SOMA. For ELAN4D, confidence is good on the central mechanism and headline result pattern, but lower on the full empirical texture because I did not exhaustively audit every table and appendix detail.

**ECHO** is the strongest paper today. Its actual contribution is not “hyperbolic memory” in the shallow branding sense. The meaningful part is that memories are organized hierarchically by abstraction level, retrieved top-down with compatibility constraints, and fused into a frozen VLA only after that filtering. The ablations matter here: short-term buffer helps, flat memory helps less, hierarchy-aware retrieval helps more, and consolidation helps most. That means the representation and retrieval policy are doing real work.

**SOMA** is the cleanest rebuttal to camera-frustum myopia in current VLAs. It assumes, correctly, that objects keep existing after they leave the current image. The paper builds a persistent spatial-semantic memory from active scanning, refines it during interaction, and retrieves task-relevant regions back into the policy. It is not a minimalist learned world model, but it is one of the better recent examples of explicit persistent state paying rent in a real robotic problem.

**ELAN4D** is more modest, but still useful. It does not maintain explicit memory or belief state. Instead, it adds training-only predictive supervision using future robot keypoint tracks derived from proprioception and forward kinematics. That makes it less interesting than a true explicit-state system, but more interesting than decorative “4D-aware” marketing, because the reported gains appear strongest under perturbations and longer-horizon settings where reactive image-to-action policies should crack.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **ECHO: Continuous Hierarchical Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it turns memory organization and retrieval discipline into part of the actual control interface, instead of treating memory as a flat cache with nicer terminology.

### 2. **Spatial Memory for Out-of-Vision Manipulation in Vision-Language-Action**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it gives a robot persistent scene memory that remains useful when the target is outside the current field of view, which is a real embodied failure mode rather than a benchmark garnish.

### 3. **ELAN4D: Embodiment-Centric 4D Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Models via Plug-and-Play Adaptation**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent mechanism paper.

Why it matters: it shows that cheap future-geometry supervision can improve robustness without pretending that a better-trained action head is already a full world model.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** ECHO.

The useful idea is not the hyperbolic geometry by itself. The useful idea is that memory retrieval is treated as a typed interface problem. The system decides what level of abstraction to retrieve, what memories are compatible with the current state, and only then lets those memories bias action generation. That is a much healthier contract than the common pattern where “memory” means throwing a giant retrieval pool at the controller and hoping semantic similarity sorts it out.

SOMA is close behind because it makes persistent scene state operational in a very grounded way. But ECHO does more to clarify a reusable design principle: structure matters when it constrains what can be recalled, reused, and fused.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**ECHO** raises the bar for VLA memory papers. A memory module should not get credit just for storing more history. It should show that representation type, abstraction level, retrieval discipline, and compatibility filtering each matter.

**SOMA** raises the bar for embodied evaluation. If a policy claims grounded competence, out-of-view target handling should be a first-class test rather than an afterthought.

**ELAN4D** is not a baseline reset, but it is a useful framing correction. There is space between pure reactive control and fully explicit world models, and compact predictive supervision can occupy that space honestly if it is evaluated on the perturbations it is supposed to address.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **ECHO** because it makes memory structure operational through hierarchical retrieval and compatibility filtering rather than vague recurrence rhetoric. **SOMA** is the best embodied systems paper because it shows that persistent spatial memory really does matter once the relevant object leaves the camera frustum. **ELAN4D** is the most modest of the three, but still useful because it demonstrates that cheap future-geometry supervision can make VLA control more robust without requiring a full explicit-state redesign. The common lesson is that structure earns respect only when it changes what the controller stores, retrieves, updates, or predicts in a way you can actually point to.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-07

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **memory and world models are becoming selection-and-state interfaces, not just bigger context**. **PatchWorld** is the most directly relevant paper because it turns logged text-agent trajectories into executable belief-state programs that can be replayed, patched, and used for planning. **Worth Remembering** is the best embodied-memory paper because it gives memory formation a causal, unsupervised write gate based on surprise in a predictive video-feature space. **LongSpace** is the strongest benchmark/method note because it asks whether video MLLMs can preserve spatial evidence across long room-tour sequences rather than merely accept more frames.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider, but it returned `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv paper pages for screened candidates returned HTTP 200, and direct arXiv pages/PDFs were used for primary-source inspection. The arXiv weekend cadence means there was no genuinely new Sunday batch; I therefore searched the recent June arXiv cluster plus one slightly older but still relevant paper that had not been preserved.

I inspected arXiv PDFs for **PatchWorld: Gradient-Free Optimization of Executable World Models**, **Worth Remembering: Surprise-Gated Robot Episodic Memory**, **LongSpace: Exploring Long-Horizon Spatial Memory from Perception to Recall in Video**, **HyperVis: Continuous Latent Visual Relational Graphs on the Lorentz Hyperboloid for Compositional Reasoning**, **LatentSkill: From In-Context Textual Skills to In-Weight Latent Skills for LLM Agents**, and **Where Should Knowledge Enter? A Layered Framework for Knowledge Infusion in Multimodal Iterative Generative Models**. PatchWorld, Worth Remembering, and LongSpace are preserved today. HyperVis and LatentSkill are useful citation material, but I am not preserving full notes for them in this run. The knowledge-infusion paper is a decent taxonomy, but not close enough to the repo's embodied/world-model center to spend a note slot today.

**PatchWorld** is the strongest direct hit. It induces Python world models with explicit symbolic belief state, transition rules, correction logic, and readout logic from offline text-agent trajectories. Prediction failures become typed counterexamples for code repair. The most important result is not just better text prediction; it is the observed frontier between observation fidelity and planning utility. The residual-memory variant predicts surface text better, while the simpler symbolic variant gives better live one-step planning utility.

**Worth Remembering** is the cleanest embodied-memory mechanism. It computes surprise in V-JEPA-2 latent space with a causal sliding-window Gaussian surrogate, stores only thresholded local maxima as visual episodes, and augments a 4D scene-graph memory. On OC-NaVQA, the surprise-gated memory improves question accuracy over DAAAM from 0.711 to 0.796 while storing about 1.7% of frames. The caveat is that the causal predictive model is still a simple Gaussian over embeddings, not a rich action-conditioned video world model.

**LongSpace** is worth keeping as benchmark and architecture pressure. LongSpace-Bench contains 445 room-tour videos, about 159 hours, and 4,073 QA pairs covering scene perception, spatial relations, and spatial memory. LongSpace combines 3D spatial-token injection with layer-aware hierarchical KV memory. The key result is that long-memory inference reaches 49.2 on LongSpace-Bench versus 36.1 for uniform 32-frame sampling and 37.7 for recent-window inference, with gains growing on longer videos.

**HyperVis** is a good citation for continuous relational structure. Its strongest point is that textual scene-graph triplets can hurt VLM accuracy, while continuous hyperbolic relation tokens improve compositional scoring. I am not preserving it today because it is static-image VQA/compositional scoring rather than embodied memory, planning, or world modeling.

**LatentSkill** is useful adjacent agent-systems material. Converting textual skills into LoRA adapters is a real interface move, but the current evidence is mainly ALFWorld and Search-QA efficiency/composition. It belongs in a future agent-skill synthesis more than today's paper daily note set.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **PatchWorld: Gradient-Free Optimization of Executable World Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it makes the world model an executable, inspectable belief-state program whose failures can be localized and patched.

### 2. **Worth Remembering: Surprise-Gated Robot Episodic Memory**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as embodied memory.

Why it matters: it gives robot memory a selective write gate tied to predictive surprise instead of storing uniform, random, or arbitrary context.

### 3. **LongSpace: Exploring Long-Horizon Spatial Memory from Perception to Recall in Video**

**Verdict:** useful direct-adjacent work.

Why it matters: it turns long-horizon spatial memory into a concrete video benchmark and shows that explicit layer-aware memory beats naive frame sampling.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** PatchWorld.

The steal-worthy idea is the repairable world-model substrate. PatchWorld treats an offline trajectory log as evidence for a compact executable hypothesis about hidden state and transition dynamics. The model is not a prompt trace, not a fine-tuned black box, and not a lookup table pretending to be structure. It is a Python module with a fixed interface: parse observation, correct belief, predict belief, read out observation, and expose action forms. That makes failure analysis concrete enough for counterexample-guided repair.

Worth Remembering is almost as important for embodied memory. The useful move is not "memory helps." The useful move is deciding what deserves a high-resolution episodic record under capacity limits. Surprise is an imperfect proxy for future utility, but it is much less lazy than keeping every frame or relying on a downstream retriever to rescue a bad write policy.

LongSpace matters because it pressures long-video and embodied-memory systems to report whether memory survives distance, viewpoint changes, route dependencies, and state changes. Bigger context windows are not the same as spatial memory. LongSpace-Bench is useful precisely because it makes that distinction harder to blur.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**PatchWorld** raises the baseline bar for "world model for agents" papers. If a paper claims planning utility, future comparisons should ask whether the world model preserves decision-relevant contrast, not only whether it reconstructs surface observations. PatchWorld's fidelity-versus-utility result is valuable because it shows those goals can diverge.

**Worth Remembering** sharpens memory-write baselines. Uniform and random episodic memory are not enough if a paper claims selective long-term robot memory. The write policy should be explicit, capacity-aware, causal if the deployment is causal, and tested against the same memory budget.

**LongSpace** raises the evaluation bar for video spatial memory. A model that processes more frames has not necessarily built memory. The benchmark pressure should be: can it retrieve evidence observed much earlier, maintain route and state information, and avoid collapsing under view ambiguity?

**HyperVis** is useful baseline pressure for scene-graph injection. Textual symbolic labels can be a lossy bottleneck; relation structure may need to stay continuous and modality-aligned.

**LatentSkill** is useful framing for agent skills. It suggests "skill memory" can become parameter-resident and modular, but the current evidence is still narrow enough that I would treat it as adjacent inspiration rather than a core cabbageland note today.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **PatchWorld** because it makes a world model into an executable belief-state object that can be inspected, tested, repaired, and used for planning. **Worth Remembering** is the best embodied-memory mechanism because it gives memory writes a causal surprise gate and beats same-budget uniform/random episodic storage. **LongSpace** is the benchmark/method to remember because it separates long-context video processing from real spatial memory. The common lesson is clean: useful memory is not accumulation, and useful world modeling is not reconstruction theater. The object being stored, updated, retrieved, or repaired has to be explicit enough to do work.

## Detailed notes

- [Worth Remembering note](../paper_notes/worth_remembering_surprise_gated_robot_episodic_memory.md)
