# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-19

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **state has to survive the moment it is not convenient**. The best papers do not ask whether a model can emit plausible surface behavior. They ask whether the hidden state, task state, or evaluation state remains explicit enough to be checked when the easy observation disappears.

I kept robotics/VLA work as a lane rather than the center. The scan deliberately covered video world-model evaluation, tool-using agents, generative-model evaluation, diffusion-LM transparency, surgical/medical deployment, neurosymbolic counterfactuals, long-video temporal reasoning, spatial tool-use agents, skill mining, and physical-AI serving. No robotics/VLA paper landed in the top three today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable for individual paper pages, but the fetched content was mostly title/navigation stubs rather than useful related-paper text. I used the arXiv API, arXiv new listings, individual AlphaXiv title checks, and direct arXiv PDFs for full-text inspection. Discovery may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

Full-text PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for **Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core**, **LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents**, **The FID Lottery**, **How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?**, **TimeProVe**, **GEN-Guard**, **DeepSWIP**, **MemoryWAM**, **S-Agent**, **SoftSkill**, **Automating SKILL.md Generation**, and **Execution-State Capsules**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core** is the most relevant paper today. It turns "world model" into an intervention test: move the camera away, return, and ask whether the object state kept evolving while unobserved. Across 9,600 videos from 23 models, the answer is mostly no; visible quality and re-observation access do not imply re-observed state correctness.

**LedgerAgent** is the cleanest agent-systems mechanism. It stores successful read-tool returns in a typed ledger, renders that observed state back into the prompt, and checks environment-changing calls against executable policy predicates before they touch the external system. It is not glamorous, but it is exactly the kind of explicit state boundary tool agents usually fake.

**The FID Lottery** is the strongest evaluation paper today. It treats FID as a random variable over both training seeds and sampling seeds, then shows that retraining the same recipe moves FID much more than redrawing samples from one fixed model. The useful lesson is not just "report error bars"; it is that many single-seed generative-model gains sit below the evaluation noise floor.

Several other papers were worth reading but stayed below the preservation line. **How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?** is a strong foundation-model behavior audit: the token bottleneck between denoising steps appears much more interpretable than the worst-case latent-reasoning story, but algorithmic transparency remains hard because the model can revise the whole canvas non-chronologically. **GEN-Guard** is a useful surgical-AI deployment paper because it names "performance leakage" in federated model selection and tests a client-blocked detection/correction stack; I kept it below the top three because the mechanism is more specialized. **TimeProVe** is a good long-video evidence search system, reducing VLM calls and cost through propose-then-verify temporal grounding, but it is less conceptually sharp than LedgerAgent today. **MemoryWAM** was the best robotics/VLA candidate, with hybrid recent-frame, anchor-frame, and gist-token memory for long-horizon manipulation, but it did not beat the non-robotics top three on transfer value.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives a direct benchmark shape for world-state persistence. A system that only resumes the last visible state when the camera returns is not modeling a world; it is replaying an observed shot.

### 2. **LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as an agent architecture pattern.

Why it matters: it moves task state out of prompt soup and into a typed, inspectable ledger that gates external writes. This is the right design instinct for any agent that changes real state.

### 3. **The FID Lottery: Quantifying Hidden Randomness in Generative-Model Evaluation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as an evaluation audit.

Why it matters: it shows that generative-model leaderboards can be reordered by training-seed randomness. If a claimed improvement is smaller than the measured seed floor, the paper has not earned the claim.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core.

The direct steal is the observability intervention. If a system claims to maintain state, hide the evidence temporarily, let the state evolve, then return and check the endpoint. This applies far beyond video: memory systems, agent ledgers, planning stacks, retrieval state, clinical monitors, and evaluation caches all need tests where the state is not continuously visible.

LedgerAgent contributes the complementary implementation pattern. Task-relevant facts should have stable addresses, update rules, and action-boundary checks. The agent can still use language reasoning, but the validity of external writes should not depend on the model re-reading an unstructured transcript and hoping it remembered the right JSON.

The FID Lottery contributes the statistical discipline. Do not compare single numbers when the training run itself is a draw. If the variance lives on the axis the paper did not sample, the leaderboard is measuring luck plus method.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core** raises the bar for world-model claims. WRBench separates camera execution, visible consistency, re-observation support, and re-observed state consistency instead of collapsing them into one attractive video score. The caveat is that this is a benchmark/diagnostic paper, not a new architecture, and the automatic evaluation still rests on human-calibrated judgments rather than a formal state oracle.

**LedgerAgent** is not novel because it invents "state"; it is novel because it enforces the boring boundary in the right place. Successful read-tool returns become schema-anchored state, and proposed write calls are checked against executable predicates before execution. The limitation is clear: the method only covers observed, structured, predicate-encoded state.

**The FID Lottery** is a useful correction to generative-model evaluation practice. It shows that sampling-seed error bars on one fixed network understate the uncertainty; training-seed variance is the larger lottery. The limitation is scope: the measured 1-2 percent coefficient-of-variation floor is for SiT flow-matching models on class-conditional ImageNet with Inception FID, not a universal constant.

**How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?** is the important runner-up. It suggests DiffusionGemma's intermediate denoising bottleneck can be compressed through a small set of interpretable likely tokens without much capability loss, reducing the apparent opaque serial-depth problem. The red flag is that similar monitorability on current evaluations does not settle single-canvas latent reasoning or future RL-trained diffusion reasoners.

**MemoryWAM** clears the robotics lane but not the top-three bar. Hybrid short-term, event-boundary, and gist-token memory is a real mechanism, and the latency/memory trade-off is useful. Still, today already had stronger non-robotics state papers, so another WAM note would have pulled the digest back toward its known robotics attractor.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all punish fake state. **Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core** asks whether a video model keeps an event endpoint alive when the camera is not watching. **LedgerAgent** asks whether a tool agent has a real observed-state object before it changes the world. **The FID Lottery** asks whether a generative-model claim survives the hidden state of training randomness. Different domains, same standard: if the state matters, isolate it, perturb observability, and make it carry the claim.

- [LedgerAgent note](../paper_notes/ledgeragent_structured_state_tool_calling_agents.md)
- [The FID Lottery note](../paper_notes/fid_lottery_generative_model_evaluation.md)

I like this because the explicit structure is not decorative. The paper is not merely adding another spatial auxiliary head while keeping the actual control pathway unchanged. It tries to align the intermediate representation with the geometry of the action space itself. That is a clean and defensible design claim. The main caveat is that the method still relies on a fairly standard learned decoder to absorb frame conversion, contact residuals, and gripper timing, so this is an alignment bias rather than a full geometric control formulation.

**TriSplat** is the strongest adjacent inspiration. The paper’s real contribution is not just another splatting variant. It notices that if the downstream use case is simulation, collision, and grasping, then a representation that still needs lossy post-hoc mesh extraction is slightly lying about being simulation-ready. TriSplat fixes that by making oriented triangle primitives the native rendering object, with normals anchored to predicted geometry and refined carefully during training. That is a good example of choosing a representation that matches the artifact you actually need later.

**AgentGrounder** is less ambitious, but more honest than a lot of “agentic 3D grounding” branding. It builds an object lookup table from point-cloud segmentation, retrieves only query-relevant candidates, applies deterministic geometric reasoning, and renders views only when color or material evidence is needed. The gains over SeeGround are real but not huge, and the system still depends on the quality of the initial segmentation stack. Still, the decomposition is legible and the selective-rendering idea is operationally sensible.

I also briefly considered **RePlan-Bot** and **AnyScene**. RePlan-Bot looked competent but more like a strong modular ALFRED stack than a paper I especially need to preserve. AnyScene looks substantial, but today’s cut favored papers with cleaner transfer into cabbageland’s interests around action-space structure, explicit geometry, and simulation-facing representations.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **OASIS: Observation-Action Space Alignment via SE(3) Trajectory Prediction for Robotic Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it makes a sharp claim that robot policies should align intermediate state with the rigid-body geometry of action, not merely enrich observation-space features and hope the decoder figures the rest out.

### 2. **TriSplat: Simulation-Ready Feed-Forward 3D Scene Reconstruction**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it picks triangle primitives because the end product needs to be a mesh for simulation and collision, not just a nice rendering primitive for novel-view synthesis.

### 3. **AgentGrounder: Zero-Shot 3D Visual Pointcloud Grounding using Multimodal Language Models**

**Verdict:** useful, with moderate novelty.

Why it matters: it is a clean retrieval-plus-geometry decomposition for open-vocabulary 3D grounding, and the selective rendering policy is more disciplined than brute-force prompting over all objects.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** OASIS.

What I like is that the paper makes a harder and better argument than “add depth” or “predict future images.” It says that if the control target is rigid-body motion, then the intermediate representation should expose pose structure that lives closer to that action geometry. The SE(3) trajectory is not the final action, but it gives the decoder a more appropriate substrate than raw visual latents alone.

This matters for cabbageland because it sharpens a recurring question in world-action and VLA work: is the explicit structure genuinely in the control loop, or is it just supervision wrapped around the same opaque policy core? OASIS does not fully solve that question, but it moves in the right direction.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**OASIS** usefully pressures a common baseline habit in robot learning. After this paper, it feels less satisfying when a manipulation policy claims strong spatial competence while keeping the decisive latent state in observation space and asking the decoder to recover 6-DoF control implicitly.

**TriSplat** also sharpens a baseline story. Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction methods look weaker for robotics or simulation-facing use once you ask whether their native representation is directly usable, rather than only visually pleasing before a lossy conversion stage.

**AgentGrounder** is less of a baseline-reset paper, but it does reinforce that “agentic grounding” should be judged by whether the decomposition actually reduces search and ambiguity, not by whether an LLM writes a plan string before doing standard retrieval.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **OASIS** because it makes an unusually clean representational claim for robotic manipulation: if action lives in rigid-body geometry, then the intermediate state should carry pose structure that is closer to that geometry instead of leaving it implicit inside an action decoder. **TriSplat** is the best adjacent paper because it chooses a triangle-native scene representation that is already the kind of object simulation systems want, rather than pretending post-hoc mesh extraction is a minor detail. **AgentGrounder** is the best smaller systems paper because it combines selective retrieval, deterministic geometry, and on-demand rendering in a way that stays legible. The shared lesson is simple: explicit structure matters most when it survives all the way to the interface that actually makes decisions or supports downstream use.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-06

## Theme

Today’s strongest paper is a clean planning paper rather than a giant platform release. **Refining Compositional Diffusion for Reliable Long-Horizon Planning** takes a real failure mode, mode averaging when overlapping local diffusion plans disagree, and fixes it with a training-free density-and-consistency guidance scheme instead of pretending score composition is already coherent. The rest of the shortlist is useful, but less architecturally sharp. **MolmoAct2** is a serious open VLA release with real substance, though it bundles many moving parts at once. **Latent Bridge** is a practical deployment optimization for dual-system VLAs, but it is still an efficiency patch rather than a representational advance.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing in the current environment. I then scouted recent arXiv submissions directly, starting from recent cs.RO listings and then inspecting primary-source arXiv pages and accessible HTML method text.

I inspected the abstract and substantial method text for **Refining Compositional Diffusion for Reliable Long-Horizon Planning**, **MolmoAct2: Action Reasoning Models for Real-world Deployment**, **Latent Bridge: Feature Delta Prediction for Efficient Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Model Inference**, and **RoboAlign-R1: Distilled Multimodal Reward Alignment for Robot Video World Models**.

**Refining Compositional Diffusion for Reliable Long-Horizon Planning** is the clearest direct hit. The paper targets a real compositional-planning pathology: when overlapping local trajectory distributions are multimodal, naive score averaging lands between modes and produces globally bad plans. The proposed fix, RCD, uses the diffusion model’s own self-reconstruction error as a proxy for local density and adds an overlap-consistency penalty at segment boundaries. That is a concrete mechanism, not just a better benchmark story.

**MolmoAct2** is important and worth tracking, but it is best read as an ambitious integrated release. The strongest specific mechanism I inspected is the action-expert interface, which conditions a flow-matching continuous-action head on the VLM’s per-layer KV cache, plus the adaptive-depth reasoning variant that only re-predicts changing depth regions. Still, the paper’s impact comes from a bundle of backbone specialization, new data, tokenizer work, architecture changes, and deployment framing all at once.

**Latent Bridge** is useful adjacent inspiration. It treats the VLM backbone in dual-system VLAs as temporally redundant, predicts feature deltas between control steps, and uses DAgger so the bridge learns on its own rollout distribution instead of only on clean synced traces. That is a sensible deployment-minded design, but it does not really change what the model knows, only how often the expensive part runs.

**RoboAlign-R1** is interesting but less convincing as a core architecture paper. Distilling an expensive multimodal judge into a cheaper reward model for world-model RL post-training is sensible, and the sliding-window re-encoding trick for reducing rollout drift is pragmatic. But most of the contribution is reward-pipeline engineering around a token video model, not a deeper structural answer to world modeling.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Refining Compositional Diffusion for Reliable Long-Horizon Planning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it identifies a real compositional pathology, mode averaging across overlapping local plans, and fixes it with a legible training-free mechanism that directly steers sampling toward high-density, overlap-consistent trajectories.

### 2. **MolmoAct2: Action Reasoning Models for Real-world Deployment**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it is a substantial open VLA release with credible deployment ambition and a few mechanisms worth remembering, especially the per-layer KV-cache action interface and adaptive-depth reasoning.

### 3. **Latent Bridge: Feature Delta Prediction for Efficient Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Model Inference**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it treats dual-system VLA latency as a temporal redundancy problem and replaces some expensive backbone calls with a lightweight learned bridge.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Refining Compositional Diffusion for Reliable Long-Horizon Planning.

The useful part is that the paper does not merely say “compose short-horizon planners better.” It names the exact failure mode, adjacent local segments independently choosing incompatible modes and then getting averaged into an off-manifold plan, and then builds guidance terms that attack that failure directly. The self-reconstruction error story is especially interesting because it reuses the pretrained diffusion model itself as a density probe instead of introducing a separate learned critic or expensive search loop.

I also like that the overlap-consistency term is concrete. If neighboring segments predict different values on shared boundary variables, the composition is structurally inconsistent whether or not the final rollout looks smooth. That is a much more honest way to talk about compositionality than papers that just concatenate modules and call it structure.

The caveat is scope. I inspected the abstract, introduction, formalization, and a substantial chunk of the method text from the arXiv HTML page, including the self-reconstruction and overlap-consistency construction, but I did not audit every experiment or appendix proof. Also, this is still a planner over short-horizon learned diffusion segments, not an explicit persistent world-state model. So the paper is strongest as a compositional-planning mechanism, not as a general answer to long-horizon memory or world representation.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

RCD sharpens a useful question for compositional planning papers: if local factors are multimodal, what prevents score composition from averaging incompatible futures into nonsense? If the answer is “sampling somehow works out,” that is weak. Here the answer is explicit guidance toward high-density and boundary-consistent regions.

MolmoAct2 matters more for ecosystem framing than for clean baseline replacement. It strengthens the case that open VLAs can be serious when they combine better embodied reasoning, better robot data, and more deployment-conscious interfaces. But because the paper bundles many changes, it is harder to extract one dominant ingredient that future work should copy first.

Latent Bridge affects evaluation taste. Dual-system VLA papers should probably stop reporting only policy quality while hiding how many nearly redundant full VLM passes they require per episode. Still, it is acceleration work, not a new model of action or memory.

RoboAlign-R1 is mostly citation material for reward alignment and evaluation pipeline design around robot video world models. The teacher-to-student reward distillation move is sensible, but it is not the kind of explicit structural commitment that should dominate the digest.

## One-paragraph takeaway

Today’s best paper wins by being specific about where compositional planning breaks and by fixing that failure with explicit guidance rather than with search-heavy patchwork or vague modularity claims. **Refining Compositional Diffusion for Reliable Long-Horizon Planning** is the one worth preserving because the mechanism is crisp and transferable. **MolmoAct2** is a meaningful open VLA release and worth watching, but it is more bundle than scalpel. **Latent Bridge** is a practical efficiency trick for dual-system VLAs, and **RoboAlign-R1** is decent reward-engineering work, but neither changes the architectural conversation as much. The general lesson is the same as usual: when a paper says “compositional,” check whether the composition operator itself is actually protected from collapse.

## Detailed notes

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-10

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **trust the measurement boundary before trusting the model boundary**. Benchmarking the Benchmarks shows that tool-agent leaderboards can be measuring evaluator artifacts instead of agent competence. CIC turns heuristic LLM uncertainty into a finite-sample abstention gate, but only under a stated calibration contract. Latent Programming Horizons finds that coding-agent hidden states carry program-success signal before edits are written, while staying honest that decodability is not causality. BrainFIBRE preserves biophysical meaning by decomposing brain microstructure information instead of fusing NODDI maps into a single latent mush. PUF does the same for 3D scene graphs: uncertainty belongs inside the fusion step, not after a hard argmax.

I kept robotics / VLA papers out of the ranked five today. The scan deliberately covered non-robotics lanes: agent evaluation validity, uncertainty calibration, coding-agent interpretability, neuro / healthcare foundation models, online 3D representation, personal-agent governance, and world-model simulator admissibility. The strongest robotics-adjacent candidate was **Validate the Dream Before You Trust Its Verdict**, but it is a workshop-positioned admissibility framework with only lower-rung driving instantiations; the non-robotics papers below had stronger evidence or more transferable mechanisms today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. I used AlphaXiv-related search trails, direct arXiv pages, and full arXiv PDFs for discovery and inspection. Discovery quality is narrower than a healthy Brave-first run, but no preserved note today is abstract-only.

For the preserved notes, I inspected the full PDFs for **Benchmarking the Benchmarks**, **Uncertainty-Aware Abstention**, **Latent Programming Horizons**, and **BrainFIBRE**. I read the method, evaluation setup, main results, ablations or guarantees where relevant, and limitations. I also inspected full PDFs for **PUF**, **Validate the Dream Before You Trust Its Verdict**, **A Definition and Roadmap for World Models**, and **SovereignPA-Bench** as ranked or runner-up candidates. I did not audit released code, rerun benchmarks, inspect every appendix table, or independently verify leaderboard claims.

**Benchmarking the Benchmarks** is the most important paper today. It attacks the evaluator layer directly: if a tool-calling benchmark disagrees with expert trace review on 18.5% of audited tasks, leaderboard deltas are not meaningful until the scoring system itself is audited.

**Uncertainty-Aware Abstention** is the cleanest calibration primitive. CIC does not pretend semantic entropy or another score is inherently trustworthy; it wraps the score in an upper-confidence-bound threshold selection rule and returns no threshold when the risk target cannot be certified.

**Latent Programming Horizons** is the most interesting mechanistic paper. It suggests coding agents may carry linearly decodable program-state and future-edit signals over long trajectories, which is useful for monitors, but the paper is careful enough to avoid claiming causal steering.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Benchmarking the Benchmarks: A Validity Audit of Tool-Calling Evaluation**

**Verdict:** must read for agent evaluation.

Why it matters: The paper audits BFCL v4, tau2-Bench Retail, LiveMCPBench, and MCP-Atlas with trace-level expert review. Across 496 tasks, official benchmark labels disagree with human judgments 92 times, for an 18.5% misalignment rate. LiveMCPBench is the worst case: 30.5% label disagreement and a 57.9% to 76.8% score range across 23 repeated runs of the same setup. The main contribution is not another agent benchmark; it is evidence that benchmark evaluators need their own reproducibility and validity layer.

### 2. **Uncertainty-Aware Abstention in Large Language Models with Provable Alignment Guarantees**

**Verdict:** highly relevant uncertainty / calibration paper.

Why it matters: CIC converts arbitrary LLM uncertainty scores into selective-answering thresholds with finite-sample risk control under exchangeability. On a calibration set, it labels accepted answers as correct or incorrect, computes an upper confidence bound for each candidate threshold, and selects the largest threshold whose bound stays below a target risk alpha. If the target cannot be certified, the method returns NULL. That last behavior is the important taste point: a reliability layer should be allowed to say "no deployable threshold."

### 3. **Latent Programming Horizons in Coding Agents**

**Verdict:** strong coding-agent interpretability paper, with causality caveats.

Why it matters: The paper collects mini-swe-agent trajectories over SWE-Bench-Verified and SWE-Bench-Pro, extracts residual streams from Laguna-XS.2 and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and trains logistic-regression probes for program properties. The probes recover current correctness, partial correctness, well-formedness, and regression signal above chance, with full-correctness AUC up to 0.83 and partial-correctness AUC up to 0.84. More interestingly, probes predict future edit outcomes above chance up to about 25 agent steps ahead. This is a promising monitoring surface, not proof that the model causally uses those representations.

### 4. **BrainFIBRE: A Foundation Model via Information Decomposition for Brain Microstructure**

**Verdict:** strong neuro / healthcare representation paper.

Why it matters: BrainFIBRE is useful because it makes the representation decomposition match the biology. It pretrains on NODDI-derived NDI, ODI, and FWF maps from 55,592 UK Biobank participants, then uses Self-supervised Partial Information Decomposition with counterfactual modality dropping / swapping to train uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy experts. The result is not just "three maps into a transformer"; it tries to preserve which microstructural compartment contributes unique, redundant, or emergent signal across age, cerebrovascular, neurodegenerative, and cognition tasks.

### 5. **PUF: Plug-and-Play Uncertainty-Aware Fusion for Online 3D Scene Graph Generation**

**Verdict:** useful 3D structure / uncertainty paper; lighter recommendation.

Why it matters: Online 3D scene graph generation usually hard-commits at the exact point where uncertainty should matter: 2D detections, partial observation, and noisy 3D lifting. PUF replaces binary node association with a probabilistic likelihood over semantic and spatial factors, propagates soft class and relation distributions through Dirichlet evidence accumulation, and optionally uses a class-conditional relation prior for sparse co-observations. On 3DSSG it reports an 18.1 point relationship Recall@1 improvement over the strongest online baseline while keeping about 15 ms per frame latency. The caveat is that its strongest relation-completion gains partly lean on dataset priors, and downstream task utility is not shown.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Benchmarking the Benchmarks.

The steal is the evaluator audit loop. OpenClaw-style systems should not accept "agent score went up" unless the scoring path preserves raw traces, decomposes tool invocation from outcome verification, supports repeated-run comparison, and has known evaluator-human agreement. The paper's concrete failure categories map almost too directly onto agent infrastructure risks: brittle state matching, trajectory lock-in, substring-based assertions, rubric drift, hallucinated completion, and answer-only scoring.

CIC gives the complementary deployment contract: use uncertainty scores as ranking signals, not as trusted probabilities, then calibrate a release / abstention decision with explicit finite-sample error control. Latent Programming Horizons points at a future internal monitor for coding agents: if hidden states carry correctness and regression signals before edits hit disk, those signals could become early abort, review, or steering hooks after causal validation. BrainFIBRE and PUF generalize the same rule outside language agents: preserve the uncertainty or modality structure at the interface where evidence is fused.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Benchmarking the Benchmarks** is valuable because it treats evaluation as an object of measurement. The strongest result is the 496-task trace audit: 18.5% aggregate evaluator-human disagreement, with LiveMCPBench at 30.5%, BFCL v4 at 20.0%, MCP-Atlas at 13.5%, and tau2-Bench Retail at 9.8%. Its repeated-run LiveMCPBench analysis is also damaging: the same 95-task configuration ranges from 57.9% to 76.8%, a spread large enough to flip leaderboard claims. Tool-Veritas is promising but preliminary: 95.5% agreement over 420 model-task evaluations, with all disagreements false negatives. The caveat is scope: the audited agents, expert process, and proposed replacement benchmark need release and reuse before the field can treat them as settled infrastructure.

**CIC** is not novel because it invents a new uncertainty score. It is useful because it refuses to trust one. The mechanism is a calibration wrapper: for each uncertainty threshold, estimate the accepted-answer error rate on held-out data, build Hoeffding-style or Clopper-Pearson upper confidence bounds, union-bound over a finite threshold grid, and pick the least conservative certified threshold. The guarantee depends on exchangeability, a fixed deployed model and decoding setup, and a valid binary alignment label. The open-ended TriviaQA experiment uses sentence-similarity thresholding, so the label itself can be noisy. Still, the design is exactly what high-risk QA needs: answer only when the risk target is certified, otherwise abstain.

**Latent Programming Horizons** has the best "future monitor" idea today. It shifts coding-agent interpretability from single generated functions to multi-step real-codebase trajectories. The evidence is broad enough to matter: 22,714 trajectories over 1,231 tasks, two open-weight models, two SWE-style benchmarks, shuffled-label controls, layer sweeps, cross-dataset transfer, and lookahead probes. The limitation is the central one the authors state: linear decodability is not causal use. A probe direction that predicts future correctness may be an observation surface, not a control handle.

**BrainFIBRE** is strong because the representation story is not decorative. NODDI already separates neurite density, orientation dispersion, and free water fraction; BrainFIBRE's SPID objective tries not to collapse that separation during pretraining. Counterfactual Candidate Construction creates modality-drop and modality-swap views, while the MoE stack assigns uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy roles to experts. The evaluation across UKB, HCP-Aging, and SINGER is more convincing than a single-cohort result, and the task-specific expert-weight patterns are useful scientific output. The caveat is that this remains a supervised-downstream neuroimaging paper, not clinical validation.

**PUF** is a compact interface fix. It keeps 2D softmax distributions alive through 3D fusion, treats spatial association as likelihood rather than a veto gate, and accumulates node and edge evidence with Dirichlet parameters. That is a clean replacement for brittle hard merging. Its main caveats are dependence on upstream 2D SGG quality, dataset-specific relation priors on 3DSSG, and no proof that better scene-graph recall improves navigation or manipulation decisions.

**Validate the Dream Before You Trust Its Verdict** was a strong runner-up and the only robotics / world-model item that seriously competed. Its admissibility ladder is conceptually right: L0 visual quality does not license a simulator verdict; action robustness, declared envelope, failure attribution, and verdict-transfer validation matter. I kept it out of the top five because it is mostly a framework plus lower-rung driving analysis, and yesterday already used the robotics / world-model slot for a diagnostic paper.

**SovereignPA-Bench** is aligned with OpenClaw personal-agent concerns and worth revisiting. The separation between agent-visible ObservableState and evaluator-only HiddenLabels is good benchmark hygiene, and the component metrics cover privacy, consent, evidence, manipulation, burden, and auditability. I did not rank it today because the tool-calling audit has broader empirical bite and a cleaner benchmark-validity target.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today converge on a hard rule: do not trust a system because the outer number looks good. Tool-agent scores need evaluator audits. LLM uncertainty needs calibrated release decisions. Coding-agent hidden states need causal validation before steering claims. Brain microstructure models need modality interactions that preserve biological meaning. Online 3D scene graphs need uncertainty carried through fusion instead of discarded at the boundary. The shared move is to make the evidence interface explicit, calibrated, and inspectable before using it to authorize action, belief, or scientific interpretation.

## Detailed notes

- [Tool-calling evaluation validity audit note](../paper_notes/tool_calling_evaluation_validity_audit.md)
- [CIC risk-controlled LLM abstention note](../paper_notes/cic_risk_controlled_llm_abstention.md)
- [Latent programming horizons note](../paper_notes/latent_programming_horizons_coding_agents.md)
- [BrainFIBRE note](../paper_notes/brainfibre_information_decomposition_microstructure.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-27

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **make the learning signal local before trusting the aggregate**. RiVER turns unknown-optimum programming tasks into calibrated relative rewards instead of pretending raw objective values are comparable. ENS gives a solver its residual field as explicit error-state instead of optimizing the residual as a proxy. SAE-guided continual learning protects task knowledge in sparse feature coordinates instead of blunt parameter coordinates.

I kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan deliberately covered non-robotics lanes: LLM reinforcement learning, scientific ML, continual learning, interpretability, root-cause evaluation, LLM-as-judge evaluation, molecular generative modeling, 3D/video generation, and healthcare-adjacent benchmarks. Robotics/control/world-model candidates inspected included **World Action Models Enable Continual Imitation Learning with Recurrent Generative Replays** and **Hallucination in World Models is Predictable and Preventable**; both were interesting, especially the hallucination paper's coverage-based failure taxonomy, but today's strongest preserved mechanisms were non-robotics.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable for arXiv pages and used as a light reachability supplement, but the actual inspection used arXiv recent listings, arXiv abstract pages, and downloaded arXiv PDFs. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on Saturday, June 27, arXiv's visible recent AI/ML/CV/CL/RO lists were still the Friday, June 26 batch. I used today's run to mine the remaining strong candidates from that batch rather than duplicating yesterday's preserved notes. I inspected full PDFs, with targeted reads through methods, experiments, results, and limitations, for **Reinforcement Learning without Ground-Truth Solutions can Improve LLMs**, **Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers**, **From Weights to Features**, **Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators**, **OpenRCA 2.0**, **Ask, Don't Judge**, **LMs as Task-Specific Knowledge Bases**, **Data-Free Reservoir Features**, **PhysiFormer**, **RayPE**, **World Action Models Enable Continual Imitation Learning with Recurrent Generative Replays**, and **Hallucination in World Models is Predictable and Preventable**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Reinforcement Learning without Ground-Truth Solutions can Improve LLMs** is the most relevant paper today. It widens RLVR from "match a known answer" to "compare executable candidates by calibrated relative quality," which is a better template for open-ended agent training.

**Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers** is the strongest scientific-ML mechanism. It argues that minimizing a PDE residual can be the wrong objective in ill-conditioned systems, then uses the residual field as input so the model can learn a correction policy.

**From Weights to Features** is the best continual-learning / interpretability bridge. It uses frozen SAE features as the coordinate system for stability and plasticity constraints, giving a concrete alternative to coarse weight-space protection.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Reinforcement Learning without Ground-Truth Solutions can Improve LLMs**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives a concrete recipe for training coding models on tasks with no gold program or optimal output, using executable feasibility checks and per-instance rank-shaped rewards rather than raw objective scores.

### 2. **Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for scientific ML and world-model-style correction loops.

Why it matters: the paper cleanly separates residual-as-objective from residual-as-state. The latter is the transferable idea: expose the model to the structured error it is making, then train a learned corrector under the real reconstruction objective.

### 3. **From Weights to Features: SAE-Guided Activation Regularization for LLM Continual Learning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for continual learning, memory, and mechanistic control.

Why it matters: it treats forgetting as a coordinate-system problem. If weights are polysemantic, weight-level importance scores are the wrong protection unit; SAE features give a more selective place to impose stability and plasticity.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** RiVER.

The steal is the environment design. A useful verifier does not need to know the optimal answer if it can reliably compare sampled candidates under the same hidden instances. That is a better fit for agents, planning, program synthesis, experimental design, and other domains where "correct" is not a single answer but better or worse behavior under constraints.

ENS gives the same lesson in physical form: do not collapse a rich residual field into a scalar optimization target too early. Let the model read where it is wrong. SAE-guided continual learning gives the representation version: do not protect "important weights" when the real unit of knowledge is a feature distributed through many weights.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**RiVER** is strong because it targets a real bottleneck in RLVR. It trains on 12 AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks where no ground-truth solution is supplied, executes sampled programs on shared hidden instances, ranks them instance-wise, and applies winner-heavy bounded reward shaping before GRPO. The main evidence is useful: Qwen3-8B improves ALE rating by 142 points and GLM-Z1-9B-0414 by 157 points, while exact-solution benchmarks also improve on average by 2.4 and 3.5 points. The caveat is scope: two coding backbones, 12 training tasks, no code audit from me, and no proof that the transfer will hold outside executable algorithmic domains.

**ENS** is strong because it names and tests the residual-reconstruction gap. PINO-style and Gauss-Newton-style methods can drive down residuals while leaving the solution inaccurate, especially in ill-conditioned systems. ENS instead feeds the residual field into a recurrent learned corrector and supervises every intermediate solution against ground truth. It is best in most reported PDE settings and is far faster than heavy hybrid test-time optimization, but the setting is still mostly known-equation 2D synthetic PDEs.

**SAE-guided activation regularization** is strong because it connects mechanistic interpretability to a practical continual-learning objective. The method builds task relevance masks over frozen Gemma Scope SAE features, then uses a protect loss for low-mask features and a guide loss for high-mask features. On TRACE it beats the tested non-architectural methods; on MedCL it leads no-replay methods but loses to larger replay buffers and O-LoRA. The important caveat is dependency on SAE coverage and validation on one main model family.

**Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators** was the strongest adjacent scientific generative paper. It replaces flow-based Boltzmann generators with exact-likelihood autoregressive proposals, gives a uniform-bin parameterization, and introduces ROBIN for transferable peptide sampling. I kept it below the note line because it is more domain-specific than today's top three, but it is worth revisiting for scientific generative modeling.

**Hallucination in World Models is Predictable and Preventable** was the strongest robotics/control-world-model runner-up. Its useful mechanism is a stagewise hallucination taxonomy tied to tokenizer reconstruction, action marginalization, and rollout divergence, plus coverage signals that can drive targeted data collection. I did not preserve it today because it sits in the already-overrepresented robotics/control lane and did not beat the top non-robotics mechanisms on balance.

**OpenRCA 2.0** is useful evaluation infrastructure: it moves root-cause analysis from outcome labels to verified causal propagation paths. It is very aligned with "correct answer, wrong reason" evaluation, but it is mainly a benchmark/protocol note rather than a reusable training mechanism.

**Ask, Don't Judge** is a solid decomposition paper for LLM evaluation. Its binary-question decomposition is clean and practical, but it is less novel than ConflictScore and other recent decomposed evaluation work already preserved.

**LMs as Task-Specific Knowledge Bases** is a sharp interpretability runner-up. The task-invariance framing is useful: a model can appear to know a fact in one query format and fail in another because task-specific parameter subsets are involved. I kept it below the line because today's SAE continual-learning paper gave a more actionable feature-coordinate mechanism.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all refuse to train on blurred signals. RiVER says raw score magnitude is not a reward until it has been calibrated by shared-instance comparisons. ENS says a PDE residual is not a solution objective until you know it tracks reconstruction accuracy; better to feed the residual field to a corrector. SAE continual learning says parameter importance is not concept importance when features are superposed. Same rule across domains: preserve the structure of the error signal long enough for the model to use it.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-17

## Theme

The best papers today all attack interface mismatch. **MemPrism** says stored history is not yet usable memory unless it is reorganized for the current decision. **Silent Updates** says a system card is not yet accountability unless it is bound to the artifact actually being served. **DreamWAM** says predicted video is not yet useful future state unless it preserves motion, geometry, and semantics that matter for action. **CliniCARE-Bench** says raw clinical accuracy is not yet trustworthy reasoning unless the investigation is evidence-grounded and shortcut-free. **WorldClaw** says a text prompt is not yet a world unless it is compiled into explicit terrain, region plans, and editable assets.

## Short overview

This Monday, August 17, 2026 run used live arXiv HTML full-text inspection across long-horizon agent memory, post-deployment model governance, world action models, clinical agent evaluation, and 3D world generation. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for all five ranked papers below.

Four papers earn preserved notes. **WorldClaw** is the strongest adjacent inspiration, but it does not clear the preserve bar because the mechanism is richer than the evidence: the pipeline is interesting, yet the evaluation is still mostly qualitative and heavily dependent on strong closed models. **Most relevant today:** **MemPrism**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **MemPrism: Task-Conditioned Relational Memory Views for Long-Horizon Agents**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the sharpest memory paper in the batch because it names the right failure mode. The problem is not always missing storage or bad retrieval. Sometimes the evidence is there, but it is organized in the wrong form for the current decision. MemPrism stores normalized event history, then builds temporary relational working-memory views on demand. On matched backbones it reaches **40.71%** ALFWorld success versus **38.27%** for LangMem, **12.87%** Mind2Web overall action accuracy versus **8.79%** for full history, and **17.7%** EB-ALFRED average success versus **11.7%** for Mem0, while also cutting prompt tokens by **33.6%** at the 50-step threshold.

### 2. **Silent Updates: Measuring and Closing the Post-Deployment Disclosure Gap**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This is one of the better field-deployment papers in recent memory because it turns vague drift anxiety into a concrete chain-of-custody audit. The paper studies **9** first-party API providers and **7** inference hosts and finds that no provider in the sample exposes a verifiable API-to-evaluation round trip, even when they publish substantial safety documentation. It also finds that **6 of 9** providers include terms that may discourage independent evaluation, then proposes a behavioral trigger system for when post-deployment changes should force disclosure or re-evaluation.

### 3. **DreamWAM: Beyond RGB Future Prediction for World Action Models**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the one robotics or VLA paper that clears the bar today because it makes a precise representational correction instead of hand-waving about "world knowledge." DreamWAM supervises future state through appearance, motion, geometry, and semantics rather than RGB alone, while remaining RGB-only at inference. On matched baselines it improves LIBERO from **98.00%** to **98.90%**, LIBERO-Plus from **69.16%** to **75.47%** with joint inference and from **51.36%** to **63.44%** without rollout, and real-robot perturbation performance from **55.6%** to **74.4%**.

### 4. **CliniCARE-Bench: Clinical Calibrated Audit of Medical Reasoning in EHR**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the non-robotics medical benchmark worth keeping because it evaluates agentic clinical audit the way it should be evaluated: through logged record investigation, evidence grounding, governing-policy use, process adherence, and calibrated abstention rather than answer-only medical QA. The benchmark covers **25** clinician-validated scenarios and **750** patient-specific cases over MIMIC-IV. Across **16** agentic systems, four-way accuracy spans **65.3%** to **76.1%**, but defect-free accuracy is **4.8** to **14.8** points lower and reorders the field. That is exactly the kind of leaderboard humiliation a domain needs.

### 5. **WorldClaw: Agentic 3D Open-World Generation at Scale**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration, not yet preserve-worthy.

Why it matters: The mechanism is more interesting than the current evidence. WorldClaw uses a clean global-to-regional pipeline: structured scene planning, semantic terrain generation, region-conditioned object composition, mesh reconstruction, and render-guided refinement into editable instance assets. That is much closer to production-minded 3D world construction than generic image-to-world vibes. The problem is that the main evaluation is qualitative, the pipeline still leans on heavy closed-model components, and the paper has not yet shown a hard quantitative case that the decomposition survives beyond demos.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **MemPrism**.

It sharpens a design rule that keeps showing up everywhere else in the digest. Storing the right facts is not sufficient. The system also needs the right decision-time interface. MemPrism makes that explicit with normalized event storage plus temporary relational views. **Silent Updates** makes the same move for governance: publishing an evaluation artifact is not enough unless it is bound to the served system. **DreamWAM** makes it for action models: predicting future pixels is not enough unless the future representation exposes action-relevant state. Same lesson across domains: a persistent artifact without the right interface is a polite way to fail.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**MemPrism** matters because it cleanly separates persistent memory from working memory. The paper's real contribution is not another memory store. It is the claim that post-retrieval representation mismatch is its own failure mode, plus evidence that dynamic relational views beat fixed history even when the underlying facts stay unchanged.

**Silent Updates** matters because it attacks a governance blind spot that most model-card discussion glides past. The useful question is not whether documentation exists, but whether an external party can verify that the served system is the one the documentation evaluated.

**DreamWAM** matters because it reframes the future-prediction target rather than just bolting on a bigger video backbone. The strongest evidence is not the in-distribution gain. It is that matched beyond-RGB supervision substantially improves robustness even when no rollout is used at inference.

**CliniCARE-Bench** matters because it shows raw accuracy can flatter clinically unsafe systems. Defect-free accuracy, process adherence, and calibrated abstention are not cosmetic extras here. They change the ranking.

**WorldClaw** matters as a framing prompt for 3D generation: global terrain and regional editable assets are a much better decomposition than trying to hallucinate an entire world in one homogeneous pass. But it is still more a promising systems sketch than a settled research result.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The August 17 lesson is that the strongest systems do not just preserve information. They compile it into the right operational interface. Good agent memory should expose the relation structure a decision actually needs. Good deployment governance should bind published evaluations to the artifact being served. Good world-action models should preserve motion, geometry, and semantic identity rather than worship RGB futures. Good clinical benchmarks should punish confident shortcutting, not reward it. Good 3D generation should keep global structure explicit while letting local assets remain editable. Same taste everywhere: do not confuse a stored artifact with a usable state.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-13

## Theme

Today’s signal is **explicit 3D belief and memory beating frame-level mush**. The strongest paper is **3D-Belief** because it tries to turn a generative world model into an actual belief state under partial observability, rather than another prettier rollout model. **AffordMem** is the most steal-worthy adjacent paper because it uses explicit cross-scene and in-scene memory to fix a real grounding failure instead of just adding a generic retrieval wrapper. **Dynamic Execution Commitment of Vision-Language-Action Models** is useful mostly as a latency-control baseline paper, not as a deeper representational advance.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run and was unavailable because the current environment is missing a Brave API key. I therefore used direct arXiv discovery and inspected accessible arXiv abstracts plus substantial HTML full text for **3D-Belief**, **Grounding by Remembering: Cross-Scene and In-Scene Memory for 3D Functional Affordances**, **Dynamic Execution Commitment of Vision-Language-Action Models**, and **PriorZero**.

**3D-Belief** is the best paper today. Its core move is to define world modeling as belief inference in explicit 3D space under partial observability, not as frame prediction or novel-view rendering. The model maintains a 3D Gaussian-splat scene belief with semantics, supports multi-hypothesis imagination for unseen regions, and updates the belief online as new views arrive. That is not just branding. The representation choice is doing real work: it gives a persistent spatial memory, a place to attach semantics, and a substrate for downstream navigation-style planning.

**AffordMem** is narrower, but honestly more satisfying than a lot of recent “memory” papers. It treats two concrete failures in training-free 3D affordance grounding as two different memory problems. Cross-scene affordance memory gives the model category-level visual priors for the small operable subregion, while in-scene spatial memory keeps a structured 3D layout of candidate parts so the system can resolve queries like “the second handle from the top.” That is exactly the kind of explicit decomposition that often gets replaced by vague retrieval language elsewhere.

**Dynamic Execution Commitment of Vision-Language-Action Models** is useful, but mostly as systems cleanup. It reframes action-chunk execution as a speculative-prefix verification problem and adaptively decides how much of a chunk to trust. That is a sensible inference-time idea, but it is still an execution-control patch on top of existing VLA policies, not a deeper memory or world-model contribution.

I also inspected **PriorZero**. It has a respectable division of labor, using language priors only at the root of latent MCTS and keeping world-model dynamics separate, but today it felt more like a solid RL architecture paper than a paper-daily keeper for cabbageland.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **3D-Belief: Embodied Belief Inference via Generative 3D World Modeling**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it upgrades “world model” from visual rollout machinery to an explicit uncertainty-carrying 3D belief state that can actually support embodied reasoning.

### 2. **Grounding by Remembering: Cross-Scene and In-Scene Memory for 3D Functional Affordances**

**Verdict:** useful, with real steal-worthy structure.

Why it matters: it uses two explicit memory mechanisms to solve two distinct grounding failures instead of hoping a generic VLM prompt will absorb both.

### 3. **Dynamic Execution Commitment of Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** mostly citation material.

Why it matters: it is a decent adaptive-horizon baseline and a clean way to talk about VLA execution trust, but it does not move the underlying representation story much.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** 3D-Belief.

The reason is simple. It treats partial observability as a belief-state problem in explicit 3D space, not as a rendering problem disguised as a world model. The paper argues that an embodied agent needs at least four things from such a model: spatially consistent scene memory, multi-hypothesis sampling over unseen structure, sequential belief updates as new observations arrive, and semantic predictions that can drive task reasoning. That decomposition is the right one.

The actual implementation is also reasonably aligned with the claim. The model predicts a 3D Gaussian-splat representation with semantic embeddings, splits it into observed and imagined components, and autoregressively replaces the imagined part when new evidence arrives. The training setup still looks expensive and fairly supervised, but the representation is explicit enough that the claimed capabilities are legible instead of mystical.

My confidence is fairly high on the core mechanism and framing because I inspected the abstract, introduction, formulation, model architecture, diffusion training description, and stated evaluation setup in the arXiv HTML. My confidence is lower on exact empirical margins and on whether the benchmark really forces hard uncertainty reasoning rather than mostly rewarding good 3D completion.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update is that a generative world model for embodied work should probably be judged by the quality of its **belief state**, not just by photorealistic prediction. If the model cannot preserve observed structure, imagine multiple unseen completions, update those beliefs over time, and expose semantics in a queryable way, then “world model” may still be too generous a label.

**3D-Belief** matters because it tries to operationalize that standard. **AffordMem** reinforces the same taste from a different angle: if a memory claim is real, it should solve a specific failure mode by storing and organizing the right structure. **Dynamic Execution Commitment** is more of a baseline paper, but it is useful for novelty positioning because many VLA control improvements are still living at the action-acceptance layer rather than the world-model or memory layer.

The skeptical update is for papers like **PriorZero**. The root-only prior injection idea is clean, but a lot of the benefit still sits in better planning and training organization rather than in a richer explicit state. Useful, yes. Core cabbageland signal, not quite.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **3D-Belief** because it makes the right conceptual move: embodied world modeling should maintain an explicit 3D belief state under partial observability, not merely predict plausible frames. **AffordMem** is the best adjacent paper because it uses explicit memory in a disciplined way, splitting category-level affordance recall from scene-level spatial disambiguation. **Dynamic Execution Commitment** is worth remembering mostly as a clean adaptive-horizon baseline. The common lesson is that structure matters when it carries uncertainty, memory, and action-relevant semantics, not when it is just another label pasted onto a latent blob.

## Detailed notes

- [AffordMem note](../paper_notes/grounding_by_remembering_cross_scene_and_in_scene_memory_for_3d_functional_affordances.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-18

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all attack the same lazy habit: letting a proxy stand in for the state that actually matters. **Proof-or-Stop** refuses to let an agent's "done" narration count as lifecycle truth unless fresh evidence can re-admit the claim. **Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?** shows that benchmark psychometrics can look rigorous while quietly collapsing under the wrong sample regime. **Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong** isolates frozen world models from their surrounding RL loop and shows how bad many of them are as standalone simulators. **xHC** turns residual-stream expansion into an actual scaling axis instead of a small-`N` curiosity. **CRISP** bets that positive-region rank is more stable than raw probabilities under medical shift and turns that into a target-free refinement scheme.

I checked the fresh `cs.AI`, `cs.CV`, `cs.LG`, and `cs.RO` arXiv category pages for **Friday, July 17, 2026**, ran an explicit non-robotics title pass for medical, multimodal, uncertainty, continual-learning, and world-model terms, and used AlphaXiv as a supplementary scout surface. Brave Search was attempted first on **July 18, 2026** via the Brave web API and failed with **HTTP 422** because the required `x-subscription-token` header is missing in this environment. AlphaXiv was reachable and surfaced overlapping candidates such as **Video = World + Event Stream**, **xHC**, and **DriftWorld**, but the final five had the cleaner mechanism or the harder evaluation lesson. No robotics or VLA paper cleared the top five today.

## Short overview

No preserved note today is abstract-only. I inspected the full arXiv HTML papers for **Proof-or-Stop**, **Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?**, **Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong**, **xHC**, and **CRISP**. For the preserved notes, I read the framing, method, main experiments, and limitation sections directly.

**Proof-or-Stop** is the most relevant paper today. The useful move is not "add more review agents." It is making lifecycle advancement an admissibility decision over fresh, code-bound evidence, so "reviewed," "tested," and "done" become gate outcomes rather than agent self-descriptions.

The strongest evaluation paper is **Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?**. Its point is simple and badly needed: AI benchmarkers keep borrowing psychometric tooling from a data regime it was not designed for, then quietly over-trusting the output. The paper shows exactly where that breaks: small model pools, skewed capability distributions, and large item banks.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence -- Loop Engineering for Verifiable Evidence-Gated Lifecycle Control**

**Verdict:** must read for autonomous coding-agent control.

Why it matters: This is one of the sharper recent papers on agent lifecycle control because it treats agent output as a claim, not as truth. The core idea is evidence gating: reviewed, tested, and done states advance only when fresh, tracked-source-state-bound receipts satisfy the gate. In the powered ablation, the gated loop cuts visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from `31/1800` to `2/1800`, and in the engine-contract suite it passes `10/10` scenarios with zero false-done.

### 2. **Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?**

**Verdict:** must read evaluation paper.

Why it matters: The paper asks a question more benchmark papers should ask before shipping fancy latent scores. Across `18,000` simulation conditions, it shows that estimator choice matters less than regime mismatch: skewed capability distributions wreck ranking recovery, `N=30` model pools are not enough for item-level inference, and some classical estimators become computationally infeasible on modern item banks.

### 3. **Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: The paper's best move is methodological before it is algorithmic. It freezes five visual world-model families, tests them as standalone simulators, and shows that strong Dyna-style agent performance can coexist with terrible frozen-model utility. Then it adds a ball-focused auxiliary loss and gets real gains in zero-shot MBRL, while still admitting that concept-region reconstruction alone does not fix the whole simulator problem.

### 4. **xHC: Expanded Hyper-Connections**

**Verdict:** highly relevant architecture paper.

Why it matters: This is one of the more concrete "new scaling axis" papers in a while. Instead of just claiming residual-stream expansion should scale, it shows why prior hyper-connection variants stall, then fixes the two bottlenecks with richer write-back and sparse stream updates. On the `18B` MoE model, the average downstream score rises from `44.8` with mHC to `48.8` with xHC; on `28B`, it rises from `50.5` to `53.6`.

### 5. **CRISP: Constrained Refinement via Iterative Squeezing Process for Robust Medical Image Segmentation under Domain Shift**

**Verdict:** useful direct paper.

Why it matters: CRISP is narrower than the four papers above, but the mechanism is real. It assumes that positive-region rank is more stable than absolute probability under shift, derives high-precision and high-recall spatial priors from latent perturbations, and refines toward the mask without using target-domain data or test-time parameter updates. The paper reports strong HD95 reductions across multi-center, demographic, and modality shifts, which is a better story than another vague "domain generalization" claim.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Proof-or-Stop

The main steal is architectural and governance-heavy in the right way: lifecycle state should be decided by admissible evidence, not by the same agent that wants credit for finishing. That matters for coding agents, workflow systems, memory-heavy assistants, and any loop where a model can narrate success before the system has actually checked it.

**Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?** is the evaluation complement: do not borrow measurement machinery from a friendlier regime and then over-read the latent scores. **Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization** is the world-model complement: a model that helps a joint RL loop can still be a bad standalone simulator. **xHC** is the architecture complement: if residual-stream expansion is going to matter, it needs a design that still works when `N` gets large. **CRISP** is the deployment complement: target-free robustness is still possible when you exploit a more stable structural signal than raw confidence.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Proof-or-Stop** is strongest because the claim boundary is explicit. It does not pretend to prove semantic correctness; it proves gate-admissible evidence under a stated trust model. Caveat: the evaluation is still one self-hosted system, one model family, and a self-application corpus with obvious selection bias.

**Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?** is strongest as a field-correction paper. It shows that ranking recovery tracks capability-distribution skewness more than estimator branding, and that `N=30` is simply too small for confident item analysis. Caveat: the study is simulation-based, so it is diagnosing reliability conditions rather than directly replacing benchmark practice tomorrow.

**Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization** is strongest where many world-model papers are weakest: it isolates the world model itself and demonstrates the gap between "helps a training loop" and "works as a simulator." Caveat: the core concept is manually specified, the scope is Pong, and even the improved frozen models remain far from being trustworthy policy-training environments.

**xHC** is strongest because it actually explains why prior large-`N` hyper-connection scaling saturates and then fixes those bottlenecks with ablations. Caveat: the results are still concentrated in MoE language-model pretraining, and the practical memory-traffic story remains part of the deployment cost.

**CRISP** is strongest as a target-free robustness mechanism. Caveat: it relies on a rank-stability assumption that may not transfer cleanly outside the anatomical structures and shifts tested here, and the paper reports single-run numbers rather than a richer multi-seed stability story.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful lesson today is to stop trusting the pretty surface artifact when the internal contract is wrong. A green agent self-report is not lifecycle evidence. A psychometric latent score is not automatically trustworthy in a tiny, skewed model pool. A high-performing Dyna-style agent does not prove its world model is a good frozen simulator. A residual-memory idea is not a scaling axis until the bottlenecks are fixed. And a segmentation confidence map is not the most stable signal under shift. # Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-01

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all refuse the lazy proxy. **OSReward** says a cheap VLM judge is not automatically a trustworthy reward signal just because it can read screenshots and trajectory text. **ReToken** says generic attention is not actually a retrieval mechanism when long visual context gets cluttered. **Chimera** says long-context visual generation should not be forced through one monolithic attention story when state tracking, global interaction, and local structure want different operators. **ORCA-bench** says oncall diagnosis is not SWE-bench with extra logs. **EndoCLIP** says routine procedure reports are not image captions, so language supervision only becomes useful after you recover the right lesion-level alignment object.

## Short overview

This run used direct arXiv recent-category inspection plus targeted arXiv API title passes rather than a broad recommendation surface. I also did the explicit non-robotics pass the repo asks for, querying title-level terms such as `clinical`, `medical`, `pathology`, `radiology`, `foundation model`, `multimodal`, `neuro`, `MRI`, and `CT`. That pass surfaced papers such as **ScaFE**, **MIND**, **PathView-Bench**, and **A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports**. The colonoscopy paper was the clear keep from that lane.

The five below are the most worth attention from this window. The top four are preserve-worthy note candidates. **EndoCLIP** is a real paper with a transferable data-engine move, but I do not think it beats the top four on direct steal value for cabbageland.

**Most relevant today:** **OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models**. The main reason is practical. If evaluation, data curation, and RL all depend on a cheap trajectory judge, then the judge itself is part of the system and needs its own benchmark, bias analysis, and cost frontier.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: It benchmarks the benchmarker. That is the right level of seriousness for computer-use agents, where noisy reward labels can silently poison evaluation, data filtering, and RL.

### 2. **ReToken: One Token to Improve Vision-Language Models for Visual Retrieval**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: This is a clean mechanism paper. Instead of pretending attention maps are retrieval, it trains an explicit retrieval token over the visual KV cache and gets real long-context gains with very little extra machinery.

### 3. **Chimera: Designing and Chinchilla-Scaling Hybrid Visual Diffusion Transformers**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy adjacent paper.

Why it matters: The paper's best move is not just architectural mixing. It treats heterogeneous long-context visual generation as something that also needs heterogeneous scaling rules, then actually fits them.

### 4. **ORCA-bench: How Ready Are Language Model Agents for Oncall?**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: This is one of the better reality checks on agent deployment claims. Root-cause analysis over noisy telemetry, source code, and ambiguous user reports is much closer to real operational work than static repo patch tasks.

### 5. **A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: The steal is the data construction move. The paper does not merely pretrain on reports; it recovers lesion-level supervision from weak routine documentation and turns that into clinically useful retrieval and transfer.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models**.

The core lesson is brutally applicable: when the whole pipeline depends on a learned judge, "the judge seems pretty good" is not a method. OSReward builds a human-gold benchmark for the judge itself, isolates a shared leniency bias, shows that the trustworthy frontier models are too expensive to run at scale, and then turns that diagnosis into a cheaper open reward model. That is exactly the kind of system discipline cabbageland needs around agents, evaluators, and training loops.

The other papers reinforce the same instinct from different angles. **ReToken** replaces vague attention-as-retrieval folklore with an explicit learned retrieval object. **Chimera** replaces one-size-fits-all scaling with module-aware scaling rules for different computation roles. **ORCA-bench** replaces toy debugging assumptions with a real telemetry stack and ambiguous incident reports. **EndoCLIP** replaces crude report-level pairing with recovered lesion-level alignment.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**OSReward** is strongest because it reframes computer-use judging as a first-class reliability problem rather than a helper component. The baseline lesson is that cost, bias, and judge failure mode matter as much as raw agreement.

**ReToken** is strongest because it cleanly separates retrieval from generic attention. The useful baseline lesson is that a VLM's existing cross-modal attention patterns are not a retrieval system just because they are there.

**Chimera** is strongest because it combines architectural heterogeneity with scaling-law heterogeneity. The important framing move is that visual long-context generation may need different operators and different transfer rules at different submodules.

**ORCA-bench** is strongest because it makes oncall evaluation structurally harder in the right ways: real telemetry interfaces, source code, ambiguous reports, time offsets, and plausible-root-cause sets instead of single canned answers.

**EndoCLIP** is strongest because it changes what counts as available supervision in routine clinical documentation. The important move is not "medical CLIP," it is recovering the missing alignment object between report findings and image evidence.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that hidden intermediates become bottlenecks unless you make them explicit and test them directly. Reward judges need their own benchmark. Visual retrieval needs its own retrieval object. Long-context diffusion needs different operators for different jobs and a scaling recipe that respects that split. Oncall agents need the real evidence stack, not a bug-fix cosplay. Clinical language supervision needs recovered lesion-level correspondence, not wishful report-image pairing. The best papers here are the ones that stop smearing task structure into a proxy and instead build around the object the task actually needs.
