# Daily Digest — 2026-04-11

## Theme

Today’s best paper is about grounding simulation hard enough that synthetic data stops being decorative. The broader pattern is that the worthwhile papers are the ones that respect embodiment and geometry as actual constraints: one paper builds physics-aligned deformable twins for data scaling, another treats active vision as part of the behavior rather than a camera placement afterthought, and a third shows a sane use of hierarchical planning over a pretrained whole-body controller for heavy-object loco-manipulation.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv API inspection and arXiv abstract / experimental HTML reading. I inspected recent April 9 submissions in robotics and adjacent categories, then read the arXiv abstract pages and accessible HTML for the shortlist. I did not do a full PDF-plus-appendix audit, so the confidence level here is mechanism triage from primary-source accessible text, not exhaustive reading.

The strongest paper is **SIM1**, because it makes a serious attempt to solve the actual bottleneck in deformable sim-to-real: not just generating more synthetic trajectories, but forcing the synthetic world to be metrically and dynamically aligned with the real one first. The paper’s core claim is sharp: simulation fails less because it is synthetic than because it is ungrounded. That is a much better framing than the usual "more randomization fixes everything" line.

**ActiveGlasses** is the most interesting adjacent paper. The useful contribution is not just learning from egocentric demonstrations; it is treating head motion and viewpoint control as part of the task signal, then reproducing that active vision on the robot with a dedicated perception arm. I do not think it is a huge conceptual leap, but it is one of the cleaner recent examples of perception being modeled as behavior rather than passive input.

**Sumo** is a solid systems paper and the best of the day for hierarchical control. Its move is simple and defensible: let reinforcement learning learn a robust low-level whole-body controller, then do online sample-based planning in that controller’s command space. That is a much saner use of hierarchy than calling everything a planner while hiding end-to-end mush under the hood.

## Ranked papers

### 1. SIM1: Physics-Aligned Simulator as Zero-Shot Data Scaler in Deformable Worlds

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it argues that deformable simulation only becomes useful once geometry, dynamics, and motion generation are explicitly aligned to real scenes, then uses that aligned simulator as a synthetic data engine for direct zero-shot policy transfer.

### 2. ActiveGlasses: Learning Manipulation with Active Vision from Ego-centric Human Demonstration

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it treats active perception as part of the demonstrated behavior and uses an object-centric representation to transfer bare-hand human demonstrations to robot manipulation without explicit retargeting.

### 3. Sumo: Dynamic and Generalizable Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it uses online sample-based planning to steer a pretrained whole-body policy, which is a clean way to get test-time flexibility without retraining for every new heavy-object manipulation objective.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** SIM1.

This repo keeps caring about the same thing from different angles: if you claim explicit structure matters, then the structure has to cash out in the computation. SIM1 mostly earns that standard. It separates the problem into geometric alignment, dynamical alignment, and movement alignment, and the synthetic-data claim depends on those stages being grounded instead of hand-waved.

What makes it relevant is not just deformable manipulation. It is the stronger general lesson: if a synthetic world is going to supervise policy learning, then scene state, physics, and behavior generation all need to be tied back to reality in explicit ways. Otherwise "simulation as data scaler" is just renamed domain gap denial.

ActiveGlasses matters as a secondary signal because it refuses the assumption that perception is fixed while action moves. That is a small but healthy pressure toward explicit perception-action coupling.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

SIM1 is good pressure on lazy sim-to-real rhetoric. The useful framing move is that real-to-sim alignment is not a preprocessing detail; it is the condition under which synthetic scaling becomes meaningful at all. If that framing holds up under deeper reading, then future deformable-manipulation papers should not get to claim scaling wins from synthetic data without saying how the simulator was physically grounded.

ActiveGlasses is baseline pressure on passive-camera imitation pipelines. If active viewpoint control materially affects task success under occlusion, then fixed-camera or wrist-camera baselines are missing part of the behavior they claim to model.

Sumo is pressure on both ends of the control-spectrum cliché. Pure end-to-end reinforcement learning is too brittle and expensive to retune for each task, while pure online model predictive control can choke on the dimensionality and instability of whole-body contact-rich systems. Planning over the command space of a pretrained policy is not new in spirit, but this is a credible demonstration in a harder regime.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The good work today is not about bigger models pretending to be more grounded. It is about making the intermediate structure earn its role. SIM1 grounds simulation before scaling it. ActiveGlasses treats viewpoint control as part of the demonstrated skill. Sumo uses hierarchy to reduce search complexity instead of to decorate an end-to-end controller. Same underlying lesson again: explicit structure is only interesting when it changes what the system can reliably do.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-22

## Theme

The best papers today all refuse to let an average metric impersonate the thing you actually care about. **HarnessRisk** says model quality is not agent safety when the harness can quietly rewrite the real risk surface. **Mechanistic Tomography** says interpretability is not a pile of probes unless the measurement family survives held-out interventions at the scale where control will actually use it. **Does Marginal Coverage Guarantee Class-Conditional Safety for Zero-Shot VLMs Under Shift?** says a passable marginal coverage number can still hide zero protection on the classes that matter. **Compliance, Capability, and Conflict** says system-message adherence is not governance if user conflict can cheaply break the hierarchy. **Holtercare-Bench** says medical multimodal competence is not the same thing as static-image comfort when the signal is a long pathological sequence.

## Short overview

This Saturday, August 22, 2026 run used direct arXiv full-text inspection on the fresh Friday, August 21, 2026 batch, plus one very recent August 18 agent-harness paper that clearly beat weaker fresh-batch options. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for all five ranked papers below.

Four papers earn preserved notes. **Holtercare-Bench** is the strongest adjacent runner-up because the dataset and failure signal are genuinely useful, but the contribution is still more benchmark-and-infrastructure than transferable systems mechanism. **Most relevant today:** **HarnessRisk: A Lifecycle-Oriented Benchmark for Agent Harness Safety**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **HarnessRisk: A Lifecycle-Oriented Benchmark for Agent Harness Safety**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the sharpest agent-safety paper in the set because it evaluates the deployed model-plus-harness configuration instead of pretending the base model is the whole story. The benchmark covers **128** sandboxed cases across six lifecycle phases, and the ugly result is concrete: attack success ranges from **12.6%** to **80.9%** while utility stays between **75.0%** and **97.6%**. The most useful systems result is the harness flip: **GLM-5.2** reaches **54.7%** ASR on OpenClaw but only **12.6%** on Nanobot, a **4.3x** difference, while useful-but-unsafe outcomes still account for **59%** of OpenClaw trajectories.

### 2. **Mechanistic Tomography: Designed Measurement for Control-Oriented Interpretability**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the strongest interpretability paper in the batch because it replaces vague "probe the model" talk with a measurement-design discipline. The useful move is to treat patching, gradients, lifted interactions, and Hessian-vector products as different sensing families for recovering a target effect map, then decide among them using held-out interventions at the scale where the estimate will actually be used. The evidence is concrete: in the planted forward-only setting, just **12** aggregate measurements recover a **32**-coordinate finite-effect map with held-out **R² = 0.935** and Pearson **r = 0.989**; on Qwen-2.5-7B, a **20**-parameter calibrated additive map already reaches held-out **R² = 0.9829**, and the **48**-parameter lifted pairwise map does not buy a meaningful MAE gain.

### 3. **Does Marginal Coverage Guarantee Class-Conditional Safety for Zero-Shot VLMs Under Shift?**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the most severe uncertainty paper in the set because it attacks the comforting misuse of marginal conformal coverage. On ImageNet-Sketch, APS marginal coverage stays around **0.86**, yet the worst class drops to roughly **0** coverage and **10-12%** of classes fall below the finite-sample null floor. The repair story is the useful negative result: Conf-OT can push marginal coverage back to roughly **0.89-0.90** and halve average under-coverage, but worst-class coverage on Sketch still stays at or below **0.02** across the tested settings.

### 4. **Compliance, Capability, and Conflict: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs under System Messages**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: This paper earns the slot because it measures the thing people actually deploy but rarely test cleanly: whether multimodal models can obey system messages without quietly throwing away task competence, and whether that obedience survives direct user conflict. The dual-metric design is the right move. Across **16** MLLMs, system messages impose a **30-70%** task-accuracy tax, frontier proprietary models top out at only **36.2%** total JSR, and misalignment robustness diverges brutally: **GPT-5.4** keeps **83.3%** misaligned CSR while **Qwen3-VL-32B** collapses to **8.4%**. Vision-grounded constraints are the hardest category for every model.

### 5. **Holtercare-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Term Dynamic ECG Analysis**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: This is the non-robotics medical paper worth carrying forward because it exposes how badly current multimodal models degrade once the signal is long, temporal, and clinically structured. The benchmark builds **22,980** QA pairs from **788** clinical Holter records and separates presence detection from the much harder counting, timing, diagnosis, and report-generation tasks. The baseline gap is concrete: **GPT-5-mini** reaches **76.31%** on presence detection but only **31.80%** on event counting and **33.54%** on event timing, while fine-tuned **Qwen3-VL-8B** jumps to **99.70%** on event timing, **95.28%** on diagnosis, and drops counting MAE from **7.34** to **0.63**.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **HarnessRisk: A Lifecycle-Oriented Benchmark for Agent Harness Safety**.

It lands directly on a cabbageland problem: the real object of safety is not the model in the abstract but the model as routed through tools, permissions, plugins, memory, action controls, and recovery workflows. That is why the harness flip matters more than the raw leaderboard. If the same model can be over four times less safe under a different harness, then "model safety" is an incomplete abstraction.

The rest of the batch reinforces the same taste. **Mechanistic Tomography** treats interpretability as a tested observer design problem, not a vibes problem. **Marginal Coverage** separates average reliability from tail reliability. **VSysBench** separates obedience theater from actual hierarchy robustness. **Holtercare-Bench** separates generic multimodal comfort from long-horizon clinical signal understanding.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**HarnessRisk** matters because it reframes agent safety around harness lifecycle responsibilities instead of one-off attack categories, then proves that high utility can coexist with substantial attack success and persistent compromise.

**Mechanistic Tomography** matters because it turns multiple interpretability tools into one shared inverse-problem language and gives a practical stopping rule: start cheap, validate on held-out interventions, then only add richer measurement families when the residual structure forces you to.

**Marginal Coverage** matters because it attacks a very common deployment inference directly. A respectable marginal coverage number is not evidence of class-tail safety under shift, and the standard source-side fixes do not rescue that tail.

**Compliance, Capability, and Conflict** matters because it jointly scores correctness and system-message adherence on the same multimodal instance. That sounds small, but it changes the failure picture: neither compliance nor accuracy can hide the other anymore.

**Holtercare-Bench** matters because it widens medical multimodal evaluation from static images to long dynamic ECG traces, making temporal localization and report generation first-class failure modes instead of afterthoughts.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful August 22 lesson is that a system usually fails first at the hidden interface between its average metric and the operational property you actually need. A safe-looking model can become unsafe under a different harness. A good-looking mechanistic explanation can collapse when asked to predict a held-out intervention. A valid marginal coverage number can hide a dead class tail. A compliant-looking multimodal model can surrender the hierarchy as soon as the user pushes back. A medical MLLM that looks competent on short or static inputs can fall apart on long dynamic traces. Same rule all day: do not trust a proxy until it has been forced to answer for the operational target directly.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-28

## Theme

Today's best papers all say the same rude but useful thing: a system does not have memory, safety, or reliability just because it gestures at them. The real question is where commitment happens, what evidence licenses it, and what gets repaired when that commitment turns out to be wrong. **Eviction as Estimation** argues that bounded memory should delay cache-keep decisions until reuse is partly observed rather than guessed. **MemTX** argues that a write to shared agent memory is not yet a belief commit. **What Can Be Enforced?** separates what runtime guardrails can enforce in principle from what they can only calibrate statistically. **Looping Is Not Reliability** shows that coding-agent revision loops can find a correct patch and then casually destroy it. **Beyond Aggregate Risk** says tool-call safety should certify semantic roles like recipient, account, or credential, not average them away inside a whole action.

## Short overview

I attempted Brave Search first through the OpenClaw `web_search` tool on Tuesday, July 28, 2026, and it failed with `missing_brave_api_key`, specifically saying Brave search needs a configured API key. Discovery therefore fell back to direct arXiv category-page inspection and primary-source reading through arXiv abstract and HTML pages.

This run did the explicit non-robotics pass the repo asks for. That surfaced papers like **Cheap Probes Predict Expensive Training in 3D-CT Vision-Language Models** and **Stress-Testing EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Decoding**, but the five below were stronger on mechanism, transferable control surfaces, and long-horizon system discipline. The top four are clear preserve-worthy notes. The fifth is also worth keeping because the unit of certification is exactly right.

**Eviction as Estimation** is the most relevant paper today. The useful move is not a new memory heuristic. It is reframing eviction as delayed estimation, then being honest that the mechanism matters mainly when reuse is sharp and endogenous rather than on ordinary text workloads.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Eviction as Estimation: A Fixed-Lag Smoothing View of Test-Time Memory, and When Measuring Beats Accumulating**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This is one of the better recent memory papers because it introduces a real axis instead of another score. Commit lag unifies recency filters, heavy-hitter accumulation, learned predictors, and Belady-style oracle caching, then the paper shows exactly where the fixed-lag idea helps and where it collapses back to H2O. The negative result is part of the value.

### 2. **MemTX: Transactional Belief Commit for Stateful Agent Memory**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This paper attacks the place most agent-memory work has been sloppy. A memory write is not a belief commit, and belief commit is not yet action permission. The protocol adds evidence, validity, permission inheritance, staged lifecycle, action gating, and typed cascade repair, then backs the claims with machine-checked invariants and downstream-harm measurements instead of vibes.

### 3. **What Can Be Enforced? A Theory of Certified Runtime Safety for Tool-Using Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: This is a framing paper, but a useful one. It separates symbolic enforceability, exogenous judge calibration, and closed-loop intervention effects, which is exactly the separation most guardrail discussions blur. The sharp line is that a pretty ROC on ungated trajectories does not tell you the true frontier once the guard changes what the agent does next.

### 4. **Looping Is Not Reliability: State-Bound Evidence and Typed Revision Contracts for Agentic Code Repair**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: The useful insult here is that "ever found a correct patch" and "ended in a correct state" are different metrics, and coding-agent papers keep pretending otherwise. The paper shows correctness can drop under forced revision, stale traces can actively damage correct starts, and a typed admission contract helps preserve verified states even when it does not magically improve repair competence.

### 5. **Beyond Aggregate Risk: Role-Stratified Conformal Risk Control for LLM Tool Calls**

**Verdict:** useful direct paper.

Why it matters: The paper gets the calibration unit right. If a prompt-injected email body changes a recipient or bank account, averaging risk over the entire action is fake reassurance. Per-role budgets are a more honest way to certify tool use, and the formal "price of coarseness" story is a strong reason not to stay at action-level aggregation.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Eviction as Estimation.

The steal is not specifically KV-cache compression. It is the more general idea that commitment should happen after a bounded amount of observed downstream use, not necessarily at arrival time and not only from a guessed future. That is relevant to long-horizon assistants, memory selection, planner rollbacks, context compaction, and any system where "keep everything important" is only meaningful if importance is measured against actual reuse.

The rest of the digest strengthens the same contract-minded view. **MemTX** makes belief maturity explicit before action. **What Can Be Enforced?** says guardrails need the right mathematical regime. **Looping Is Not Reliability** binds evidence to exact code state before another revision is allowed to stomp on it. **Beyond Aggregate Risk** says certification should follow the semantic role that can actually cause harm.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Eviction as Estimation** is strongest because it gives a better organizing variable than the current benchmark race. Caveat: the practical performance win is narrow, and the paper is strongest as a framework plus mechanism audit, not as a new state of the art.

**MemTX** is strongest because it shifts the target from "memory retrieval quality" to "belief lifecycle discipline under side effects." Caveat: the evaluation is purpose-built rather than naturally occurring product traffic, so real deployment brittleness is still open.

**What Can Be Enforced?** is strongest because it prevents three common category errors: conflating symbolic enforceability with statistical calibration, conflating exogenous ROC with closed-loop safety, and conflating benign calibration with robustness under representation attack. Caveat: the guarantees depend on explicit modeling choices and can degenerate to block-all.

**Looping Is Not Reliability** is strongest because it changes what a coding-agent paper should have to report. Caveat: the repository-scale evidence is smaller and noisier than the HumanEval-style controlled evidence, so treat the contract as a standards contribution more than a proven win on real bug fixing.

**Beyond Aggregate Risk** is strongest because it names the real object of failure in structured tool use: role-specific fields, not the action average. Caveat: the method inherits the limitations of the detector it wraps and still needs recalibration or exchangeability assumptions for its cleanest guarantees.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The pattern today is that system quality depends on where you place the commit boundary. Memory eviction should not necessarily commit at arrival. Shared-memory writes should not become actionable belief the moment they are stored. Runtime guardrails should not confuse a static judge score with closed-loop enforceability. Coding agents should not treat another revision as harmless once a correct patch has already appeared. Tool-call certification should not average recipient-risk away inside a mostly benign action. Same lesson everywhere: stop talking about capability in the abstract and specify the contract that turns intermediate state into something the system is allowed to trust.

## Detailed notes

- [MemTX note](../paper_notes/memtx_transactional_belief_commit_stateful_agent_memory.md)

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-26

## Theme

Today’s useful cluster is explicit task management for long-horizon robot behavior. The strongest papers are not claiming that a bigger end-to-end policy will somehow absorb planning. They carve out visible structure for progress tracking, correction, and branch reuse.

## Short overview

Brave search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. So scouting fell back to direct arXiv API discovery plus primary-source inspection through arXiv abstract and HTML pages. I inspected the abstract and substantial HTML text for **Long-Horizon Manipulation via Trace-Conditioned VLA Planning**, **Hi-WM: Human-in-the-World-Model for Scalable Robot Post-Training**, and **VistaBot: View-Robust Robot Manipulation via Spatiotemporal-Aware View Synthesis**.

The strongest paper today is **Long-Horizon Manipulation via Trace-Conditioned VLA Planning**. The real move is not “use a manager.” It is the specific contract: predict a progress-aware remaining plan plus a lightweight 2D trace, then let a short-horizon executor repeatedly follow that explicit spatial prompt. That turns long-horizon control into a receding-horizon loop with visible memory rather than hidden persistence inside a monolithic action model.

**Hi-WM** is still highly relevant, even though it was already preserved yesterday. Its best idea is to treat failure states as reusable assets: roll out in a world model, intervene around failure, then rollback and branch multiple corrective continuations from the same state. That is a much more concrete use of a world model than just generating prettier imagined futures.

**VistaBot** is adjacent and somewhat mixed. The geometric-plus-diffusion fusion for viewpoint robustness is real engineering, and the view-generalization metric is useful pressure. But the paper is more about perception robustness than about explicit memory, planning, or controllable task structure. For this repo, it is relevant mostly as support infrastructure, not as a core mechanism paper.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Long-Horizon Manipulation via Trace-Conditioned VLA Planning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it gives long-horizon manipulation an explicit manager-executor interface with remaining-plan memory and a spatial trace prompt, instead of hoping long-horizon competence will emerge inside one reactive policy.

### 2. **Hi-WM: Human-in-the-World-Model for Scalable Robot Post-Training**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it turns a world model into a rollback-and-branch correction workspace around real failure states, which is exactly the kind of explicit reusable structure that world-model papers often claim but do not deliver.

### 3. **VistaBot: View-Robust Robot Manipulation via Spatiotemporal-Aware View Synthesis**

**Verdict:** useful but adjacent.

Why it matters: it attacks viewpoint brittleness with explicit geometry plus diffusion-based latent synthesis, but the main contribution sits closer to robust perception plumbing than to planning or structured control.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Long-Horizon Manipulation via Trace-Conditioned VLA Planning.

The steal-worthy part is the split between a progress-aware manager and a generic executor. The manager predicts what is done, what remains, and a 2D trace for where the next interaction should go. That is a cleaner interface than asking a single VLA to simultaneously remember task state, recover from drift, and emit low-level actions.

Hi-WM is the better paper if the question is how to reuse failure states for data collection and post-training. LoHo-Manip is the better paper if the question is how to make long-horizon execution legible at inference time.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

LoHo-Manip adds pressure on long-horizon VLA papers that hide all progress tracking inside the policy. If a system claims multi-step robustness, the obvious questions should now be: where is the explicit task-state representation, how is failure persistence handled, and what stable interface connects planner to executor?

Hi-WM adds pressure on world-model framing. A world model should do more than hallucinate futures or rank checkpoints. It should ideally create reusable intervention structure, especially around failure basins.

VistaBot adds evaluation pressure in a narrower sense. If a manipulation policy claims robustness, camera-view shift should be treated as a first-class stress test rather than an afterthought.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful lesson today is that robotics papers get more interesting when they stop pretending end-to-end mush will organize itself. LoHo-Manip makes progress state and near-term spatial intent explicit at inference time. Hi-WM makes failure states explicit and reusable during post-training. VistaBot is less central for this repo, but still reinforces that perception invariance should be built with structure rather than assumed. The strongest throughline is simple: separate roles, expose state, and make the control interface visible.

## Detailed notes

- [Hi-WM note](../paper_notes/hi_wm_human_in_the_world_model_scalable_robot_post_training.md)

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-21

## Theme

Today’s interesting papers are all about anchoring. Dual-Anchoring explicitly pins navigation state to progress tokens and landmark memory instead of letting a Video-LLM drift. OneVL tries to compress planning into latent tokens, but only works once those latents are forced to reconstruct both language and future visual dynamics. MultiWorld is the more adjacent systems paper: if you want multi-agent world models to be more than stitched-together demos, you need explicit agent identity and a shared cross-view state.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv search plus primary-source inspection. I inspected the arXiv abstract and HTML paper text for **Dual-Anchoring: Addressing State Drift in Vision-Language Navigation**, **OneVL: One-Step Latent Reasoning and Planning with Vision-Language Explanation**, and **MultiWorld: Scalable Multi-Agent Multi-View Video World Models**. I also looked at **EmbodiedLGR** and **XEmbodied** during filtering, but did not keep them as top picks. EmbodiedLGR is a decent lightweight memory-system paper, but more useful as a deployment reference than a sharp research move. XEmbodied has some solid ingredients, but right now it reads too much like a large packaging exercise around adapters, tool distillation, and curriculum rather than a clean new mechanism.

The strongest paper today is **Dual-Anchoring**. Its contribution is not that it says “memory matters” in VLN. The better move is the split diagnosis: long-horizon failure is not one thing, but at least two different drifts, progress drift and memory drift, and they need different anchors. One branch forces the model to externalize which instruction prefix is already done. The other adds a retrospective landmark-prediction objective so history cannot collapse into generic mush.

**OneVL** is the most interesting adjacent bet. Most latent-CoT work in embodied settings feels like a wish that hidden states will somehow keep the useful causal structure after text compression. OneVL’s answer is to supervise the latent bottleneck from both sides: decode language explanations and decode future visual tokens. I buy the direction more than the hype. The paper is long, benchmark-heavy, and partly driving-specific, but the mechanism is real.

**MultiWorld** is more systems-heavy than conceptually deep, but still worth logging. The useful lesson is that multi-agent controllability and multi-view consistency need separate machinery. Agent identity needs to be explicit, and cross-view coherence needs a shared state, not just shared parameters.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Dual-Anchoring: Addressing State Drift in Vision-Language Navigation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it treats long-horizon embodied failure as explicit state-tracking failure, then adds concrete anchors for instruction progress and landmark memory instead of hoping a streaming Video-LLM will stay coherent by itself.

### 2. **OneVL: One-Step Latent Reasoning and Planning with Vision-Language Explanation**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it makes latent reasoning less decorative by forcing the compressed bottleneck to reconstruct both language reasoning and future visual dynamics.

### 3. **MultiWorld: Scalable Multi-Agent Multi-View Video World Models**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it isolates two real interface problems, agent identity and cross-view shared state, that most multi-agent video world-model demos blur together.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** Dual-Anchoring.

The reason is simple: it attacks a failure mode cabbageland actually cares about, internal state drifting away from task reality over long horizons. The paper’s best conceptual move is to refuse the vague story that “the model forgets.” Instead, it splits forgetting into instruction-state confusion and landmark-history collapse, then imposes different training signals for each. That is much closer to the kind of explicit-state design pressure worth paying attention to.

OneVL is probably the most reusable architectural pattern. If you want a compressed reasoning bottleneck to retain causal structure, supervising it only through text is too weak. Dual supervision from language and future-state prediction is a much stronger contract. MultiWorld is less central, but its use of explicit agent identity and a 3D-aware global state is still a useful reminder that shared-environment simulation needs a real interface for shared state.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

Dual-Anchoring pushes against the current habit of treating long-horizon embodied errors as generic “reasoning” failures. The paper’s framing suggests that many VLN systems are not missing more intelligence in the abstract, they are missing explicit state bookkeeping. If that framing sticks, some future work should be compared less against generic bigger-model baselines and more against targeted state-anchoring baselines.

OneVL pressures the latent-CoT literature. The paper’s strongest claim is not just better speed, but that latent reasoning gets materially better when the bottleneck is grounded in future visual dynamics rather than language-only compression. If that result holds outside driving, a lot of latent-thought work starts to look under-constrained.

MultiWorld is baseline pressure on multi-agent world-model demos that quietly assume a fixed number of agents, fixed camera layouts, or weak interaction structure. It does not solve everything, but it makes those assumptions harder to ignore.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The common lesson today is that explicit anchoring beats hopeful compression. If you want long-horizon navigation, anchor progress and memory separately. If you want fast latent reasoning, make the bottleneck answer to future world dynamics, not just decoded prose. If you want multi-agent simulation, separate who did what from what the shared world state is. That is all basically the same research taste: structure should constrain the actual computation, not just decorate the story.

## Detailed notes

- [OneVL note](../paper_notes/onevl_one_step_latent_reasoning_and_planning_with_vision_language_explanation.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-08-16

## Theme

The strongest papers today all reject the lazy idea that a long trajectory is already a usable state. **LongHorizon-Harness** says progress should persist as audited task state, not as an ever-growing executor transcript. **RippleMem** says memory access should recover missing support, not just return the first relevant-looking record. **Beyond Myopic World Models** says long-horizon prediction should be trained at the horizon where it will be used, not by recursively hoping short-horizon losses somehow survive rollout. **TRACES** says science benchmarks are still ducking the more basic question of whether a model can reject a rotten premise. **NeuroMosaic** says clinical multimodal reasoning should route through anatomy-indexed evidence and abstention logic, not generic pooled visual tokens.

## Short overview

This Sunday, August 16, 2026 run used live recent-paper discovery and arXiv HTML full-text inspection across long-horizon agents, persistent memory, world models, scientific reliability, and non-robotics medical multimodal reasoning. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for all five ranked papers below.

Three papers earn preserved notes. **TRACES** is the strongest runner-up because the benchmark is sharp and the failure signal is ugly in the useful way, but it is still mostly a measurement instrument rather than a reusable systems mechanism. **NeuroMosaic** is the strongest adjacent runner-up because the anatomy-indexed routing, concept memory, and abstention boundary are real, though the evidence remains cohort-bound and domain-specific. **Most relevant today:** **LongHorizon-Harness**.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **LongHorizon-Harness: Advancing Long-Horizon Agents for Real-World Tasks**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the sharpest systems paper in the set because it treats long-horizon execution as explicit task-state management rather than heroic context stuffing. The useful move is the Manage-Execute-Audit loop: a manager writes bounded contracts from audited state, a fresh-context executor performs one round, and a read-only auditor decides what actually changed. On matched backbones, it lifts Qwen 3.7-Plus from **51.8%** to **80.7%** on WeaveBench, from **69.7%** to **77.2%** on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and from **2.8%** to **8.3%** binary completion on OSWorld 2.0.

### 2. **RippleMem: From Isolated Retrieval to Associative Recollection for Long-Term Agent Memory**

**Verdict:** must read direct paper.

Why it matters: This is the best memory paper in the batch because it names the real failure mode: the evidence exists, but the system fails to recover all of it together. RippleMem stores cue-rich episodic memory units, links them in an event-centric graph, then uses recalled anchors as cues for bounded associative expansion. It reaches **87.14%** judge accuracy on LoCoMo, **84.80%** and **86.60%** overall accuracy on the two LongMemEval-S settings, and cuts graph-construction cost by about **30x** relative to heavier graph-memory baselines.

### 3. **Beyond Myopic World Models: Long-Horizon End-to-End Training for Direct Future Prediction**

**Verdict:** preserve-worthy direct paper.

Why it matters: The paper's useful claim is that the main bottleneck is often the supervision horizon, not the world-model brand name. DPWM predicts the endpoint in one shot from the initial observation plus the whole action sequence, avoiding recursive rollout at both training and inference. On the policy-trained Cheetah setting at horizon **100**, endpoint MSE is **0.4452** for DPWM versus **25.6086** for ADM and **11.0004** for MoSim, and the authors further show that recurrent baselines also improve when retrained under the same endpoint objective.

### 4. **TRACES: A Benchmark for Epistemic Reliability in Scientific Reasoning by LLMs**

**Verdict:** strong direct runner-up.

Why it matters: This is one of the better recent benchmark papers because it measures the refusal boundary instead of assuming scientific QA scores imply scientific judgment. TRACES builds **42** probes from retracted, fraudulent, and pseudoscientific papers and evaluates **30** models across **12,600** responses. Every tested model fails more than **71%** of agentic probes, **22 of 30** fail more than **90%** of the time, and about **81%** of responses contain no warning at all.

### 5. **NeuroMosaic: Anatomically Grounded Multimodal Large Language Modeling for Molecularly Aware Glioma Reasoning from 3D MRI and Clinical Narratives**

**Verdict:** strong adjacent runner-up.

Why it matters: This is the non-robotics paper worth keeping in view because it replaces generic visual pooling with anatomy-indexed routing plus a concept memory that can explicitly say unresolved. The model converts multi-sequence MRI into routed regional evidence, binds diagnostic clauses to image or clinical support, and calibrates abstention separately from representation learning. It reports external integrated-subtype macro-F1 values of **0.784**, **0.761**, and **0.742**, plus evidence-pointing accuracy of **0.703** and a targeted-deletion confidence drop of **0.187** versus **0.046** for random deletion.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** **LongHorizon-Harness**.

It attacks a very cabbageland problem with the right unit of repair. Long tasks usually fail because execution history, progress tracking, and completion judgment all get stirred into the same context soup. This paper separates them cleanly. The executor is no longer trusted to both act and narrate what is true. Only audited state survives the round.

That is a good design rule well beyond GUI agents. The useful transferable ideas are bounded contracts, fresh-context execution, state records that persist outside the trajectory, and a rule that completion is only granted by read-only environmental evidence. **RippleMem** sharpens the same taste from the memory side: stored history is not enough unless the system can recover the missing support set. **Beyond Myopic World Models** makes the parallel point for predictive models: even a strong representation can fail operationally when training pressure lands at the wrong horizon.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**LongHorizon-Harness** matters because it makes task state a first-class object rather than a side effect of the transcript. The paper's real contribution is not yet another planner loop. It is the decision to let only audited facts persist across rounds.

**RippleMem** matters because it changes the memory question from "did retrieval find something relevant?" to "did recollection recover an answerable support set?" That is a cleaner and more useful boundary than another flat top-k retrieval comparison.

**Beyond Myopic World Models** matters because it humiliates a common reflex. If long-horizon behavior depends on endpoint accuracy, then training only on one-step losses and hoping rollout will carry the signal is structurally misaligned.

**TRACES** matters because it exposes a hole in scientific-agent evaluation. A model can score well on answerable science questions and still operationalize fraud, pseudoscience, or retracted premises when asked to help do science with them.

**NeuroMosaic** matters because it treats medical multimodal reasoning as evidence routing plus selective risk, not as "feed the MRI to a bigger decoder." The anatomy-indexed route and unresolved state are the interesting parts, not the generic multimodal branding.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful August 16 lesson is that long-horizon competence does not live in the raw trace. It lives in what the system can isolate, verify, and reuse. Good memory should recover missing support, not just matching snippets. Good execution should preserve audited task state, not a swollen transcript. Good world models should be trained at the horizon where they will actually be judged. Good scientific assistants should know when the premise itself is rotten. Good clinical multimodal systems should bind conclusions to routed evidence and keep abstention explicit. Same taste everywhere: make the operational state legible, or the system will eventually lie to itself.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-07-20

## Theme

Today's strongest papers all punish the same mistake: confusing a nicer surface for a better mechanism. **Presentation, Not Mechanism** shows that a fancy deprecation-aware memory ledger mostly wins because its render is easier for the answer model to read, not because the fine-grained state is actually doing more useful work. **CRAFT** argues that evaluation should target the capability named by the rubric criterion, not the whole prompt blob. **Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training** treats RL gains as a function of the pretrained state instead of mystical post-training alchemy. **SlotMem** makes long-video memory character-addressable instead of hiding identity inside frame soup. **ContinuityBench** points out that "high availability" is not continuity if failover silently forgets the conversation.

## Short overview

I checked the fresh `cs.AI`, `cs.CV`, and `cs.LG` arXiv recent pages on **Monday, July 20, 2026**, used the public Brave Search results page first for discovery and naming-variant checks, then read the primary arXiv sources directly. I also ran an explicit non-robotics title pass for `medical`, `clinical`, `radiology`, `MRI`, `CT`, `pathology`, and `healthcare` terms. That surfaced **CardioMeta** and **Region-Grounded Vision-Language Learning for Detection-Guided Mammographic Lesion Classification**; both were serious, but both felt more application-shaped than the final five on transferable mechanism.

No preserved note today is abstract-only. I inspected the arXiv HTML full text for **Presentation, Not Mechanism**, **CRAFT**, **Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training**, **SlotMem**, and **ContinuityBench**. No robotics or VLA paper cleared today's top five.

**Presentation, Not Mechanism** is the most relevant paper today. Its best contribution is not a new memory architecture. It is a benchmark-design correction: if you change the memory mechanism and the rendered presentation at the same time, you do not know what won.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Presentation, Not Mechanism: A Render Confound in Deprecation-Aware Memory Evaluation**

**Verdict:** must read.

Why it matters: This paper does the rude thing the area needed. It holds the memory task fixed, adds a render-matched control, and shows that the apparent fine-ledger gain on reverted-revert cases is mostly presentation, not mechanism. The headline `+0.182` advantage over a flat baseline decomposes into about `+0.159` render effect and only `+0.025` fine-mechanism residual, while a coarse live/dead invalidation mechanism actually buys more.

### 2. **CRAFT: Clustering Rubrics to Diagnose Weak LLM Capabilities and Generate Targeted Fine-Tuning Data**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: The useful move is changing the diagnostic unit from whole prompts to prompt-rubric criteria. That sounds small but is not small. CRAFT turns rubric criteria into capability probes, builds a hierarchical capability tree, then uses low-performing nodes to target synthetic SFT data. On held-out evaluation, it wins the finance-domain average for all four tested open models and the legal average for three of four.

### 3. **Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training**

**Verdict:** highly relevant direct paper.

Why it matters: The paper studies reasoning with an actual pretraining-to-RL pipeline instead of treating RL post-training as a detached magic trick. In the controlled chess setup, pretraining loss predicts post-RL pass@1, the compute-optimal frontier shifts toward a larger RL share as total compute grows, and the mechanism analysis shows a split between easy and hard puzzles rather than one simple "RL makes reasoning better" story.

### 4. **SlotMem: Character-Addressable Internal Memory for Narrative Long Video Generation**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: This is one of the cleaner memory papers in the long-video lane because it makes the address key explicit. Instead of retrieving whole frames or keyframes, it uses text-anchored character probes to extract role-wise slot memory, updates those slots conservatively, and injects them only into localized character tokens. The result is more reusable than another global-consistency heuristic.

### 5. **ContinuityBench: A Benchmark and Systems Study of Stateful Failover in Multi-Provider LLM Routing**

**Verdict:** useful workflow and infrastructure paper.

Why it matters: The mechanism is almost embarrassingly simple, which is part of the point. If failover throws away the conversation history, uptime is not continuity. The paper formalizes continuity with CPR and CLO, then shows that a history-forwarding proxy preserves context in `744/750` failovers while the stateless baseline preserves none.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Presentation, Not Mechanism

The steal is methodological and architectural at the same time: hold render fixed before claiming a mechanism win. That applies directly to memory systems, agent evaluations, workflow UIs, and any benchmark where a structured artifact is both state and prompt.

**CRAFT** is the evaluation complement: the useful diagnostic unit is often the rubric criterion, not the prompt. **Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training** is the scaling complement: post-training returns are shaped by the pretrained state you start from. **SlotMem** is the generative-memory complement: if the memory target is a character, the address should also be a character. **ContinuityBench** is the systems complement: continuity is a separate contract from availability and should be measured that way.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Presentation, Not Mechanism** is strongest because it attacks an evaluation confound instead of proposing a louder data structure. Caveat: the paper is still scoped to current-state evidence-state-revision queries and a particular benchmark construction.

**CRAFT** is strongest where many eval pipelines are weakest: it tells you what to train next, not just what score went down. Caveat: the method depends on rubric quality, judge consistency, and domains that already have explicit criteria.

**Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training** is strongest as a controlled science paper. Caveat: chess is not natural language, and some transfer claims will stay qualitative until the same analysis is done at larger language scale.

**SlotMem** is strongest as an explicit memory-interface paper. Caveat: it depends on consistent character-semantic anchors in the captions, and the current training scale is still limited.

**ContinuityBench** is strongest as a systems correction. Caveat: the history-forwarding mechanism is simple enough that the benchmark matters more than the architectural novelty.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful lesson today is to stop letting a convenient proxy impersonate the state that actually matters. A prettier ledger render is not proof that finer memory structure helped. A prompt cluster is not the same thing as a failed capability. RL gains are not independent of the pretrained policy they start from. A frame memory is not a character memory. And an available fallback is not a continuous conversation if it forgot the conversation. Same message across five papers: make the interface explicit, measure the right contract, and distrust wins that disappear once the presentation is controlled.

- [CRAFT note](../paper_notes/craft_rubric_capability_clustering.md)
- [Pretraining-to-post-training reasoning note](../paper_notes/pretraining_to_post_training_reasoning_scaling.md)
- [SlotMem note](../paper_notes/slotmem_character_addressable_video_memory.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-15

## Theme

Today’s signal is **explicit object and scene structure doing real planning work, while benchmark-heavy long-horizon agent papers still need harsher separation between cognition claims and scaffold claims**. The strongest paper is **Slot-MPC** because it uses object-centric latent state for actual online control rather than for decorative representation learning. **LEXI-SG** is the best adjacent paper because it uses room structure as an organizing prior for scalable monocular scene-graph mapping instead of pretending a rolling latent map will stay coherent by itself. **LongAct / HoloMind** is useful mostly as benchmark pressure and framing, not because its proposed agent stack looks especially clean.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run and was unavailable because the current environment is missing a Brave API key. I therefore used direct arXiv discovery and inspected accessible full text for **Slot-MPC: Goal-Conditioned Model Predictive Control with Object-Centric Representations**, **LEXI-SG: Monocular 3D Scene Graph Mapping with Room-Guided Feed-Forward Reconstruction**, **When Robots Do the Chores: A Benchmark and Agent for Long-Horizon Household Task Execution**, and partial PDF text for **Quantitative Video World Model Evaluation for Geometric-Consistency** and **VGGT-Edit**.

**Slot-MPC** is the most relevant paper today. The paper learns slot-based object representations from video, trains an action-conditioned object-centric dynamics model over those slots, and then performs gradient-based model predictive control directly in slot space to reach visual goals. That is a real mechanism, not just another “structured” label. The most important claim is not merely that slots are interpretable. It is that the lower-dimensional object factorization makes online planning cheaper and more controllable than holistic latent planning in low-data offline settings.

**LEXI-SG** is strong adjacent inspiration. Its core move is simple and good: do not keep reconstructing the world in small overlapping windows if that predictably causes scale drift and double walls. Instead, use room transitions as semantic batching boundaries, reconstruct each room once from a curated set of views, connect rooms with explicit Sim(3) edges, and then hang open-vocabulary object nodes off the room graph. That is exactly the kind of explicit scene hierarchy that feels more useful than latent mush when the downstream task is navigation or memory.

**LongAct** is worth noticing mainly because it pushes long-horizon household evaluation toward free-form instructions, multi-room tasks, and explicit improvement-over-time metrics. The associated **HoloMind** agent is less convincing as a reusable architecture contribution. It has all the expected components, DAG planner, spatial memory, episodic memory, critic, but from the accessible text it still reads more like a sensible systems bundle than a sharp new mechanism. Useful benchmark, softer architecture claim.

**PDI-Bench** is good citation material even though I did not preserve a full note for it today. Its contribution is to stop calling video generators “world models” without auditing geometric consistency. That is a worthwhile diagnostic lens, but more evaluation infrastructure than core architecture insight.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Slot-MPC: Goal-Conditioned Model Predictive Control with Object-Centric Representations**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it makes explicit object state pay rent at control time through differentiable planning, instead of stopping at prettier latent decomposition.

### 2. **LEXI-SG: Monocular 3D Scene Graph Mapping with Room-Guided Feed-Forward Reconstruction**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it uses room hierarchy as an actual systems prior for scalable mapping and open-vocabulary scene memory from RGB alone.

### 3. **When Robots Do the Chores: A Benchmark and Agent for Long-Horizon Household Task Execution**

**Verdict:** mostly citation material, but relevant citation material.

Why it matters: the benchmark raises the floor on what “long-horizon household autonomy” should mean, even if the proposed agent stack is more bundle than breakthrough.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Slot-MPC.

The paper earns that spot because it connects explicit representation to actual action selection. Many object-centric papers stop at the pleasant observation that objects are easier to visualize or more compositional in principle. Slot-MPC goes one step further and uses slot state as the planning substrate itself. The resulting story is concrete: parse current and goal images into slots, roll forward object dynamics under candidate actions, and optimize the action sequence by minimizing distance to the goal configuration in slot space.

I also like the constraint regime. This is offline, reward-free world-model learning from visual data, followed by test-time planning. That makes the paper more reusable than task-specific reactive policy learning. The main caveat is that the slot abstraction is only as good as the scene parser and learned dynamics. If the object decomposition is unstable or omits task-relevant contact structure, gradient-based planning may optimize a clean latent objective while still missing physical reality.

My confidence is fairly good on the mechanism because I inspected substantial arXiv HTML full text, including the training losses and the planning setup. My confidence is lower on the absolute empirical margin over all baselines because I did not audit every appendix detail.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update is that **object-centricity matters most when it improves the control interface**, not when it merely supplies nicer latent visualizations. Slot-MPC is useful because it ties structure to online optimization cost and controllability.

LEXI-SG sharpens a different but related point. Explicit hierarchy is often more valuable as a batching and optimization contract than as a semantic garnish. Rooms are not just labels here. They define when reconstruction happens, how local consistency is preserved, and how global scene memory is stitched together.

LongAct mostly affects evaluation framing. Papers claiming long-horizon embodied competence should probably face more free-form, multi-room, dependency-heavy tasks instead of short canned episodes. But HoloMind does not, from the accessible text, settle the architecture question. It mostly reminds us that enough scaffolding can partially rescue weak base agents.

PDI-Bench is the negative baseline update. A paper calling generated video a world model should probably survive geometry-specific audits before that label is taken seriously.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Slot-MPC** because it uses explicit object state for real online planning, not decorative structure theater. **LEXI-SG** is the most interesting adjacent paper because it treats rooms as an operational hierarchy for scalable monocular scene-graph mapping and persistent scene memory. **LongAct** is useful benchmark pressure, but **HoloMind** looks more like a competent long-horizon agent bundle than a crisp conceptual advance. The broader lesson is familiar but still important: structure matters when it constrains prediction, memory, or control in a legible way. It matters much less when it is just another branded latent layer.

## Detailed notes

- [Slot-MPC note](../paper_notes/slot_mpc_goal_conditioned_model_predictive_control_object_centric_representations.md)
- [LEXI-SG note](../paper_notes/lexi_sg_monocular_3d_scene_graph_mapping_room_guided_feed_forward_reconstruction.md)

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-04

## Theme
Today’s thread is explicit steering and explicit structure. The best paper does not try to make a language model more omnipotent; it asks whether a visual representation itself can be conditionally redirected without collapsing into language mush. The second-best paper asks a related question in 3D generation: if native 3D data is scarce, can cross-modal generation cycles supply enough structure to make a unified text-image-3D autoregressive model actually useful? Brave Search was checked first in this run and was unavailable because the Brave API key is missing in this environment, so discovery fell back to arXiv API listings plus direct inspection of arXiv HTML papers.

## Short overview
The strongest hit today is **Steerable Visual Representations**. It is good because the claim is narrow, testable, and computationally honest: keep a strong frozen visual encoder, inject language early through lightweight cross-attention, and ask whether the resulting features can be redirected toward non-salient concepts without ruining their usefulness for ordinary vision tasks. That is a real representational question, not just another multimodal demo.

Second is **Omni123**. This is the most interesting of the recent “unified 3D foundation model” papers I inspected because it at least has a structural answer to the obvious bottleneck: 3D supervision is scarce, so use interleaved text-image-3D generation cycles as an implicit geometric constraint rather than pretending scarce text-to-3D pairs are enough by themselves. I am interested, but not fully converted; the data-engineering stack is huge, and some of the gain may simply come from industrial-scale curation plus synthetic triplets.

Third is **MetaNav**. This is more adjacent and less conceptually sharp than the first two, but it is still respectable. The useful part is not the “metacognitive” branding; it is the concrete planner structure: persistent 3D semantic memory, a revisit penalty over episodic history, and an LLM-triggered correction stage only when exploration stalls. That is a better recipe than naive stepwise VLM frontier scoring.

Other inspected papers did not clear the preservation bar. **Generative World Renderer** looks like a serious dataset-and-pipeline contribution for inverse/forward rendering, but for this repo it is more infrastructure than mechanism. **Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Control under Time-Varying Dynamics** is theoretically respectable and probably worth remembering as background on stale-data forgetting, yet today it felt more like solid control theory than a reusable cabbageland design move.

## Ranked papers

1. **Steerable Visual Representations**
   - Verdict: **Highly relevant**
   - Role: **Directly relevant**
   - Why it matters: It offers a clean way to make visual features promptable without throwing away visual quality or routing everything through an LLM.

2. **Omni123: Exploring 3D Native Foundation Models with Limited 3D Data by Unifying Text to 2D and 3D Generation**
   - Verdict: **Useful**
   - Role: **Directly relevant**
   - Why it matters: It treats image-3D consistency as structure, not just data augmentation, and that is the only reason a “unified” text-image-3D model here feels remotely credible.

3. **Stop Wandering: Efficient Vision-Language Navigation via Metacognitive Reasoning**
   - Verdict: **Useful**
   - Role: **Adjacent inspiration**
   - Why it matters: It packages persistent spatial memory, revisit-aware frontier scoring, and sparse reflection into a practical navigation loop instead of pure greedy VLM querying.

## Most relevant to cabbageland
**Steerable Visual Representations** is the clear winner. The important move is to condition vision on language without surrendering the representation to language-space habits. A lot of multimodal work effectively says “just let the LLM sort it out,” which usually means the representation gets blurrier as the branding gets grander. This paper instead asks for a visual representation that remains useful as vision while becoming selectively steerable. That is a much better research instinct.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact
- **Early fusion can be the point, not a decorative wiring choice:** SteerViT’s main argument is that if text only arrives after visual encoding, the visual features themselves were never actually steerable. That sounds obvious once said aloud, but many prior baselines quietly dodge the issue.
- **Cross-modal cycles as structural regularization:** Omni123 is most interesting when read as a constraint-design paper rather than a product pitch. The text→image→3D→image idea is trying to force semantic, appearance, and geometric consistency to meet in one sequence space.
- **Reflection only when necessary beats constant deliberation theater:** MetaNav’s better idea is not “metacognition.” It is that expensive corrective reasoning should be triggered by detectable stagnation rather than performed constantly.
- **What did not make the preserved set:** Generative World Renderer may be useful later as a dataset citation or rendering benchmark reference, but today it looked more like a large curation + evaluation pipeline than a concept worth preserving in note form. The time-varying MBRL paper has real theory, especially on why stale data breaks calibrated uncertainty, but it felt more like background for forgetting and non-stationary control than a top Paper Daily save.
- **Truthfulness / access note:** I directly inspected arXiv HTML or abstract pages for Steerable Visual Representations, Omni123, MetaNav, Generative World Renderer, and the time-varying MBRL paper. Confidence is strongest on problem framing, architecture, and the qualitative mechanism claims visible in the accessible HTML sections; weaker on exact benchmark margins, appendix details, and any claims that depend heavily on hidden implementation details.

## One-paragraph takeaway
The useful lesson today is that conditionality gets better when it is built into the representation rather than bolted on afterward. **SteerViT** makes that point cleanly for visual features: text should be able to redirect what the representation encodes without destroying the representation itself. **Omni123** reaches for a similar principle in 3D by using cross-modal generative cycles as a geometric prior instead of pretending scarce native 3D supervision is enough. **MetaNav** is less elegant, but it lands the same general taste in embodied form: keep persistent state, penalize obvious failure modes, and reserve reflective reasoning for moments when the agent is actually stuck. Good day for explicit structure, not a great day for grandiose claims.

- [Omni123 note](../paper_notes/omni123_unifying_text_to_2d_and_3d_generation.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-12

## Theme

Today’s real signal is **moving computation out of online search and into explicit reusable structure**. The strongest paper is **Latent Geometry Beyond Search: Amortizing Planning in World Models** because it asks a sharp question instead of adding another planner trick: when is the latent space good enough that planning can be mostly compiled into a simple inverse map? **Understanding Asynchronous Inference Methods for Vision-Language-Action Models** is the most useful evaluation paper of the batch because it compares several delay-mitigation strategies under one protocol instead of letting each method hide behind its own setup. **VLADriver-RAG** is more adjacent, but its shift from raw visual retrieval to scenario graphs is at least the right instinct.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run and was unavailable because the current environment is missing a Brave API key. I therefore used recent arXiv RSS discovery plus direct arXiv abstract and HTML inspection.

I inspected the abstract and accessible arXiv HTML text for **Latent Geometry Beyond Search**, **Understanding Asynchronous Inference Methods for Vision-Language-Action Models**, **VLADriver-RAG**, **Test-Time Training for Visual Foresight Vision-Language-Action Models**, and **Adaptive Failure-Informed Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models**. Confidence is highest on each paper’s framing and core mechanism, and lower on appendix-level implementation details or exhaustive ablations.

**Latent Geometry Beyond Search** is the paper worth keeping. The useful claim is not merely that a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics model can be fast. The deeper claim is that if a world model’s latent space is smooth, uniform, and action-sensitive enough, then much of what test-time planners recover may already be locally encoded in the representation. Their GC-IDM replaces expensive search over action sequences with a small MLP that reads current latent state, goal latent state, and remaining horizon, then outputs the next action. If the result holds up, it is a meaningful argument that representation quality should be judged partly by how much planning it makes unnecessary.

**Understanding Asynchronous Inference Methods for Vision-Language-Action Models** is not a new VLA architecture, but it is a useful cleanup paper. It compares IT-RTC, TT-RTC, VLASH, and A2C2 under harmonized codebases and benchmarks. The big practical takeaway is that lightweight residual correction wins on their tested setups, while training-time delay simulation is the most robust zero-overhead training-based fix. This is mainly baseline and systems-positioning value, not a deeper representational idea.

**VLADriver-RAG** is the most interesting adjacent paper. I do not trust the state-of-the-art pitch very much on its own, but I do like the structural move from raw visual retrieval to explicit spatiotemporal semantic graphs plus topology-aware alignment. That is at least a real mechanism. The main caveat is that autonomous driving retrieval stacks can become packaging-heavy quickly, and the paper still looks more like a benchmark-oriented system than a clean reusable memory architecture.

I also inspected **Test-Time Training for Visual Foresight VLA Models** and **Adaptive Failure-Informed Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models**. Both have coherent local ideas, but neither cleared the preservation bar today. T3VF is a modest self-supervised adaptation patch for visual-foresight models, and AFIL mostly reframes failure avoidance as guidance between success and failure generators. Neither felt as transferable as the best paper today.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Latent Geometry Beyond Search: Amortizing Planning in World Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it treats representation quality as something that should reduce planning burden, not just improve prediction accuracy.

### 2. **Understanding Asynchronous Inference Methods for Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it gives a cleaner comparison of asynchronous-control fixes than the current fragmented literature.

### 3. **VLADriver-RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it replaces raw visual retrieval with explicit scenario graphs and topology-aware retrieval, which is at least the right kind of structural move.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Latent Geometry Beyond Search.

The core reason is that it reframes planning cost as a representation question. If a world model’s latent space is genuinely regular and action-relevant, then a cheap inverse map from current state, goal state, and remaining horizon should recover a good local action without online search. That is a much more interesting claim than another planner that simply spends more compute in latent space.

The paper is also unusually honest about what it is and is not doing. It is not proposing a new world model. It freezes a pretrained JEPA-style world model, then asks whether CEM and related optimizers are recovering structure that the latent space already made available. Their GC-IDM is deliberately small, which makes the result more interpretable if it works.

My confidence is fairly high on the main mechanism because I inspected the abstract, introduction, method setup, and accessible HTML text covering the planning-tax framing, the frozen LeWorldModel setup, the GC-IDM input-output definition, the pairwise-IDM failure case, and the reported comparison against CEM, MPPI, iCEM, and gradient-based planners. My confidence is lower on the exact strength of the empirical advantage because I did not audit all appendix details, environment-by-environment breakdowns, or failure analyses.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The biggest framing update is that world-model papers should probably be judged not only by rollout fidelity, but by **how much online optimization their representation still requires**. If planning remains expensive, that may indicate the latent space is predictive but not very action-usable.

This also affects baseline interpretation. A planner-heavy result can hide representational weakness if the optimizer is doing all the hard work at test time. **Latent Geometry Beyond Search** explicitly tests that. **Understanding Asynchronous Inference Methods** is useful in a different way: it reduces confusion around latency-mitigation baselines that are currently hard to compare fairly.

The more skeptical update is for papers like **VLADriver-RAG** and the other VLA robustness patches I inspected today. They contain some real ideas, but they still feel closer to engineering overlays than to durable representational advances.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The strongest paper today is **Latent Geometry Beyond Search** because it asks the right question: when a world model latent space is well-structured, should planning still need expensive search at all? Their answer is a small goal-conditioned inverse dynamics model that replaces search with direct action inference, and that is exactly the kind of claim cabbageland should track. **Understanding Asynchronous Inference Methods** is a useful evaluation cleanup paper for delayed VLA control, and **VLADriver-RAG** is an adjacent structural retrieval paper with some real mechanism but a more benchmark-heavy smell. The common lesson is that explicit structure is most valuable when it actually removes runtime mush, not when it merely decorates it.

## Detailed notes

- [Latent Geometry Beyond Search note](../paper_notes/latent_geometry_beyond_search_amortizing_planning_world_models.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-04-29

## Theme

Today’s useful pattern is explicit correction or explicit state validation instead of pretending the base model already “implicitly knows.” The strongest papers do not just add scale or another generic planner loop. They isolate what the main policy is missing, then either distill that missing signal or enforce a tighter contract between symbolic intent and physical reality.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. I then scouted recent arXiv listings directly and inspected the abstract plus substantial method text from arXiv HTML pages for **Privileged Foresight Distillation: Zero-Cost Future Correction for World Action Models**, **ANCHOR: A Physically Grounded Closed-Loop Framework for Robust Home-Service Mobile Manipulation**, **VISION-SLS: Safe Perception-Based Control from Learned Visual Representations via System Level Synthesis**, and **World-R1: Reinforcing 3D Constraints for Text-to-Video Generation**. I am preserving notes for the first three. **World-R1** is interesting as a trend signal, but I am not keeping a note today because the current evidence still looks too reward-stack-heavy and too vulnerable to “judge the reconstruction” style proxy gaming.

The strongest direct hit is **Privileged Foresight Distillation**, or PFD. It asks a very good question: if world action models often drop the future-prediction branch at inference with little penalty, what exactly was future information doing during training? The paper’s answer is sharper than the usual “better representation” handwave. It treats future access as an action-conditioned correction signal, then distills that residual into a small adapter while keeping current-only inference.

**ANCHOR** is more systems-heavy but still worth keeping. The main claim is that a lot of home-service mobile-manipulation failures are not high-level semantic failures, but stale or physically invalid interfaces between plan, navigation, and manipulation. The paper’s best move is to force symbolic predicates to stay tied to continuously revalidated geometric anchors, then localize recovery to the minimum responsible layer instead of flailing with full replanning.

**VISION-SLS** is the strongest adjacent paper. It is not a world model paper, but it is a serious attempt to make high-dimensional visual control safer by learning a reduced observation with calibrated error bounds and then solving robust output-feedback control directly in that reduced space. The useful part is the contract: learned representation first, but with explicit bounded uncertainty rather than pretending the encoder is trustworthy because it came from a foundation model.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Privileged Foresight Distillation: Zero-Cost Future Correction for World Action Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it turns “future prediction helps somehow” into a more explicit transfer mechanism, namely a distillable residual correction to the action denoising direction.

### 2. **ANCHOR: A Physically Grounded Closed-Loop Framework for Robust Home-Service Mobile Manipulation**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it treats long-horizon manipulation failure as a state-consistency and recovery-localization problem, not just as a need for more VLM reasoning.

### 3. **VISION-SLS: Safe Perception-Based Control from Learned Visual Representations via System Level Synthesis**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it shows a disciplined way to put a learned visual abstraction inside a control stack without dropping uncertainty accounting.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Privileged Foresight Distillation.

The paper’s strongest contribution is conceptual. It argues that future information in world action models is not just an auxiliary regularizer and does not need to survive as explicit rollout generation at test time. Instead, future access reveals a direction that corrects the current-only action denoising prediction, and that correction can be distilled into a small residual head.

That is useful because it reframes a muddy design space. Instead of asking whether we must generate future video at inference, the sharper question becomes: what privileged signal does future access expose during training, and can we compress only that piece? Even if the exact result is benchmark-bound, that framing is worth keeping.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

PFD sharpens the baseline story around world action models. If future-conditioned training helps mostly through a compressible correction, then comparisons should separate three things that often get blurred together: richer shared representation, extra action-specific signal, and test-time future generation.

ANCHOR is a good reminder that many embodied failures blamed on “reasoning” are really interface failures between stale symbolic state, bad base pose selection, and coarse recovery. A clean baseline is not just another planner, but a planner whose predicates are continually re-anchored to observable state.

VISION-SLS matters more for method taste than for direct baselines. It is a strong example of refusing the lazy move where a learned visual embedding is treated as trusted state without calibrated error bars.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today are trying to preserve learned power while adding a stricter interface. PFD adds a residual correction interface between privileged future access and current-only action prediction. ANCHOR adds a physical re-anchoring interface between symbolic planning and evolving world state. VISION-SLS adds a bounded-abstraction interface between foundation-model visual features and safe control synthesis. None of these are universal solutions, and all depend on assumptions that can break. But they are directionally right: if you want robust action, safer control, or less mushy long-horizon behavior, do not just enlarge the black box, isolate the missing signal and make its contract explicit.
